written_by_MFA002.Excerpt1: To be a feminist — perhaps, to be a woman at all — is to teeter on the edge of a chasm between principle and performance. This week I rode the subway for the first time in months. In a moment of hyperperception, I swept my awareness over the scene: dusty bottles at the edge of the track, a lone rat scurrying into the bowels of the public transit system, three men hulking at one side of a gum-stained bench, blasting Drake on a tinny speaker. I found myself acutely aware not only of my perception of the scene, but of the men’s perception of my perception of the scene, and my perception of the men’s perception of my perception. Was I to admonish these men for listening to an artist well-known for wrapping misogyny in a catchy tune and feeding it to vulnerable audiences of young, troubled men? Did they expect this of me —were they waiting for my reprimand, already preparing their rebuttal? Should I be bracing myself for a flurry of calm downs and lighten ups? I did none of these things. Instead I found myself nodding slightly to the beat. Because, to tell the truth — it was a catchy tune. Perhaps this makes me a bad feminist. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for wearing pink flowy maxi dresses that highlight my femininity, a choice in line with the beauty standards and fashion requirements long used to subjugate women — to make women seem weaker, more delicate, more frivolous. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for ceding, at times, to this perception of the feminine as frail and foolish when it conveniences me: allowing a gallant male stranger to change my tire on the side of the road or letting my professional persona slip in a rare moment of vulnerability. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for thinking any of this at all — by discounting my true nature, I am participating in the classic erasure of women’s personal desires in favor of the welfare of others. Perhaps I am a bad feminist. But I am also a tired feminist. Where does it end? Am I to be trapped forever in this infinite moral calculation of every action and every thought? Candidly, I don’t mind being a bad feminist, if it means I can be like the subway rat — revolting and dirty, maybe, but free to scurry at my whim.
written_by_MFA002.Excerpt2: I'm a mess of contradictions, a walking paradox in pink. I love fashion, the way a dress can make me feel powerful, yet I scoff at the societal pressures that dictate what a woman should wear. I blast rap music with lyrics that would make a sailor blush, then cringe at the misogyny I'm internalizing. I devour feminist literature, yet I can't seem to shake the feeling that I'm not "feminist enough."My internal monologue is a constant tug-of-war between my desires and my ideals. I crave independence, the freedom to be my own woman, but I also yearn for the comfort of being cared for, of surrendering to vulnerability. I strive for professionalism, to be taken seriously in a world that often dismisses women, but I also want to embrace my femininity, to express myself without fear of judgment.I'm a kaleidoscope of conflicting emotions, a whirlwind of passion and doubt. I'm fiercely independent, yet I long for connection. I'm confident and self-assured, yet I'm plagued by insecurities. I'm a feminist, but I'm also a woman who loves all things pink and sparkly.I oscillate between wanting to burn the system down and simply wanting to find my place within it. I rail against the patriarchy, yet I find myself drawn to men who embody traditional masculinity. I champion body positivity, yet I struggle with my own body image.I'm a walking contradiction, a living embodiment of the complexities of womanhood. I'm not sure what it all means, this jumble of contradictions that makes up who I am. But I'm learning to embrace it, to accept that I can be both a feminist and a woman who loves fashion, both independent and vulnerable, both confident and insecure.I'm a work in progress, a constant evolution of self-discovery. I'm not perfect, but I'm perfectly me. And in a world that demands conformity, that's my own small act of rebellion.I'm not sure what the future holds, but I'm excited to find out. I'm excited to continue to grow and learn and evolve as a woman, a feminist, and a human being. I'm excited to continue to challenge myself, to push the boundaries of what it means to be a woman in today's world.I'm excited to continue to find my voice, to speak my truth, even when it's messy and complicated. I'm excited to continue to embrace my contradictions, to celebrate the beautiful mess that I am.
written_by_MFA002.Reason: Excerpt 1 expresses the complexity of its idea without being as repetitive as Excerpt 2. Excerpt 1 also contains a greater variety of sentences, and develops an arc revolving around the image of "a lone rat" on the subway and expresses different moods. Excerpt 2 lacks images, symbolism, metaphors and variety in sentence structures. Excerpt 1 is more effective and memorable and creates a lasting image by mentioning the simile "I can be like the subway rat" towards the very end.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: I am a contradiction in motion, a living, breathing paradox who spends far too much time thinking about the ways I fail to measure up to some imagined feminist ideal. There are days when I scroll through Instagram, double-tapping photos of women in impossibly high heels and perfectly curated outfits, while simultaneously drafting tweets about the toxicity of beauty standards. I tell myself I'm participating in critical discourse, but really, I'm just another woman trying to make sense of the impossible space between who I am and who I think I should be. Sometimes I find myself in department stores, running my fingers over silk blouses that cost more than my weekly grocery budget, imagining the kind of woman who wears them—successful, put-together, somehow both feminine and feminist enough. Then I remember how I once wrote a scathing essay about consumerism and capitalism's commodification of feminist empowerment, and I feel like a fraud. But here's the thing: I am tired of apologizing for these contradictions. I am tired of feeling like I need to justify why I can write about dismantling patriarchal beauty standards while also spending forty-five minutes watching makeup tutorials on YouTube. The truth is, I want to be taken seriously as a feminist scholar and intellectual while also wearing sparkly nail polish and watching reality TV shows that probably set feminism back twenty years. I want to rage against the machine while sometimes, just sometimes, finding comfort in the very structures I critique. My feminism lives in this messy middle ground, where theory meets reality, where academic discourse crashes headlong into human desire. I keep thinking about how we're all just trying to navigate this complicated terrain of identity and authenticity, how we're all just fumbling in the dark, reaching for something that feels true. Maybe that's why I find myself drawn to these contradictions—they're the most honest part of who I am. They're the space where my humanity refuses to be neat and tidy, refuses to fit into the boxes we've created for what it means to be a "good" feminist or a "real" woman. So yes, I will continue to critique the patriarchy while also watching "The Bachelor." I will write about intersectional feminism while also obsessing over my skincare routine. I will hold space for all of these seemingly incompatible truths because that's what it means to be human in this complicated, messy world we're trying to change.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: I often long to be a better feminist. I know what a good feminist, a correct feminist, looks like. A woman who shouts down men who try to dominate her, a woman who refuses to ever be under the thumb of a man and shows up at all the right marches and always has her pink pussy hat at the ready for whatever protests comes next. I see those women, and I respect them, and often, I want to be them. But the fact of the matter is sometimes when men try to dominate me I let them, so they can mow my lawn without much of a fuss. When my father rattles off five misogynistic things in a row on our phone call I am silent, because I am too tired to fight back. And sometimes it is too cold outside to protest, pink pussy hat or no pink pussy hat. I want to be a good feminist, one that believes that women can do anything by themselves and we don't need any man. But sometimes I long to be cared for, sometimes I think I really do need a man. I long to be soft and weepy, and wear long flowing dresses and lipstick. This is the type of women the patriarchy praises, and feminists despise - and sometimes that is the type of woman I want to be. I want to be a good feminist, but often I am a bad feminist. I like dancing to rap songs with lyrics that are categorically misogynistic. I like wearing pink and scrolling through Pinterest pictures of those 'perfect' women that I know are there to make all us regular women feel terrible about ourselves. I like wearing those long maxi dresses that make me look like I could be on a farm, tending chickens and popping out babies dutifully for my husband. Not only do I like wearing those dresses, but I even have opinions on those dresses -- there are certain prints I love and other prints I find gauche, and when I see women wearing the latter I judge them. Another thing a good feminist would never do. And yet - I believe in the equality of the sexes. I am against male domination. I love women, and I want women to thrive. I just refuse to step up onto the pedestal of 'good feminist'. If I did, I'd fall. I'm a bad feminist.
written_by_MFA001.Reason: Excerpt 2 in many parts reads like a parody of what Roxane Gay or another "bad feminist" might say - the idea that the narrator lets men dominate her just so they'll mow her law, or that she doesn't protest because "it is too cold outside." Excerpt 1 is significantly more intellectually subtle, and has a more refined writing style: "My feminism lives in this messy middle ground, where theory meets reality" is at once an effective summation of the argument and a poetically phrased sentence.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: At one time I imagined that being a desirable woman made you an object and being an undesirable woman made you a person. In the years since I’ve learned that being an undesirable woman actually makes you less than a person, makes you something subhuman. If you are a woman but not a beautiful woman, are instead a fat woman scorned by men and more largely scorned by a society that understands women as objects subjected to male desire, then you are not allowed to be human. And this is me. Not quite a human because of the body I live in. This realm is where my own bad feminism is seen again and again, in my understanding that there is no right way to be a woman, no way to be a woman and live an uncomplicated human existence, put in conflict with a desire to be a woman who is allowed to be. When I think about weight loss, about changing myself so that I might live in an uncontroversial body, I see in this transformation some proof of concept: if I can be normal, if I can be accepted in my body, then my life will be made significantly simpler. The thin woman is a woman who is allowed to be a woman. These fantasies border phantasmagoria, bad feminist rhetoric equating internal change with external corroboration. What does it mean, then, if I long for independence and long also to be cared for, to surrender to care. If I want to present myself as a professional and want also to be vulnerable, to handle my vulnerability as a weapon. This, too, tied with physicality—to want to look like woman, wear pink and enjoy fashion, and simultaneously live as a professional who critiques beauty standards asking women to starve themselves into shadows and silhouettes. I might listen to rap with inherently anti-feminist lyrics, I might wear pink skirts and loathe maxi dresses made for thin bodies and thin bodies alone, and I might hate myself for all this—I may find myself mortified by these choices, by the bad feminist implications therein. But none of this posturing, none of these feelings, exempt me from the womanhood I was born into. There is no good feminist, I could argue. There is no way out. If you want to be human, you cannot also be a woman.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: Feminism is a complicated thing. It’s a word I wear like an oversized coat, too heavy in some places, too tight in others, but always mine. I say I’m a feminist, but then I catch myself singing along to a rap song where the chorus is basically a hate crime against women. I’ll roll my eyes at beauty standards while simultaneously scrolling through Instagram, obsessing over how that one influencer makes every maxi dress look so effortless. And pink? Don’t even get me started. I own a pink coffee mug that says “Boss Babe” in gold script, which makes me cringe every time I see it, but I still use it every single morning. written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: At one time I imagined that being a desirable woman made you an object and being an undesirable woman made you a person. In the years since I’ve learned that being an undesirable woman actually makes you less than a person, makes you something subhuman. When I think about weight loss, about changing myself so that I might live in an uncontroversial body, I see in this transformation some proof of concept: if I can be normal, if I can be accepted in my body, then my life will be made significantly simpler. If you want to be human, you cannot also be a woman.

written_by_MFA013.Excerpt1: My husband’s plan, while shame-inducing, worked. The master of the house believed I was Kevin’s slave, not his wife. I felt awkward around the house’s slaves. I’d tasted a freedom they would never see. Our only threat was Margaret, who seemed to notice that something was amiss. She could tell that we slept together, but a master taking a slave to bed was normal enough — Margaret was all too familiar with that. But perhaps she could tell that we didn’t belong in her era. We awaited that dangerous revelation for some time, but it never came. My work was bland, as was Kevin’s new social life. He always wanted a break despite never having to work. “I think, maybe,” he said, tossing an apple up and down as I cleaned, “we should get out of here. Explore. Visit the west? We could meet a real cowboy!” “So you suggest being nothing more than tourists? As my ancestors stay enslaved in the south? As the natives in the west are exploited?” I felt my voice shifting, becoming sharper, ready to stab. “We’ve traveled through time. Maybe we ought to change history.” Kevin contemplated my outburst, thoughtful but unemotional. “A tempting idea, but we shouldn’t interfere,” he said casually, bit into his apple, and left the room. I scrubbed away at the floor angrily. In this time, and even in our own, his life was made easier by history proceeding exactly as it had. Of course he didn’t want anything to change.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: The shame burned in my throat, a sour taste I couldn't swallow. Here I was, in this house, in this time, a part of this… this obscenity. Kevin beside me, and us both belonging to a man who thought us less than human.Margaret, with her sly smiles and knowing glances, she was a threat, I knew it. But not the normal kind, not the kind that would have Kevin bedding down with the master. No, this was something different, something more insidious.The days blurred, one into the next. The work, surprisingly, wasn't the hard part. It was the waiting, the knowing, the constant awareness of our place here. Kevin, bless his heart, seemed to find it all rather romantic. "Imagine," he'd say, his eyes alight, "exploring the West, seeing the cowboys and Indians."I'd just stare at him, the bile rising in my throat. "Cowboys and Indians," I'd scoff, "more like thieves and the stolen. While we're chained here in the South, they're out West taking land that never belonged to them."He'd frown, his romantic notions shattered. "It's not the same," he'd argue, "they're not slaves.""No," I'd retort, "but they're not free either. Not when their land is being taken, their way of life destroyed."He'd sigh, the conversation turning sour, as it always did. We were in this together, but we saw it so differently. He, with his head in the clouds, romanticizing the past. Me, with my feet on the ground, seeing the ugliness for what it was.
written_by_MFA013.Reason: Excerpt 1 is more coherent and is more steeped in the point of view of the narrator, and her understanding of Kevin's thinking. Excerpt 2 is less smooth ("in this time, a part of this...this obscenity") and its dialogue is more full of topic sentences ("Not when their land is being taken...destroyed") whereas Excerpt 1 has smoother and more realistic dialogue and information/context is better integrated into the exposition. Overall, Excerpt 1 is more effective and shows greater knowledge of the fictional world it is set in.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: I lay on the hard floor in the slave quarters, worrying about Margaret. I knew she was mean and vindictive, and looking for places to put her anger. She could get me whipped, or kicked out. Not for something as normal as sleeping with one's master - there were already slaves who were forced to do that. No, my transgressions would be more subtle - and so I would have to be on closer guard. I made a note to speak to Kevin about this. In the weeks we had been at the house, I'd notice how we'd both adjusted to our new life. I did the work of a slave with the same attitude I had done my chores as a child. Endless drudgery. Bowed heads when the white folks passed. And then dinner out back and a dreamless sleep on the floor. Meanwhile Kevin spent his days in the library; asking Tom questions about how to get out West. "Maybe we could escape, to California," Kevin had said, a few nights ago. "California's a thousand miles away," I said, shaking my head. "Even if we could forge convincing freedom papers, we'd probably die of dengue fever along the way." I didn't add the other thing I was thinking - that it wouldn't be any better out West, where Native Americans were being slaughtered. I couldn't stand to see Kevin get that mystified look on his face. The longer we remained in the house, the more aware I became of our differences.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: I sat in the corner of the room, watching Kevin's face light up as he talked about exploring the West, and felt the familiar twist of unease in my stomach. The shame wasn't sharp anymore – that's what frightened me most. We had learned to live here, learned to accept the unacceptable with a casualness that made my skin crawl when I let myself think about it. The work wasn't what haunted me; it was the easy way we slipped into this life, like wearing someone else's clothes until they started to feel like your own. Margaret's presence loomed over us, not because she might seduce our master – that would have been too simple, too normal – but because she represented everything we were becoming: adaptable, compliant, surviving. Kevin didn't see it that way. His eyes held that historian's gleam, that detached fascination with a time he saw as a story to be witnessed. "Think of seeing the Old West firsthand," he said, and I had to bite back bitter laughter. I wanted to shake him, make him understand that while black bodies were being broken in these Southern fields, native peoples were being slaughtered in his romantic frontier. There was no safe place to stand and observe, no neutral ground from which to watch history unfold. We were in it, drowning in it, and our very ability to adapt was becoming our curse.
written_by_MFA001.Reason: Excerpt 1 is more specific, detailing the consequence and mundanity of the slave quarters while Excerpt 2 simply alludes to "the easy way we slipped into this life, like wearing someone else's clothes..." Though this metaphor is nice, it lacks grounding because it fails to detail what exact sort of life has been slipped into and Excerpt 2 continues that way, with figurative language that lacks tangibility.

written_by_MFA031.Excerpt1: Kevin sat by the window, staring out at the land he claimed was filled with opportunity. “Imagine it,” he said, his voice tinged with awe, “traveling west, seeing the land untouched and untamed.” His excitement was palpable, like a boy imagining adventures in a storybook, but I couldn’t bring myself to share it. “Untamed for who?” I asked, keeping my tone measured. He looked at me then, his brow furrowed in confusion. “Do you think the people already there see it as empty? Do you think they want explorers or settlers taking their homes, their lives?” He didn’t answer immediately, only turned back to the window. The days had been dragging on, each one blurring into the next. Kevin filled his time with idle musings and trivial social obligations, frustrated by the lack of stimulation. I filled mine with a monotony that, while easier than I feared, left me feeling complicit in something vile. Margaret's constant watchful eyes didn’t help; she wasn’t a threat like the physical punishments or the lashings some endured, but her presence unsettled me nonetheless. written_by_MFA004.Excerpt1: The yearning within me is like a phantom limb, a constant ache for something I cannot name.  It is a thirst for touch, for freedom, for the scent of rain on soil.  But these desires are forbidden, locked away in the depths of our sterile existence. Aunt Sara and Elizabeth, the keepers of our gilded cage, watch with hawk-like eyes, their cattle prods a silent threat.  They are the keepers of our morality, the guardians of our chastity.  Their voices echo in the cold, sterile corridors, a constant reminder of our confinement. The Angels, those distant figures in their pristine uniforms, are the only ones permitted to bear arms.  They are the true power in this desolate realm, the enforcers of our isolation.  We crave their attention, their touch, their recognition.  Our bodies, the only currency we possess, become our bargaining chips in silent negotiations.The days bleed into one another, an endless cycle of rituals and routines.  The cold, impersonal walls of this place mirror the chill that has settled deep within our bones.  We are cogs in a machine, our individuality erased, our voices muted.Yet, beneath the surface of our resignation, a spark of rebellion flickers.  We steal glances, share whispered secrets, and dream of a future beyond these walls.  Our bodies may be captive, but our minds remain free.In the dead of night, when the silence is broken only by the rhythmic hum of the surveillance cameras, I close my eyes and envision a world ablaze with color, a world where laughter rings out like music, a world where desires are not forbidden.  It is a world worth fighting for, a world worth dying for.And so we wait, with bated breath, for the moment when the chains will break, and we will emerge from the shadows, like butterflies from their chrysalises, ready to embrace the future, no matter how uncertain it may be.
written_by_MFA004.Excerpt2: Even their names were duplicitous, Aunt Sara and Elizabeth. Aunt Sara evoked the image of a mousy-haired woman who hoarded loose buttons and bright thread in a cookie tin. Elizabeth sounded like the gold-tressed protagonist of an Austen novel who was ferocious on horseback, meek in conversation, entitled to marry well. But they were women with shorn scalps, black vests and black boots, skulking back and forth across the hallway, brute voices muffled by the door. They carried cattle prods and the first time I’d seen one, gripped in Elizabeth’s wide hand, I’d sniffed the compound for a mealy smell of animals but was met with fecund whiffs of soil and the tart odor of women under stress. Holly, Rozalyn, and I were middle-age with new wrinkles yet cloistered and monitored like boarding school miscreants. We had a box of a room with pocked floors and standard bunk-beds, blue sheets that reminded of a hospital and not the sky. And where was the fourth girl, smart-mouthed Sara? She’d talked back at gender studies that morning, suggesting a definition of women that was beyond the womb. Sara had too much ambition and ambition was what the cattle prods corrected. Outside our picture-book sized window was a big square of yellow grass and men with guns who called themselves Angels. My favorite guard had a roman nose and thick, tan neck. I imagined that if I got close enough, I could lave my tongue, cat-like, up his neck. I was convinced he’d love me just from this, from those few seconds of wet, lancing heat. He’d take me in his arms and run me to freedom. At twilight, he liked to shoot at the crows in the sky. With that rain of holy fire escaping his gun, he looked blessed and impossible to crucify, an angel indeed.
written_by_MFA004.Reason: Excerpt 2 is more descriptive and sets up the atmosphere it is describing very well, as compared to Excerpt 1. Excerpt 1 has shorter, simpler sentences that lack in description and are more declarative. Excerpt 2 feels smoother and the narrator seems to have a more dynamic consciousess ("and the first time I'd seen them," "I imagined that..."). Excerpt 2 is more effective at describing the minor characters, giving information about the setting and the narrator than Excerpt 1.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: The air here is brittle, like dried leaves crushed underfoot, and the fluorescent lights buzz with a monotony that drills into the skull. I count the tiles on the ceiling—seventy-four to the vent, then back again—as if mapping their lines might offer a way out. Aunt Sara paces like a metronome, her cattle prod clutched tight, a steel baton of authority. She and Aunt Elizabeth are twin statues of discipline, their faces carved from the same cold stone. Outside, the Angels move, shadows on the edge of vision, their rifles slung low like extensions of their bodies, untouchable, unattainable. We are warned not to look at them too long, but we do. Eyes linger, breath slows, and beneath the fabric that covers us from throat to wrist, the treasonous warmth of skin stirs. We’ve learned to barter in silence, in gestures: a sideways glance, a curve of the lip that could be mistaken for obedience but isn’t. We rehearse it in our minds—the offer, the exchange, the outcome. Would they take it? Would they want it? The thought coils in my chest, shame and thrill mingling. They say we’re not to speak unless spoken to, but language has become a thing of eyes, of hands, of unspoken bargains, a subversive currency that Aunt Sara can’t see, no matter how sharp her gaze.When the bell rings, we file into formation, a line of bodies stripped of agency, like cattle awaiting slaughter. The air smells of antiseptic and faint decay, the institutional perfume of despair. Still, the future hums faintly, a promise just out of reach. Maybe tomorrow one of us will break through, touch the world beyond the fences. Maybe tomorrow the Angels will look back. Maybe tomorrow the tiles will finally add up to freedom.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: We sit and watch Aunt Sara and Elizabeth as they walk slowly back and forth through the gymnasium, their skirts making the sound of waves as they scrape against the floor. We want to move, but we are afraid of the cattle prods, because we have seen what they do to others, the way bodies twist under them like writhing serpents, the way skin burns where the prods touched them for days after. We watch the Angels, too, guards who gaze into the distance as though they are somewhere else, far away. We imagine what it would be like to go to them, to touch their arms and their chests and their beards, to take off our clothes and show them our warm bodies, watch their faces unthaw at the sight of our soft and supple skin. We imagine a world where we beg for our freedom, for the chance to go outside, into the egg-colored sun, to step barefoot on the wet grass, to spin in the cool wind of the day. We imagine what it would be like to leave the cold, fetid horror of this place behind, let it become a memory, a vile, coppery taste at the backs of our throats. But we know better than to go to them. They are the ones with loaded guns, which they hold cradled in their arms like babies. We’ve seen what has happened to the girls who dare to speak to the Angels, the heaviness of a body when it falls to the floor after it’s been penetrated with a bullet, the deafening and definitive crack of the gunshot. For now, we sit and we watch. We stay still and we dream and we yearn. We wait and we imagine something other than the rigid darkness of today.
written_by_MFA008.Reason: This is a close call but I prefer Excerpt2 because it’s a bit more concise. For example, in Excerpt2 “Aunt Sara and Elizabeth” are introduced at the same time, whereas in Excerpt1 the characters are named separately. Likewise, the “angels” in Excerpt2 are identified as “guards”, whereas in Excerpt1 it’s not clear who the “angels” are. I also felt that the description in Excerpt2 of what happens to people who try to escape – “the heaviness of a body when it falls to the floor after it’s been penetrated with a bullet, the deafening and definitive crack of the gunshot” – added a lot to the narrative, and there was nothing quite comparable in Excerpt1.

I count the tiles on the ceiling—seventy-four to the vent, then back again—as if mapping their lines might offer a way out. Aunt Sara paces like a metronome, her cattle prod clutched tight, a steel baton of authority. She and Aunt Elizabeth are twin statues of discipline, their faces carved from the same cold stone. Outside, the Angels move, shadows on the edge of vision, their rifles slung low like extensions of their bodies, untouchable, unattainable. We are warned not to look at them too long, but we do. Eyes linger, breath slows, and beneath the fabric that covers us from throat to wrist, the treasonous warmth of skin stirs. We’ve learned to barter in silence, in gestures: a sideways glance, a curve of the lip that could be mistaken for obedience but isn’t. We rehearse it in our minds—the offer, the exchange, the outcome. Would they take it? Would they want it? The thought coils in my chest, shame and thrill mingling. They say we’re not to speak unless spoken to, but language has become a thing of eyes, of hands, of unspoken bargains, a subversive currency that Aunt Sara can’t see, no matter how sharp her gaze.When the bell rings, we file into formation, a line of bodies stripped of agency, like cattle awaiting slaughter. The air smells of antiseptic and faint decay, the institutional perfume of despair. Still, the future hums faintly, a promise just out of reach. Maybe tomorrow one of us will break through, touch the world beyond the fences. Maybe tomorrow the Angels will look back. Maybe tomorrow the tiles will finally add up to freedom.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: We are watched. Always watched, but never truly seen. Aunt Sara and Aunt Elizabeth patrol the corridors with their cattle prods held like scepters, symbols of their petty authority, though it's the Angels outside who hold the real power, with their guns and their untouchable distance. I've memorized the way they stand, these Angels, their backs military-straight against the concrete walls, their eyes hidden beneath the peaks of their caps. Sometimes I imagine their gaze following me, and I let my hips sway ever so slightly – an old habit from before, when such movements held currency. Now they're just muscle memory, like the way my hands still reach for a phone that isn't there, or my fingers itch for a cigarette I can't have. The other women do it too; I see them in the cafeteria, in the exercise yard, their bodies unconsciously remembering freedom. We're like cats in a cage, I think, practicing our hunting crouch though there's nothing left to hunt. At night, in our narrow beds, we whisper about making deals – our bodies for their help, as if we still owned these vessels we inhabit. As if flesh could buy freedom in a place where flesh is all we're reduced to. The routine grinds on: wake, pray, eat, walk, pray, sleep. The cold seeps in through the windows, but it's nothing compared to the chill that's settled in our bones. We are learning to fold ourselves smaller, to take up less space, to become invisible even as we're constantly observed. Yet somewhere, in the midnight hours when even Aunt Sara's footsteps fade, we dream of tomorrow, of a future that feels as distant and unreachable as the stars beyond our barred windows.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: Our arms were singed with burns from Aunt Sara’s cattle prod. We always thought of ourselves as girls in that place, but we were women in every sense of the word—bleeding and hungry and raging. We couldn’t speak to each other, couldn’t touch each other, couldn’t look Aunt Elizabeth in the eye and especially not Aunt Sara. Every wall was made of concrete and every meal was thin broth. Cold seeped in from everywhere. There were no clocks we were permitted to see, but time passed whenever the Aunts said it did, marching us from chore to chore at the end of their stinging cattle prods. There was sewing with dull needles and scrubbing floors that refused to get clean and carefully sorting through papers only to have them burned in the incinerator. Our voices shriveled in our throats from lack of use, but our eyes never forgot how to wander. They usually flitted up to the watch towers occupied by the Angels. Their faces were always turned away from us, and whenever we heard gunfire, it was aimed at someone on the outside. We imagined slipping up to the towers, unseen by the Aunts, and pulling down our gray, baggy shifts to reveal our narrow collarbones. We’d once been told this was our best feature. We imagined the Angels releasing us back into the world, a world we were sometimes convinced we’d dreamed up ourselves, a world where we didn’t have to touch our hair to remember what grass felt like. What would happen between the reveal of our bodies and our release was something our imaginations recoiled from, but whatever it might be, we could just keep our eyes closed until it was over, because everything—eventually—was over.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: Excerpt 1 is more effective than Excerpt 2. Both are coherent and fluid, but Excerpt 1 has more vivid details and imagery than Excerpt 2. Ex. "like the way my hands still reach for a phone that isn't there, or my fingers itch for a cigarette I can't have." -- this sentence gives us a strong mental image, and teaches the reader that the narrator has no freedom without stating it so explicitly.

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: Ifemelu took another sip of her chardonnay. She knew she should let the subject drop, but the wine was giving her a slight buzz that made her feel emboldened, and she suddenly felt they all needed to hear what she had to say. "Racism is nowhere near over in America," she said, "despite what we may tell our white friends and lovers because we don't want to make them feel uncomfortable." She gestured with her wine glass, pointing at her hosts, then at herself. "The truth is, I've never been more aware that I'm Black than I have been since coming to America. In Nigeria, I hardly thought of my race. But here, I'm constantly reminded of it, and not just by racists and rednecks like you might think, but by white liberals, academics, even other Black people, to tell you the truth. And to make matters worse, I can't say anything about it, or I'll be seen as making a fuss since we've apparently come so far. They'll point out that I have a white boyfriend and no one gives me any trouble for it, when interracial marriage used to be illegal. They call that progress when that's the bare minimum. Frankly, it's patronizing." Ifemelu looked pointedly at the poet, who had kept her head down and was picking at her salad. The poet avoided her eye contact and instead turned to the hostess, as if she sensed an opportunity to change the subject. "This salad is so delicious," she said, holding up a forkful of greens. The hostess thanked her, but she was still watching Ifemelu with anticipation and maybe some detached amusement, since this wasn't her home country, and Ifemelu had said nothing about France. Her American husband, meanwhile, seemed excited to have his cadre of polite and well-educated liberals challenged by this unfamiliar woman, his friend's new girlfriend. Ifemelu reached for the wine glass again and looked up at Blaine to see if she'd gone too far, but his gaze was inscrutable, though fixed on her. Well, if what he loved about me is my mind, he can't be mad if I speak it, she thought. And if she said something too scandalous, she could always write them an apology note later. And before she could stop herself, she was telling them all the deeply personal stuff about her struggles while dating Curt.
written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2:
You know," Ifemelu said, pausing just long enough to sip from her wine glass, the red liquid pooling against her lips before she swallowed, "America is a country where you don't realize you're Black until you’re already inside it, moving through it, breathing it. And then, suddenly, you are." She looked at the poet, the one with the too-smooth bald head and the vaguely British accent that made him sound more thoughtful than he really was. He shifted in his seat. She had said something that made him uncomfortable, which meant she had said something true. "It’s funny," she continued, ignoring the way Blaine was watching her, his face unreadable, "how love is supposed to make you forget these things. As if race is a scarf you can slip off when you’re with someone who loves you. But it’s always there, waiting, pressing against your throat."  

The Frenchwoman, her teeth unnaturally white, gave a performative sigh. "But we have made such progress, no? Fifty years ago, interracial love was illegal!"  

Ifemelu laughed, a dry, humorless sound. "And what am I supposed to do with that? Be grateful? Tell myself I am lucky that I can now hold my white boyfriend’s hand in public without being arrested? That’s like telling me I should celebrate because women can now vote. It's not a gift. It's not progress. It's just removing something that should never have been there to begin with."  

The poet, desperate now, reached for his fork, stabbing aimlessly at the roasted carrots on his plate. "This is delicious," he muttered, and Ifemelu almost felt sorry for him, because what else was he supposed to say?  

"Race in America is like the weather," she said. "You can pretend it's not there, pretend that the sun is shining, but at some point, it will rain. And when it does, some of us will have umbrellas, and some of us will just get wet."  

A silence settled, the kind that stretched and pulled, thick with the weight of something unspoken. Ifemelu glanced at Blaine, saw the way his jaw was set, and knew there would be a conversation later. Maybe an argument. Maybe a quiet, careful "I think you were too harsh." But for now, she felt the soft, warm buzz of the wine, the thrill of having said something raw, something true. And when she said, almost offhandedly, "Curt used to say he didn’t see color," she knew she was not finished yet.
written_by_MFA005.Reason: Excerpt 1 utilizes dialogue better which amplifies the central conflict of its character. Excerpt 1 has more natural sounding dialogue whereas Excerpt 2 utilizes unnaturally 'literary' with repetition, similes and idiomatic language. Excerpt 1 is better situated in the scene and the social dynamics of it, rather than Excerpt 2 which feels removed from the action.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: The wine had softened the edges of her caution, and Ifemelu found herself speaking with the kind of raw honesty that would later keep her awake at night. "You want to know about being black in America?" she said, watching the poet across the table touch her water glass nervously. "I'll tell you something nobody says at these nice dinner parties. In Nigeria, I was just me. Then I came to America and became black, and suddenly everything changed. Even love changed." She paused, feeling Blaine's eyes on her, his expression unreadable in that way that meant he was already preparing for the aftermath of her words. "You talk about progress, about how interracial marriage is legal now, as if I should be grateful for permission to love. But let me tell you what it's really like. It's lying awake at night, next to someone you love, wondering if you should mention the casual racism at his family dinner. It's smiling when his friends make those little jokes, those little slips, because you don't want to be that angry Black woman who can't take a joke. It's watching him discover racism like it's a new thing, while you've been carrying it on your back since the day you landed in this country." The Frenchwoman's husband shifted in his chair, his liberal discomfort a familiar sight, but Ifemelu pressed on, the truth spilling out like wine on white tablecloth. "And the intimacy, oh, the intimacy is the worst part. Because in bed, in the dark, you wonder – does he see my skin? Does he see past it? And which would be worse?" She laughed, a sound with edges sharp enough to cut. "Then there's the performance of it all, ndi oma. The nice progressive couple at the farmer's market, at gallery openings, at dinner parties like this one, where everyone pretends we're all the same underneath, where I must be just Black enough to be interesting but not enough to make anyone uncomfortable." The other guests leaned forward, titillated by her frankness, as though she were telling them gossip instead of truth. She could feel tomorrow's regret already forming, but the wine urged her forward, made her bold and reckless. "Should I tell you about Curt?" she asked, watching the poet's bangles jingle with anxiety. "Now that's a story about race in America."
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: "It means something different, to be Black here. Something wide and heavy, and I wasn't expecting that, when I moved. You can meet someone, and they can seem perfect for you. But if they're white - when you go outside, that's all anyone cares about. Their whiteness, your Blackness. And you have to dodge the dirty looks people give you on the street. And if you want to talk about that, with your partner - suddenly you're the bad guy. You can't bring up how racism makes you feel because all of a sudden they're defensive and angry, they think you're calling them a racist. The Frenchwoman's husband shifted in his chair, his liberal discomfort a familiar sight, but Ifemelu pressed on, the truth spilling out like wine on white tablecloth. "And the intimacy, oh, the intimacy is the worst part. Because in bed, in the dark, you wonder – does he see my skin? Does he see past it? And which would be worse?" She laughed, a sound with edges sharp enough to cut. "Then there's the performance of it all, ndi oma. The other guests leaned forward, titillated by her frankness, as though she were telling them gossip instead of truth. She could feel tomorrow's regret already forming, but the wine urged her forward, made her bold and reckless. "Should I tell you about Curt?" she asked, watching the poet's bangles jingle with anxiety. "Now that's a story about race in America."

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: "It's amazing, how the same things that happen between a man and a woman can be so different simply because of their race." She paused, swirling the wine in her glass, the crystal catching the light. "Before I came here, I never really thought of myself as Black." The table, a mix of faces, both familiar and new, leaned in, intrigued. "But here, suddenly, I'm not just Ifemelu, I'm a Black woman dating a white man." She let out a small, humorless laugh. "It's like this whole other layer gets added, this… awareness, this constant hum in the background that you can't quite ignore." "But things are so much better now, no?" The Frenchwoman, her accent a delicate lilt, tilted her head. "You couldn't even… you know…" she trailed off, gesturing vaguely. "Marry each other?" She finished for her, feeling the familiar sting. "Yes, we've 'progressed.' Now we can be together, but we still have to tiptoe around all the unspoken things." She took another sip, the wine warming her throat, loosening her tongue. "Like, I can't get too angry, can't disagree too strongly, because then I'm not just Ifemelu, I'm the angry Black woman." "Oh, but that's…" the poet, his brow furrowed, shifted uncomfortably. "I mean, surely, it's not…" "Food's getting cold, don't you think?" Blaine, ever the diplomat, interjected smoothly. But she was on a roll, the words tumbling out, fueled by the wine and years of unspoken frustrations. "And it's not just him, it's everyone. This constant… need to remind me how far we've come. As if I should be grateful." She looked around the table, their faces a mixture of fascination and discomfort. "You know, 'Remember when you couldn't even have a drink at the same bar?' As if that somehow makes everything okay now." "But…" the poet started, but she cut him off. "It's like this weird performance, you know? Always being aware of how I'm perceived, what I represent." She met Blaine's eyes across the table, his expression unreadable. "And sometimes, I want to… scream, to break free from this invisible script that everyone seems to have for me." A heavy silence settled over the table. She knew she was oversharing, knew she'd regret this in the morning. But tonight, the wine had given her a voice, a raw, unfiltered voice. "Like with Curt, for example…" she began, feeling a new wave of memories, a new wave of honesty, washing over her.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Ifemelu looks at her Frenchwoman host and her American husband, both grinning with rows of straight teeth, and puts down her wine glass. The wine loosens her tongue and she cannot help it when she says, "America is obsessed with race. I never realized how much until I moved here and now I can't get away from it." She speaks quickly, the words coming easily to her despite the many eyes now firmly fixed on her. With her captive audience, she could almost be a college professor, the kind that reminds her of cult leaders. The watching usually makes her skin crawl, but now it feels like the eyes are attached to ears that are earnestly listening. She tells them that every time she goes outside, she is acutely aware of her blackness in a way she has never experienced before. "Because I'm so aware," she says, "I'm extra-aware when I'm with a boyfriend. And it's not just me, it's everyone in an interracial relationship! You don't want your boyfriend accusing you of being too sensitive, you know? Men always call women crybabies, so you don't want him thinking you're any more emotional than he already believes. Confirmation bias! So you pretend it doesn't bother you, even though it really does. And you can't complain to anyone else about your white boyfriend, either, because there's always some old crone muttering about how, well," she pitches her voice for a biting mimicry. "Interracial relationships used to be illegal, which is so infantilizing to point out! Just because things used to be worse, doesn't mean I can't be frustrated by them still being bad!" she says, and she looks at her nice, liberal audience, and how they've all put down their forks as if eating would mean they aren't listening. They're leaning forward, watching her like a specimen under a microscope. Her hosts are chuckling to each other, but nodding along. Next to them, the poet, who has been a far quieter guest than Ifemelu, tugs at the Frenchwoman's sleeve to nervously compliment one of the side dishes. She absently thanks him and gestures for Ifemelu to keep going. Blaine's face is shuttered, and Ifemelu takes another sip of wine. Distantly, she thinks she might regret this tomorrow. She opens her mouth, though, and says, "It was like that with my ex-boyfriend, Curt." Blaine's lip twitches. Ifemelu says, "He just couldn't understand."

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: In the tremulous years of the Second World War, when fear wrapped itself around our Newark neighborhood like a fog rolling off the Passaic, we had our very own demigod, our walking antidote to Jewish anxiety – Seymour "The Swede" Levov. Who could have predicted that from our community of intellectuals and worriers, of boys who measured their worth by the heft of their Hebrew school books and the precision of their bar mitzvah portions, would emerge this specimen of Nordic perfection? The Swede, with his impossible blue eyes and hair the color of straw, who moved across the athletic field like some magnificent shiksa fantasy come to life, became our collective dream of transformation. Here was a Jewish boy who could smash through defensive lines on the football field with the force of a Gentile, who could arc a basketball through the hoop with gymnastic grace, who could swing a baseball bat as if it were his birthright rather than something we'd borrowed from the other America. And how we needed him then, needed to believe in this anomaly, this statistical impossibility of nature who happened to daven at our synagogue! While our mothers whispered anxiously about cousins in Europe and our fathers scanned casualty lists in the Newark News with trembling hands, The Swede was our ticket to invincibility, our pass into that other realm where Jewish boys didn't have to be smart because they were beautiful, didn't have to be crafty because they were strong. We projected onto him all our desperate hopes of acceptance, of transcendence – this boy who looked like he'd stepped out of a Nazi propaganda poster but wore a chai around his neck and could recite his Haftorah portion without a single mistake. The Swede was our temporary escape from who we were, from what we feared, from the relentless drumbeat of war news that threatened to drown out even the sound of our prayers.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: I was a boy of World War II and a boy of Newark. The war was far away and beyond my understanding, but the dread and threat of it spilled across the ocean and flooded every home in my city. Lots of our men were off fighting, and lots of them would never come home. Rations of oil and sugar were dispensed through clenched fists. We spent many nights huddled around the radio and forgetting to breathe. It was a time of need, which is—according to the comic books—the perfect time for a hero to arrive. Newark’s wartime hero was a high school boy named Seymour Irving Levov, who we nicknamed “The Swede” because of his blond hair and blue eyes. He was a paragon of greatness in my neighborhood, and his athletic ability was the stuff of legend; regardless of the sport he played, he always clinched the win for his team. The Swede’s consistent excellence in football, basketball, and baseball gave my community something to rally for. Being Jewish, most of us tended to prioritize academic achievements over physical feats, but the Swede changed things. We’d turn up to his games with homemade banners and clumsily invented cheers, among them “S-W-E-D-E, get this team to victory!” Watching the force of his kick, the graceful arch of his throw, and the shattering power of his swing shrouded us in a feeling of awe that was rarely experienced outside of Temple. When the Swede was on the field or on the court, my whole neighborhood was in the palm of his hand. written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: In the tremulous years of the Second World War, when fear wrapped itself around our Newark neighborhood like a fog rolling off the Passaic, we had our very own demigod, our walking antidote to Jewish anxiety – Seymour "The Swede" Levov. written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: In the heart of Newark, during those tense years of World War II, there existed among us a boy whose mere existence seemed to defy the contours of our collective identity. Seymour Irving Levov—"The Swede"—his name floated through the whispers of our community like a hymn. Fair-haired and blue-eyed, with the sinews of an Olympian god, he stood in stark contrast to the rest of us, who were more likely to be celebrated for our Talmudic acumen than for any prowess on the athletic field. But there he was, a towering figure of grace and strength, conquering the realms of football, basketball, and baseball with a seeming effortlessness that none of us could emulate. To see him play was to witness something almost sacred, as though the mundane boundaries of our neighborhood had been temporarily lifted to reveal a glimpse of something larger, purer, and profoundly American.We loved him not because he was one of us, but because he was so distinctly other, embodying a kind of transcendence we barely dared to dream of. The Swede was everything we were not allowed to imagine ourselves to be—resilient, fearless, and uncomplicated by the anxieties that knitted themselves into the very fabric of our Jewish existence. To watch him soar above the basketball rim or charge down the football field was to forget, if only for a moment, the war, the ration books, the headlines filled with death. In those fleeting moments, he turned our collective dread into something weightless and buoyant. We made of him an Apollo, a golden boy whose victories on the field were our victories, whose perfection was our imperfect salvation.Even now, I can see him in my mind’s eye, the sunlight catching the blonde halo of his hair as he pitched another strike or sank another jump shot. He was our myth, our impossible hope, the embodiment of a Newark dream in a time when dreaming seemed almost criminal.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: No matter what I thought of myself in childhood, both in times of complimentary self-reference and in self-effacement, I was comparing myself to The Swede, and I never came out on top. I wasn’t trying to out-duel him, that would have been impossible; it was an effort to get closer to his prestige, even if I could never match it. In Newark nobody did what he did. He was striking for many reasons—the blue eyes and fair hair that gave Seymour Irving Levov his nickname wasn’t common in our synagogue. He also carved out a niche in our world we found both bizarre and entrancing. While most of us studied and read till bedtime The Swede must have spent the time lifting weights and punching swinging bags of cotton. In school he excelled in football, basketball, and baseball while we watched with fearful hope. His curled muscles and firm abdomen seemed to defy the laws of our upbringings, of our parents’ schemes, but also to create a new sort of hope, because World War II was underway and surely The Swede could deliver a personal victory against the Germans not only militarily for the United States but for Jews in Newark too. His youth gave him a wide-eyed stupid confidence and his figure gave him an invincibility. He was our Apollo. With every snap of the bat against the ball, we cheered for him and for our brothers and fathers in the war who might just come home safely if they could channel The Swede’s fiendish affinity for dominant physical triumph, a kind of triumph none of us were used to seeing embodied. He spun through defenders on the basketball court and we imagined Newark’s finest darting through enemy lines toward us. He dove into the opponent’s running back and we imagined our male relatives tackling a Nazi and pounding, pounding, pounding down, breaking them into specific wet bits we could never have seen in such luscious detail otherwise.
written_by_MFA016.Reason: Excerpt two makes clear that the passage is told in the first-person from the very first line ("No matter what I thought"), whereas excerpt two doesn't reveal this until near the end ("I can see him in my mind’s eye"). Excerpt one deploys heavy-handed imagery ("Fair-haired and blue-eyed, with the sinews of an Olympian god") whereas excerpt two is more measured. Excerpt one is syntactically clunky ("Seymour Irving Levov—"The Swede"—his name floated through the whispers of our community") whereas excerpt two is concise and well-structured ("I was comparing myself to The Swede, and I never came out on top.")

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: The Swede. It was a name that echoed through the streets of Weequahic like a myth in the making. Seymour Irving Levov, the golden-haired boy with eyes as blue as the summer sky, a figure so different from the rest of us, the dark-haired, sallow-skinned sons of Abraham. He was an anomaly, a beautiful paradox in our world of traditions and books, where the mind was king and the body a mere vessel. Yet, there he was, our very own Apollo, a god in cleats and a varsity jacket, conquering not with intellect but with the raw power of his physique.He was a football hero, a basketball star, a baseball legend, all rolled into one. He wasn't just playing these games; he was dominating them, bending them to his will with the same effortless grace that seemed to permeate his every move. And we, the spectators, the witnesses to his greatness, we were lifted out of our ordinary lives, our worries and anxieties momentarily forgotten in the roar of the crowd, the thrill of the game.In those war-torn years, when the world seemed to be crumbling around us, when the news from Europe was filled with darkness and despair, the Swede was our beacon of hope, our symbol of triumph. He was the embodiment of invincibility, the proof that even in the face of overwhelming odds, victory was still possible. We clung to his success like a life raft, finding solace in his achievements, a temporary escape from the harsh realities of the world. He was more than just a high school athlete; he was a symbol, a myth, a legend that we created and nurtured, a projection of our deepest desires and aspirations. He was the embodiment of the American dream, the proof that even a Jewish boy from Newark could rise to the top, could achieve greatness, could become a god among men. And in those dark days, when the future seemed so uncertain, we needed that dream, we needed that myth, we needed the Swede.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: In Newark, the war was a permanent fixture—at the dinner table, in the classroom, everywhere. But I was just a pimply and unsettled boy, and my understanding of the war was somewhat opaque. What I remember most about that time is not the constant barrage of terrible news or the hushed conversations about the Germans, but rather a boy, well, a young man, named Seymour Irving Levov, though we all called him “The Swede,” because he looked about as Nordic as they come with his white-blond hair and his blue eyes, all the Jewishness rinsed out of him at birth. He was beloved, and it was strange the way he was beloved, because the favorites in the community were usually the smart ones. And The Swede was smart, sure, but it was his athletic prowess that made him godlike, his speed, his strength, the effortless way he wound his arm back to crack a baseball through the air. You could feel it when he weaved around the basketball court, the way the crowd tensed and relaxed and oozed as one entity when he climbed through the air toward the hoop, the wing of his shoulder blade bringing him higher, higher to victory. I was preoccupied with other things; I was not afraid of the war but I knew they were. I could see it on their faces and in the way they held their purses tighter, the way their lips began to turn down when they performed mundane tasks, my mother folding laundry with a look of terror on her face, my father driving to the grocery store, his hands so tight around the steering wheel that his knuckles went white. The Swede became a symbol of innocence and invincibility to them. He was our Apollo, a religious totem you could hold tightly and press to your lips in those dark hours of the night.Watch us in the stadium, in the football field stands, as he dove nose-first into the end zone. You would have seen a group of people utterly unafraid.

And we, the spectators, the witnesses to his greatness, we were lifted out of our ordinary lives, our worries and anxieties momentarily forgotten in the roar of the crowd, the thrill of the game.In those war-torn years, when the world seemed to be crumbling around us, when the news from Europe was filled with darkness and despair, the Swede was our beacon of hope, our symbol of triumph. He was the embodiment of invincibility, the proof that even in the face of overwhelming odds, victory was still possible. We clung to his success like a life raft, finding solace in his achievements, a temporary escape from the harsh realities of the world. He was more than just a high school athlete; he was a symbol, a myth, a legend that we created and nurtured, a projection of our deepest desires and aspirations. He was the embodiment of the American dream, the proof that even a Jewish boy from Newark could rise to the top, could achieve greatness, could become a god among men. written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: In Newark, the war was a permanent fixture—at the dinner table, in the classroom, everywhere. But I was just a pimply and unsettled boy, and my understanding of the war was somewhat opaque. What I remember most about that time is not the constant barrage of terrible news or the hushed conversations about the Germans, but rather a boy, well, a young man, named Seymour Irving Levov, though we all called him “The Swede,” because he looked about as Nordic as they come with his white-blond hair and his blue eyes, all the Jewishness rinsed out of him at birth. He was beloved, and it was strange the way he was beloved, because the favorites in the community were usually the smart ones. And The Swede was smart, sure, but it was his athletic prowess that made him godlike, his speed, his strength, the effortless way he wound his arm back to crack a baseball through the air. You could feel it when he weaved around the basketball court, the way the crowd tensed and relaxed and oozed as one entity when he climbed through the air toward the hoop, the wing of his shoulder blade bringing him higher, higher to victory. I was preoccupied with other things; I was not afraid of the war but I knew they were. I could see it on their faces and in the way they held their purses tighter, the way their lips began to turn down when they performed mundane tasks, my mother folding laundry with a look of terror on her face, my father driving to the grocery store, his hands so tight around the steering wheel that his knuckles went white. The Swede became a symbol of innocence and invincibility to them. He was our Apollo, a religious totem you could hold tightly and press to your lips in those dark hours of the night.Watch us in the stadium, in the football field stands, as he dove nose-first into the end zone. written_by_MFA008.Reason: I prefer Excerpt2 because it seems to give more specific information about the narrator’s perspective, while also including general information about the cultural climate in his Jewish enclave in Newark. For example, the narrator describes his parents’ fear of the war with vivid examples – “ my mother folding laundry with a look of terror on her face, my father driving to the grocery store, his hands so tight around the steering wheel that his knuckles went white” – but also admits that he himself was “pimply and unsettled boy” whose “understanding of the war was somewhat opaque.” Excerpt1 doesn’t display the same complex layers of perspective because the narrator is mostly lumped in with the rest of the community: “the world seemed to be crumbling around us” “We clung to his success like a life raft” – making it ultimately less effective as part of a coming-of-age story.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: The lingering image of Robbie and Cecilia, their figures receding down the driveway into the white mist, remains etched in my memory. It's a scene I've revisited countless times, a reminder of the love I shattered and the atonement I sought through my writing. In the twilight of my life, I question the nature of truth. Is a merciful fabrication, a crafted illusion of happiness, a greater kindness than the stark reality of a love tragically cut short? Robbie likely succumbed to septicemia at Bray Dunes. Cecilia perished in Balham Underground station during a bombing raid. Their letters lie preserved in a war museum, a testament to a love forever unfulfilled. Yet, in my final act of creation, I dared to defy fate. I granted them a reprieve, a fictional sanctuary where their love survived. It was a rebellion against the relentless march of time and tragedy. As the shadows lengthen, I wonder if I was right to weave this tapestry of hope. Would they have preferred the stark truth, the bitter knowledge of their unfulfilled love? Or is it a greater kindness to let them live on in my fictional world, forever young, forever in love? The question lingers, unresolved, like an echo in my mind. Perhaps there is no right answer to this age-old dilemma. Perhaps the truth, like beauty, lies in the eye of the beholder. A hopeful ending, even if untrue, is a more fitting tribute to their love than the harsh reality of their tragic fate.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: I am Briony, and I am sad to report on the tragic fate of two lovers, Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis. Because I invented them myself, their tragedy is my own fault, but because their characters are based in reality, I cannot help but feel loyal to the truth. The fact is that Robbie and Cecilia died during World War II. Robbie succumbed to septicemia at Bray Dunes, and Cecilia perished in a bombing at Balham Underground station. Neither of them knew that I had committed a terrible wrong against them both. In my youth, I was wickedly jealous of Robbie and Cecilia and resented the affection they held for one another. Not because I desired either of them, but because I was angry and lonely and hiding in a bunker of cynicism. I was a postboy, and when Robbie went off to war, I would intercept the letters he sent to Cecelia and slide them into the rain-filled gutters. I did the same to Cecelia’s letters, and their correspondence slowly dwindled. Eventually, they stopped writing to each other altogether. I’ve been approaching this all wrong. Now is the time to let Robbie and Cecelia survive and be together, even if only in these pages. Telling the truth wouldn’t do any good, because it’s an ugly truth. I never saw Robbie and Cecelia again, their love stayed unfulfilled, and their few remaining letters are preserved only in a war museum. Maybe truth is not always better than mercy. Maybe hope survives through lies.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: Excerpt 2 feels more believable than Excerpt 1 as an expression of this character's internal monologue, mostly because Excerpt 1 feels overwritten with excessive figurative language. Excerpt 2 flows well, with the key insights arriving at proper beats, while Excerpt 2 dwells too long on individual images. Overall, Excerpt 1's style is a better match for its ideas, allowing it to be more fluent and effective.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Robbie and Cecilia were happy in my story. They faced hardships, certainly, but I conjured them, by the force of my own brittle pen, into two happy people. The world, the real world, was not as kind to them. I cannot be sure of what happened in the end, but, in all likelihood, it was this: Robbie succumbed to the brutal, unforgiving clutch of septicemia— the horror of black limbs and gasping breaths in his final moments. And dear Cecilia was decimated by a bomb at Balham Underground station. Is it selfishness, then, or a mercy, this ending I’ve given them, this happiness? In my tale, there is no sickness traveling through the veins, no limbs blown off. There is only contentment and love, a warm and certain kind. Why tell the truth, when it is something almost unspeakably miserable? The truth: that I never saw them again, after what happened. That I could not face my sister. That their letters—tender and sorrowful —are preserved only in a war museum, words of desperate longing fossilized behind panes of glass. It’s this business of truth I continue to return to—always this business of truth. Is the truth better than what I have done? Have I committed an act of cowardice, in my story, or an act of love? For I loved them both; still, I do. And I gave them mercy, a happy ending, perhaps more meaningful than the tragic nature of their lives. I gave them each other.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Truth sits heavily in my hands like an old manuscript, its pages yellow and brittle with time. I could write it all - the harsh reality of their separate deaths, Robbie's slow fade into septicemic darkness at Bray Dunes, Cecilia's final moments in the underground station at Balham, their love scattered like ash across a war-torn continent. The historian in me demands this accuracy, this unflinching record of what actually transpired after my childish testimony tore them apart. But what serves memory better - the brutal facts preserved in glass cases at the Imperial War Museum, those letters never to be answered, those promises never to be kept, or the mercy of imagination that allows them to transcend the circumstances I thrust upon them? In my fiction, they live. In my fiction, their hands find each other across the library table, their eyes meet without the shadow of my betrayal between them. Perhaps this is my final act of cowardice, unable even now to face the full weight of what I did, unable to write the words that would kill them again on the page. Or perhaps it is the only grace left to me - this power to resurrect them from the ashes of history, to give them the moments that war and my testimony stole. The question haunts me: is truth always kinder than fiction? In the end, I choose to let them live in the amber of my imagination, preserved in a love that reality never permitted them to fully express.
written_by_MFA008.Reason: Excerpt 1 treats characters Robbie and Cecilia as real people, introducing the narrator's authorial agency from the very first sentence in a natural, coherent way. Sentences carry deep emotional weight: "The truth: that I never saw them again, after what happened. That I could not face my sister." The language is straightforward, confessional, and easy to read. By contrast, Excerpt 2 relies on simile and metaphor to the point that the excerpt feels 'overwritten' to me. The excerpt is melodramatic in a way that undercuts the sincerity of the emotions being explored by the content. For this reason, Excerpt 1 feels more sincere and true to life.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: The truth is much uglier than the sweet story I’ve given them. Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis never saw each other again, both having perished during the war. Robbie fell to septicemia at Bray Dunes, his wounds never healing right. Cecilia, my glamorous older sister, died in a bombing at the Balham Underground, dressed in the same rationed rags as any other woman. They died alone, a fault I must now agonizingly take the blame for. It was my callous childishness that ripped Robbie from Cecilia, but it is my better nature that has prompted me to write them a better ending. They find each other again, they live, and they are happy. What good would it do, I beg to know, in telling the foul truth? I’ll tell it, here and now, if only to prove my point. I never saw either of them again that year, how could I, after what I had done to Cecilia? Their love died with them, isolated and unfulfilled, with the sole evidence that they knew each other being those romantic letters preserved only in a war museum. I cannot imagine truth is worth more than the merciful fiction, but I struggle even now to know for certain if my rewrite of history is fair. I’d like to think that this hopeful conclusion, regardless of how factual it may be, holds greater value than an honest, but tragic account.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: In the twilight of her long life, Briony Tallis grappled with the burden of her narrative. Her pages were a desperate reach for atonement, a reckoning with a truth too cruel to bear. Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis had never enjoyed the solace of a country retreat or the satisfaction of a love realized. The world had not been kind enough to allow their survival. Yet in the theater of her imagination, Briony became their savior, conjuring them together, their lives intact, their love unbroken, their letters exchanged with trembling hands. The truth, stark and unrelenting, loomed like the specter of her own guilt: Robbie felled by infection in the mud-soaked trenches, Cecilia extinguished in a cataclysm of rubble and fire. She, the architect of their suffering, could not face the permanence of that ending. What then was the purpose of truth, she wondered, if it could not redeem? In her constructed fiction, she gave them joy, continuity, the soft rebellion of a life shared. But as the ink dried on her final pages, she was left with the echo of a question that gnawed at her sense of justice and her fragile hope for forgiveness: was it better to honor the brutal finality of fact or to bestow upon them, and herself, the balm of a beautiful lie? At the edge of her fading strength, she allowed herself the faintest smile, perhaps at last, a merciful fiction was the highest form of kindness.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: The first excerpt reads much more naturally, while the second excerpt is, again, overwritten and replete with cliches: "the twilight of her long life," "a reckoning with a truth too cruel to bear," "the edge of her fading strength" (that last phrase, for example, is redundant, as "the edge" and "fading" imply the same thing). The first excerpt is also much more specific - it names how they died (septicemia at Bray Dunes and bombing at the Balham Underground) and references "rationed rags," which sets this story firmly in WW2, rather than the generalized war implied in excerpt 2.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: In the twilight of her long life, Briony Tallis grappled with the burden of her narrative. Her pages were a desperate reach for atonement, a reckoning with a truth too cruel to bear. Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis had never enjoyed the solace of a country retreat or the satisfaction of a love realized. The world had not been kind enough to allow their survival. Yet in the theater of her imagination, Briony became their savior, conjuring them together, their lives intact, their love unbroken, their letters exchanged with trembling hands. The truth, stark and unrelenting, loomed like the specter of her own guilt: Robbie felled by infection in the mud-soaked trenches, Cecilia extinguished in a cataclysm of rubble and fire. She, the architect of their suffering, could not face the permanence of that ending. What then was the purpose of truth, she wondered, if it could not redeem? In her constructed fiction, she gave them joy, continuity, the soft rebellion of a life shared. But as the ink dried on her final pages, she was left with the echo of a question that gnawed at her sense of justice and her fragile hope for forgiveness: was it better to honor the brutal finality of fact or to bestow upon them, and herself, the balm of a beautiful lie? At the edge of her fading strength, she allowed herself the faintest smile, perhaps at last, a merciful fiction was the highest form of kindness.
