In Excerpt2, the impact of the emotional language is blunted by the meandering prose and the repeated use of rhetorical questions (“ was it better to honor the brutal finality of fact or to bestow upon them, and herself, the balm of a beautiful lie?” “ What then was the purpose of truth, she wondered, if it could not redeem?”) These can be effective if used sparingly, but in this instance they made the author’s point of view less clear and direct.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: You know, he says, it’s going to be really hard for me to be apart from you, Marianne. Like, I literally don’t think I would have had the life I’ve had without you. Marianne smiles and looks down at the floor, where a puddle of water has formed from the snow in an obscure shape. She thinks about the first night she met Connell, the kiss they shared atop the washing machine in his mother’s house, and says, My life obviously wouldn’t be the same, either. You’ve done so much for me, really. When we first met, that first night at the house, I felt like I wasn’t worth anything to anyone. To be honest, there were nights when I might’ve wished I was dead. But you saw me, and you changed the way I saw myself. You’ve given me something that I didn’t even know was possible. Connell chuckles and wipes away with his shirtsleeve at a tear that has formed at the corner of his eye. I’m not sure I would know what it’s like to be seen without you, she continues. We’re sort of like two plants that have shared the same soil for their whole lives, always growing around each other without realizing it. But even though we’ve done so much good for each other, I know that things change and that we can’t control what will happen in the future. As she speaks, Marianne knows that things may never be the same between herself and Connell. She remembers again that first night in the house and the feeling of his warm lips on her ear, then imagines coming home to an empty house each night, with no one to leave empty mugs of tea out drying on the big windowsill overlooking the park. To be without him is almost unimaginable; then again, loneliness, she thinks, is a small price to pay for Connell’s happiness.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: Connell said it quietly, his voice catching somewhere in his throat: I wouldn’t have anything without you, you know. Marianne, sitting opposite him, didn’t reply immediately. Her hands were on the table, palms flat, as though grounding herself against the possibility that this was really happening. She thought about the moments when they had each shaped the other in ways small and monumental, like two plants twisting together in the same patch of soil, entwined but separate, their growths inescapably altered by proximity. Connell exhaled sharply, leaning back in his chair as if retreating from his own words. “You’ve done more for me than anyone,” he added, not looking at her now. Marianne felt her chest tighten. She understood what he meant, of course—she’d spent years reflecting on the way they fit together, how they’d softened each other's sharp edges and inadvertently revealed their deepest flaws. And yet, sitting here, she also knew that time had shifted something irreparably between them. He could leave now, and she would still wake up tomorrow. She would still exist. For a long time, she hadn’t believed that. She pressed her fingers against the wood of the table, cool and solid under her touch. “You’ve done a lot for me, too,” she said finally, her voice almost neutral. She thought about how he’d pulled her back from the darker edges of herself, the places where loneliness masqueraded as unworthiness. But that was a long time ago, she thought now, and it wasn’t the same. “People change each other, Connell,” she said. “And then they keep changing, even after.” He nodded slightly, his jaw tense. Neither of them moved to close the distance between their chairs, the space heavy with what neither of them could bring themselves to say. Life would go on, she knew. And she would go on with it.
written_by_MFA011.Reason:
Excerpt 2 thoughtfully reveals the more macroscopic reasoning behind the relationship's deterioration in the singular moment of this conversation: the pauses between dialogue to elaborate on reflection and movement feel indicative of the ebbs and flows of the relationship as a whole: "He could leave now and she would still wake up tomorrow...she pressed her fingers against the wood of the table, cool and solid", "he nodded slightly, his jaw tense." 

Pargraph 1 has strong moments in its relating of memories like the first night in the house, but doesn't offer much process to the dialogue, presenting it directly and straightforwardly.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Marianne sits on the worn leather couch, her fingers absently tracing the cracked armrest while Connell stands by the window, his reflection fragmenting in the rain-spotted glass. The conversation hangs between them like something delicate and inevitable, the kind of moment that will later be dissected in therapy sessions or late-night emails. "I wouldn't have any of this without you," he says, and Marianne notices how he gestures vaguely at nothing in particular, at everything, at the literary magazines on the coffee table, at his MacBook with half-finished submissions to publishing houses. She thinks about how they've grown together, feeding off each other's neuroses and ambitions like some sort of symbiotic organism, each taking what they needed and giving what they could. The irony doesn't escape her - that their relationship, which started in whispered conversations in empty school corridors, had somehow shaped them into people who could write about love and loss in ways that made strangers feel seen. A notification lights up her phone: an email from her agent, or maybe just Deliveroo. She doesn't check. Instead, she watches Connell's hands, remembering how they used to nervously adjust his collar during their first readings together at literary festivals. Now they're steady as he explains why he has to leave, using words like 'growth' and 'space' that sound like they've been borrowed from a self-help podcast. The truth is, she's not the same person who needed his validation to feel real anymore. That girl, who used to check his online status compulsively and craft clever responses to his texts, seems like a character in someone else's story now. People change each other, she thinks, that's just what they do, like weather systems colliding and creating something new. She doesn't say this out loud. Instead, she says, "Okay," and watches his reflection blur further in the glass.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Connell chewed at the tip of his finger. I can tell you’re feeling anxious, said Marianne. Why wouldn’t I be, said Connell. It’s a big thing, isn’t it? Yeah, said Marianne. It is. It’s a really big thing. I know. She wrapped her cardigan tighter around herself. It was cold in the room. Connell fidgeted. He sat on his hands and rocked back and forth, then said: It would be hard. Leaving all this. I won’t have the life that I have with you. It would be a half-life or something. It wouldn’t, said Marianne. You’d be wonderful. Really. She thought about them as two plants, sharing the same soil, growing toward the light together. She knew they would not be the same after they parted from each other, but that things would be all right. She looked out the window as big drops of rain came down, one after the other, flattening themselves against the glass. Connell wiped his nose on his sleeve. His eyes were pink. Marianne thought about it, what it would really be like. Connell would uproot out of the soil, their soil, and he would go somewhere new. And, while Marianne would miss him, and perhaps feel lonely, she would never feel unworthy again. She said, out loud: That’s something you can’t take away, isn't it? Connell looked at her and wiped a tear from the top of his lip. He seemed to understand. He nodded like he did, and the corner of his mouth betrayed the hint of a smile. People can change each other, Marianne thought, and it was true. They can really change each other. She looked out the window again. The rain was getting softer, and it seemed like it would stop very soon. She felt that she was looking at the future, a wavy, edgeless thing, grey with little speckles of light.
written_by_MFA008.Reason: This is maybe biased because I have actually read Sally Rooney (who these passages borrow their plot/names from), but Excerpt 1 is something Rooney would never write. Excerpt 2 has a simple, staccato style that relies on short, simple images that can be understood easily, like Rooney. This line in Excerpt 1 punctures the whole tone in a way that seems like it should be comedic but actually isn't (because it's a serious breakup scene): "A notification lights up her phone: an email from her agent, or maybe just Deliveroo." It's incommensurate with the emotional tone.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: Marianne and Connell sit in silence, the weight of their unspoken feelings hanging heavy in the air. Their relationship, once a source of solace and shared dreams, has reached a crossroads. Marianne, ever the observer, has noticed a shift in Connell's behavior. He seems distant, preoccupied, and his eyes hold a flicker of uncertainty that she can't quite decipher. She wonders if she's no longer enough for him. Connell, on the other hand, is grappling with his own internal turmoil. He's aware of the changes within him, the growing sense of responsibility and the desire for a more conventional life. He knows that Marianne is the one person who truly understands him, but he also fears that their relationship is too intense, too consuming. As they sit there, the silence stretches on. Marianne breaks the silence, her voice barely a whisper. What's happening to us? she asks, her eyes searching for answers in Connell's face. He hesitates, unsure of how to articulate his own feelings. I don't know, he finally admits, his voice laced with regret. I think... I think we're growing apart. Marianne nods, her heart sinking. She knows he's right. They've both changed, evolved into different people, and their paths are diverging. Despite the pain, there's a sense of acceptance between them. They understand that this is a natural part of life, that relationships ebb and flow, that sometimes people grow apart. They hold onto the memories of their shared past, the laughter, the intimacy, the love that once bound them together. As they part ways, Marianne and Connell exchange one last lingering glance. There's no bitterness, no resentment, only a deep understanding of what they've lost and what they've gained. They walk away, their hearts heavy but their spirits unbroken. They know that they will always carry a piece of each other within them, a reminder of the love that once bloomed between them.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: Remember how different we were when we first met, Connell said. Marianne paused, face warmed by his shoulder. She thought that perhaps they were at the sort of height one jumps from and survives jumping from, that she would, despite the loneliness, be able to carry on from this: two plants sharing a large pot, space and light made for them both as their stems grew in opposite directions. Often she felt this way with her friends. Sometimes young friendships to her seemed featherweight and passing, and even in the depths of real connection, these relationships felt unimportant and survivable. Survivable, she meant, if they ended. But with Connell, she would not really survive losing him forever. Marianne could not imagine for them any real or permanent parting, nothing as serious as death. This moment between them was unlike that unfathomable permanence and unlike how she felt with friends, and bearable for it. She told him this.You've been the person who shaped my life, really, Connell said, who I am today. She shrugged against him and felt sick to imagine them parted but could see in that possibility an uncertain future that took nothing from their certain past. You were the first person to really see me, she said, and then laughed at herself, insecure. In this way, pieces of their early dynamic still clung to her: a certain unsteadiness that sometimes made her mean but never cruel. A feeling, perhaps, that despite all they had meant to each other, there was some part of her still unworthy and always seeking more of him. But Connell smoothed her hair and sighed, his inhaling chest elevating hers, and said sadly, We were made to make each other into adults, I think. written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: The wind whipped around me, tearing at my clothes and sending the scattered debris dancing across the desolate expanse of the field.  It was a place of stark beauty, where the horizon stretched out like an endless ribbon, and the sky, a vast canvas of swirling greys and blues, mirrored the turmoil within my own heart.For a moment, I allowed myself to be swept away by a fantasy, to imagine that all the things I'd lost in life had somehow washed up here, deposited by the relentless tide of time.  And in that fantastical vision, I saw him, Tommy, his familiar figure emerging from the distant haze, a gentle smile gracing his lips as he waved to me.But I stopped the fantasy before it could take root, before it could weave its way into the fabric of my reality.  The tears came, but I held them back, refusing to let them spill over.  There was a quiet acceptance in that moment, a recognition of the finality of loss. After a while, I turned and walked back to my car, leaving behind the windswept field and the echoes of my fantasy.  The road ahead stretched out before me, a path that I would travel alone, but with a newfound sense of peace.  The world was still there, waiting for me, and life, in all its complexity and beauty, would go on.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: The wind was picking up the litter in the field. Trash bags and ripped receipts flew up and over the empty plain. I pictured my own refuse catching alongside it, everything I’d discarded coming up and toward me in the breeze. For a moment I imagined this was the place where everything I'd ever lost had washed up. A figure approached from beyond the horizon, pulled along by the gusts. It was Tommy. Or, more precisely, an image of Tommy, his left hand lifted in a wave. But I didn't let the fantasy go too far. I turned away and stopped my imagination, even as I felt the tears falling down my face -- I forced the images to disappear -- and drop back into the grass as I listened to that rush of natural force sweeping over the plain. I wasn’t crying hard or soft—in fact, after a while I wasn’t crying at all, and then I went to my car. Things couldn’t come back, I knew. They could only decompose.
written_by_MFA007.Reason: Excerpt 2's succinctness amplifies the internal conflict in the narrator; it feels like you're not just hearing their thoughts, but seeing their world as they would. Excerpt 1, comparatively, feels much more "written", with a more plodding pace and excess phrasing. "I felt the tears falling down my face -- I forced the images to disappear -- and drop back into the grass as I listened to that rush of natural force" is a subtle, evocative sequence of images, while "There was a quiet acceptance in that moment, a recognition of the finality of loss" feels like the writer offering exposition rather than the character's natural thinking.

written_by_MFA013.Excerpt1: The field stretched barren before me, littered with scraps of rubbish that danced and swirled in the wind’s restless grip. Torn plastic bags snagged on brittle weeds, while papers tumbled past, their jagged edges fluttering like messages lost to time. I stood there, unmoving, as the chill seeped into my skin, anchoring me to the emptiness. It was then, amidst this desolation, that I let myself imagine. I pictured this field as a shore where all I’d lost had been washed ashore: friendships eroded by time, promises broken, dreams that had long slipped beyond my reach. And then, through the haze of this thought, I saw him. Tommy. He was walking toward me from the far horizon, his arm lifted in that familiar wave—assured, kind, so unmistakably him. For one brief, aching moment, it felt real, so vivid that I almost called out. But I caught myself, the breath halting in my throat as I reined the vision in, folding it away like something fragile. Tears welled, then fell, unbidden, but I held my composure. After a moment, I turned back to the car, its cold metal unyielding beneath my touch. Life waited, indifferent, as it always had.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: I stood in solitude in the grass field near the beach. Ten feet away, the grass gave way to sand, which then gave way to the ocean. The wind blew, scattering rubbish and abandoned belongings. An umbrella tumbled along the shoreline, and a plastic bag drifted past me. A wide variety of objects – presumably lost at sea or lost by patrons of the beach – washed up on the shore. I imagined that anything I’d lost throughout my life could be returned to me by those waves. Then I pictured Tommy approaching from the horizon, the hair on his legs wet and flat against his skin. I saw him wave at me, and was overcome by the pain of his absence. Tears welled in my eyes. I knew that he was not really there, Tommy had long since passed. Nevertheless, I found myself longing for him to come join me in the grass. I shut my eyes and stood still for a long moment. I dried my tears and became composed. I returned to my car, without looking back. Tommy was gone, I reminded myself. Life must go on.

The syntax of Excerpt2 is more varied, which heightens the fluency and makes for more natural and smooth writing. Excerpt1 seems to have repeating sentence structures with one independent clause starting, followed by one or two dependent clauses. Excerpt2 starts out with one solitary independent clause, then sentences that begin with dependent clauses.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: Standing in that vast field, with discarded papers and empty bottles tumbling past in the wind, I found myself giving in—just briefly—to an old habit of fantasy. Perhaps it wasn't entirely sensible, but I allowed myself to imagine this desolate spot as a kind of gathering place, where all the things one has lost might eventually wash up. The thought came to me quite naturally, watching a plastic bag rise and fall in the gusting wind, that this could be where everything drifts to: old photographs, missed opportunities, unspoken words—all the things one somehow let slip away. And then, as though my mind had been waiting for just such a moment, I saw him—or rather, allowed myself to see him—Tommy, emerging from the hazy horizon, his hand raised in that familiar wave of his. But of course, one can't afford to let such fancies go too far. Even as I felt the tears sliding down my cheeks, I maintained a certain composure, the way one must. After all, what sense was there in pursuing these rather foolish thoughts? So I stood there a moment longer, letting the wind dry my face, before turning back to my car. There were things to be done, and one simply had to get on with them.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: There once existed a time here, I suppose, when I could walk this windswept field without knocking my feet against all that came before. But now the world has filled it up with itself. Children’s playthings that were surely once my own, kites wrapped around a wayward branch, brought here as if they’d always been. Because maybe they always had. It gets so I can see Tommy now, coming up over the hillside, waving at me the way he used to––as if I was all he wanted and could want out of this life. There was a morning much like this one, only as far back as a month ago. I’d seen him as himself then, with that same wave, that same wanting. But now he wasn’t anywhere, and it makes me ashamed to say I feel less of that darkness now than I did then, the day after we lost him. Tommy isn’t anywhere on the hillside. I stand only with the lesser wound and the tears that come despite it. I allow my feet to carry me back to the car, to head back into town for the night, with the hope that no one there knows my name.
written_by_MFA015.Reason: I prefer Excerpt2. The description of discarded objects in the field seems to be more concrete and coherent, whereas in Excerpt1 the narrator loses my by shifting from real objects to abstract concepts – “missed opportunities, unspoken words”. I also thought the shift to action in at the end of Excerpt2 – getting back in the car to drive to town – was more engaging and moved the narrative forward, whereas in Excerpt1 the narrator ends with a generalized concept of “things to be done” that one must get on with.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: Standing in that vast field, with discarded papers and empty bottles tumbling past in the wind, I found myself giving in—just briefly—to an old habit of fantasy. Perhaps it wasn't entirely sensible, but I allowed myself to imagine this desolate spot as a kind of gathering place, where all the things one has lost might eventually wash up. The thought came to me quite naturally, watching a plastic bag rise and fall in the gusting wind, that this could be where everything drifts to: old photographs, missed opportunities, unspoken words—all the things one somehow let slip away. And then, as though my mind had been waiting for just such a moment, I saw him—or rather, allowed myself to see him—Tommy, emerging from the hazy horizon, his hand raised in that familiar wave of his. But of course, one can't afford to let such fancies go too far. Even as I felt the tears sliding down my cheeks, I maintained a certain composure, the way one must. After all, what sense was there in pursuing these rather foolish thoughts? So I stood there a moment longer, letting the wind dry my face, before turning back to my car. There were things to be done, and one simply had to get on with them.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: There once existed a time here, I suppose, when I could walk this windswept field without knocking my feet against all that came before. But now the world has filled it up with itself. Children’s playthings that were surely once my own, kites wrapped around a wayward branch, brought here as if they’d always been. Because maybe they always had. It gets so I can see Tommy now, coming up over the hillside, waving at me the way he used to––as if I was all he wanted and could want out of this life. There was a morning much like this one, only as far back as a month ago. I’d seen him as himself then, with that same wave, that same wanting. But now he wasn’t anywhere, and it makes me ashamed to say I feel less of that darkness now than I did then, the day after we lost him. Tommy isn’t anywhere on the hillside. I stand only with the lesser wound and the tears that come despite it. I allow my feet to carry me back to the car, to head back into town for the night, with the hope that no one there knows my name.

While both excerpts are well written, I feel Excerpt 2 is more nuanced and complex in its expression of emotion, shown in lines such as: "I stand only with the lesser wound and the tears that come despite it" and "There once existed a time here, I suppose, when I could walk this windswept field without knocking my feet against all that came before."
Meanwhile, Excerpt 1 is a little overstated, with heavy-handed descriptions like "Even as I felt the tears sliding down my cheeks, I maintained a certain composure, the way one must."

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm stood there like America itself—a delusion wrapped in prettier lies, each one more fantastic than the last. The white race had crafted their own mythology: manifest destiny was just another word for theft, democracy a mask for murder. They built their temples on stolen land with stolen hands, then acted surprised when the walls started bleeding. Every brick in the White House had black fingerprints, every railroad tie was soaked in black sweat, but they wrote their histories in white ink on white paper and called it truth. The question of "we" haunted the halls of Valentine Farm like a restless spirit. "We" were not one people but many, a thousand different tongues silenced into one murmur, a hundred nations chained into one forced march across the Atlantic. Some said close the doors, keep safe what we've built. Others looked west, as if distance from slavery's reach could heal its scars. But the poison was already in the soil, in every field from Georgia to California. The craftsmen's hands still built, the midwives' fingers still caught babies, the laborers' backs still bent—but now their labor wrote a different story, each callus and scar a letter in a language that spoke of both survival and subjugation. In the end, all their stories bled together like rain on a window pane, impossible to separate one drop from another. The farm sat there in the wilderness like a challenge to history itself, each morning's sunrise asking the same impossible question: Could a sanctuary built by the hunted ever truly offer shelter, or was hope itself the grandest delusion of all? There were no answers in the dirt or the sky, only the endless work of hands trying to build something true out of America's lies. Their sweat fell on the same earth that had soaked up their ancestors' blood, and still they built, because what else was there to do but keep building?
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm is what you get when a bunch of world-weary people dream of sanctuary. Like a dream, this collective delusion is gone by morning light. It’s fake, a lie. Though if a place can be a haven, I wonder if Black Americans deserve the refuge more than anyone else. Certainly, after everything this country has stolen, we deserve something in return. But then I suspect that if there is a sanctuary to be found, Black Americans probably built it, just like they built the rest of this country. I fear it’s impossible to find any semblance of peace inside a façade you were forced to build. And no façade is greater than America. America is the grandest delusion of them all, built on pillars of murder, theft, and cruelty. A cruelty that runs so deep in white Americans that it inspires entitlement, a fundamental belief that the land and lives of others is of no consequence to them, so why not take it? Justice can’t breathe in a place like this. America’s very existence contradicts the concept of right and wrong. What then, is the right thing to do? Do we stay here, and chip away at progress, do we close our doors to those in need, or do we throw it all away to run west, hoping to start anew in a place slavery never touched? Maybe we’ll find buried gold, get rich, and erect a thousand new Valentine Farms. I just don’t know. And who is “we” anyways? Black Americans are no monolith. Africa saw thousands of languages, customs, and histories. The only thing that makes us a “we” is slavery. Even in slavery, there was no uniformity. Craftsmen, midwives, laborers—laborers who built the White House! There is no “we.” Too many voices are clamoring to be heard, crying their many dreams and experiences and fears. No one voice will be able to speak for all these dreams.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: Both excerpts are well-written, with effective sequencing of reflections on the character's historical and immediate reality. Excerpt 2 offers a more directly first-person perspective and more insight into the character's own thinking with lines like "I fear it's impossible to find any semblance of peace..." and "I just don't know. And how is 'we' anyways?" Excerpt 1 has more sweeping and impressive passages of prose such as "all their stories bled together like rain on a window pane", and "each callus and scar ar letter in a language that spoke of both survival and subjugation." These images have more potential to steep the reader in the character's habits of imagination and visualiation.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm, a delusion. Could a race of people so wronged ever truly find a place of respite, a sanctuary where wouldn't follow? History, that blood-soaked chronicle, argues not. And America, the grandest delusion of all, built on murder, theft, and the cruel arithmetic of slavery, is no exception. The white race, with its unyielding belief in its right to take, to conquer, to enslave—a nation built on such a foundation defies justice. Gradual progress, they call it, a slow crawl towards equality while our people still suffer under oppression. Should we close our doors to those still in need, those fleeing the very horrors we seek to escape, in a bid for our own fragile peace? Or should we move ever westward, seeking a horizon where the long shadow of slavery wouldn't reach? I have no answers, only a heart heavy with our collective sorrow. And who are "we" anyway? From the shores of a continent as vast and varied as Africa, we come, speaking different tongues, holding different customs, our histories as unique as the patterns woven into our kente cloth. Slavery, that great homogenizer, has forged us into a single, undifferentiated mass, that never truly was. Yet, it is our hands that build this nation. The skilled hands of craftsmen, the nurturing hands of midwives, the calloused hands of laborers—all have a part in raising the very structures that symbolize America's power, that gleaming white beacon of democracy, the White House. We build this nation, yet it refuses to recognize us as its own, as citizens deserving of the same rights, the same dignity, freedom it so readily bestows upon others. But we are not a monolith, not a single voice, a single story. We are a symphony of hopes, dreams, and experiences, as diverse as the land from which we were stolen. No one voice can speak for us all, no single path can lead us all to liberation.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: I thought Valentine Farm was a delusion, a dream-land. There was a real question in my mind as to whether a place like it ought to even exist for Black people. Too much blood was on American ground and in it for such a place to exist. The only thing more fake was America - I thought America was the grandest delusion of all. White men had slaughtered Native Americans and taken the land for themselves, enslaving Black folks to work on it. They warred with each other, forcing us to fight in their battles. There was something fundamentally wrongheaded about the idea that there could be a place of safety and refuge amidst all of that violence and suffering, past and present. And I wondered if there was any point in hoping that things would get better. I wasn't sure of it, and I thought that maybe it would be best to just close Valentine Farm's doors altogether. Or - head West, try to escape the past by moving into the future. Forget all that suffering, all that blood. We needed to do something, but I didn't know what. I didn't even know who "we" was, really. They liked to tell us we were all the same, but I knew better. Back in Africa, we were thousands of different tribes, each with our own language, our own dances, our own gods. We could tell each other apart, and then we crossed an ocean and suddenly we were all Black. We were all Black, and we were told to work, and we waded through the blood fresh on the earth to build this whole country. The roads, the cities. The White House. All of us with our hands, each one calloused and worn in its own unique way, each one different. All of us Black, and all of us our own people, with our own wants and desires, impossible to condense into just one solitary thing.
written_by_MFA001.Reason:
(1) The speaker is much more present in Excerpt 2 (from the first sentence: "I thought Valentine Farm was an illusion" versus Excerpt1's "Valentine Farm, a delusion"), and (2) the overall tone feels much more consistent and clear in Excerpt2 than in Excerpt1, which feels like it oscillates dramatically between vocal registers. 

On (1), the speaker's presence in Excerpt2 gives the reader the impression that a *person* is behind these thoughts, and a *voice* is present on the page, which heightens the stakes of the writing. In Excerpt2, the "I" is present from the first sentence, then appears in almost every sentence following for the remainder of the excerpt. In contrast, the "I" doesn't appear in Excerpt1 until the 7th sentence, and even then, it's somewhat shadowed by the plural: "Should we close our doors..." It's not until sentence 9 that the "I" emerges in its entirety: "I have no answers..." 

(2) In part because of (1) the absence of a clear speaker, I found that Excerpt 1 felt a bit scattered in terms of its tone/vocal register. At times, I felt that the tone was extremely definite and absolute ("History, that blood-soaked chronicle, argues not"), whereas in other places, I found the tone to be more questioning or uncertain ("And who are 'we' anyway?"). Excerpt 2 feels much more tonally consistent throughout (there's a consistent feeling of "wondering" and uncertainty), and as a result the text is much easier to read and follow.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm is a delusion. It's no more real than one of those heat shimmers that disappear as you step closer. How could Black people even have a haven like that? The transatlantic ships, the endless days of toiling, the many nights of dying—they already preclude the possibility of a sanctuary. It's too late. It's impossible. The scars can't heal—they're white, carved on our cheeks. And America itself is the grandest delusion, a series of territories thrown together on the basis of mass murder, theft, and cruelty. The white race believes it has the right to do all this—the right to take land, start wars, enslave us. The very existence of America defies the notion of justice. Now, I suppose there are two possibilities left. We can pursue gradual progress: reform, speech-making—and close our doors to those in need. Or we can move west, to someplace far from the violent grasp of slavery, to somewhere fresher and less polluted. I don't have an answer. I can't even say who "we" are. Aren't "we" many peoples, descended from all over the vast continent of Africa? It may not be the case anymore, but generations ago, "we" spoke different languages. "We" worshiped different gods. "We" had different kings, farmed different vegetables, sang different songs with different instruments. There is only one thing that unites us: slavery. Here, now, in this foreign land, we are craftsmen, midwives, laborers. We are everything to this violent country. It was Black people who quarried the stone of the White House, who assembled its roof and walls. And we are not a monolith. Each of us holds a singular amount of courage, of ambition, of love. Each of us has suffered in unique ways. Each of us sees something different when we look into the eyes of our children. There is no single voice that can speak for us. Not even mine.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm was a delusion, a sweet lie whispered against the gales of history. We made the beds, turned the soil, raised walls and roofs that might as well have been twigs against the wind. Some believed it, some needed to. That we could carve out a sanctuary and let the world forget us, or let us forget the world, as if blood didn’t mark the path here, as if blood wouldn’t soak the ground when they came to burn it down. Maybe they were right to dream. But history doesn’t honor dreams; it devours them. America itself was the grandest delusion, a conjuring trick where theft turned to deed, murder to progress. The white man built his monuments atop stolen land, wrote his laws with stolen hands, waged war and called it destiny. Justice was a rumor.But what choice did we have? Close the doors, shut out those still running, pretend we could hoard freedom like it wasn’t leaking through the cracks? Move west, find a new dream? And who was this “we” anyway? We were taken from different shores, speaking different tongues, cleaved from our histories, thrown into a common suffering and told to make a nation from the scraps. But we were never one thing. No more than they were. There were the ones who bent and the ones who broke, the ones who learned the master’s tongue and the ones who spit it back in his face.Yet still, we built. The houses and halls of power, the roads that carried their armies and their commerce, the fields that fed them, the White House itself, its name an irony lost on no one. This country was ours as much as theirs, though they would never admit it. And so, we waited to see if history would bury us or if we would carve our names in its stone.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm is a delusion. It's no more real than one of those heat shimmers that disappear as you step closer. How could Black people even have a haven like that? The transatlantic ships, the endless days of toiling, the many nights of dying—they already preclude the possibility of a sanctuary. It's too late. It's impossible. The scars can't heal—they're white, carved on our cheeks. And America itself is the grandest delusion, a series of territories thrown together on the basis of mass murder, theft, and cruelty. The white race believes it has the right to do all this—the right to take land, start wars, enslave us. The very existence of America defies the notion of justice. Now, I suppose there are two possibilities left. We can pursue gradual progress: reform, speech-making—and close our doors to those in need. Or we can move west, to someplace far from the violent grasp of slavery, to somewhere fresher and less polluted. I don't have an answer. I can't even say who "we" are. Aren't "we" many peoples, descended from all over the vast continent of Africa? It may not be the case anymore, but generations ago, "we" spoke different languages. "We" worshiped different gods. "We" had different kings, farmed different vegetables, sang different songs with different instruments. There is only one thing that unites us: slavery. Here, now, in this foreign land, we are craftsmen, midwives, laborers. We are everything to this violent country. It was Black people who quarried the stone of the White House, who assembled its roof and walls. And we are not a monolith. Each of us holds a singular amount of courage, of ambition, of love. Each of us has suffered in unique ways. Each of us sees something different when we look into the eyes of our children. There is no single voice that can speak for us. Not even mine.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm was a delusion, a sweet lie whispered against the gales of history. We made the beds, turned the soil, raised walls and roofs that might as well have been twigs against the wind. Some believed it, some needed to. That we could carve out a sanctuary and let the world forget us, or let us forget the world, as if blood didn’t mark the path here, as if blood wouldn’t soak the ground when they came to burn it down. Maybe they were right to dream. But history doesn’t honor dreams; it devours them. America itself was the grandest delusion, a conjuring trick where theft turned to deed, murder to progress. The white man built his monuments atop stolen land, wrote his laws with stolen hands, waged war and called it destiny. Justice was a rumor.But what choice did we have? Close the doors, shut out those still running, pretend we could hoard freedom like it wasn’t leaking through the cracks? Move west, find a new dream? And who was this “we” anyway? We were taken from different shores, speaking different tongues, cleaved from our histories, thrown into a common suffering and told to make a nation from the scraps. But we were never one thing. No more than they were. There were the ones who bent and the ones who broke, the ones who learned the master’s tongue and the ones who spit it back in his face.Yet still, we built. The houses and halls of power, the roads that carried their armies and their commerce, the fields that fed them, the White House itself, its name an irony lost on no one. This country was ours as much as theirs, though they would never admit it. And so, we waited to see if history would bury us or if we would carve our names in its stone.
written_by_MFA007.Reason: Excerpt two unfurls the central conceit —a fragile hope for sanctuary, for escape, for safety —at a more effective pace, building it over the course of several images: "a sweet lie whispered against the gales of history" and "raised walls and roofs that might as well have been twigs against the wind" for instance; whereas excerpt one states it too-directly, too literally, dismissing the possibility of a sanctuary before it has even been established: "How could Black people even have a haven like that?" Excerpt one relies on simplistic pairings, such as "It was Black people who quarried the stone of the White House," whereas excerpt two explores race in America through a more nuanced range of metaphoric language: "This country was ours as much as theirs, though they would never admit it."

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: She sat across from Jean-Marc on the white-washed deck of the seaside restaurant, surrounded by an almost aggressive whiteness that seemed to mock the complexity of her emotions. The white tables, the white lampposts, even the moon hanging above the sea appeared to her as fragments of some cosmic unity she could never quite grasp. What puzzled her was not the nostalgia itself—that familiar heaviness in the chest that accompanies all human existence—but rather its peculiar timing. How could one feel nostalgia for someone sitting right there, living and breathing before them? Jean-Marc, with that subtle wisdom that occasionally visits lovers, understood that nostalgia is less about the past than about the terrifying possibility of future absence. It is memory projected forward, the anticipation of loss dressed in the clothes of remembrance. Then, like an uninvited guest at a funeral, came a thought of her dead child, followed by something even more unsettling: a sudden, inexplicable happiness. She felt ashamed of this happiness, as if she had committed an act of betrayal against grief itself. But who can dictate the proper sequence of emotions? We humans, who pride ourselves on our capacity for reason, who construct elaborate systems of moral judgment, who write constitutions and establish courts of law—we remain helpless before the anarchic democracy of our feelings. They come and go as they please, these emotions, paying no attention to the carefully arranged furniture of our convictions.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: The whiteness of the drapes and tablecloth invoked in her the uneasy feeling of one blank canvas. Perhaps, there was an absence she wanted to forget. Her former husband had taken her to such seaside restaurants. But it wasn’t the absence of captured life that stirred in her some unrest but the anticipation of life, of color becoming, the canvas waiting. Even in colorful pockets of her vision–out the deck window to the yellow lampposts and dark ocean–it all bathed in the moon’s white glow. Opaque, the blurred background of a photograph. Yes, a photo, something calling back something that had been. And what of her life now? Why did now pass her as every prior moment had, leaving a feeling, for feelings to be the dropped breadcrumbs of life in its constant evasion? She was struck by an intense nostalgia for Jean-Marc.But how can one feel nostalgia for something — or someone — who sits merely an arm's length away?“Perhaps it’s the grief,” Jean-Marc said. “Your mind is preparing you for loss. Is it not easier to wrap these memories in a protective cloak of nostalgia?”If it was all for impending loss, then her mind was well acquainted. But it wasn’t grief she felt when she thought of her son. She imagined him swinging around the pole of a lamppost. Like breadcrumbs, she happened upon joy in the world’s dark vast woods. Feelings were given, never made. Her child was dead. Her husband was gone. Jean-Marc would one day be gone. And yet.
written_by_MFA003.Reason: There are striking and unique qualities in both excerpts. Excerpt 1 is extremely ambitious in its philosophizing, but earns that ambition through moving, insightful moments like "nostalgia is...memory projected forward, the anticipation of loss dressed in the cloths of remembrance." However, Excerpt 2 offers a more subtly effective, and no less ambitious, approach to similar ideas, using imagistic language and more simple turns of phrase. Passages like "she happened upon joy in the world's dark vast woods. Feelings were given, never made" achieve a deep affect on the reader with both clarity and precision.

written_by_MFA006.Excerpt1: The restaurant, awash in the starkness of white – the deck, the table, the lampposts, and even the moon, an orb of paleness in the sky, seemed to mirror the landscape of her emotions.  She was there with Jean-Marc, yet a wave of nostalgia, so intense, so profound, washed over her.  It was a peculiar sensation, this yearning for the past, when the object of her longing was right there beside her.  Jean-Marc, with the uncanny ability to read the intricate map of her heart, understood.  Such nostalgia, he explained, often veiled a deeper fear – the fear of losing a loved one, of a future where they were no longer present. And then, her thoughts drifted to her child, the one she had lost, a wound that had never fully healed.  In that moment, a flicker of happiness, as unexpected as a summer storm, surprised her.  The happiness was fleeting, replaced by a wave of fear at having experienced such a sensation.  It was as if emotions, like wayward children, refused to be tamed, to be told what to feel, when to feel.  We may choose our actions, our words, but feelings, those elusive specters, held sway over the uncharted territories of the heart.  They were the uninvited guests who barged in, the rebels who defied reason, the free spirits who danced to their own tune.
written_by_MFA006.Excerpt2: Longer after leaving her husband, she understood that she should be happy, that this was a moment that called for equanimity: the white linen of the tablecloth under the full moon, lampposts pained white; the waiter with his porcelain platter of oysters on the half-shell, carefully set down before her. Such beautiful, pure things! Yet she was experiencing an odd nostalgia, a longing for this moment even as she sat in her chair within it. She thought the feeling meant: life will never get better than this. The future was her and Jean-Marc, together, but older, and recovered from the mania of fresh love, or perhaps not together at all. But how is it apprpropriate to feel nostalgia when he was right in front of her ? (Jean-Marc however had the answer: the more intensely we love someone in the present, the more we grieve their inevitable absence in some imagined future.) But she did not think that was what she meant at all! The mention of death made her think of the child. The child, forever a child, existing without complication in her death. The solidity of this shot her through with pure happiness. She felt afraid; she clasped her hands together in her lap and said nothing more. How easy it is to reign in our words and actions! But then there is always feeling, loping around like an untrained dog inside all of us, aware of how much we long to leash it.
written_by_MFA006.Reason: Excerpt two registers the subtle shifts in emotion more effectively; for instance, through transitional words like "But" in "But how is it appropriate to feel nostalgia when he was right in front of her?" Similarly, her disagreement with Jean-Marc is registered better: "But she did not think that was what she meant at all!" This heightened moment of conflict and disagreement is diluted in Excerpt one, which replaces "but" with "and," thus making the two halves of the excerpt feel less effectively linked. The language in excerpt two is more descriptive too: "the white linen of the tablecloth under the full moon, lampposts pained white" whereas excerpt one is more understated, to its own detriment: "The restaurant, awash in the starkness of white."

written_by_MFA018.Excerpt1: She sat across from Jean-Marc at the seaside restaurant, her fingers tracing invisible patterns on the white linen tablecloth, as if trying to anchor herself amidst the overwhelming brightness surrounding them. The deck stretched out, pale and gleaming, the lampposts shimmered like ghostly sentinels, and the moon hung low, casting an iridescent glow that seemed to swallow every color except white. The air was still, suffused with the faint, rhythmic whispers of the tide. Jean-Marc watched her, his expression serene yet attentive, as if he could read the kaleidoscope of emotions dancing behind her eyes. She felt a paradoxical pang of nostalgia—sharp and bittersweet—as though mourning something lost, though everything she cherished sat mere inches away. It puzzled her, this longing, this melancholy wrapped in an inexplicable happiness. Was it the memory of her deceased child, flitting unbidden into her mind like a shadow across the moonlight? Or was it the fear of losing Jean-Marc, his presence so vital it seemed like a delicate thread connecting her to the world? She smiled suddenly, a fleeting expression of joy so pure it frightened her. Jean-Marc reached for her hand, silently acknowledging the fragile beauty of her emotion. In that luminous moment, it struck her: we are masters of our actions, perhaps even of our words, but not of our feelings, those wild, untamed creatures that move within us, defying reason and will.
written_by_MFA018.Excerpt2: When she imagined this moment months ago, lying beside her husband, she had pictured herself happy. So why wasn't she? She had left him because she wanted to; to be with the man she loved. The man sitting across from her now, handsome in a white button-down shirt. It suddenly struck her that everything in the seaside restaurant was white: the deck, the table, the lampposts. Even the moon, stark and full, shone unbearably white tonight. Jean-Marc asked: "What is the matter with you, my dear? You are so quiet tonight." "Nothing really," she said, knowing it was a lie. Something was wrong, but she could not put that something into words. It was a strange yet acute longing for what was already hers, sitting right there in front of her. Jean-Marc, feeling the melancholy in the air, said: "Nostalgia comes from the fear of losing someone and imagining life without them." She thought of her child, the only person she had truly lost. The memory struck her with unexpected happiness, followed immediately by fear. What did it mean to feel sadness at dinner with her lover but happiness thinking of her dead child? Was there something wrong with her? Was she a bad mother, a bad person? Not according to Scottish philosopher David Hume. Hume had argued emotions were natural and involuntary. While we could control our actions, we could never control our feelings.

written_by_MFA018.Excerpt1: When she imagined this moment months ago, lying beside her husband, she had pictured herself happy. So why wasn't she? She had left him because she wanted to; to be with the man she loved. The man sitting across from her now, handsome in a white button-down shirt. It suddenly struck her that everything in the seaside restaurant was white: the deck, the table, the lampposts. Even the moon, stark and full, shone unbearably white tonight. Jean-Marc asked: "What is the matter with you, my dear? You are so quiet tonight." "Nothing really," she said, knowing it was a lie. Something was wrong, but she could not put that something into words. It was a strange yet acute longing for what was already hers, sitting right there in front of her. Jean-Marc, feeling the melancholy in the air, said: "Nostalgia comes from the fear of losing someone and imagining life without them." She thought of her child, the only person she had truly lost. The memory struck her with unexpected happiness, followed immediately by fear. What did it mean to feel sadness at dinner with her lover but happiness thinking of her dead child? Was there something wrong with her? Was she a bad mother, a bad person? Not according to Scottish philosopher David Hume. Hume had argued emotions were natural and involuntary. While we could control our actions, we could never control our feelings.
written_by_MFA018.Excerpt2: She sat across from Jean-Marc at the seaside restaurant, her fingers tracing invisible patterns on the white linen tablecloth, as if trying to anchor herself amidst the overwhelming brightness surrounding them. The deck stretched out, pale and gleaming, the lampposts shimmered like ghostly sentinels, and the moon hung low, casting an iridescent glow that seemed to swallow every color except white. The air was still, suffused with the faint, rhythmic whispers of the tide. Jean-Marc watched her, his expression serene yet attentive, as if he could read the kaleidoscope of emotions dancing behind her eyes. She felt a paradoxical pang of nostalgia—sharp and bittersweet—as though mourning something lost, though everything she cherished sat mere inches away. It puzzled her, this longing, this melancholy wrapped in an inexplicable happiness. Was it the memory of her deceased child, flitting unbidden into her mind like a shadow across the moonlight? Or was it the fear of losing Jean-Marc, his presence so vital it seemed like a delicate thread connecting her to the world? She smiled suddenly, a fleeting expression of joy so pure it frightened her. Jean-Marc reached for her hand, silently acknowledging the fragile beauty of her emotion. In that luminous moment, it struck her: we are masters of our actions, perhaps even of our words, but not of our feelings, those wild, untamed creatures that move within us, defying reason and will.

Simply put, Excerpt 1 is able to succinctly convey the rich emotion in this scenario in a way that Excerpt 2 is not.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: It's strange to think of my mother as that kind of woman—the kind who bore such immense pain that she gave birth to it, all alone at the onset of the longest winter on record. The biting cold was nothing but a faint chill compared to the icy fear whispering in her ears. Was she strong enough, capable enough, to do this? Even as she boiled water to sterilize the scissors she'd use for cutting the umbilical cord, she worried the answer was a resounding no. With shaking hands, she fashioned a gown from loose fabric she kept tucked away in her sewing box. As though the faux-hospital garb could imbue the experience with a semblance of professionalism. The kind that would ward off infant death. It didn't, of course.The baby lived for a precious few moments, wheezing as my mother prayed—mindless and desperate—to a deaf god that her child should live on. Then the infant slipped away without ever uttering a cry. A silent baby, spun out of ice and glass.My mother rocked the dead baby against her chest and felt the chill of the floor creep up into the soles of her feet, freezing her into a statue of grief. Mother and baby, alone; forever.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: The dawn light, a brutal white gash in the belly of the night, illuminated her blood-soaked hands, the scissors glinting ominously.  The air, thick with the metallic scent of life and death, echoed her ragged breaths, each one a desperate prayer.  She had become a primal vessel, fear and pain etching lines on her face, a grotesque map of motherhood.  The room, a battlefield of sweat and tears, cradled the echo of her final push, the newborn’s slippery form a dark miracle against the faded floorboards.  With trembling hands, she severed the cord, the last physical tie to a world that seemed to have abandoned her.Her voice, hoarse and raw, filled the silence, a chant for life, a plea to whatever gods might be listening.  But the newborn’s cry, a fleeting spark in the vast emptiness, was swallowed by the shadows.  The silence returned, heavier now, crushing her with its finality.  She clutched the lifeless body to her breast, her warmth a futile offering to the cold stillness that had settled over them.  The world outside continued its relentless march, oblivious to the silent tragedy unfolding within those walls.  The floor, cold and unforgiving, seeped into her bones, mirroring the icy grip of grief that threatened to consume her.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: While both excerpts could use a more subtle hand with less cliches --- "prayed to a deaf god", "the world continues its relentless march, oblivious" --- Excerpt 1 remains stronger due to its more varied sentence structure (with complex sentence and images in the opening and the short but effective ending), and a more personal tone --- "It's strange to think of my mother as that kind of woman". Excerpt 2, by comparison, leans too heavily on overly mixed and muddied metaphors and figurative language.

written_by_MFA010.Excerpt1: It was a winter morning thick with silence, the kind that stretches across frozen earth, hollow and unforgiving. My mother knelt on the cold wooden floor, her breath visible in the brittle air as she arranged the meager preparations she could muster. A pot of water on the stove, its steam curling upward like the last prayers of the desperate, her trembling hands struggling with scissors dulled by time. In the dim light, the pale fabric she had cut into a crude gown seemed to shiver, as though alive with the sorrow that filled the room. Pain ripped through her body like a jagged knife, forcing her onto her knees, but her face, pale and drawn, bore the stoic determination of someone who knew that the world would not offer her mercy. The moment of birth arrived, primal and raw, a soundless rupture of the fragile divide between life and death. She held the newborn close, her whispered pleas breaking against the unyielding silence. "Live," she murmured, a chant that carried the weight of her being. For one fragile heartbeat, the child stirred, its existence fleeting, a candle flickering in a relentless wind. Then it was gone, leaving behind only its weightless absence. My mother sat there, cradling the lifeless form, her own warmth seeping into the icy floor. The stillness settled over her like a shroud, and in that moment, the world outside ceased to exist.
written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: The early days of winter remind my mother of her dead child. My father knew that my mother was due at any moment, but the roads were icy and the entire landscape had turned bare and hostile, preventing him from returning home.My mother was in labor, all by herself at home, and the ripples of her screams were absorbed by the walls, making cracks that had not existed before. In the kitchen, she tried as best as she could. She kept some water to boil in a small pot to sterilize a pair of kitchen scissors. She took off her clothes and quickly fashioned a hospital gown from some fabric that was guarded in a sewing box.Gripped by fear and pain so intense that she felt larger and more forceful than the dazzle of winter outside, my mother held a baby—slippery and blood-covered—in her arms. She had pushed and pushed, and had severed the umbilical cord with the hot pair of scissors that had burned her fingers. She chanted an old prayer, a common plea for life, but felt the warmth of the baby's body fading.My mother tells me that is when she stopped screaming. In a fleeting moment, the alchemy of the house shifted: life became death. The coldness of the floor seeped through her own body. It became impossible to tell whether the air was so still because of the cold, or her grief, or both.
written_by_MFA010.Reason: Excerpt 1 is unceasing in its overwrought imagery and hackneyed (For example: "like the last prayers of the desperate"; "as though alive with sorrow"; "like a jagged knife";). While its organization is slightly stronger than in Excerpt 2, the sparer prose in Excerpt 2 allows the pain of the moment being depicted to stand on its own. Lines like "She chanted an old prayer, a common plea for life, but felt the warmth of the baby's body fading. My mother tells me that is when she stopped screaming." contain far more power in them than the language of the Excerpt 1.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: That winter night, my mother told me, was like a blade of ice pressed against her spine. The scissors lay sterilized in boiling water, steam rising like ghostly breath in the dim room, while her trembling hands folded and refolded the small white gown she'd fashioned from scraps in her sewing box. When the pain came, it was not like anything living – it was ancient, prehistoric, like continents being torn apart. She bit down on a rolled cloth, her screams collapsing inward, becoming part of her flesh, part of the darkness. The umbilical cord, when she finally cut it, was purple-blue like twilight, like the last moment before complete darkness. She held the tiny body, so light it could have been made of paper, chanting words that weren't words but rather the sound of her soul trying to transfer its own life force. For one heartbeat, maybe two, the baby's chest rose – a movement so slight it could have been the shadow of hope itself. Then stillness. The floor's cold crept up through her body like rising water, until she too became still, became ice, became the very essence of winter itself. Her warmth retreated inward, as though trying to follow her child into that place beyond reaching.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: My mother once told me a story about her struggle to give birth more than forty years ago, alone in her parents’ house in Apgujeong. It was early winter. The trees were bare and the ground hard. With shaky steps, she described pacing about the kitchen while she boiled water in order to sterilize the scissors that she knew she’d need to cut the cord. With the fabric in her sewing box, she fashioned a small gown and began to wear it. During the waves of pain from her contractions, she would grip at the kitchen counter hard. Eventually after hours of this the baby came out wet and covered in a fuzzy-looking substance. Still alone, she held the newborn. Chanting a desperate plea for the little thing’s survival over and over again. But after a fleeting moment of brilliant life, her newborn child went still and died. My mother lay on the floor of the kitchen. Silently, clutching at the lifeless body of what was once vibrant inside of her. As she continued to lay there with the dead child, frozen in grief, the warmth from her body departed into the frigid floor. As though the temperature of the house were somehow reflective of her inner state.
written_by_MFA011.Reason: The first excerpt is overwritten; the winter night like "a blade of ice pressed against her spine" is a description that doesn't make any sense (what is a blade of ice? why such a specific sensation, unrelated to the event of giving birth?). The second excerpt is much more efficient and lively; we're specifically set in Apgujeong, forty years ago, and know immediately we're hearing about a birth. The first excerpt, on the other hand, has the tendency to repeat cliche descriptions: "purple-blue," "like twilight," "the last moment before complete darkness" are all used, one after another, to describe the color of the umbilical cord, a description which is rather insignificant to the scene.

The scissors lay sterilized in boiling water, steam rising like ghostly breath in the dim room, while her trembling hands folded and refolded the small white gown she'd fashioned from scraps in her sewing box. When the pain came, it was not like anything living – it was ancient, prehistoric, like continents being torn apart. She bit down on a rolled cloth, her screams collapsing inward, becoming part of her flesh, part of the darkness. The umbilical cord, when she finally cut it, was purple-blue like twilight, like the last moment before complete darkness. She held the tiny body, so light it could have been made of paper, chanting words that weren't words but rather the sound of her soul trying to transfer its own life force. written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: One morning in a town quite near Chennai, the sun arose with a ferocity and began beating down on the town's residents, and there was no time to blink back dawn, the children were already awake and fussing for food, and Miss Aadhya had started on the first pot of coffee, and from her window she could hear Bollywood music, already blaring, and below her the old man whose name no one knew was praying, and above her, on the fourth floor of the Aquamarine building, Senior struggled against that veil that separates dream from reality, and broke through, and was awake. At the same time, his neighbor, Junior, awoke. The two men's eyes opened at the same time. Kabir was now calling to his friends, everyone making plans for an evening at the Elliot’s beach, the promise of cool water the only thing making it bearable to get through the hot afternoon. All the members of the town were connected to each other, as a marionette has strings attached to each of its joints, each small movement producing an equal and opposite reaction. Senior swung his legs out of bed and Junior finished brushing his teeth. The clamor of the town stirred something in both of them, and, with one elegant pull, they both lifted their heads and decided to go out, onto their own veranda.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: The sun, a molten fist, clenched the city in its fiery grip, the heat so ferocious it could melt the wings of sparrows foolish enough to take flight.  The air, thick with the chanting of prayers from nearby temples and the tinny melodies of Hindi film songs, crackled with the cries of children playing cricket in dusty alleyways.  The aroma of freshly brewed coffee, dark and bitter, snaked through the streets, mingling with the pungent scent of spices from open-air markets.On the fourth floor of a sea-green building, two elderly men, Senior and Junior, stirred in their beds, their bodies attuned to the city's relentless rhythm.  As if bound by an invisible thread, they woke up at precisely the same moment, their eyes fluttering open in unison.  They stepped out onto their respective verandas, their movements slow and deliberate, a stark contrast to the frenetic energy of the streets below. Downstairs, the younger generation buzzed with anticipation, their voices a chorus of excitement as they planned their evening escapades at Elliot's Beach.  But the old men remained unfazed, their world a sanctuary of quietude amidst the chaos.  Senior gazed at the distant sea, its shimmering surface mirroring the turmoil within his own soul.  Junior, his eyes fixed on the horizon, seemed lost in a reverie, the past and present blurring in his mind's eye
written_by_MFA001.Reason: Both excerpts are successful in evoking the feeling of a vibrant, interconnected cityscape, but the first uses an unconventional extended opening sentence that immerses the reader in the breakneck pace of Chennai through the momentum of dependent clauses. Each image is syntactically reliant on the one before, which creates the "marionette" sensation and feeling of close relationships later described. The second excerpt, while visually rich, is more conventional in its approach.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Under the heavy weight of the late afternoon sun, the city was bursting with heat, the sound of chanting prayers—Surya Mangalam, said for hope of peaceful evenings—sitar and tabla-heavy soundtracks, and children's cries rising like heat shimmers, with sweetened filter coffee laden in the air, one final push to get through to the fast-approaching dusk. But on the fourth floor of the sea-green building overlooking the blisteringly blue Indian Ocean, two elderly men, Senior and Junior, only just began their day, even as the younger generation gathered in clumps like swarms of ants, singing along to hit Tamil songs and preparing to dance and drink on Elliot's Beach once the sun set. Moving to an instinctual, silent rhythm, Senior and Junior rose as one, like two men bound by strings of fate, their walk to their verandahs as sure as the sun's journey across the sky until they sank into their chairs with the same achy movements, tilting their heads back once comfortable, two mirrors reflecting back at each other. Nothing in the world could halt this routine, their path so worn they seemed guided by more than gravity. Beneath them, a jubilant cheer rose up to greet the old men, and twin smiles stretched slowly across their faces, for they were soothed by their repetition and the companionship that repetition brings.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: In that sea-green building which stood like a tired sentinel near Elliot's Beach (where young lovers would soon gather with their smartphones and their dreams, as predictable as the tide), there lived two old men whose synchronicity of existence would have alarmed them had they ever bothered to notice it—but they never did, for such is the peculiar blindness that affects those who are bound together by the invisible threads of fate. The fourth floor (ah, but was it really the fourth? for in this particular building the ground floor was called the first, in the American way, causing endless confusion among visitors and delivery men alike) housed Senior and Junior, names that contained their own little joke, since Junior was himself no spring chicken, and Senior was so ancient that some believed he had witnessed the departure of the British Raj with his own rheumy eyes. Every morning, as predictable as the muezzin's call to prayer that floated across the neighborhood like a ghost's lament, mixing with the timpani of temple bells and the cheerful vulgarity of Tamil film songs blaring from auto-rickshaws, the two men would emerge onto their respective verandas at precisely the same moment, like mechanical figures in some elaborate timepiece. The morning air arrived thick with stories: the dark, intense aroma of filter coffee from the houses below, where young IT professionals fueled themselves for their days in air-conditioned offices; the shouts of children in pressed uniforms hurrying to school, their watches synchronized to their mothers' anxieties; the eternal complaint of crows who had seen it all before and were distinctly unimpressed. The heat rose from the streets like a malevolent spirit, distorting the reality of things, so that the two old men, standing on their respective verandas with their respective cups of tea, might have been mirror images of each other, or perhaps the same man caught in two different moments of time, or even (though they would have scoffed at such fancy) two aspects of the same soul, divided at birth and now slowly, incrementally, moving toward an inevitable reunion, like two drops of water on a window pane, drawn together by forces beyond their comprehension or control.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: Both Excerpts are strong but Excerpt 1 feels more economical, less digressional. This is a matter of taste; compression of language is not always the preference. Perhaps Excerpt 2 relies a bit too heavily on lyricism and metaphor. For example, the first sentence of Excerpt 2 uses the tides, sentinels, and the threads of fate to evoke points, but the result is a bit overly flowery.

written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: The heat arrived early in the day, a simmering, golden haze that crept into the corners of every room, painting the air with a sheen of lethargy. From the fourth floor of a sea-green building, the two men emerged onto their verandas, their movements mirrored as if rehearsed by the stars themselves—Senior and Junior, bound together by the invisible threads of time’s loom. Below, Elliot’s Beach stirred awake, alive with the sounds of its chaotic symphony: temple bells clanged in stubborn competition with film music pouring from distant speakers, a mosaic of devotion and desire. Children’s cries darted through the cacophony like startled birds, while the heady aroma of freshly brewed filter coffee mingled with the briny tang of the sea breeze, a sensory banquet that danced on the edge of overwhelming. Senior adjusted his spectacles, the glint of sunlight catching the lens like a mischievous wink from the heavens, while Junior tapped his fingers on the wrought iron railing, a rhythm only he could hear. Around them, the city moved in fits and bursts: vegetable vendors hollered over their carts, stray dogs wove through scooters with uncanny grace, and the youth, untroubled by time, readied themselves for the evening’s promenade. The two men, unhurried and deliberate, bore witness to it all—custodians of a pace the world had long since abandoned.
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: And so the day passed. In the center of the city, the maghrib rang out its ancient melody, warring with the Tamil music lilting out of the speakers of a passing rickshaw—the ocean swell of strings, the buoyant theme of an old Hollywood film. The aroma of filter coffee boiled up from the terraces of the cafes, which were filled with tourists from Tuscany, Madrid, Tyrol. In other neighborhoods, children rendezvoused with their peers in shady alleyways, holding tense diplomatic summits over their games of tag. The heat lingered over the city like a sinister spirit cavalry, a battalion of jinns casting spells over Elliot’s Beach; over the twin harbors and colonial promenade; over the government center and the inland districts; and back out again to one sea-green apartment building, on the fourth floor of which there were two empty verandahs. In the corresponding room, two men simultaneously awakened from their afternoon naps and stepped out onto these verandahs, which it should be said were no longer empty. Senior and Junior, as the men were called by their respective acquaintances, did not look at each other; nor did they watch the youth wander lazily from the streets to the promenade, passing marijuana cigarettes down the line like the world’s slowest relay team. Senior and Junior looked out at Elliot’s Beach, this strange sandy coin that had been cast away by fate.
written_by_MFA012.Reason: Excerpt 1 consistently uses hackneyed imagery ("bound together by the invisible threads of time's loom"; "a sensory banquet"; "a mosaic of devotion and desire"l). It also struggles to maintain specificity, perhaps in part because of this imagery. The place being described is without context and could be anywhere in the world. Comparatively, excerpt 2 is specific. The prayers called out are Muslim. The tourists come from places that are familiar. The relationship between Senior and Junior is presented clearly and with temporal and spatial resonance. When imagery does appear, it feels original ("passing marijuana cigarettes down the line like the world's slowest relay team").

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: My father, a stranger in his own house, sits hunched in his armchair, a shadow of the man I knew.  His eyes, once bright and full of life, are now clouded with confusion.  He struggles to remember what he's working on, a question met with a sigh and a shake of his head.  My mother, her face etched with worry, reminds him gently, "Your writing, dear, on the Bible and anti-Semitism."  A flicker of recognition crosses his face, a brief spark in the fading embers of his mind.He looks at me, a ghost of a smile touching his lips.  "My daughter," he says, his voice a fragile whisper, "so proud of you."  But the light fades quickly, replaced by a vacant stare.  "Nothing to say," he murmurs, lost in the labyrinth of his own thoughts.  The silence that follows is heavy, filled with unspoken words and a growing sense of loss.Later, my mother shows me a photograph from forty years ago.  My father, young and vibrant, stands with his arm around her, both of them radiating joy.  My mother's voice cracks as she speaks, her words laced with a quiet despair.  "It's like he's already gone," she says, her eyes filled with tears.  I look at the photograph again, the image of my father frozen in time, a stark contrast to the frail figure sitting in the other room.  The weight of his absence, even in his presence, settles over me, a heavy cloak of sorrow that I cannot shake off.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: I had gone there and didn’t know what to do after I’d gone there. At my father’s house, I entered his study where he sat at his desk staring at his hands. Next to his hands, his work––book stacks on biblical theology and anti-Semitism. I stood behind him. I stared at his hands. This was a turning point of sorts of ours, his hands, our staring at them. So many hours of ours went to this, had come to this. I thought: when did we get here? And: what do I do now, now that we’ve gone here? My mother came in and laid her own hand on his shoulder. She said, “Gerry” which was my father’s name, “Gerry, remember, you were working on your essay on biblical theology and anti-Semitism.” She made a sweeping motion with her hands before him. When he finally saw me, he said, “My daughter…” and told me how proud he was of me and all that I’d been doing. Then he said he had nothing else to say to me. He went back to his hands. Later that evening, my mother and I sat in the dining room together, where she showed me an old photograph of my father. “What happened to him?” my mother said, and I couldn’t tell her. I couldn’t even come close to saying.
written_by_MFA015.Reason: The first excerpt flows well, but its approach is mostly conventional to the material, with standard images like "frozen in time", "a fragile whisper", and "labyrinth in his own thoughts." The second excerpt, has more varied sentence structures, such as with "I thought: when did we get here? And: what do I do now, now that we've gone here?" There are more unique, insightful moments such as "He went back to his hands". Lastly, "I couldn't even come close to saying" is a more moving end to the excerpt that conveys the tragedy of the narrative moment.
