written_by_MFA027.Excerpt1: I visit my father and immediately notice new changes. The way he holds his coffee cup with both hands now, like a child. The way his eyes move around the room without settling. When I ask about his work, he stares at the wall behind me. My mother quickly fills the silence: "Tell her about your writing on the Bible, dear. The anti-Semitism research." He nods, but I can see he's already forgotten the prompt. "I'm proud of you," he says to me suddenly, then adds, "though I have nothing to say." I wonder if this is what therapy feels like - this careful observation of painful things while maintaining a scholarly distance. Later, my mother pulls me aside to show me a photograph. "Look," she says, "this was forty years ago." In it, my father stands straight-backed beside a podium, papers spread before him like fallen leaves. I notice how his collar sits perfectly against his neck, how his hands rest purposefully on the wooden edge. My mother's fingers tremble slightly as she returns the photo to its drawer. I think: This is how we measure time now - not in years or months, but in the growing distance between who he was and who he is becoming.
written_by_MFA027.Excerpt2: I barely recognized my father when I entered the kitchen, which was probably because he completely failed to recognize me. All my life I had felt only he knew my name. I was a stranger to everyone else, even to my mother, whose voice had repulsed me ever since I was a girl. I probably should not have said this, but I was relieved when I realized I was not the only fact of his life he forgot. "What was I when I was?" he asked my mother in the kitchen. She ran to the bookcase. "You wrote this all yourself," she told him, extra nasally. "It was a Bible on the Bible. A seminal take-down of anti-Semitism." I could tell he was not listening. Then suddenly he turned to me. Suddenly I was me again. When he said my name I returned to my skin. "What are you?" he asked me, and when I told him, his eyes filled with something I recognized. "If I had any words left I'd spend them on voicing just how proud I..." he stuttered before a long pause. "I have nothing to say," he whispered. Night fell again. When he went to sleep in the kitchen I was not sure he would wake up, but my mother decided tonight was a fine time to dig up their 40-year-old wedding pictures. "He is a gorgeous man," she said, then yawned the word "was."
written_by_MFA027.Reason: Excerpt 1 is the stronger of the two because the interactions between the characters feel more realistic. The flow of the dialogue feels natural, whereas Excerpt 2's dialogue is sometimes a bit stilted. The imagery in Excerpt 1 is more vivid and descriptive as well, with lines like "papers spread before him like fallen leaves." There is also more context given in Excerpt 1 about the father's weakening condition and the physicality of his behavior. Ultimately, Excerpt 1 has more genuine characterization and a clearer illustration of the scene.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: I went to see my father and found him in a much worse state than I had left him. He was disoriented and dazed, mumbling to himself about taxes and missionaries knocking on the door. He couldn't remember much about what he was working on. My mother gently reminded him that he was writing about the Bible and anti-Semitism. "Oh yes," he said, "that's right," and nodded as if to confirm this to himself. While the three of us ate supper, he turned to me and told me that he was quite proud of me. "You are a good kid," he said. "Always have been." "Is that so?" I asked. He nodded again. "I just have nothing to say to you," he said, and I told him I understood. After my mother and I washed the dishes together, she showed me a photograph from forty years ago. In it, my father had a full head of dark curls. His eyes were alert and his smile untroubled. I was perched in his lap like a small pet, staring up at him as if I had just noticed he was there. All five of my fingers could fit around his thumb. Everything that would follow in the years to come might never happen. "This was such a nice day," said my mother, stroking the photograph. "You probably don't remember, do you?" I had forgotten what her smile looked like, so I told her I remembered it perfectly.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: He sat in the chair by the window, where he always sat, though I wasn’t sure if he recognized the chair. He had been writing about the Bible, about anti-Semitism, about something urgent, something that had mattered. My mother told him this. “Your work,” she said. “You’ve been writing about the Bible.” He nodded, as if this was something he could accept, though not something he quite believed. He looked at me and said he was proud of me, but then added, almost apologetically, that he had nothing to say to me. I nodded back. We sat, the three of us, not saying anything. He looked out the window, or at the window. My mother left the room and came back holding a photograph. “This was him,” she said. “Forty years ago.” I looked at it. She held it up next to his face, as if she could prove something that way. He did not look at the picture. He closed his eyes. My mother sighed. Later, she would tuck the photo back into the album, where it belonged. He would remain in his chair, where he belonged. I would leave, where I belonged. It was not that we did not love each other, only that love had become a kind of stillness, a sitting together, a waiting for words that had already been forgotten.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: Excerpt 1 delivers the scene of the father's dissolving health more effectively than excerpt 2, with more coherent prose that flows better. Where Excerpt 2 describes, in an adequate way, that th efather "had been writing about the Bible, about anti-Semitism," Excerpt 1 folds that information into domestic drama: "My mother gently reminded him that he was writing about the Bible and anti-Semitism. "Oh yes," he said, "that's right," and nodded as if to confirm this to himself." Notice how that same information packs a far heftier dramatic punch when delivered from the mother than when stated outright.

written_by_MFA010.Excerpt1: That Christmas morning, my father handed me an envelope, thick with cash, along with a brochure for Disney World, its glossy pages showcasing artificial castles and choreographed joy. "We leave next week," he said, his voice carrying that familiar mixture of authority and hesitation that had marked our relationship since my mother's death. I watched Chitra in the kitchen, methodically preparing tea, her movements precise and deliberate, like someone navigating through a space that wasn't quite her own. Through the window, I could see Rupa and Piu in the backyard, their matching winter coats making them look like mirror images as they built a lopsided snowman. I manufactured an excuse about a winter session course, watching their small shoulders slump when my father relayed the news. The girls had wanted to share their Disney princess fantasies with their older sister, not understanding that I was a relic of a different fairy tale, one that had ended with my mother's last breath in a stark hospital room. Later, as I folded the crisp bills and tucked them into my wallet, I caught Chitra's fleeting glance – a look of relief poorly disguised as sympathy. My father busied himself with travel arrangements, his enthusiasm slightly too pronounced, betraying the comfort he found in my absence. I recognized then that we were all performing our roles: they as the new family looking forward, me as the keeper of memories, standing still in a house that held too many ghosts.
written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: I was home during winter. On Christmas morning, my father entered my room with a thin, white envelope in hand. Inside, there were ten twenty-dollar notes, totalling a sum of two hundred dollars, the most generous amount I had ever received from my father. I thanked him profusely, but it seemed like a prologue to the real question my father wanted to ask me. He invited me to Disney World, where he was planning to take Chitra, his new wife, and my two half-sisters, Rupa and Piu, during spring break. But I felt distant from his new family, like a string being pulled from both ends. I fabricated some excuse about having to be on-campus during that time since I was a Resident Assistant, and declined his invitation. Later that week, as we sat on the floor circled around the Christmas tree in our living room, Rupa and Piu expressed their disappointment. They could not understand why I would not want to join them in Disney World. "It's Disney World," they exclaimed. But I kept thinking of my late mother, and everything I owed her. I felt a responsibility to hold back, to stay with her memory, as if her place in our family was still untouched and unoccupied, in the same way that Rupa and Piu symbolized and remained committed to their father’s legacy. written_by_MFA010.Excerpt1: I was home during winter. On Christmas morning, my father entered my room with a thin, white envelope in hand. written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: That Christmas morning, my father handed me an envelope, thick with cash, along with a brochure for Disney World, its glossy pages showcasing artificial castles and choreographed joy. "We leave next week," he said, his voice carrying that familiar mixture of authority and hesitation that had marked our relationship since my mother's death. I watched Chitra in the kitchen, methodically preparing tea, her movements precise and deliberate, like someone navigating through a space that wasn't quite her own. Through the window, I could see Rupa and Piu in the backyard, their matching winter coats making them look like mirror images as they built a lopsided snowman. I manufactured an excuse about a winter session course, watching their small shoulders slump when my father relayed the news. The girls had wanted to share their Disney princess fantasies with their older sister, not understanding that I was a relic of a different fairy tale, one that had ended with my mother's last breath in a stark hospital room. Later, as I folded the crisp bills and tucked them into my wallet, I caught Chitra's fleeting glance – a look of relief poorly disguised as sympathy. My father busied himself with travel arrangements, his enthusiasm slightly too pronounced, betraying the comfort he found in my absence. written_by_MFA032.Excerpt1: The crisp bill tucked into my palm felt unfamiliar, the weight of its promise as foreign as the characters etched onto its surface.  My father, in his crisp suit and polished shoes, stood before me, the scent of his new life – a blend of unfamiliar spices and expensive cologne – clinging to him like a second skin.  His words echoed in the sterile expanse of the hotel room, an invitation to a world I no longer recognized.  "Disney World," he'd said, the syllables rolling off his tongue with a practiced ease that made my stomach clench.  "Just you, me, Chitra, and the girls."My mouth formed the words of refusal, a practiced excuse about school and looming deadlines, but the lie tasted like ash.  In their eyes, the disappointment was a tangible thing, sharp and cutting.  Rupa's lower lip trembled, a mirror of the tremor in my own heart.  Piu, ever the stoic, simply stared, her dark eyes pools of confusion.  They were a part of him, just as I was a part of her, the ghost that lingered in the corners of our lives.Later, as I stood on the balcony, the city lights blurring into a sea of neon, I felt a strange sense of relief emanating from them.  They wanted to move on, to build something new, untainted by the past.  And I, the keeper of memories, the guardian of a love lost, was a burden they no longer wished to carry.  The distance between us was a physical manifestation of the years that had passed, the laughter and tears that had reshaped our lives.  It was a gulf that could not be bridged, a chasm carved by grief and the relentless march of time.
written_by_MFA032.Excerpt2: Neither were presents he could have wrapped, he said, in a tone at once defensive and apologetic. “You didn’t have to get me anything,” I said. But he continued explaining, and all the while his eyes remained trained on his girls, who were prostrate under the tree. First, he conjured a creased envelope from his shirt pocket, inside which were two crisp hundred-dollar bills, but no note, no card. The invitation to Disney World came next, in that same laconic way. Unlike the cash, it was entirely intangible. Not a ticket on a red-eye to Orlando, not a room at the same overpriced hotel or a paid-for day pass—-it was simply these words: “And of course, you can join us at Disney World, if you would like.” From the kitchen, Chitra added her ringing voice to his: “Only if you want! There’s no pressure.” Meanwhile, Rupa bounded toward me and Piu followed, talking over each other as they hammered out the details.I was still holding the envelope when it struck me that the tree in their living room was new-—a real Douglas Fir, not the artificial tree, which had infused the winters of my own youth, which my mother decorated with the ornaments I made at preschool. “I would love to,” I said, looking at my father, whose eyes remained elsewhere, “but classes are starting up so soon, and with the teaching load this semester… I should work.” The girls crumpled immediately. “But, but, but why?” My father simply nodded his head gravely, as if we had come to a painful, but just, compromise. “I understand,” he said, “I understand.”
written_by_MFA032.Reason: Excerpt 2 is far superior to Excerpt 1. Excerpt 1 is immensely overwritten, with overwrought descriptions such as "the weight of its promise as foreign as the characters etched onto its surface," while the descriptions in Excerpt 2 are natural and precise: "I was still holding the envelope when it struck me that the tree in their living room was new." Excerpt 1 over-explains the subtext: "I, the keeper of memories, the guardian of a lost love, was a burden they no longer wished to carry." Meanwhile, excerpt 2 allows the emotional weight to exist in small, subtextual details: "no note, no card."

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: I held the cash, folded in my hand, and my father asked the question again. Would I like to use the gift to join them for a trip to Disney World? I looked around the room, at the expectant faces of Piu and Rupa, and Chitra’s reserved smile. My mother had always sat in the velvet chair Chitra now inhabited and my mother had even donned a similar posture to hers, pert and classic. I tried to mimic Chitra’s smile. Maybe, I said, of course I’d love to, but exams will be especially wicked this year. I don’t expect to have enough time to get away for a vacation. Piu and Rupa knitted their brows, faces falling for a spell, sensing rejection—hadn’t we been getting close? Chitra’s composed smile remained as if painted on her face. I looked back to my father, hoping to convey my gratitude. A piece of me did want to go. I hadn’t been able to say much to him since the new woman became his world, two half-daughters making him young again. The American family getaway might have been an olive branch to me. Certainly Chitra would not have chosen it. I was surprised to see no resignation in his face, no disappointment, but relief instead.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: At breakfast, my father handed me an envelope thick with cash, a gesture both startling and unsettling. "For Christmas," he said with forced cheer, his eyes flicking toward Chitra, who was sipping her tea, avoiding my gaze. He added, almost apologetically, “And Disney World, with us. The girls are excited.” Rupa and Piu, dressed in matching holiday sweaters, looked at me expectantly, their bright faces blurring into one as I fumbled for words. “I can’t,” I said, the excuse tumbling out. “There’s a project—due after break.” The lie felt hollow, but I let it stand. Chitra placed a dish of fruit on the table, her movements brisk, her expression neutral, as if my refusal required no comment. My father leaned back, resigned, a faint relief softening the tension in his jaw. I sensed how the trip would be easier without me—how my presence reminded them of another family, one they had worked hard to unwrite. Later, when I passed the girls in the hallway, they whispered in hurried tones, their laughter abruptly silenced when I appeared. I thought of my mother, the spaces she had filled now occupied by others, and felt caught between loyalties, between memory and their momentum forward. Outside, the winter sun broke through, exposing everything.
written_by_MFA016.Reason: Excerpt 1 allows significantly more implication and trusts its reader to understand what is occurring without overtly spelling it out ("Maybe, I said, of course I'd love to, but exams will be especially wicked this year. I don’t expect to have enough time to get away for a vacation" as opposed to "'I can’t,' I said, the excuse tumbling out. 'There’s a project—due after break.' Excerpt 2 also uses descriptions which veer into the surreal in their use of imagery ("Rupa and Piu, dressed in matching holiday sweaters, looked at me expectantly, their bright faces blurring into one as I fumbled for words") where excerpt 1 maintains clarity. This clarity gives the ending betrayal on the part of the narrator's father significantly more weight than the imagery at the end of excerpt 2.

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: "There is a speck of ash at the bottom of this cup of tea." He was not sure why he was telling this to the waiter, because he couldn't tell if it was real ash or maybe just little crumbs from the tea itself."Oh dear, I'm sorry sir. I'll get that swapped out for you right away.""He didn't even think to argue. Part of me wants him to tell me to go back to whatever 'istan' I'm from. That's what they used to tell me when I first arrived. Before my voice began to sound like theirs, before I knew what a three-piece coat was, before I knew how to take the trolley.And now, he insists on talking to me as if I'm just one of them. 'Sir,' he calls me, 'sir.' Like part of me has rotted to be like the forever rotten core of them and they smell it too. But isn't that what I always wanted? Isn't that why I came to this country? To join the ranks of those torn, of those divided? I swear these warring sides of myself must have migrated to my reproductive organs, for just look at my children," said Samad bitterly."I think of the children. Varush, he just sticks out that stiff upper lip all day and god, that accent—sometimes I just want to unhook his jaw and stuff it full of chai, and tell him to go back where we came from. But then Malik, the other boy, always complaining that everything is offensive and everyone is oppressing us. These children, I swear, sometimes I just want to walk away from them.""Oh, that's not true, surely," Irie says."Please do not underestimate the ability of a father to forsake his children! If I was a man before I made the devil's pact and came here, I am something less now.". The waiter is taking long. Samad drinks the tea and the ash all in one gulp. "I want to feel all of its worlds inside me. But really, they just vanish, like they never existed at all", he says.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: Samad sat there, his fingers drumming against the pub table, each tap a tiny rebellion against the polished oak surface that had witnessed centuries of English contemplation. "You see," he began, his voice carrying that particular tone of a man who has rehearsed his grievances in the mirror, "this country, this England, it's like one of those fancy department stores where they let you browse but never expect you to buy anything." He paused, taking a theatrical sip of his whiskey—a drink he'd adopted precisely because it made him feel like a fraud. "My son—the one who wears those ridiculous pinstripe suits—he thinks he's fooled them all. Barrister this, Westminster that. But they see through it, oh yes, they do. And the other one?" He laughed, but it was the kind of laugh that carries more warning than humor. "He's gone and done exactly what they feared we all would. Turned himself into their worst nightmare, hasn't he? A proper fundamentalist. Both of them are just different sides of the same bloody English pound." Irie, who had been watching this performance with the patient attention of someone who had seen it many times before, interjected softly, "Oh, that's not true, surely." But Samad was already racing ahead, carried by the momentum of his discontent. "When I came here, I thought—just a few years, make some money, go home a success. Instead?" He spread his arms wide, encompassing the pub, the street outside, the whole of London, "Instead, I've become this strange creature who belongs nowhere. Not here, where they 'tolerate' us—" he spat the word like a pip from a bitter fruit—"and not there, where I'm now too English to fit in. Tell me, what is a birthplace anyway? A cosmic accident? A life sentence? Or just another pretty lie we tell ourselves while we're busy being lost?" He turned back to his whiskey, his reflection in the mirror behind the bar showing a man caught between what he was and what he had become, between where he was from and where he had landed—a man trapped in the hyphen of British-Bengali identity.

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: Samad sat there, his fingers drumming against the pub table, each tap a tiny rebellion against the polished oak surface that had witnessed centuries of English contemplation. "You see," he began, his voice carrying that particular tone of a man who has rehearsed his grievances in the mirror, "this country, this England, it's like one of those fancy department stores where they let you browse but never expect you to buy anything." He paused, taking a theatrical sip of his whiskey—a drink he'd adopted precisely because it made him feel like a fraud. "My son—the one who wears those ridiculous pinstripe suits—he thinks he's fooled them all. Barrister this, Westminster that. But they see through it, oh yes, they do. And the other one?" He laughed, but it was the kind of laugh that carries more warning than humor. "He's gone and done exactly what they feared we all would. Turned himself into their worst nightmare, hasn't he? A proper fundamentalist. Both of them are just different sides of the same bloody English pound." Irie, who had been watching this performance with the patient attention of someone who had seen it many times before, interjected softly, "Oh, that's not true, surely." But Samad was already racing ahead, carried by the momentum of his discontent. "When I came here, I thought—just a few years, make some money, go home a success. Instead?" He spread his arms wide, encompassing the pub, the street outside, the whole of London, "Instead, I've become this strange creature who belongs nowhere. Not here, where they 'tolerate' us—" he spat the word like a pip from a bitter fruit—"and not there, where I'm now too English to fit in. Tell me, what is a birthplace anyway? A cosmic accident? A life sentence? Or just another pretty lie we tell ourselves while we're busy being lost?" He turned back to his whiskey, his reflection in the mirror behind the bar showing a man caught between what he was and what he had become, between where he was from and where he had landed—a man trapped in the hyphen of British-Bengali identity.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: "There is a speck of ash at the bottom of this cup of tea." He was not sure why he was telling this to the waiter, because he couldn't tell if it was real ash or maybe just little crumbs from the tea itself."Oh dear, I'm sorry sir. I'll get that swapped out for you right away.""He didn't even think to argue. Part of me wants him to tell me to go back to whatever 'istan' I'm from. That's what they used to tell me when I first arrived. Before my voice began to sound like theirs, before I knew what a three-piece coat was, before I knew how to take the trolley.And now, he insists on talking to me as if I'm just one of them. 'Sir,' he calls me, 'sir.' Like part of me has rotted to be like the forever rotten core of them and they smell it too. But isn't that what I always wanted? Isn't that why I came to this country? To join the ranks of those torn, of those divided? I swear these warring sides of myself must have migrated to my reproductive organs, for just look at my children," said Samad bitterly."I think of the children. Varush, he just sticks out that stiff upper lip all day and god, that accent—sometimes I just want to unhook his jaw and stuff it full of chai, and tell him to go back where we came from. But then Malik, the other boy, always complaining that everything is offensive and everyone is oppressing us. These children, I swear, sometimes I just want to walk away from them.""Oh, that's not true, surely," Irie says."Please do not underestimate the ability of a father to forsake his children! If I was a man before I made the devil's pact and came here, I am something less now.". The waiter is taking long. Samad drinks the tea and the ash all in one gulp. "I want to feel all of its worlds inside me. But really, they just vanish, like they never existed at all", he says.
written_by_MFA030.Reason: Excerpt1 is of better writing quality than Excerpt2. The voice feels much more specific and alive (“both of them are just different sides of the same bloody English pound”) vs the more passive and dull voice of Excerpt2 (“Varush, he just sticks out that stiff upper lip all day”). I feel the characters anger in his specificity in Excerpt1, while the descriptor “stuff him full of chai” in Excerpt2 feels almost parodic. I’m also unsure where I am in time and space much more in Excerpt2, whereas in Excerpt1 we are grounded in the specific scene setting of the pub table and the whiskey that he drinks “precisely because it made him feel like a fraud.”

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: "It's all a joke, a cosmic joke and God is laughing somewhere, but me? I ask to raise two good Muslim sons in this country and walk away feeling as though I've made a devil's pact," Samad cried. "One son has fully converted, a pukka Englishman. He tells his mother he wants to wear those ridiculous wigs and practice law. My other son, a fundamental terrorist! I just don't understand it, you raise your children the best you can, but they still grow into strangers."Irie said tentatively, "Oh, that's not true, surely."The disembodied loneliness of the past 20 years collapsed in on Samad as he thought about the state of his family, the state of himself."It's this place. I know it. You come here for all the right and righteous reasons. You don't mean to stay, not forever, but this place, it traps you. It's cold and wet here, and no one knows how to love, but you stay because things are working. By the time you realize you've made a mistake, you've been stained," Samad said. He looked at Irie, desperate to get the words out. "You can never fully be here, be English, because you're from someplace else, but you can never go back there, either! I know I can't. I'm tainted from my time here. I can never go home. I'm from nowhere now, and I'm going nowhere."
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: "Bloody hell! One son a pukka Englishman lawyer, the other a fundamentalist terrorist. And me, I'm stuck here in this bloody country, this England, this devil's pact of a place! They said it was temporary, they said it was a stepping stone, but they lied! Thirty-odd years and I'm still here, still tolerated, still an immigrant, still not one of them! My sons, they've got it figured out, they fit in, one way or another. But me, I'm neither here nor there, a bloody ghost, a man without a country! This England, it sucks you in, chews you up, and spits you out! There's no place for us here, no place for anyone who doesn't fit their mold!"Oh, that's not true, surely," Irie offered, her voice a gentle counterpoint to Samad's bitter outpouring."True? Of course, it's bloody true! Look at me, look at my life, what does it mean? What am I? A joke, a parody, a failed experiment! They talk about birthplaces, about roots, about belonging, but what do they know? What do they know about being torn from your home, about being a stranger in a strange land, about never truly belonging anywhere? This England, it's not my home, it will never be my home, and now, after all this time, I can't even go back to where I came from. I'm adrift, I'm lost, I'm a man without a place, without a home, without a bloody identity!"
written_by_MFA025.Reason: Both pairs of dialogue achieve a similar impact, but Excerpt 1 does so in a slightly more realistic manner; the monologue is less repetitive and melodramatic. Sentences like "its cold and wet here, and no one knows how to love" are original and do not rely on cliche. Overall, slightly more expertise is shown in how Excerpt 1 portray's Samad's frustrations.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Samad leaned back, fingers tightening around the stem of his glass, watching the amber liquid swirl, gathering his thoughts like a man recalling a half-forgotten dream. "You know, Irie, I did not come here to stay," he began, with the kind of dramatic pause he enjoyed, as if delivering some great revelation. "No. It was meant to be temporary, a short stint, a little adventure before going home, but then—ah, then!—this country does something to you, something insidious. You come thinking you are a visitor, and before you know it, you have children who speak back to you in accents you don’t recognize, who call you old-fashioned, who think the way you eat, the way you pray, the way you exist is some sort of historical relic." He sighed, gesturing vaguely at the street outside. "One son, a lawyer. A proper pukka Englishman, with his nice suits and his nice house and his nice friends who politely pretend not to see the color of his skin. The other?" A mirthless laugh. "A warrior. A martyr. At least that’s what he believes. This place—it stretches you, splits you down the middle. And you, you keep asking yourself: where do I belong? Here? There? Nowhere?" He shook his head. "They tolerate us, Irie. Tolerate. Like a mild skin condition." Irie frowned. "Oh, that’s not true, surely." Samad just smiled, a tired, knowing thing.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: "If I could tell my own father about this!" cried Samad. "One son, with his marmite on toast and his football games. The other, a downright fundamentalist! More Bengali than I ever was. What would he have done, my father, if he could see me now? He would have said, It serves you right, Samad. That is what you get for going somewhere you are only tolerated." Samad paused and took a long sip of his tea. "Oh, Irie," he continued. "If I’d known that England was the way that it is. A place where we are merely tolerated. A place where belonging and not belonging both feel like a trap. Was it not pure foolishness, then, to come here? Not sometimes, but every single day, I know it was a mistake. We should have stayed put. What didn’t we stay put?” Irie shook her head. “That is not true, surely, Samad,” she said. “It’s England. It’s what we have always wanted. We dreamed of this place all our lives." "We dreamed of a version of this place, certainly," said Samad. "Truthfully, I don’t know what I believe anymore. I thought I knew what it meant to be born somewhere. But now? What does it matter where you are born? How can you belong anywhere if you feel... adrift. Every day. Completely adrift."
written_by_MFA008.Reason: Excerpt 2 is more coherent and effective in delivering emotional punches. Where Excerpt 1 belabors its points, stretching the idea that one father has two sons who've assimilated differently to the tortuous, "A proper pukka Englishman, with his nice suits and his nice house and his nice friends who politely pretend not to see the color of his skin. The other?" A mirthless laugh. "A warrior. A martyr. At least that’s what he believes.," Excerpt 2 gives us the far punchier, and arguably more illustrative, "One son, with his marmite on toast and his football games. The other, a downright fundamentalist! More Bengali than I ever was." Here, concision and fluency produce a stronger emotional impact than Excerpt 1 does with more words.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: The Manhattan skyline at night is, for me, an argument against the concept of singularity, not merely because it’s the result of innumerable hands and minds, bundled debts, and traces of antidepressants in the water but because the multiplicity of its forms evokes a sublimity alien to natural landscapes. Standing there, breathing in air tinged with blossoms or exhaust fumes, my gaze skips between the architectural vastness and the tiny illuminated windows, each a human-scale element folded into a collective fabric that feels, somehow, alive. The skyline is not a skyline; it is a second person plural, an as-yet-unrealized "we" that all art addresses, even the most intimate. This thought emerges less like revelation than residue, clinging stubbornly to my attempts to organize experience into some semblance of narrative. The more I reflect on the idea of this "we," the more it unravels into the sublime traffic of urban life—the shifting weather patterns mirrored in high-rise glass, the ebb and flow of bundled debts that keep the city afloat, and the anonymous networks of pipes, trains, and storm drains humming just below the surface.It is in this interwoven complexity that I find my vocation as an artist, not to produce artifacts but to transform what I’ve termed “bad forms of collectivity” into fleeting glimpses of unity—never full, never final, but enough to sustain a flicker of hope for a communal body. In this endeavor, Noor—or, perhaps, the fiction of Noor—becomes a locus, a gravitational pull around which my fragmented thoughts and projects reorganize themselves. Noor is not Noor; they are the shorthand for an idea, an abstraction that reminds me how little of myself is mine, how often I am alien to my own being. And yet, in that discomfort, that acknowledgment of not being fully identical with oneself, there lies the faint shimmer of possibility—a utopian flicker in which past and present collapse into a unified whole, not resolved but reinterpreted.I am, however, just a body on a bench at midnight, my bandanna flattening my hair, my hands sticky with the juice of unsulfured mango as I project myself into futures too many to count. A mild lacrimal event—a phrase borrowed, revised—wets my cheek. The tears are neither despair nor ecstasy but a texture of the moment, the salt of an urban meditation that hovers between the profound and the ridiculous. I do not attempt to resolve it, knowing the real art is in letting the tension linger, illuminating the skyline from within.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: The Manhattan skyline at night is, for me, an argument against the concept of singularity, not merely because it’s the result of innumerable hands and minds, bundled debts, and traces of antidepressants in the water but because the multiplicity of its forms evokes a sublimity alien to natural landscapes. Standing there, breathing in air tinged with blossoms or exhaust fumes, my gaze skips between the architectural vastness and the tiny illuminated windows, each a human-scale element folded into a collective fabric that feels, somehow, alive. The skyline is not a skyline; it is a second person plural, an as-yet-unrealized "we" that all art addresses, even the most intimate. This thought emerges less like revelation than residue, clinging stubbornly to my attempts to organize experience into some semblance of narrative. The more I reflect on the idea of this "we," the more it unravels into the sublime traffic of urban life—the shifting weather patterns mirrored in high-rise glass, the ebb and flow of bundled debts that keep the city afloat, and the anonymous networks of pipes, trains, and storm drains humming just below the surface.It is in this interwoven complexity that I find my vocation as an artist, not to produce artifacts but to transform what I’ve termed “bad forms of collectivity” into fleeting glimpses of unity—never full, never final, but enough to sustain a flicker of hope for a communal body. In this endeavor, Noor—or, perhaps, the fiction of Noor—becomes a locus, a gravitational pull around which my fragmented thoughts and projects reorganize themselves. Noor is not Noor; they are the shorthand for an idea, an abstraction that reminds me how little of myself is mine, how often I am alien to my own being. And yet, in that discomfort, that acknowledgment of not being fully identical with oneself, there lies the faint shimmer of possibility—a utopian flicker in which past and present collapse into a unified whole, not resolved but reinterpreted.I am, however, just a body on a bench at midnight, my bandanna flattening my hair, my hands sticky with the juice of unsulfured mango as I project myself into futures too many to count. A mild lacrimal event—a phrase borrowed, revised—wets my cheek. The tears are neither despair nor ecstasy but a texture of the moment, the salt of an urban meditation that hovers between the profound and the ridiculous. I do not attempt to resolve it, knowing the real art is in letting the tension linger, illuminating the skyline from within.

written_by_MFA027.Excerpt1: The night air, maybe tinged with the scent of some flowering tree I can’t identify, swirls through the gaps in the fencing.  The thrill elicited by this view—the tiny illuminated windows, the way human-scale elements are visibly enmeshed with the inhuman scale of the skyline—is something I associate with urban spaces.  The Hudson River, the Palisades on the other side, even the movement of the clouds, fail to trigger the same response.I breathe deeply, trying to identify the chemical compounds in the air.  I’m high up enough to see the bridges spanning into Brooklyn and Queens.  I imagine the collective exhalation of eight million people, the collective inhalation, the movement of hands over innumerable screens, the scrolling, the tapping, the repetitive stress injuries.  I picture the vast network of pipes, mains, and cables extending below the streets, the nighttime deliveries to bodegas, the movement of trains underground.I see the skyline as the material manifestation of a second person plural, a collective to which all art, even the most intimate, is addressed.  A yet-to-exist “we” glimpsed in the bundled debt, the traces of antidepressants in the water supply, the elaborate traffic system, the weather patterns.  I resolve to become the kind of artist who can transform bad forms of collectivity—bedbugs, or the crowds now surging toward Times Square—into glimpses of their potential for a kind of unity, a communal body.    And then there’s Noor, around whom the fiction of the world reorganizes itself.  I’m always trying to get back to her, but she’s never fully available, and this unavailability is central to her function.  She’s here, but only in the form of a promise I’ve made to myself to get up early and run the loop of the park, a promise I’ve already broken.I’m trying to think my way into a future state, but I’m too aware of my body on the bench to achieve the desired self-alienation.  I feel the pressure of the chain-link fence against my back, the bandanna flattening my hair.  I’m eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, the juice running down my chin.  I’m having a mild lacrimal event, quietly tearing up.I’m never fully identical with myself.  There’s always a part of me that’s alien to me.  And this is where the hope, the utopian glimmer, resides—in the self-estrangement that enables me to imagine the past and present merging into something reinterpreted, whole.
written_by_MFA027.Excerpt2: The scent of blossoms colors the night, and New York in its entirety fits very neatly and completely into my hands. For instance, between my thumb and my index, lights flicker on and off in a miniature window. If I elongate my fingers I could also hold the silver skyscrapers tearing into the clouds. How astonishing; the skyline’s ants and beasts fit right, and wrong, into my palms. Back in my father's village nothing, absolutely nothing, fit into my hands. There were no neat edges anywhere, no contrast, nothing for me to want to try to hold. In short, there is no place I feel less alone than here, alone on this bench in New York, where the skyline is ours, and we are the skyline, my eyes staring straight into the material manifestation of a second person plural. In the future, they will say this skyline was synonymous with every art, every intimate form that has ever, or will ever, exist. To say we are the skyline is to confirm a collective identity, to confirm a stake in what makes up the city's sublime marrow; bundled debt, traces of antidepressants in the water, traffic networks, and shifting weather patterns. As an artist it will be my mission to transmute bad forms of collectivity into a sculpture of the communal body of the future. There is something Noor said once, in response to my ideas about the fiction of the world, that I am desperately trying to forget. We were not speaking the way people speak, necessarily, but more like skies, or skylines, when a passing cloud whispered something about a mirror. The disembodied voice said one cannot recognize oneself and at once be identical with oneself. But one plus one plus one equals three, if my math is correct. So maybe we multiply, keep multiplying, and our past and present and future selves never leave, and maybe that is what Noor really meant when she said the world has no genre you can name. The midnight air does nothing to unflatten my hair beneath the bandana. I would mistake this moment for a dream if I had not just consumed an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, the juice all over my fingers. I vaguely remember a dream of myself as an old man, maybe an old woman, my fingers free of both tiny windows and the stain of fruit, and with this memory of the future I experience a mild lacrimal event, and I feel very alone, and very together.
written_by_MFA027.Reason: While both excerpts are deeply internal and reflective, Excerpt 1 approaches this interior narrative with a confidence that draws readers into the furtive, misty headspace of the narrator: "I’m trying to think my way into a future state, but I’m too aware of my body on the bench to achieve the desired self-alienation.  I feel the pressure of the chain-link fence against my back, the bandanna flattening my hair." This tangibility is more affecting that the interiority of Excerpt 2, which leans more abstract/subjective.

written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: Gazing upon the skyline of Manhattan, I inhaled the stench of the sewers, the smoke of the gyro stand, and the fragrance of blossoms. For me, steel landscapes always followed this progression: first coarseness, then delectability, then something more subtly appetizing. The longer I looked, the more thrilling the tableau revealed itself to be, with the yellowed hued windows forming a jagged arcade. The buildings were so immense that I didn’t think of mountains so much as other buildings, particularly the skyscrapers-in-progress I had recently encountered in an architecture magazine. Granite ranges—not to mention waterfalls, alluvial plains, verdant valleys, desert mesas, and the like—have seldom made an impression on me. Yet this skyline, being the result of over a century of steel-hewn collective striving, provoked a deeper recognition; in the risings and falls of the rooftops, I pinpointed a material beyond that which the builders had worked with—something all-encompassing, a “you” to which a work of art would surely be addressed. Perhaps every work of art in the history of humankind—from the verses of Sappho, to the triumphs of Muslim architecture, to brush strokes of the Dutch masters, to the Goldberg Variations—had been addressed to this “you.” All the bundled debt of midtown was merely a muse to a Greek woman’s pen; pigments intermingled in the city water supply with the traces of antidepressants; the gridlock on the Brooklyn Bridge recalled the stylings of Ibn Tulun. Did the fog setting in over the river contain a hint of Bach? I couldn’t quite tell. written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: I remember those college days. The grass peeking over cement, the columns of the buildings thick, stuffed, presumably, with knowledge. Though, admittedly, I had a hard time juggling it all, having joined the Panthers on campus, less for their social cause, and more to reject the budding questions about my Blackness. Needless to say, it didn't work. Everywhere I went, strangers, white and Black, would tell me I wasn't Black enough. The white friends wanted to know why I didn't keep a gun, like a real Black Panther, and the Panthers wanted to know why I was so busy doing the white man's homework. Once, an entire basketball court stopped the game to laugh for five minutes when they heard me mutter egads after missing a shot. I can take these teases in everyday life, but when it comes to my literature, that's when the blade cuts deepest. The most recent was a slack-mouthed reviewer who wondered why my last novel, a retelling of Aeschylus, did not portray adequately, as they put it, "the Black man's experience." This was no unusual comment. At a literary party, I was once told to abandon my passion for classic retellings in favor of "true, gritty real stories of Black life." There were millions to be made here, an agent had said. When I refused their suggestion, telling them that all of my stories are stories of Black life, because I, a Black life, made them, they moseyed over to a performance artist, with whom they spent the rest of the evening talking about sword-swallowing. I looked at the paintings on the walls of the luxury Harlem apartment, all of Black strife, contorted faces, hands in yearning, bodies that seldom looked like bodies. Pictures of poverty worth millions. I couldn't say that I believed in race at all - I saw it merely as a construct. And yet, its grasp over me and those around me felt crushing, inevitable, real. I knew if I burned the apartment to the ground, as I felt the growing desire to do, the newspaper would not say "Established Author Sets Party Ablaze in Fit of Misplaced Justice." No, it would simply say, "Black Man Commits Arson." That would be how I would be remembered.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: As a college freshman, I joined the Black Panther Party. I didn't quite fit in; I didn't wear my beret tilted just right, didn't raise my fist with enough fury, didn't speak with the necessary cadence that marked the truly radical. I muttered "Egads" during basketball games, to the collective horror of my teammates, who were often split between exasperation and bemusement. White classmates with their predictable condescension said I was "articulate," while Black peers muttered under their breaths, "Not Black enough." A professor once called me “fascinatingly displaced,” as though I were a museum artifact. This dislocation seeped into my writing. My first novel was a retelling of Aeschylus—a reviewer described it as “a charming but ill-advised venture into the Greeks, woefully devoid of authentic Black experience.” I reread the critique three times, marveling at how one could misinterpret authenticity as a monolith.Years later, I stood in a dim Manhattan loft at a literary party where the wine was as dry as the wit was acidic. A literary agent in a glinting blazer cornered me by the hors d’oeuvres, leaned in conspiratorially, and said, “Listen, you’ve got talent, but all this Greek tragedy nonsense—leave it behind. Write something real. Something gritty, raw, Black life in the streets. That’s what sells.” He patted my shoulder, as though certifying my potential to commodify my identity, then floated off to fawn over a performance artist wearing a gown made of egg cartons.I sipped my wine, the bitterness cutting through my amusement. The transactional nature of the room was suffocating, the smiles wide but hollow, the handshakes quick but calculating. Authenticity, here, was a currency as fleeting as the trends that shaped it. I thought of race—the way it sat heavy on me when others decided it should, the way I refused to believe in it except when guilt or societal violence forced it into my consciousness. Guilt for what? For not being Black enough? For being too Black? It was endless. I walked to the window, feeling the cold glass against my palm, and let the city’s hum drown out the noise of the room. “Authenticity,” I whispered, watching my breath fog the glass, “is just another mask they want me to wear.”
written_by_MFA030.Reason: Excerpt 1 is more scenically detailed, allowing for deeper immersion and, subsequently, emotional attachment to this narrator's interiority: "I remember those college days. The grass peeking over cement, the columns of the buildings thick, stuffed, presumably, with knowledge." This initial scene setting makes the narrator's grappling with his black identity feel more individual and less didactic.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: There came a point in my life when I seemed to have to "prove" my Blackness, despite my inherent identity as a Black man. As a result, I joined the Black Panther Party in college. I needed some validation that I was, indeed, who I appeared to be, not only on the outside but on the inside as well. Both Blacks and whites alike told me that I was "not Black enough" for them (they saw the way I played basketball, muttering "Egads" under my breath with every foul or missed layup—Egads). This applied not only to my physical appearance and manner of speech but also extended to my intellect and my books.My most recent manuscript was denied by every major publisher. From a reviewer: "While somewhat compelling and an interesting take on the retelling of Aeschylus, we just don't see how it relates to the Black experience." Despite my being a Black writer, the book was, apparently, not written from a Black perspective. At the latest New York literary party, a well-known literary agent told me, "You should forget those retellings of yours; classical works aren't what the market is looking for. What we're seeking are the true, gritty stories of Black life—write that, then give me a call."I told him, "My stories are Black stories." And in their own way, it was true. Was I not a Black writer? The agent shuffled past me to attend to a performance artist so they could see what they could do for one another, before never speaking to each other again.I didn't know how to contend with any of it: how to portray myself as "Black enough," the backward, ill-feeling guilt behind not being so, and how to fit into the mold that society made of Black men. We all had to be gangsters, rappers. But why should I have been anything other than who I was? Race was a construct I didn't believe in and rarely dwelt on, until those moments arose when guilt compelled me to see the "other side" of the matter. written_by_MFA002.Excerpt1: I joined the Black Panthers in college, not out of revolutionary fervor but from a peculiar need to authenticate my Blackness, as if membership cards and raised fists could offset my tendency to mutter "Egads" during pickup basketball games. The Panthers, to their credit, were more amused than offended by my professorial affectations, though one member did suggest I try saying "damn" instead. My novels drew similar bewilderment – a reviewer once wrote, "While technically accomplished, his adaptation of Aeschylus' Oresteia to a housing project seems more interested in postmodern discourse than authentic Black experience." As if authenticity came with a manual, complete with approved vocabularies and prescribed narratives. At a Manhattan literary soirée, between sips of overpriced wine and precisely cubed cheese, a literary agent cornered me with the air of someone about to dispense life-changing wisdom. "Look," she said, adjusting her horn-rimmed glasses with manicured precision, "nobody wants to read about Black people discussing Aristotelian ethics. Write something real, something gritty. Give me projects and pimps, give me struggle." She might as well have asked me to perform a soft-shoe routine. The irony of being told my Black experience wasn't Black enough by someone whose closest connection to the culture was probably watching "The Wire" wasn't lost on me. I watched her glide away to fawn over a performance artist who'd painted himself in crude oil to protest environmental racism – now there was some authentic Blackness she could sell. Standing alone by the cheese plate, I contemplated how race was like quantum mechanics: a construct I didn't believe in but couldn't ignore, something that only seemed to materialize when observed or when guilt compelled me to notice it. Yet its consequences were undeniably real, manifesting in broken bodies and broken dreams, in rejection letters suggesting my characters weren't "relatable enough" to my own people. The violence of these expectations was subtle but persistent, like water wearing away stone, and I found myself wondering if authenticity was just another mask we wore to please the observers of our particles, another performance in the endless theater of racial identity where even our silences were scripted and our rebellions came with stage directions. I smiled at my reflection in the wine glass, watching it distort and fragment like truth itself.
written_by_MFA002.Excerpt2: My awkward undergraduate years are better left undiscussed, but lately I have found myself turning them over in my head in search of an insight that has eluded me since – what drove me to join my university’s chapter of the Black Panther Party? Ostensibly I supported the movement and its ideologies, but in retrospect – and in all honesty – my desire to resist the oppression of my people was, perhaps, not the most pertinent factor in my decision. Really I joined the Party as a means of proving myself – more specifically, proving my Blackness. And to whom was this posturing directed? Certainly at the white and Black basketball players alike who laughed me off the court when I mumbled “Egads” upon a fumbled shot. Certainly at Todd Henderson, the literary critic who called my retelling of Aeschylus’s Prometheus Bound “disconcertingly cerebral” for an author like me. And candidly, perhaps at myself. I needed to convince myself that I was Black enough. And maybe I still do, decades later. The other day I attended a literary party in the city and somehow found myself sucked into a conversation with an agent of an acquaintance. “Don’t bother with the Achilles,” the agent told me. (Privately I considered correcting his pronunciation of Aeschylus, then decided it wasn’t worth the effort.) “It’s not what they want. They’re looking for true, gritty, real stories of Black life. They want authenticity.” This puzzled me. I asked him to define authentic. What makes me, a Black man writing material guided by my lived experience, not authentically Black? To this, the agent laughed, clapped me on the shoulder, and moved on to debate the prevalence of body shaming in social media with a bemused performance artist perusing the hors d’oeuvres. Today, as I write, I consider my opinion on it all – Blackness, whiteness, authenticity. I don’t really believe in race. I regard race as a construct of convenience, a societal demarcation on which I rarely dwell. And yet, I recognize the self-indulgent folly in the popular adage, I don’t see color. I am not blind to the concrete consequences of racial divides: oppression, discrimination, violence, subjugation. But there’s something artificial and contrived about the Blackness that I feel I must actively demonstrate.
written_by_MFA002.Reason: The second excerpt is very flowery, unnatural for a first-person narration, and constantly interrupted by overly formal questions that make for awkward/clunky transitions: "And to whom was this posturing directed?" The first excerpt uses the "Egads" detail as an efficient and very funny punchline, but that detail, in the second excerpt, is buried in a much-too-formal and much-too-descriptive sentence, which completely stifles the joke. The narrator's understanding of race is also much more nuanced in the first excerpt ("like quantum mechanics: a construct I didn't believe in but couldn't ignore, something that only seemed to materialized when observed"). This is a brilliant comparison that extends as the narrator contemplates whether "authenticity was just another mask we wore to please the observers of our particles." The second excerpt doesn't capture the nuance of how the demand for authenticity plays into racial identity, and how race is not something that one can cast aside.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: I was seven months pregnant and couldn’t button my coat, which was how I ended up waddling into the room where my soon-to-be ex-husband Mark was laughing with his friends about something—or more likely, nothing—completely inconsequential. That’s when I said it. I said, “It’s funny, you know, Mark’s not available for affairs right now because he’s pregnant with me.” And they laughed. Oh, they laughed all right, but it wasn’t the right kind of laugh. It was that awkward, pitying chuckle that makes you realize your joke is less of a joke and more of a moment everyone wishes they weren’t part of. I felt like a stand-up comic bombing on open-mic night, only instead of hecklers, I had my own humiliation.That night, after crying for the hundredth time that week, I tried to find some solace in my father’s apartment, which was a masterpiece of misery. His brown corduroy couch sagged like it had given up on life, and every corner of the room was decorated in a way that screamed, “I haven’t been redecorated since Nixon resigned.” It was the kind of place that made sadness feel inevitable. And there I was, crying over Mark, who I now knew had been sneaking around with a woman named Thelma Rice—a name so cloyingly sweet it felt like it belonged on a box of cookies, not the antagonist of my life.The worst part? The discovery. A children’s songbook. A little gift from Thelma to Mark, inscribed with some nauseating drivel like, “For all the songs you’ll sing.” Songs he’d apparently been singing for her while our toddler, Sam, sang solo in his crib. I couldn’t believe the audacity, the gall, the absolute polyester pantsuit-ness of it all. And Thelma herself! I mean, have you seen Thelma? She looked like she spent her weekends alphabetizing her collection of decorative soaps. Yet there I was, a hormonal, bloated mess, crying into a pillow that smelled like mothballs. It was unbearable. And yet, somehow, it was also just another Tuesday.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: I'm seven months pregnant, and Thelma Rice is sleeping with my husband, so I'm sleeping with no one. Thelma Rice does not understand the struggle of dating inherent to being a 38-year-old pregnant woman, though maybe one day she will! It's a thought I comfort myself with, and it makes me laugh. I miss laughing. I don't think the joke would make anyone so much as giggle, not when said out loud and especially not when I look at it written on paper. It's just pathetic, I can hear the awkward chuckles now, the kind clusters of people make when trying to be sympathetic, or to prevent tears. I'm crying now, but I'm pregnant so it's to be expected. My life has turned quite ugly, filled with droll tragedy and my father's hideous furniture. It's good of him to let me stay in his New York apartment, but the place is so grey and miserable that it makes me grey and miserable. The lights in all the lamps flicker, and the few windows face a brick wall, so the apartment resembles a cave more than a home. It's fitting, I suppose. A nice cave, buried deep in the building, where I can retreat to lick my wounds. If my father's apartment had looked like a real home, I would have been reminded of what I lost. Ever since I found that crude inscription, in a book of children's songs of all places, I've had no home. Thelma Rice, with her endless entitlements, dragged Sam into this too, scrawling out her wantonness on the pages of a book suited for a small child, not a grown man. I can just see her now, her short and stubby fingers clutching at the pen as she tried to rhyme words together into her approximation of a clever lyric. I imagine her chewing her pen with her crooked teeth and smudging her lurid lipstick down her chin. It makes me feel...better, to think of her this way. Like I can see her truest self.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: Excerpt 1 contains a surprising and comedic voice, allowing us to feel the dual comedy and tragedy of the narrator's situation: "I was seven months pregnant and couldn't button my coat, which is how I ended up waddling into the room where my soon-to-be ex husband Mark was laughing with his friends..." The ambivalence rendered here allows for a more realistic impact rather than the straightforward, journalistic nature of excerpt 2.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: When I started living at my father's place in New York I couldn't stop crying. The weeping would be long and drawn out, dramatic affairs, and through my vision blurred with tears I would see my father's awful furniture, everything wooden and overly embellished, and the ugliness of the space I was in would only make me cry more. Often as I cried, I would think about how he told me about Thelma Rice. What made it all the more horrible was how utterly mundane it was. I was looking through Sam's little bookshelf for something to sing him to sleep. I was on autopilot, already thinking about what I would do after Sam fell asleep. I was not scrounging through my husband's letters, or stalking Thelma on the streets. I just pulled a book at random and flipped it open to the first page and there, in the most flowery, idiotic handwriting, a note: for the man with a mouth do a lot more than singing, love, Thelma. Disgusting, especially because it was a children's book, one that was on my son's bookshelf. Just thinking about her handwriting could make me cry for twenty minutes. To make myself feel better I would think about how ugly she was. Not very women's lib, I know, but she was my husband's mistress. And she was ugly, it was a fact. She had these bulging eyes and a veiny neck and nothing about her face was symmetrical. I would think about that and stop crying and then think about that note and the whole cycle would start all over again. In public, I put on a brave face. One night I went to dinner and at one point I said, no one wants to take out a lady who's seven months pregnant, she'll eat twice as much! It's not very funny when I write it down. When I said it, though, people laughed. Although, now I wonder if they were laughing because it was funny, or because they pitied me. I was certainly quite pitiable.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: I suppose there's nothing quite like discovering your husband is having an affair when you're seven months pregnant. The timing is exquisite, really – your body has morphed into something between a beach ball and a whale, your ankles have disappeared into puffy clouds, and you're crying at paper towel commercials. And then there's Thelma Rice, with her perfect figure and that irritating habit of inscribing children's books with suggestive little notes, as if marking her territory like some literary-minded cat. I tried making jokes about it, naturally. That's what I do – turn tragedy into comedy, preferably before dessert. But somehow, quipping about being undatable while sporting a seven-month baby bump didn't land quite the way I'd hoped. The laughter that followed had that distinct pitch of pity, the kind that makes you wish you could crawl into a hole, except you can't because, well, pregnant. So here I am in my father's apartment in New York, surrounded by furniture that looks like it was rejected from a 1950s detective novel, crying into tissues and wondering how my life turned into this particularly unfunny sitcom. Sam, my toddler, doesn't understand why Mommy keeps staring out windows like she's auditioning for a Tennessee Williams play. The truth is, betrayal is a peculiar thing – it doesn't just break your heart, it retrospectively ruins perfectly good memories. Like how that book of children's songs, the one with Thelma's nauseating inscription, has now tainted every lullaby I've ever sung to Sam. The whole thing would be almost comedic if it weren't so tragically predictable – the younger woman, the secret notes, the pregnant wife. It's like someone took every cliché about infidelity and decided to stage it in my living room, with me as the unwitting star of this domestic drama. At least I can say this: nothing makes you reevaluate your life choices quite like finding your husband's mistress's handwriting in your child's bedtime stories.
written_by_MFA001.Reason: Excerpt 2 is the more effective piece of writing. Where excerpt 1 attempts a vernacular voice that's somewhat oral but ultimately flat, Excerpt 2 produces a more authentic version of a similar voice. Take two comparable sentences, one from Excerpt 1 ("One night I went to dinner and at one point I said, no one wants to take out a lady who's seven months pregnant, she'll eat twice as much!") and another from Excerpt 2 ("The timing is exquisite, really – your body has morphed into something between a beach ball and a whale, your ankles have disappeared into puffy clouds, and you're crying at paper towel commercials."), and notice how the second sentence conveys a similar idea in a funny, vernacular voice that is also rhythmically complex and richer in sensory detail.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: It’s something you don’t expect from a second husband. Or, I don’t know, maybe you should suspect it more from a second husband. And that name. Thelma Rice. Like a villain in a Roald Dahl book. Imagine my shame, telling people I had been cheated on, at thirty-eight, with a woman named Thelma Rice? I would have gotten him back, I really would, but it’s difficult to date when you’re seven months pregnant. That’s a joke. I’m laughing as I write it. I admit that it feels sad when it’s on paper. The laughter I can hear now is the worst kind: sympathetic laughter. The truth is, I don’t laugh often these days. I cry and cry and cry. I cry in a lot of places, but I do most of my crying in my father’s New York apartment, surrounded by that mocking cuckoo clock and all the uncomfortable plastic furniture. But there is laughter. How can I not laugh when I think of the moment I found out? Sitting on the floor of the nursery, amongst the blocks and the plush toys, cherubic Sam on my knee, opening that children’s song book I found out later was a gift to my husband from Thelma called “The Hungry Hippo.” On the first page, in lascivious handwriting: My darling. Let this be a reminder of how hungry I am for you. xoxo- Thelma. I remember the sound as I snapped the book shut. I remember Sam grabbing for it, wondering why story time was over before it had begun. I can see her when I close my eyes, hunched over that sweet and unassuming book, a hippo herself with that round, smug face, those manly teeth, that grayish skin. To be cheated on when you are seven months pregnant, by your second husband, is one thing. To be cheated on with a woman who resembles a cartoon hippo is entirely another. This, more than anything, is what makes me cry when I’m alone with just my father’s cuckoo clock and the rubber loveseat to keep me company.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Picture this: me, seven months pregnant, sprawled on the couch in my father's dreary New York apartment, tears streaming down my face. The backdrop? A symphony of beige, a decor so monotonous it could make a nun scream. The cause of this melodramatic scene? My second husband, Mark had just pulled a classic man move. He'd fallen in love with another woman. Now, I'd always been the type to handle heartbreak with a dash of humor. So, when I told my friends, "I'm not going to be able to date for a while because I'm seven months pregnant," I expected a chuckle. But the joke fell flat, and the silence was deafening. Maybe it was the delivery, the sheer absurdity of the situation. Whatever the reason, the only response I got was a smattering of pitying laughter. Back in my father's apartment, surrounded by furniture that seemed to mock my misery, I couldn't help but feel like a character in a bad sitcom. The beige walls, the lumpy couch, the faded floral wallpaper – it was all a recipe for despair. And then there was the discovery. The inscription in the book of children's songs, a gift from Thelma Rice to my husband. "To Mark, with love, from the other woman." It was like a punch to the gut, my husband's betrayal. Thelma Rice. The name echoed in my mind, a caricature of a woman with a voice like nails on a chalkboard and legs that went on for days. I pictured her, all blonde hair and fake smiles, and my anger burned even brighter. But amidst the tears and the anger, there was a flicker of determination. I wouldn't let this break me. I would pick myself up, dust myself off, and start over. I would find a way to be happy, even if it meant navigating the world of dating with a baby on my hip. After all, I was a woman, and women are resilient. We bend, we don't break. We fall, we get back up. We cry, we laugh. We love, we lose, we love again. And through it all, we find a way to keep going.
written_by_MFA008.Reason: I prefer Excerpt 1. It offers more information -- the inscription from Thelma, for example, is more specific and feels more real. Excerpt 1 is written in a kind of controlled ironic tone, whereas Excerpt 2 hackneyed phrases in a way that doesn't clearly become satire (e.g. "Mark had just pulled a classic man move"). Excerpt 2 is an odd melange of tones that then ends with a somewhat forced-feeling "redemptive" ending that sounds like a cliche. Excerpt 2 uses hyperbolic language, whereas Excerpt 1 has more grounded imagery, like the mocking clock.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: It’s something you don’t expect from a second husband. Or, I don’t know, maybe you should suspect it more from a second husband. And that name. Thelma Rice. Like a villain in a Roald Dahl book. Imagine my shame, telling people I had been cheated on, at thirty-eight, with a woman named Thelma Rice? I would have gotten him back, I really would, but it’s difficult to date when you’re seven months pregnant. That’s a joke. I’m laughing as I write it. I admit that it feels sad when it’s on paper. The laughter I can hear now is the worst kind: sympathetic laughter. The truth is, I don’t laugh often these days. I cry and cry and cry. I cry in a lot of places, but I do most of my crying in my father’s New York apartment, surrounded by that mocking cuckoo clock and all the uncomfortable plastic furniture. But there is laughter. How can I not laugh when I think of the moment I found out? Sitting on the floor of the nursery, amongst the blocks and the plush toys, cherubic Sam on my knee, opening that children’s song book I found out later was a gift to my husband from Thelma called “The Hungry Hippo.” On the first page, in lascivious handwriting: My darling. Let this be a reminder of how hungry I am for you. xoxo- Thelma. I remember the sound as I snapped the book shut. I remember Sam grabbing for it, wondering why story time was over before it had begun. I can see her when I close my eyes, hunched over that sweet and unassuming book, a hippo herself with that round, smug face, those manly teeth, that grayish skin. To be cheated on when you are seven months pregnant, by your second husband, is one thing. To be cheated on with a woman who resembles a cartoon hippo is entirely another. This, more than anything, is what makes me cry when I’m alone with just my father’s cuckoo clock and the rubber loveseat to keep me company.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Picture this: me, seven months pregnant, sprawled on the couch in my father's dreary New York apartment, tears streaming down my face. The backdrop? A symphony of beige, a decor so monotonous it could make a nun scream. The cause of this melodramatic scene? My second husband, Mark had just pulled a classic man move. He'd fallen in love with another woman. Now, I'd always been the type to handle heartbreak with a dash of humor. So, when I told my friends, "I'm not going to be able to date for a while because I'm seven months pregnant," I expected a chuckle. But the joke fell flat, and the silence was deafening. Maybe it was the delivery, the sheer absurdity of the situation. Whatever the reason, the only response I got was a smattering of pitying laughter. Back in my father's apartment, surrounded by furniture that seemed to mock my misery, I couldn't help but feel like a character in a bad sitcom. The beige walls, the lumpy couch, the faded floral wallpaper – it was all a recipe for despair. And then there was the discovery. The inscription in the book of children's songs, a gift from Thelma Rice to my husband. "To Mark, with love, from the other woman." It was like a punch to the gut, my husband's betrayal. Thelma Rice. The name echoed in my mind, a caricature of a woman with a voice like nails on a chalkboard and legs that went on for days. I pictured her, all blonde hair and fake smiles, and my anger burned even brighter. But amidst the tears and the anger, there was a flicker of determination. I wouldn't let this break me. I would pick myself up, dust myself off, and start over. I would find a way to be happy, even if it meant navigating the world of dating with a baby on my hip. After all, I was a woman, and women are resilient. We bend, we don't break. We fall, we get back up. We cry, we laugh. We love, we lose, we love again. And through it all, we find a way to keep going.
written_by_MFA008.Reason: I prefer Excerpt1. There is more variance in the length and rhythm of each sentence, the details are more specific (the “villain in the Roald Dahl” book, for example) and the narrator seems to have more personality, alternating between vulnerability (“I cry and cry and cry”) and irony (“to be cheated on with a cartoon hippo”). By contrast, Excerpt2 starts off fine but gives into Hallmark-style cliches by the end, with lines like “women are resilient” and “we bend, but don’t break”.

written_by_MFA022.Excerpt1: Dr. John Montague stood before Hill House, a place that loomed as though waiting, its cold stones heavy with silence. The house, not sane, appeared to lean slightly forward, its dark windows watching him with a lifeless gaze, as though withholding secrets that could never be pried free. Hill House had stood for eighty years, holding within its walls an impenetrable darkness that even sunlight seemed reluctant to touch. The hills rose sharply behind it, framing its stark isolation; the house seemed less built than grown, an aberration of nature. Dr. Montague, meticulous in his methods yet quietly burdened by self-doubt, adjusted his glasses, a gesture as habitual as his reliance on his title—"Doctor of Philosophy in Anthropology"—to shield himself from skepticism. For years, his inquiries into the supernatural had been met with thinly veiled disdain, but Hill House represented his long-sought grail: an authentic haunting, a house with whispers in its foundation. He had rented the property at a steep price, its rooms and halls offered not for comfort but as a proving ground for his theories. As he crossed the threshold, the air seemed to shift, pressing lightly against his skin as though the house was tasting him. He paused, glancing back at the gravel drive that led away, the thought fleeting: nothing here would let him leave unmarked. The door shut behind him with a finality that echoed briefly, then faded, swallowed entirely by the unbroken, unnerving silence of Hill House.
written_by_MFA022.Excerpt2: Hill house, not sane, stood alone amongst the darkness. A house born within a garden of oleander, no person alive could claim witness to its birth, and so the poisonous intentions of the house were known only to itself. Only Dr. Montague, snaking up the thorn-lined driveway in a car packed with books, would observe the house’s final blooming, though even he, a man of scholarship and philosophy, a fastidious believer in the supernatural, would come to doubt what the Hill House had to show him. Dr. Montague was a man of doubt, not of the world, or of the unspoken phenomena hidden within it, but of himself, and his instincts, which he sought to justify through scholarship; Indeed, he arrived at Hill House surrounded by the false safety of his books on an errand of study, having rented the home at considerable personal and financial cost, with the hope of producing definitive work on psychic disturbances and their accompanying phenomena. He believed himself, after conducting a lifelong search for a haunted home, to have found Hill House; this was a false belief. It was Hill House that found Dr. Montague, alone in his study, nursing his failures with cognac in hand as he lingered over a newspaper clipping which happened to mention, offhandedly, the strange occurrences of a mansion atop a hill in a small New England town. This home could contain answers, he thought, slowing his car to park beneath the ominous gaze of the house's front windows, answers only I can find.
written_by_MFA022.Reason: Excerpt 2 contains fewer muddled images and sharper language than 1: "Hill house, not sane, stood alone amongst the darkness." This personification of Hill House differentiates it from other houses and establishes the "why" for the story immediately while also clarifying that Hill House is the central character. Excerpt 1 starts with the doctor, falsely making it seem like his story is penultimate.
