written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: At the end of the road, Hill House stood alone with jaws full of silence. Its windows stared unblinkingly. Its long shadow loomed like the hood of a cobra. The tight and winding corridors were not unlike veins, but rather than blood and life, all that ran through them was darkness. Hill House was not sane. Rather, it was a place where reality wobbled and warped into something unrecognizable. And now Dr. John Montague had come to cross the threshold. A Doctor of Philosophy in anthropology, Montague had dedicated his career to the study of supernatural phenomena. He was a reasonable sort of man who insisted on his own soundness of mind. He was stubborn and dogged in his pursuits, but always shuffled shyly around the fringes of academia, insecure about the reputation he had built for himself. He clung to his title of “doctor” with ferocious pride and brandished it like a badge at the slightest hint of skepticism from his colleagues. His ultimate goal had always been to find a genuine haunted house: a place that would offer up evidence so absolute that there could be no room for argument. It was a tumultuous and often disappointing journey that had, at last, led him to Hill House. After several fruitless grant applications for his proposed experiment on psychic disturbances, Montague decided to make a personal investment in the project and rent Hill House using his own savings. The cost was significant, but so was Montague’s belief that it was well worth the price.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: Hill House waited, its brooding silence pressing against the walls like a living thing, holding darkness within its brick and timber bones as it had for eighty years. Through its malevolent windows, it watched Dr. John Montague approach, his academic credentials clutched like a shield before him, as though his doctor of philosophy might protect him from whatever dwelled in the house's shadowed corners. He came with his leather briefcase and carefully organized notes, believing that science could explain away the whispers in empty rooms, the footsteps that followed no feet, the cold spots that lingered like breath on glass. The locals spoke of Hill House only in whispers, their eyes sliding away when they mentioned its name, but Dr. Montague saw only the promise of scholarly recognition, of footnotes and bibliographies and peer reviews. He paid his considerable rent to the Sanderson family without hesitation, never noticing how quickly they pocketed the money, as though it might carry some taint of the house itself. In his hotel room, preparing for his first night in Hill House, he arranged his instruments with precise care - thermometers, cameras, tape recorders - tools of rationality to measure the irrational. He did not yet understand that Hill House had been waiting for him, had perhaps called to him through all his years of searching, and that his arrival was merely the beginning of what the house had planned, as it stood against its hills, patient and hungry, its doors sensibly shut against the approaching night.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: Excerpt 2's anthropomorphizing of the house ("Through its malevolent windows, it watched...") is really effective, and adds a degree of suspense and high stakes that's lacking in Excerpt1, which relies solely on description that at times seems overdone ("It's long shadow loomed like the hood of a cobra," "The tight and winding corridors were not unlike veins, but rather than blood and life, all that ran through them was darkness"). While Excerpt1 feels like it's being told from an omniscient third person speaker or even a speaker close to Dr. Montague, Excerpt2 has the curious effect of feeling like it's being told by the house itself, or by a speaker *inside*/deeply familiar with the house. This effect is really unique.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Up on the tallest hill sat the aptly named Hill House, a place not entirely sane. From its high point, Hill House lorded over the town, judgmental in its solitude. The house enjoyed its loneliness, and the town preferred the continued isolation of Hill House. The windows were ever shuttered, the rusted main gate always locked, keeping the world out and the occupants in. Dr. John Montague was the latest resident, a man far more foolish than his doctorate in anthropology would lead one to believe. His path of study brought him not to the study of people, but deceased people. Dr. Montague considered himself an expert in paranormal happenings, a fact that left him with few peers. Academics shunned him, and he shunned ghost hunters. Formally organized academia needed to be inserted into the field of the supernatural if there was ever going to be a proper study done, and Dr. Montague was more than willing to use his credentials to move things along. Renting Hill House came at significant financial cost to Dr. Montague, but he was quite certain that this was the avenue that would lead him to career success. No one could look at Hill House and dismiss that it was a truly haunted house. Dr. Montague had researched the house himself and found its past riddled with the occult. Once he conducted his study and produced a paper that could double as a guidebook to the paranormal, the checks written to rent the house would cease to matter.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Hill House, a structure with a mind of its own, rested against the hills, its darkness palpable, its sanity questionable.  For eighty years it had borne silent witness to untold horrors, and eighty more it might endure, its walls upright, its floors firm, its doors closed, a tomb of secrets.  Within its depths, Dr. John Montague, a man of letters and a scholar of the unseen, sought to unravel the mysteries that clung to the house like cobwebs.  His excitement was a tangible thing, a nervous energy that thrummed beneath his skin as he surveyed his conquest.He had come seeking a haunted house, and Hill House, with its malevolent reputation, seemed to fit the bill.  It had cost him dearly, this pursuit of the paranormal, both in the coin of the realm and the currency of his reputation.Yet, he was undeterred, his resolve as firm as the foundations of the house itself.  He would have his proof, his definitive study of psychic disturbances, a testament to the unseen world that whispered just beyond the veil of perception. Dr. Montague, a man who clung to his title as if it were a life raft in a sea of skepticism, was determined to conquer the mysteries of Hill House.  He would face the darkness, the unseen forces that lurked within, and emerge with the truth, or be consumed by the shadows that stretched long and hungry within the walls of the house.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: Excerpt 1 personifies Hill House in an engaging, effective way. We transition smoothly from the introduction of the home to an introduction of Dr. John Montague. The writing is smooth, confident, and polished. "From its high point, Hill House lorded over the town, judgmental in its solitude." By contrast, Excerpt 2 relies on cliches: "a structure with a mind of its own", "a tangible thing, a nervous energy that thrummed", "clung to his title as if it were a life raft." The reliance upon cliched language makes Excerpt 2 less engaging and interesting to read.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Up on the tallest hill sat the aptly named Hill House, a place not entirely sane. From its high point, Hill House lorded over the town, judgmental in its solitude. The house enjoyed its loneliness, and the town preferred the continued isolation of Hill House. The windows were ever shuttered, the rusted main gate always locked, keeping the world out and the occupants in. His path of study brought him not to the study of people, but deceased people. Dr. Montague considered himself an expert in paranormal happenings, a fact that left him with few peers. Academics shunned him, and he shunned ghost hunters. Formally organized academia needed to be inserted into the field of the supernatural if there was ever going to be a proper study done, and Dr. Montague was more than willing to use his credentials to move things along. written_by_MFA025.Reason: In terms of efficacy, the narration of 1 is slightly less "insistent upon itself" in casting a foreboding tone, where 2 seems too strongly to insist on its characters being judged, whether it be the house judging the town or the narrator judging Dr. M for being "more foolish than his doctorate in anthropology would lead one to believe." written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: And before long lying in bed in this room my senses narrowed in totality. There was no escaping the shadow on the sash of the curtains flooding out in further shadows darkening the windowsill and washing the floorboards in lengthening patches of darker darknesses though still I attempted to move away from them even as they drifted over my legs in bed. They almost had me then. But I would not let them. No I would never let them. Not once. Because once is always. And the ticking hiccups of my grandfather’s watch that my father gave me in my pocket I could not either escape. Its rhythm beating hiccups against my leg made me think only of my father and every word he ever gave me to hold on to. The inescapability of clocks never outweighed by the conquered, momentary kingdoms of victories, he said, never outdone by wordly doings done in the face of all that we are faced with. These are but illusions and facades in the battlegrounds of time, he once said. But consider Jesus walking forty days forty nights and the long and lonely light-rays and consider even still Saint Francis’s Little Sister Death, consider the weight of Jesus and light and death, he said. Consider them. Thinking of my father in this way and his words in bed amid the shadows and the ticking he gave me so long ago only deepened my fear of the inevitable. The ineffable. The possible, terrible pointlessness of it all.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: The shadow of the sash curved across the dim curtains, and the watch on the nightstand ticked steadily, a quiet insistence that time itself bore witness to all that was and all that ever would be. I could feel it in my chest, that weight, a pressing reminder of my grandfather's words—words handed down through my father like a relic, tarnished by the grime of despair, polished by futility. Time does not pause, does not forgive. Its victories are hollow, its passing immutable, carving grooves into the soul like water wears down stone, relentless and unyielding.The ticking grew louder, or perhaps it was my thoughts that gave it resonance, filling the room, saturating the air. And in that sound, that metronome of inevitability, I found the tether of memory and the dread of its permanence. Was it my father’s voice I heard or my own thoughts as they spiraled? His words wrapped around my consciousness like the fraying tendrils of a dream that refuses to die. Jesus walked once, on light-rays long and lonely, and Francis whispered to Death as though she were kin, a sister who waited not cruelly but certainly.I lay there, the watch’s rhythm tethering me to the present even as my spirit floated, weightless, into the past and future. Time, unbroken and unseen, bore its teeth, gnawing at the fragile membrane between what is and what is not, what could be and what will never be. I closed my eyes, and still, the ticking remained.
written_by_MFA015.Reason: Excerpt 1 begins with sharp stiking language and without the passive voice of excerpt 2: "And before long lying in bed in this room my senses narrowed in totality." This embeds us as readers in the narrator's sensorial zone of interest, allowing us to experience the totality of how their environment is affecting them.

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: The shadow of the sash falls down the curtain, a pallid crescent in the gloom of the room.  I can hear the ticking of the watch, a steady pulse in the quiet.  It was Grandfather’s watch, and now it is Father’s, and someday it will be mine.  The watch ticks on, a metronome marking the inexorable passage of time.  Father said, “You cannot conquer time.  You can only try to forget it.”  But how can one forget time when it is always there, ticking away, a constant reminder of our mortality?  The watch hands move, a slow, relentless dance towards the end.  “Time is a relentless and hungry force,” Father said.  “It devours all things – youth, beauty, even memory.”  The watch ticks on, a tiny machine marking the moments of our lives.  Each tick brings us closer to the end, to the final silence.  “Victories in life are fleeting,” Father said.  “They are but illusions in the face of time’s infinite and hungry maw.”  The watch ticks on, a constant reminder of our mortality.  It is a sound that haunts me, a sound that echoes the futility of our existence.  “Jesus walking on Galilee,” Father said, “and Saint Francis, speaking to his Little Sister Death.  Both of them knew that time could not be conquered, that it could only be endured.”  The watch ticks on, a steady beat in the silence of the room.  It is a sound that I cannot escape, a sound that reminds me of my own mortality.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: The chiffon curtain like a pleated hourglass hung cinched by the dark of the sash. It stood unstirred in the limpid bedroom air. No, the empty air was preoccupied with the counting of its ceaseless age. My grandfather’s watch–which still belonged to my father even after his death as dogs belong to their buried owners, circling their grave and howling the premonitions my grandfather had uttered in his own bed: life being one big fever dream, all its hills and troughs in one fell swoop wrenched from under you, a dream from which you will be wrenched, and you wake in the unending dark where you take no triumphs with you, and the ceaseless hounds of timestamp flat your burial mound and the sky’s days pass beyond–ticked incessantly somewhere in the dark. My father talked about the dark in a similar night’s stifled room. How Saint Francis welcomed Little Sister Death as the dark all around Jesus when he walked along the long and lonely light-rays. Beyond that dark is nothing but dark, that we only know dark from the little light we got. We only know time because we count it, but countless time goes unticked in the unending dark, so much time there is no before, no after, the unnumbered breezes with no curtain to shape them. No, my time is never truly had. I felt the air too thick to breathe.
written_by_MFA003.Reason: Both excerpts have some melodramatic elements but Excerpt 2 is using more novel approaches, fresh languages, and playful language ("the chiffon curtain like a pleated hourglass"). Excerpt 2 seems to be taking a more original approach and playing with sentence structure, length, and cadence, while Excerpt 1 is a bit repetitive and clunky. Phrases like "The doom of the room," with their rhyming cadence, are overly melodramatic.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: A moment came when I stirred from my private twilight and noticed two things. First, the stain of shadow upon the curtains. Then, the ticking of the watch. It was a fine instrument that had been passed down from my grandfather to my father to me. Both of these men were long dead, and it seemed that in my inheriting the watch, I had inherited their fate: the impending loss of a war with time. It was a fate my father had tried in vain to prepare me for.“Time,” he once said to me, “is inexorable. It can be fought, but never conquered. Our victories are as futile as our struggles.” Time was and is and had and always would win. All I could do was lay in bed and listen to the steady, measured thump of its advance, like the footsteps of an army unafraid of being spotted by its enemy. The ticking seemed to stop coming from the watch. Now, it was coming from everywhere. Time bled from the walls and windows and floors, and with the flood came memory. I thought of my father describing Jesus walking along long and lonely light rays. I thought of his stories about St. Francis’s “Little Sister Death” who left no flower un-plucked. The waters of time rose and roiled around me. I wondered if I would be able to float, and as swiftly as the question came upon me, so did its answer. Time would rise; I would sink.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: The shadow moved like time itself across the curtain, not marking but mocking, and I could hear it, the watch, grandfather's watch (not mine because how can time belong to any man when time owns all men), ticking away beneath my pillow where Father had placed it saying Time is the mausoleum of all hope and desire, boy, and you'll learn that too, and I lay there hearing it not with my ears anymore but with my blood, my bones, each tick-tick-tick like Christ's own footsteps walking not on water but on those long golden light-rays that stretched across eternity, across all the Compson failures and pride, across Sister Death herself who waited patient and humble like that shadow on my curtain, and I knew then what Father meant about time being dead until the clock stops because I could feel it dying with each breath, each tick, could feel it running through my fingers like the river I would find later, running away from all the Quentins that ever were or would be, and still that shadow moved, and still that ticking came, and I thought about how Father said a man is the sum of his misfortunes, and how that sum was ticking away beneath my pillow, beneath my head, beneath my thoughts that weren't really thoughts anymore but just the sound of time itself, marking nothing, changing nothing, just being, like that shadow, like that watch, like all the Quentins that ever were.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: Excerpt two formalizes the effect of time's passage through its winding sentences and breathless syntax (the excerpt is one long sentence), where excerpt one has a staccato rhythm, which dilutes the character's emotional state. Excerpt one expresses ideas so simply as to be unimpactful: "Time was and is and had and always would win." Excerpt two instead deploys figurative language that strikes a more resonant chord: "Time is the mausoleum of all hope and desire." Excerpt one tends to feel repetitive, in part because of its routine usage of short sentences and stock statements about mortality, whereas the language of Excerpt two continues to surprise and arrest readers.

This simile is such an egregious cliche that, by comparison, nearly any writing would be preferable to it. Unfortunately, the similes of this variety continue as the excerpt goes on, becoming more overwrought and less impactful as they go ("… like Christ's own footsteps walking not on water but on those long golden light-rays that stretched across eternity"). The run-on sentences accentuate this problem, creating a vortex of meaning unbound to any particular scene, with images moving in and out of different metaphors. The more restrained prose of excerpt 2, while also often dealing in cliche, is consistent in scene and in introducing memories and concepts, which themselves are given internal scenes ("It was a fate my father had tried in vain to prepare me for. 'Time,' he once said to me, 'is inexorable. It can be fought, but never conquered. Our victories are as futile as our struggles.'"). Because excerpt 2 is clear about the position of its narrator ("All I could do was lay in bed and listen") and grounds itself in relationship to its contents, its moments of flowery language are much more coherent.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: First, in the south, we were stormed by the spotted sickness, little red bumps that went from the blanket to the body; then, by the gun, we moved westward to Dakota land, thousands of us dragging our feet across endless miles. Those of us who didn't drop dead from the spots signed a treaty. Before long, we moved once more, condemned to exile, our land taken away by right of the government's stamped document. 1914: Another sickness called 'consumption' rolled in as a terrible storm does, its invisible winds running into our mouths and choking us. After all that, we coughed to our deaths. It came slowly: not like a massacre but like a lost war. We were living six to a room back then, and the cough jumped from one Anishinabe brother to another. The whole Pillager family became ill within a fortnight, the eight of them wasting away in a single room. My whole family went, too. Our tribe, once a tightly woven quilt, unraveled; the knots came loose, the patterns disintegrated into bright threads. Merely fifty years have passed since my birth, yet I am now called an elder, the last of the Nanapush. I remember the end of our lives, the final rites of our traditions. I led the last buffalo hunt. I saw the last bear shot. I trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt. I felled the last birch tree older than a sapling. I remember how, as the sickness razed our people, I went into the room with the eight members of the Pillager family. I fed them water, buffalo meat, and bread. I brought them wet cloths and herbs to ease their fever and coughing. I saved the last of them, the daughter. And I remember receiving the government papers that would rid us of our land and rights. I refused to sign.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: The spotted sickness came first, creeping up from the south. It stole through the village like a hungry ghost, leaving empty spaces where laughter and life once thrived. Then came the long walk westward, the elders leaning heavily on their canes, the children clinging to their mothers’ skirts. We signed a treaty in Dakota land, our fingers tracing unfamiliar symbols on the white man's paper. But treaties are as fragile as spiderwebs in the wind, easily torn and forgotten. The government men came again, their words like sharp stones cutting through our hearts. Exile. Loss. Land stolen, not by force, but by the stroke of a pen on official documents.In 1914, a new sickness arrived, a slow, insidious cough that consumed the lungs and the spirit. Consumption, they called it. It spread through the reservation like wildfire, leaving behind a trail of sorrow and empty beds. The Pillagers, huddled close in their crowded homes, succumbed one by one. My family, my friends, my neighbors, all taken by the relentless disease. I watched them go, helpless to stop the tide of grief that threatened to drown me.And then, there was only me. Nanapush, the last of his line, an elder at fifty, my hair prematurely streaked with the white of winter. I led the last buffalo hunt, the thundering hooves echoing through the vast emptiness of the plains. I saw the last bear fall. I trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt. I felled the last old birch tree, its leaves whispering secrets to the wind.But even in the face of such overwhelming loss, I found the strength to resist. I saved the last of the Pillager family, their faces etched with the same sorrow that mirrored my own. I refused to sign the government papers, those insidious documents that would erase us, make us invisible in our own land.

The "little red bumps that went from the blanket to the body" is a much more chilling, evocative way to describe the "spotted sickness [that] came first" from Par 2. I also think that the images in Par. 2 are much more expected and rote than the ones in the Par. 1. "It spread through...like wildfire" "the children clinging to their mother's skirts" -- both of these are images I've seen and heard many times before, and just don't hold a candle to the more startling "rolled in as a terrible storm does" or the tribe as "a tightly woven quilt, unraveled." I also think that the sentences have more variation and fluidity in Par. 1 than they do in Par. 2, which I think speaks to a higher fluency. written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: First it was the spotted sickness that unfurled from the south. I was not there, but I remember. Then forced migration westward, to Dakota land, and the Anishinabe signed a treaty. These were made to be broken and to break us. After came more displacements, the government making exiles of us again. So many documents and so much displacement. I lie on my back and these papers press hard on my chest when I think of them. In 1914 it was consumption, creeping slowly through the reservation like woodsmoke. Taking us one by one, and unraveling us, and my family could not escape it either. The Pillagers were unraveled by this new sickness and so was our community, huddled so close together as we were. Unable to escape each other, shoulder, pressed to shoulder, and unable to escape the sickness. I was the only one of us who lived. Nanapush, the sole survivor. For this suffering I am already an elder, but I am only fifty years old. And for this terrible privilege I have been witness to the end of the traditions. I have led the last buffalo hunt, saw the last bear killed. Trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt, and felled the last old birch. Sometimes we understood we were doing these things for the final time. Other times, we didn't realize until after. The loss hurts in my teeth. It lives in my early wrinkles and sore body. But I have saved the Pillager family. When the government comes with more papers, more opportunities to strip us of our land and our identity, I have resisted. I did not sign. I will not sign—we will not be exiles again. Too much has already been taken. The Anishinabe persist, and I will continue to resist for the Pillagers who are lost, and for those of us who carry on.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: In the damp quiet of that reservation, I stood as the last thread holding together the vast, frayed tapestry of our people, the Anishinabe. Sickness had come, spotted and relentless, rising from the south to crawl across our bodies, marking us for the grave. We fled westward, believing Dakota land might swallow us whole and offer peace, only to be met with treaties that tangled words into chains we could never untether. The land we walked became paper; paper became exile. Yet it was not over. In 1914, another ghost, slow and smothering, stalked us—consumption, it was called. It seeped through the fragile walls of our homes, latching onto breath, pulling entire families under its cold, merciless blanket. I saw the Pillagers go, one by one, slipping into the quiet where I alone remained. Fifty years old, they called me an elder, though my face bore fewer lines than my spirit. Time had sped in its cruelty. I had seen the last buffalo fall beneath our arrows, the last bear stagger through our woods, the final beaver with a pelt worth holding. The birches I once leaned against as a child, their bark aglow with the sun, were nothing but broken stumps. Each loss carved another hollowness, and still, I stood. I saved what was left—the last of the Pillager family, the name that carried its own strength. When they brought papers, government seals pressed flat against the lives they meant to strip away, I took the pen in my hand but never let it touch the page. They could take everything—our animals, our trees, even the air that filled our lungs. But they would not take the land, not from me, not from what I carried. I stared back at them, unflinching, as if daring them to try harder, without fear, without shame.
written_by_MFA026.Reason: This was close but overall I thought the sentences in Excerpt2 were more dynamic. For example, these lines in Excerpt2 – “I had seen the last buffalo fall beneath our arrows, the last bear stagger through our woods, the final beaver with a pelt worth holding. The birches I once leaned against as a child, their bark aglow with the sun, were nothing but broken stumps” – are varied and interesting; the deaths of the animals are depicted using active language (“stagger, fall”), allowing us to visualize these moments, and the example of the birches is depicted with a childhood memory. By contrast, in Excerpt1 this sequence reads more like a list (‘last buffalo hunt”, “last bear killed”).

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: I am Nanapush, and my people, the Anishinabe, have borne floods of suffering that rose like tidal waves over the generations. We’ve learned to endure the violent waters. First, there was the terrible spotted sickness that came from the south, killing us by the dozens and scarring the faces of the living. There was the long migration west, where we were marched to the Dakotas with an army at our backs, and the treaty we signed at gunpoint. Then came another exile—a slow dismemberment of the land that remained, bled dry by a series of laws and documents. My people were left alone for some time after that. But in 1914, consumption began to prowl the perimeter of the reservation. Its footfall was silent, though its presence was anything but invisible. When consumption snapped its jaws, it unraveled the community death by death, trapping families like the Pillagers inside, left to huddle in their close quarters and wait out the disease. I see now that the disease was waiting them out instead. The Pillagers succumbed to the sickness one by one—all of them but me. Although I am only fifty, I have risen through the ranks by default. I am considered an elder now. In truth, I am merely a survivor. It is under my watch that our traditional way of life has finally been extinguished. It was I who led the final buffalo hunt, trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt, and felled the last of the old birch trees. Loss is my constant companion. It visits me as it visited my ancestors, but I have found a small mercy within its grasp. I have preserved the last of the Pillager family, refusing the men from the government who come with more papers to sign, seeking more ways to strip the Anishinabe of their land and identity. As long as my name is Nanapush, I will not forfeit that final power.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: The spotted sickness came first, creeping up from the south like a shadow that darkens the earth before a storm. We didn't know then that it was just the beginning, just the first thread being pulled from the fabric of our world. I was young when we were pushed westward to Dakota land, our feet leaving tracks in soil that wasn't ours, our hands reaching out to sign papers we couldn't read. The government men smiled with teeth like tombstones while our people's names were written down, recorded, filed away in drawers that would never open again. Then came 1914, and with it the consumption—slow, patient, hungry as winter. It ate through our families like fire through dry grass, starting with the Pillagers who lived close as bark to wood. I watched them fall, one after another, until the silence in their cabin was louder than any drum. My own family went the same way, leaving me to carry their names like stones in my pocket, weighing me down, making me an elder at fifty though my hair had barely grayed. I led the last buffalo hunt, my heart heavy as I watched the dust rise from their hooves. I was there when the last bear fell, when the last beaver with a mature pelt swam into my trap, when the last ancient birch dropped its leaves for the final time. The old ways slipped through our fingers like water, impossible to hold. But I refused to let it all go. When I saved the last of the Pillagers, I held on tight, my fingers cramping around what remained. Those government papers came again and again, whispering promises of money, of progress, of change. But I knew better. I'd seen enough of their promises turn to dust in our mouths. This time, I kept my pen still, my name unwritten, my piece of earth ungiven.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: While both passages are quite floral and elaborate, I feel that Excerpt 1, despite its many metaphors, is more fluent and coherent than Excerpt 2. "When consumption snapped its jaws, it unraveled the community death by death, trapping families like the Pillagers inside, left to huddle in their close quarters and wait out the disease" (Excerpt 1) is slightly overwritten but not necessarily condescending, whereas "The government men smiled with teeth like tombstones while our people's names were written down, recorded, filed away in drawers that would never open again" (Excerpt 2) feels like a stereotype-ridden attempt to emulate Indigenous fiction. It was difficult to read Excerpt 2, so I'm selecting Excerpt 1 as the stronger excerpt here!

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: I am Nanapush, and my people, the Anishinabe, have borne floods of suffering that rose like tidal waves over the generations. We’ve learned to endure the violent waters. First, there was the terrible spotted sickness that came from the south, killing us by the dozens and scarring the faces of the living. There was the long migration west, where we were marched to the Dakotas with an army at our backs, and the treaty we signed at gunpoint. Then came another exile—a slow dismemberment of the land that remained, bled dry by a series of laws and documents. My people were left alone for some time after that. But in 1914, consumption began to prowl the perimeter of the reservation. Its footfall was silent, though its presence was anything but invisible. When consumption snapped its jaws, it unraveled the community death by death, trapping families like the Pillagers inside, left to huddle in their close quarters and wait out the disease. I see now that the disease was waiting them out instead. The Pillagers succumbed to the sickness one by one—all of them but me. Although I am only fifty, I have risen through the ranks by default. I am considered an elder now. In truth, I am merely a survivor. It is under my watch that our traditional way of life has finally been extinguished. It was I who led the final buffalo hunt, trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt, and felled the last of the old birch trees. Loss is my constant companion. It visits me as it visited my ancestors, but I have found a small mercy within its grasp. I have preserved the last of the Pillager family, refusing the men from the government who come with more papers to sign, seeking more ways to strip the Anishinabe of their land and identity. As long as my name is Nanapush, I will not forfeit that final power.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: The spotted sickness came first, creeping up from the south like a shadow that darkens the earth before a storm. We didn't know then that it was just the beginning, just the first thread being pulled from the fabric of our world. I was young when we were pushed westward to Dakota land, our feet leaving tracks in soil that wasn't ours, our hands reaching out to sign papers we couldn't read. The government men smiled with teeth like tombstones while our people's names were written down, recorded, filed away in drawers that would never open again. Then came 1914, and with it the consumption—slow, patient, hungry as winter. It ate through our families like fire through dry grass, starting with the Pillagers who lived close as bark to wood. I watched them fall, one after another, until the silence in their cabin was louder than any drum. My own family went the same way, leaving me to carry their names like stones in my pocket, weighing me down, making me an elder at fifty though my hair had barely grayed. I led the last buffalo hunt, my heart heavy as I watched the dust rise from their hooves. I was there when the last bear fell, when the last beaver with a mature pelt swam into my trap, when the last ancient birch dropped its leaves for the final time. The old ways slipped through our fingers like water, impossible to hold. But I refused to let it all go. When I saved the last of the Pillagers, I held on tight, my fingers cramping around what remained. Those government papers came again and again, whispering promises of money, of progress, of change. But I knew better. I'd seen enough of their promises turn to dust in our mouths. This time, I kept my pen still, my name unwritten, my piece of earth ungiven.

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: I call them the Spaghetti Days (they lasted an entire week but the singular week standing alone bothers me). On my way home from work, I’d pass the kitchen utility store where, in the shop window, there sat a stack of metal pots. I wanted the bottom one, the one shining against the rain the day I stepped through the shop door. Buying an empty pot felt wrong—too spacious—so I also bought an egg timer. But it rattled hollow around the pot. I kept walking until I reached the foreign supermarket with its crates of imported tomatoes under the awning. I put some tomatoes in that pot along with white onions, garlic, oregano, a green glass bottle of olive oil, and boxes and boxes of dry spaghetti. This, for me, was the start of a deep ritual. Steam from the boiling water fogged my kitchen window as I imagined having guests share my tea and salad. They’d comment on the nuance in smells and praise my subtle changes with the sauce and spices. But an audience would have been too much, too cramped and restricting. Spaghetti was best enjoyed alone. And being alone, there were always leftovers I’d scoop into a plastic container. At the end of the week, when it couldn’t fit any more spaghetti, I emptied all of it into the trash. No matter how hard I scrubbed the container, I couldn’t get the red stains out. I threw out the container too.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: For an entire year, spaghetti became the core of my existence—a solitary ritual that shaped my days. I’d visit a dimly lit specialty store downtown, where the air carried the faint tang of aged balsamic and oregano, to buy the essentials: a large pot, a precise kitchen timer, and an assortment of imported ingredients. Supermarkets catering to foreigners became my haunts, offering me tomatoes that smelled of distant summers, garlic as pungent as a whispered confession, and every conceivable variety of pasta. Back in my small apartment, I experimented tirelessly with sauces. Rich tomato-based ones simmered for hours, creamy carbonaras that threatened to stick to the pan if I turned my back even for a second. The scent of garlic sizzling in olive oil seeped into my walls, my furniture, even my clothes. Eating spaghetti became a meditative act, the fork twirling endlessly in a repetitive choreography that mirrored my own existence. Tea steeped nearby, a salad of crisp lettuce and vinaigrette sat untouched until the last strand of pasta disappeared. There was no music, no voices, no distraction. Just the warm embrace of routine, filling the cracks left by loneliness. Each Sunday bled into the next, the days indistinguishable but somehow comforting, as if the rhythm of boiling water and clinking plates was a language only I could speak.
written_by_MFA003.Reason: This one is more difficult to me, as I feel like these excerpts are of similar quality. I prefer one to two at the end of the day, though. I think 2 also loses some effectiveness because it gets bogged down in its own images and meanings ("the fork twriling endlessly in a repetitive choreography that mirrored my own existence."). In terms of fluency, the writing in 2 feels a bit overly ornate and sophomoric, while the writing in 1 is comparatively plainspoken but effective in expressing the contents of the excerpt.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: During that time I was much consumed by spaghetti. The process of cooking it was satisfying, but the idea of perfecting it was addictive. Like any dedicated student, I gathered the necessary equipment. I purchased a large pot and a kitchen timer from the specialty store across town and stocked up on spices, tomatoes, and all the pastas under the sun. The supermarket I bought the ingredients from was a place that catered to foreigners, but no one seemed to question my presence there. In a way, spaghetti and I were still strangers to each other. Back in my apartment, the experimenting began. What I lacked in formal training I had to make up for in creativity. I cooked feverishly. The smell of garlic was in my hair; the smell of onion was in the carpet; the smell of olive oil was in the wallpaper. Spaghetti sauce consumed me and the place I called home. It even spilled into my dreams. It was very important that I only ate spaghetti alone. It’s the kind of dish that insists on solitude. Before I knew it, I was following a new routine. Spaghetti was the centerpiece of every meal—balanced out, of course, by tea and a simple salad. My blissful Spaghetti Days stretched on and on from Sunday to Sunday. If there was an end in sight, I didn’t want to see it.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: There was a time when spaghetti became an obsession, a solitary ritual in my small apartment.  I had this idea that spaghetti was a dish best enjoyed alone, savoring every twirl of the fork, every subtle nuance of the sauce.  It was a dish that demanded solitude, a quiet contemplation of the simple things in life. I had made a pilgrimage to a specialty store, a treasure trove of culinary tools, where I acquired a large pot, a gleaming stainless steel monument to my spaghetti ambitions, and a kitchen timer, its ticking a metronome marking the passage of time until my spaghetti was cooked to perfection.  From supermarkets catering to foreigners, I gathered exotic spices, plump tomatoes, and an assortment of pasta brands, each promising a unique spaghetti experience. My small apartment transformed into a spaghetti laboratory, filled with the rich aroma of garlic, onion, and olive oil, a fragrant symphony that clung to the curtains, the furniture, even my clothes. I experimented with countless sauces, each simmering on the stove, a testament to my dedication to the art of spaghetti. Sundays marked the beginning of my spaghetti week, a repetitive cycle of cooking and consuming spaghetti, my days revolving around this singular dish.  Tea and a simple salad were the supporting players, but spaghetti was the star, the center around which my culinary world revolved.  There was a comfort in this ritual, a sense of order in the twirling of the spaghetti, the methodical consumption of the dish.Spaghetti Days, I called them, stretching from Sunday to Sunday, a solitary symphony of flavors and textures, a testament to my love affair with this humble dish.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: I don't really have a clear preference here, because each has different strengths, but I've ultimately gone for Excerpt 1. What I appreciate about Excerpt 1 is that it feels more humorous on balance, which fits with the tone of this somewhat bizarre quest the narrator is on. I also appreciated the relative economy of the opening line: "During that time I was much consumed by spaghetti." Something I did like about Excerpt 2 is that it is more specific about images: e.g. "a kitchen timer, its ticking a metronome marking the passage of time until my spaghetti was cooked to perfection."

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: Around seven years ago now I would go down to the Italian Market, weekends, to stock up on what I soon deemed the essentials: oregano, bay leaves, fennel seeds, butter, lemon. Among others. Nothing in my life pointed to this beginning. No crises or wayward desires, no history of culinary skills resurfaced, and I cannot say, exactly, what became of me during this time. Why I found myself in the aisles of specialty stores, several miles from home. Why I, each weekend, sought a furtherance: going beyond what I had cooked the week prior, with more tools, sauces, and research on what breed of spaghetti I would cook next. I tracked down a Le Creuset stockpot, a pasta roller, an egg timer. I spent too many hours over my stove at home, simmering garlic in olive oil, and over the cutting board on my countertop, chopping onions, tomatoes, basil. Though innocent at first, soon this meal prep encompassed every evening, Sunday through Sunday, and in this way I practiced what I now call my Spaghetti Days. During this time I never shared a meal with anyone else, coming to believe that spaghetti, along with my evening earl gray and caesar salad, was best enjoyed alone. Soon I realized it wasn’t desire that brought me to the habit, but ritualistic necessity. It was about hands, and what it meant to keep them moving. As soon as this realization came, all the magic of preparing spaghetti washed away.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: It was during that strange winter when I began my obsession with cooking spaghetti. Like a monk devoted to a peculiar religion, I wandered through foreign grocery stores, filling my basket with olive oil bottles that gleamed like ancient artifacts and tomatoes so red they seemed to hold secrets from another world. The specialty shop owner—a thin man with circular glasses who looked like he could speak to cats—sold me a deep blue pot that seemed bottomless and a kitchen timer that ticked with the precision of a heartbeat. Strange how such ordinary objects can suddenly feel magical, as if they've crossed over from a parallel universe where pasta is a sacred thing. In my small apartment, which felt more like a submarine than a living space, I'd stand at the stove watching the water boil, counting the bubbles like stars. The steam would rise and fog my windows, creating a barrier between my spaghetti sanctuary and the outside world. I never invited anyone to these meals—somehow, I knew this was a ritual meant for solitude, like writing poetry at midnight or counting clouds. Every Sunday, I'd prepare the same meal: spaghetti swimming in sauce that I'd cooked for exactly twenty-seven minutes, a green salad that seemed to whisper ancient mysteries, and tea that tasted of distant memories. The garlic and onion fragrance would seep into my clothes, my books, my dreams, until I couldn't tell where the cooking ended and I began.
written_by_MFA015.Reason: Excerpt one makes use of unintuitive syntactical constructions, such as: "Around seven years ago now I would go down to the Italian Market" which presents a past habit in an ambiguous way; whereas excerpt two does it clearly and simply: "It was during that strange winter when I began my obsession with cooking spaghetti." Similarly, excerpt one dilutes the emotional resonance of narrative moments; where excerpt two makes the reader feel some melancholy around the narrator's obsessive spaghetti-making, excerpt one presents it more whimsically, without the undertone of pathos. Excerpt two is seamed through with religious and cosmic imagery ("Like a monk..." and "I'd stand at the stove watching the water boil, counting the bubbles like stars") which lends the activity a grandeur; excerpt one presents it merely as "Spaghetti days," as if it were a hobby.

Why I found myself in the aisles of specialty stores, several miles from home. Why I, each weekend, sought a furtherance: going beyond what I had cooked the week prior, with more tools, sauces, and research on what breed of spaghetti I would cook next. I tracked down a Le Creuset stockpot, a pasta roller, an egg timer. I spent too many hours over my stove at home, simmering garlic in olive oil, and over the cutting board on my countertop, chopping onions, tomatoes, basil. Though innocent at first, soon this meal prep encompassed every evening, Sunday through Sunday, and in this way I practiced what I now call my Spaghetti Days. During this time I never shared a meal with anyone else, coming to believe that spaghetti, along with my evening earl gray and caesar salad, was best enjoyed alone. Soon I realized it wasn’t desire that brought me to the habit, but ritualistic necessity. It was about hands, and what it meant to keep them moving. As soon as this realization came, all the magic of preparing spaghetti washed away.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: It was during that strange winter when I began my obsession with cooking spaghetti. Like a monk devoted to a peculiar religion, I wandered through foreign grocery stores, filling my basket with olive oil bottles that gleamed like ancient artifacts and tomatoes so red they seemed to hold secrets from another world. The specialty shop owner—a thin man with circular glasses who looked like he could speak to cats—sold me a deep blue pot that seemed bottomless and a kitchen timer that ticked with the precision of a heartbeat. Strange how such ordinary objects can suddenly feel magical, as if they've crossed over from a parallel universe where pasta is a sacred thing. In my small apartment, which felt more like a submarine than a living space, I'd stand at the stove watching the water boil, counting the bubbles like stars. The steam would rise and fog my windows, creating a barrier between my spaghetti sanctuary and the outside world. I never invited anyone to these meals—somehow, I knew this was a ritual meant for solitude, like writing poetry at midnight or counting clouds. Every Sunday, I'd prepare the same meal: spaghetti swimming in sauce that I'd cooked for exactly twenty-seven minutes, a green salad that seemed to whisper ancient mysteries, and tea that tasted of distant memories. The garlic and onion fragrance would seep into my clothes, my books, my dreams, until I couldn't tell where the cooking ended and I began.
written_by_MFA015.Reason: The second excerpt is overwritten, including metaphors that don't make any particular sense or seem to have much of a purpose; for example, the line "olive oil bottles that gleamed like ancient artifacts and tomatoes so red they seemed to hold secrets from another world" isn't very coherent - ancient artifacts don't have a particular gleam and redness doesn't convey a "secret from another world." The first excerpt is much more grounded, and in contrast to that realist grounding, the surreality of this spaghetti obsession becomes ever stranger. It also ends on a note of particular realization, a thematic cap (that the cooking is a "ritualistic necessity" born from the narrator's pleasure in keeping their hands moving); the second excerpt, however, veers into meaningless abstraction: "The garlic and onion fragrance would seep into my clothes, my books, my dreams, until I couldn't tell where the cooking ended and I began."

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: She had it all planned out, she said, though she wouldn't tell me exactly when. Like the coming of the Lord, she joked, no one knows the day or the hour. Her voice was steady but her hands shook as she arranged and rearranged the little heap of mail on her bedside table. I thought about my own mail piling up at home—how long would I need to stay?—and felt ashamed for thinking of such things. The practical always intrudes on the sacred, I suppose. She spoke of her body's betrayals with a kind of weary impatience, the way you might discuss a chronically late friend who nevertheless remained dear to you. Don't ask me about the pills, she said. I won't tell you what they are or where they came from. It's better that way. For your protection, she added, though I wondered if it wasn't more for her peace of mind. The secret felt heavy between us, like a third presence in the room. Looking at her face, lined with pain but still beautiful in its determination, I found it unthinkable to ask the questions that pressed against my throat: When? How soon? Will I be here? Later that night, I called S. and told her everything, breaking my promise of silence before it was even a day old. "I just need someone else to know," I said, and she understood, or said she did. But afterward I lay awake, thinking about loyalty and betrayal, about the boundaries between caring for someone and caring for yourself. About how even in death—especially in death—we are never quite as alone as we might wish to be.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: A good friend of mine told me about her plans for death. More precisely, she told me she was planning to take matters into her own hands. I asked her what she meant by this, and she just gave me a look that said, are you going to make me spell it out for you? No, I wasn’t going to make her spell it out, and she went on, saying that she had gotten quite impatient about the whole thing. She was ready, she said, and she wanted to bow out while there was still time. My friend’s body had never fared well when it was invaded by illness. It also didn’t fare well when it was invaded by medicine. As a teenager, she had lots of problems with headaches. Stomachaches, too, but she didn’t talk about that as much. She was also allergic to many things. Of dying, she said this: I want it to feel natural, without anything getting in the way. She wouldn’t say how this would happen. Just like the coming of the Lord, nobody would know until it was already here. I had two main concerns. One of them was practical—if I came to stay with her and supervise her wellbeing, my mail would pile up. The other was that I found it unthinkable to ask her any direct questions. Questions like, when? Questions like, where? My friend insisted on secrecy and made me promise not to tell anyone about her plan, and especially not about her drug of choice. She said this would bring her peace and give me protection. To be honest, I did want both of those things. But sometimes I can’t help myself. I told someone without even meaning to. I made him promise not to tell.
written_by_MFA029.Reason:
I think Excerpt1 is better than Excerpt2. Firstly: Excerpt1 feels more grounded in scene than Excerpt2, which feels floaty and out of time and space. While we get the same sort of high-concept thoughts in both (Excerpt1: "When? How soon? Will I be here?" Excerpt2: "Questions like, when? Questions like, where?") these meandering thoughts feel more attached to reality and have more emotional weight in Excerpt1 due to the fact that they are grounded in a scene of an exchange of dialogue rather than the recounting of an exchange of dialogue, as it is written in Excerpt2. written_by_MFA010.Excerpt1: I remember things. I remember how I felt when my friend talked about taking her own life. She wasn’t planning to commit suicide exactly. But she wanted her life to come to an end, she said. Her honesty made me pause and I wondered what I should do in such a situation. Could I make her change her mind? Would I have to look after her things and live with guilt? It would’ve been different if my friend didn’t want to handle “her situation” on her own terms. She, who had always been a planner, had even decided which drug she wanted to use to die, and asked me to keep it a secret, both for her sake and for my “protection,” whatever that meant. What concerned me though was that she wanted to do it soon. She said it slowly and calmly, but her tone was riddled with impatience and readiness. My friend had been ill for a long time and her body had not been responding well to treatments. She had spent so much in hospitals that now she wanted death to feel natural, without any interventions or disruptions. Smooth and clean. She hoped death would arrive like an unexpected guest. “Like the coming of the Lord, you know?” she said, with a laugh. I was in two minds. I wanted to know when she was planning for it all to go down, but it felt unthinkable to probe directly about her timeline. And, I felt equally concerned with more practical issues. If I were to stay with my friend during her final days, my mail would pile up. What would I do then? And what would happen to everything she had? It was all this and more about her, including her choice of pill, that I recounted to another friend of mine later in the day.
written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: She’d said, “I want to handle this in my own way, on my own terms.”Her words hung in the air, heavy with finality and a hint of defiance.“I’m tired of waiting,” she continued, her voice a mix of weariness and determination.“I’m tired of this body failing me, of the endless treatments, the uncertainty.”She spoke of wanting to die peacefully, naturally, without any interference.“I don’t want any interventions, any disruptions,” she’d said.“I don’t want anyone trying to prolong this… existence.” She paused, a wry smile flickering across her face.“I don’t want anyone trying to play God,” she added, her tone a blend of humor and solemnity.Her words echoed in my mind as I walked down the street, the weight of our conversation pressing on me.I thought about her situation, her desire for autonomy, her frustration with the slow, unpredictable decay of her body.I thought about her wish for a peaceful, natural death, her refusal to let anyone “play God.”I thought about her insistence on secrecy, her plea for me not to mention her plans to anyone, not even my closest confidantes.I felt a knot of tension tighten in my chest, a conflict between my loyalty to her and my own need to process this heavy situation.I thought about the consequences of her choice, the potential legal ramifications, the emotional toll it would take on those who cared about her. I thought about my own role in this, my promise to support her, my fear of being implicated, my desire to protect her and myself.I felt a surge of guilt, a sense of betrayal, as I remembered the conversation I’d had with my therapist, the one person I’d confided in, breaking my promise to her.I tried to justify my actions, telling myself that I needed someone to talk to, someone to help me navigate this emotional minefield.But the guilt lingered, a constant reminder of my broken promise.
written_by_MFA010.Reason: While Excerpt 2 does contain some somewhat cliched language (e.g. "someone to help me navigate this emotional minefield," "a constant reminder of my broken promise") I still prefer it because the various devices employed make the scenario feel more immediate, engaging, and real. The use of dialogue and specific details in 2 contrast with the more streamlined and sterile tone of 1. 2 feels like it contains more insight into the psychology of the friend who is planning to die. Meanwhile, a phrase like "for it all to go down" in 1 reads as oddly informal given the clean, abstracted tone of the overall passage.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: I’m ready now, my friend said, and I said nothing because I didn't know what to say. There were ways people did these sorts of things, she explained to me, certain drugs people used. But she couldn't tell me which drugs. For my protection. Protection against what?, I wondered, but I didn't ask her. That seemed wrong to say. I wanted to ask her about when she was planning on taking these drugs, exactly, but I worried that line of questioning was unthinkable, morbid. I didn't want it to seem like I wanted a date so I could put it on my calendar and plan around it. Already, though, I was thinking about my plans. The mail stacking in the mailbox with each day I stayed with my friend. You don't have to tell me anything you don't want to, I said -- and then I worried that made it sound like I didn't really want to hear anything at all. But she just said, this way it's all in my hands. Her hands: frail, slightly shaking. She was ready to die, she told me, she wanted to get it over with, it felt like that was the way her body was heading. All the ups and downs with the treatments just delaying the inevitable. She was bound to die, just like the coming of the Lord was bound to happen, she said. She glanced upwards and my eyes followed hers. Nothing and no one appeared, and she looked back at me. Just promise you won't tell anyone, she said. I won't, I said -- it was a lie. The weight of the secret was too great. Her plans were too great, too serious. I didn't know what to do. I had already told someone else.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: It’s strange, how quickly we adapt to the unthinkable. Sitting across from her that day, I tried not to fixate on her trembling hands or the way her voice, once so commanding, now wavered. “I don’t want to know when,” I said, a cowardly dodge that felt both honest and unkind. She gave a short laugh, the kind that cuts, and said, “You think it’ll be like the Rapture—poof, and I’m gone? Sorry to disappoint.” The drugs were hidden somewhere, and I knew better than to ask. Still, I couldn’t stop my mind from wandering to the mechanics of it: where, when, how. She didn’t want witnesses, she said, though she spoke about it with the eerie calm of someone discussing weather forecasts. “No surprises,” she added, “except maybe for you, if you’re still here.” She wanted the mail collected, the apartment left tidy, as if planning for a long vacation. But I could see in her eyes a quiet insistence: this wasn’t for my benefit. It was for hers.I nodded along, complicit in the silence she demanded, though guilt sat heavy in my chest. “It’s your choice,” I managed, the words dry in my mouth. I didn’t tell her about the conversation I’d already had, late one night, with someone who wasn’t her. Someone who had listened as I stumbled over explanations and shared the weight she was handing me. My betrayal, small and selfish, would never reach her ears, but it lived between us nonetheless, a thing unspoken but palpable. And when she turned back to her tea, her gaze distant and inward, I wondered how much she already suspected. In that moment, she seemed to belong not to this world or the next but to the narrow, flickering space between.
written_by_MFA001.Reason: To me, Excerpt 2 is superior to Excerpt 1 for a variety of reasons. The first is that the language in Excerpt 1 is dry and repetitve without any clear intention: for example, "The weight of the secret was too great. Her plans were too great, too serious." and "...says, and I say nothing because I don't know what to say." both repeat words ("great" and "say") multiple times in quick succession without clear artistic intent. A second reason is that the flow of the scene is far more suspenseful in Excerpt 2. In Excerpt 1, information is stated outright, whereas in excerpt 2 it's gradually revealed and not made explicit.

She was bound to die, just like the coming of the Lord was bound to happen, she said. She glanced upwards and my eyes followed hers. Nothing and no one appeared, and she looked back at me. Just promise you won't tell anyone, she said. I won't, I said -- it was a lie. The weight of the secret was too great. Her plans were too great, too serious. I didn't know what to do. I had already told someone else.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: It’s strange, how quickly we adapt to the unthinkable. Sitting across from her that day, I tried not to fixate on her trembling hands or the way her voice, once so commanding, now wavered. “I don’t want to know when,” I said, a cowardly dodge that felt both honest and unkind. She gave a short laugh, the kind that cuts, and said, “You think it’ll be like the Rapture—poof, and I’m gone? Sorry to disappoint.” The drugs were hidden somewhere, and I knew better than to ask. Still, I couldn’t stop my mind from wandering to the mechanics of it: where, when, how. She didn’t want witnesses, she said, though she spoke about it with the eerie calm of someone discussing weather forecasts. “No surprises,” she added, “except maybe for you, if you’re still here.” She wanted the mail collected, the apartment left tidy, as if planning for a long vacation. But I could see in her eyes a quiet insistence: this wasn’t for my benefit. It was for hers.I nodded along, complicit in the silence she demanded, though guilt sat heavy in my chest. “It’s your choice,” I managed, the words dry in my mouth. I didn’t tell her about the conversation I’d already had, late one night, with someone who wasn’t her. Someone who had listened as I stumbled over explanations and shared the weight she was handing me. My betrayal, small and selfish, would never reach her ears, but it lived between us nonetheless, a thing unspoken but palpable. And when she turned back to her tea, her gaze distant and inward, I wondered how much she already suspected. In that moment, she seemed to belong not to this world or the next but to the narrow, flickering space between.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Since John’s death, my memories (of him, but also of most things), once acute, have become soft and mudgy. For a while, I was able to maintain a handle on reality by way of an elaborate method of timekeeping. It was calming to look back at what John and I were doing one year ago, and keep track of the days that way. One year ago today, I would remind myself, we were in Mexico, preparing a dinner of heavily spiced chicken in our rented kitchen. One year ago today, we were at the Met, looking at the new rooftop exhibit, which John loved but I disliked for its uninspired crudeness. These memories were vivid, acute, and I was able to almost watch them, like one would a television show. And then, December 31, 2003 arrived. In that moment, one year ago no longer included him. John had morphed, officially, into a part of the past and not the present. I came to this burning realization while I was crossing Lexington Avenue. I had a bag of groceries in my hand. It was snowing, quite faintly. I realized I had spent the year trying to keep him alive, because I have always believed, been told, that it is our duty to keep the dead alive. But what about the living? I realized it, then, that the key to all of this was to keep them dead. There was no other way, in my view, to continue living myself.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: It is December 31, 2004, and I find myself at the intersection of memory and absence, crossing Lexington Avenue on a day John never knew. The light changes, the traffic hums, but the world feels displaced, as though operating on a parallel timeline I can no longer inhabit. I ask myself where we were this day a year ago, but the question folds into itself, unanswered. There was no "we" then. There is no "we" now. It is just me, standing on the edge of a moment I never thought would arrive, tethered to someone who no longer exists in the present tense.Time has turned traitorous, reshaping vivid recollections into something blurred, soft-edged, mudgy. I want the sharpness back—the sound of his voice calling my name, the exact tilt of his head when he laughed—but instead I am left with echoes that refuse to hold their shape. For months I kept time through him: what we ate, where we sat, how the hours unfolded a year ago. That tether, too, is breaking, and I know it must. To live is to keep the dead where they belong, not erased but sequestered, a layer beneath the surface of everything we do and feel. I loved him, love him still, but loving him has become the act of holding his absence, acknowledging the permanence of it, walking forward through the days he will never know. This is the life left, the one that does not wait.
written_by_MFA008.Reason: Excerpt1 is better than Excerpt2 -the first sentence in Excerpt1 is more fluid/natural and emotionally gripping, whereas the opening sentence of Excerpt2 is much more cold and flat in affect in a way that feels unintentional and unsuccessful. While I think Excerpt2s ideas flow together in a more natural way, the vivid descriptions and time jumps from Excerpt1 held my attention and were overall more effective. I feel like I can “see” Excerpt1 — the “heavily spiced chicken” and “quite faintly” falling snow.Excerpt2 just sort of feels like abstraction.

Without specificity, neither John nor the narrator feel like they ever lived to me at all.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Time moves in peculiar circles when you're carrying the dead. I found myself caught in this ritual of backward glancing, measuring each day against its twin from the year before, when John was still here, still breathing, still marking time with me. It became a kind of obsession, this constant calculation – where were we last March, what were we doing that April afternoon, did we have dinner at that place on Second Avenue in May? The memories started clean, sharp-edged, but they grew mudgy around the corners, like old photographs left too long in sunlight. Then came that morning on Lexington Avenue, unremarkable except for its mathematical significance: December 31, 2003, a date John never saw. The realization hit me with the force of a physical blow – I had crossed some invisible line into a time he never knew existed. We tell ourselves we keep the dead alive through memory, through these endless retrospective inventories, but perhaps what we're really doing is learning to keep them dead. It's a peculiar arithmetic, this subtraction of the living from the dead, this slow release of what was into what is. The truth about grief, I was learning, is that it operates on its own timeline, indifferent to our careful calculations, our desperate attempts to hold onto what slips away with each passing day, each remembered and then half-remembered moment.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Time erodes memory, smudging away the finer details of a scene until all that remains are stage directions. Grief forces us to look back, to fall into stories that lack the danger of surprise. It was possible for me to sit across from John’s empty seat at the table so long as I could fill that chair with all my memories of him sitting in it. 2003 folded into 2004, the dates layered on top of one another. I wanted to believe I was pulling John’s ghost along with me. On December 31, 2004, as I was crossing Lexington Avenue, I realized that I was chasing after his echo, instead. Every day of that first year was endurable, if only because the date was glossed over by what John and I had been doing the previous year. No longer could I use this crutch. December 31, 2003 was the first full day I was a widow. Those memories remains sharp, regardless of if I’d prefer them smudged. Agonies are often the loudest in hindsight, whereas comforts are soft and slippery. After a death, we cling to empty air. We turn back, and we turn back again to memories until our fingerprints have worn them fuzzy. This is all there is now. Memories and photographs and people who knew him. Death draws a fine line between then and now, and if one wishes to live, they must let their dead be dead.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: Again, my opinion is surely informed by having actually read "The Year of Magical Thinking" by Joan Didion, but I prefer Excerpt 1. Excerpt 2 does not sound like anything she would ever write and is of lesser quality overall. "The memories started clean, sharp-edged, but they grew mudgy around the corners, like old photographs left too long in sunlight" is an interesting, memorable, and Didion-esque sentence because it is at once elegant, clean, and yet uses an interesting word choice ("mudgy") that is totally idiosyncratic. Excerpt 2 devolves into generalities and cliches that aren't rooted in a specific emotion.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: The air in the apartment is heavy, thick with the scent of lilies and the ghost of his presence.  Time, that relentless tide, keeps moving, yet I seem stranded, caught in the undertow of grief.  It's been a year and four months since John, my John, slipped through the veil, and the world insists on reminding me.The calendar, that cruel arbiter of time, mocks me with its relentless march forward.  Each day is a faded echo of the one before, a year removed.  I find myself trapped in a loop, rewinding the reel of memory, asking, "Where were we a year ago? What were we doing?"  It's a futile attempt to hold onto him, to keep him alive in the only way I know how.Yesterday, I crossed Lexington Avenue, the same way I've done a thousand times before.  But this time, it was different.  This time, I carried the weight of December 31, 2003, a date that exists in my world but not in his.  It was the day he ceased to be, the day the world shifted on its axis.And in that moment, I realized the terrible truth.  We who are left behind, we try to keep the dead alive in our memories, clinging to their fading essence like a lifeline.  But in doing so, we create a purgatory, a liminal space where they are neither here nor there.  To truly live, to move forward, we must keep them dead.  It's a harsh reality, a bitter pill to swallow.  But it's the only way to navigate the treacherous terrain of grief.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: When I think of John now, whether in grief or joy, time makes a mirage of our parting. Memories are distant, those vibrant, vivid images inevitably softened by the passing days and nights into muddy and distorted reflections. My practice of keeping time in relation to what John and I were doing last year is a game of questions. When he was alive, who did we see today? Where did we go together? Above all: What did he say to me then? Crossing Lexington Avenue in the wintry haze enveloping New York, a cold, damp curtain hung above the city, I come across the date—December 31, 2003—and realize John never saw this day last year. My exercise for keeping time has expired, and my husband lives in the distant past. I might transplant him here, invite him as memory into this moment to maintain our profound connection, the sort unsevered by death so long as he is kept within the perfect safety of memory. Yet it occurs to me—in this exercise of resurrection, I am only ensuring that I, too, never see December 31, 2003. That I, like John, live only in my recollections. Thus: we must keep them dead. To continue living, to draw oneself up from the smudged and mildewy twilight of the place where memory is real to us, there can be no resurrection; for the living to carry on, the dead must remain dead.
written_by_MFA026.Reason: Excerpt 1 lacks specificity and relies on overwrought imagery to develop its narrative: for instance, "The calendar, that cruel arbiter of time, mocks me with its relentless march forward" or "Time, that relentless tide…" Likewise, while it suggests memories of John, they remain vague. The reader has to trust that there are memories, we are not shown them. In Excerpt 2, there is greater specificity. While there remains a fair bit of overwrought imagery, it is contained by the clear position of time the narrator places themselves in relationship to John. Memories are given slightly more specificity: not only "where we were a year ago? What were we doing?" but also "… who did he see today? Where did we go together? Above all: What did he say to me then?" These questions create a clearer sense of what the narrator is imagining. As such, the approximation of memory makes more sense. I prefer Excerpt 2 for these reasons, but these two are relatively similar in quality.
