written_by_MFA006.Excerpt1: The billionaire had invited me to lunch with him at a London club. When I arrived, I was surprised by how casually he dressed, in jeans and a white button-down. He was generous: on account of my enormous suitcase, he offered to call me a taxi to the airport when it was time to leave. He told me he was working on a software project that could predict an employee's capacity to betray their company. I didn't know why we were talking about this—we were meeting under the pretense of discussing a literary magazine that the billionaire was interested in starting—but I sat there and did my best to listen. He wanted to tell me many things, his whole life story. He had grown up poor, he said, but that hadn't lasted long, and now he had a floating windfarm that doubled as worker housing, and an idea for a scheme to keep lawyers out of people's personal business. He told me about the rock band he played drums in, and that he was expecting his eleventh child soon. This was in addition to the four Guatemalan quadruplets he had already adopted. It felt like too many children to me. I wondered if perhaps he thought that by creating this magazine, he might also fashion himself as a writer capable of being published in it. The idea seemed a stretch to me, but perhaps the billionaire was used to spanning such extreme logical leaps. The leap from man to billionaire was certainly larger than billionaire to writer. I was struggling to follow my own line of thinking. The waitress kept appearing, bringing brightly colored drinks and dishes that alternated between tasting too rich and too pungent. It had the opposite effect on the billionaire. Amidst the bright colors and flavors, the billionaire's face shone like a young boy who had been suddenly surrounded by mountains of his favorite sweets. When the food and drink had finally been swept away and the bill paid, he put me and my heavy suitcase in the taxi. Enjoy yourself in Athens, he said, which was a surprise. I hadn't recalled ever mentioning my destination.
written_by_MFA006.Excerpt2: The club's interior held that particular London stillness, a cultivated hush that seemed to absorb and neutralize the city's chaos beyond its walls. The billionaire sat opposite me in jeans and a t-shirt, his casualness a subtle assertion of power in this formal setting, as though the rules that governed others were merely suggestions to him. He spoke rapidly about his software project - designed to predict employee betrayal - with the enthusiastic self-absorption of someone unused to interruption. I found myself studying the way he moved his hands, which were unexpectedly delicate, as he described algorithms that could detect disloyalty in email patterns. The waitresses appeared and disappeared like synchronized dancers, bearing plates of increasingly elaborate food that he barely seemed to notice. When he mentioned the literary magazine he wanted to start, I recognized in his tone that particular quality of the very wealthy - the assumption that anything could be acquired or created through the application of sufficient capital. His life story emerged in fragments between courses: the humble beginnings, the Guatemalan quadruplets, the floating wind farm with its worker housing, each achievement recounted with a child's pride in showing off their toys. I noticed how he used the word "just" before describing extraordinary accomplishments - "I just bought an island," "I just started a rock band" - as though trying to diminish their significance while simultaneously drawing attention to them. The scattered nature of his focus felt familiar to me, reminiscent of the way wealth itself tends to fragment experience into consumable pieces. When he mentioned my upcoming trip to Athens - something I hadn't told him about - I felt a curious shift in the air between us, as though the careful performance of our lunch had momentarily slipped to reveal something else beneath. But he was already moving on to another topic, and I found myself wondering if I had imagined it, the way one sometimes imagines connections between unrelated events in an attempt to create meaning from randomness. The taxi he insisted on paying for waited outside like a full stop at the end of a run-on sentence.
written_by_MFA006.Reason:
These are very close to me in terms of quality, and I could make a case for either being superior to the other (it feels, at the end of the day, about a question of taste: do you prefer to read a scene and feel as if you are present inside it, or do you prefer to read a speaker's intelligent reflections about a scene that's at more of a distance from you?) I prefer the former, so I vote Excerpt 1, even though I think excerpt 2 has more poignant revelations/observations. 

Excerpt1 has descriptions of the conversation that feel a lot more like dialogue happening in real time ("he said," "he told me,") that feels untouched by the judgement/reflections of the speaker, whereas Excerpt2 feels like it almost exclusively has the kind of description that's clouded by the speaker's musings ("he spoke rapidly... with the enthusiastic self-absorption of someone used to interruption:). While Excerpt2 therefore gives a lot more meaningful characterization of both the speaker and the billionaire, it also loses some of the suspense and mystery that comes from Excerpt1 leaving much of this up to the reader to interpret/decide. And ultimately, I feel much more "present" in the scene of Excerpt1, which is the kind of reading experience I prefer.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: The club's mahogany-paneled dining room felt both intimate and imposing, much like the billionaire himself who sat across from me in his unexpectedly casual attire - a contradiction that seemed to epitomize the entire encounter. He spoke of his software project with the same blithe enthusiasm one might discuss a hobby, though its purpose - to predict employee betrayal - carried an unmistakable darkness beneath its technological sheen. I found myself watching his hands as he gestured, noting how they moved with the unrestrained energy of someone unaccustomed to constraint, while waitresses appeared and disappeared around us like temporal markers, each bringing increasingly elaborate dishes that created their own kind of narrative. The literary magazine, ostensibly the reason for our meeting, seemed to float between us as an abstraction, less substantial than the wine being continuously poured into our glasses. When he mentioned his floating wind farm, complete with worker housing, I recognized in his tone the particular cadence of someone who had grown accustomed to reshaping reality according to their whims - a power that seemed to have preserved in him something childlike, even as it had presumably destroyed other, more ordinary qualities. The adopted Guatemalan quadruplets entered the conversation with the same matter-of-factness as his rock band drumming, both details that seemed to resist integration into any coherent whole. Throughout lunch, I felt myself becoming increasingly passive, as though I were merely a surface upon which his life story was being projected - his humble beginnings, his current affluence, his schemes to eliminate lawyers from personal matters - all of it washing over me in waves that left me struggling to maintain my own sense of reality. When he finally deposited me in the taxi with a casual "Enjoy yourself in Athens" - a destination I was certain I hadn't mentioned - I felt as though I had experienced something that existed outside the normal boundaries of social interaction, an encounter that had its own internal logic but one that, like his software, seemed designed to predict something I couldn't quite grasp.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: Before I left the country, a billionaire invited me to lunch at a London club. I’m working on a software for HR operations, he said. He wore an outfit that defied the club’s dress code: a dark T-shirt and darker jeans. It uses a predictive algorithm, he said, that scrapes employee backgrounds, e-mails, and market trends to identify which ones are likeliest to betray their companies. But I’ve been getting carried away. I’m starting a literary magazine; let’s discuss it. Unfortunately, by the time the literary subject came up, I’d already finished my entree and needed to leave for the airport. He insisted on paying for my taxi, which I accepted. I was late for my flight and carried a heavy suitcase. The billionaire had spent most of our lunch sharing his life story, which began with him as a humble public-school student and ended with him becoming the wealthy man leaning back in the chair across from me. I figured he wanted to use the literary magazine as a launchpad to becoming a writer himself. It wouldn’t be a ridiculous notion—he bought his way into a number of things. He told me he’d built a floating wind farm, located offshore from the township he was designing to house its workers. He also said he had a scheme to eliminate lawyers from people’s everyday lives and personal problems. For fun, he played drums in a psychedelic rock band, though he wasn’t writing any original songs. He was expecting his eleventh child, a surprise pregnancy; he and his wife had recently adopted quadruplets from Guatemala. Throughout the lunch, I found it difficult to respond thoughtfully, or even adequately, to the billionaire’s many ventures and projects. The waitresses kept bringing in appetizers on porcelain plates—foie gras, baked brie, oysters—and drinks in crystal glasses—mimosas, champagne. The billionaire jumped from topic to topic, and when his voice rose an octave as he described eliminating inefficiencies, he reminded me of a child barreling through the halls of an opulent mansion. At the end of lunch, he put me in the taxi and said, Enjoy yourself in Athens. I didn’t remember telling him where I was going?
written_by_MFA007.Reason: Excerpt 2 is the more effective piece of writing. Where Excerpt 1 uses the essayistic format of the excerpt to put a very fine point on certain ideas, like when it tells us that the billionaire's knowledge that the narrator is visiting Athens feels like a breach of "the normal boundaries of social interaction," Excerpt 2 lets the mystery of this moment speak for itself: "At the end of lunch, he put me in the taxi and said, Enjoy yourself in Athens. I didn’t remember telling him where I was going?" Notice how the second example gives you, as a reader, a better chance to experience the breach of boundaries, because it provides it in scene, instead of telling you that it happened.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: The glass partition reflected my spectacled face, sallow and withdrawn, as we sat at the group table near the kitchen. My father's hands, roughened by work, rested uneasily on the paper placemat while we waited, ignored by the waiters who glided past with studied indifference. At the next table, a girl my age lounged with casual elegance, her summer-bronzed skin gleaming against a crisp white blouse. She spooned yogurt—a food I had never tasted—with the natural grace of someone who had always known its existence. Her father, well-dressed and at ease, gestured expressively as he spoke to her. They had ordered à la carte, their plates arranged with careful precision by attentive staff. When our fixed-price meals finally arrived, the mashed potatoes sat in a grayish heap, unmolded from some industrial container. My father ate in silence, his shoulders tense, his fork scraping the institutional plate. For days afterward, he would mutter about the "pig slop" they had served us, each repetition of the phrase carrying the accumulated weight of a lifetime of similar humiliations. I understood then that the restaurant had sorted us, placed us in our proper social category—the cheap seats, the hurried service, the institutional food. We belonged to the world of fixed-price menus and group tables, while others inhabited the realm of individual choice, of yogurt and carefully plated dishes, of being seen and served with deference.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: We sat there, my father and I, at the group table. Anyone looking our way could see our discomfort. I touched my spectacles and watched myself in the great wall mirror - each time finding myself paler and more repulsive. My father grew more agitated, too, letting our meager conversation drop, because the waiter had still not come with his mashed potatoes after so many dreary minutes. I watched a girl near my age across the room dining at her own special table with an older man. I watched her through the mirror in case she might meet my eye. She was tan and lifted a spoon of creamy yogurt to her lips. I was lost, for a moment, in imagining its flavor. I had never tasted yogurt before. When our food came at last, it looked nothing like the pretty plate in front of the tan girl - the same way my clothes looked nothing like hers - the same way my skin matched the grey sky outside while hers glowed like the sun in the tropics. Later, in the streets and at home, my father repeatedly talked about the "pig slop" they served him at the restaurant and vowed never to return. It took me years to understand how he was complaining - in his own way - of the hurt that came with seeing, but never ordering, "à la carte."
written_by_MFA016.Reason: The narrator is not centered in Excerpt 1 -- the writing is merely a list of observations about what other people are doing, experiencing, seeing, feeling. It's more of a list-style rundown of people dining in a restaurant than something that tells us anything about the narrator. Excerpt 2, meanwhile, is much more centered, and everything is filtered through the narrator's "I"; even observations about the other diners are a window into letting us know how he sees himself, his father, his circumstances. The writing feels about equal in both options -- neither is overdone, both are solid -- but the difference, to me, lies in what Excerpt 2 tells us about the narrator versus what Excerpt 1 fails to illuminate.

written_by_MFA033.Excerpt1: My father wanted to take me to lunch. He found a restaurant unlike any I’d ever been to, unlike anything that existed in C. Any excitement I felt disappeared quickly. The waiter looked us up and down, seeing what we were immediately. I was pale from the winter, dressed in my worn, washed clothes. I wore spectacles, awkward and out of fashion, the kind you could buy at a steep discount. The waiter directed us to a shared table at the back of the restaurant, in front of the wash closet. At first my experience of discomfort was limited only to me. My father still had a big smile, ear to ear. But then I saw another father-daughter pair at a table in the restaurant’s big window. The girl was around my age, and pretty. She dealt with the restaurant staff confidently, with a confiding air, like they shared a special secret. I watched the girl longingly. Her tanned legs ended in delicate buckled shoes. I watched her eat food I could not identify. Back then, I’d never had yoghurt.As the waiter laughed and spoke to them in earshot of us, I saw my father growing red. “Those potatoes were pig slop,” he said after we left the restaurant, again and again. It embarrassed me. It was clear enough to both of us what had happened. At least, it was clear that we’d both had a bad time. I knew what he was saying. We had been treated as second-class citizens because we ordered the prix fixe, instead of selecting expensive dishes à la carte like the more sophisticated clientele. I wanted to forget about it. If we didn’t speak of the event, then perhaps it wasn’t real.
written_by_MFA033.Excerpt2: At the restaurant, a dim-lit corner housed a long table where we were seated, our pale faces barely catching the flicker of candlelight. The service was indifferent, the kind that signaled our place—second-class, among the unremarkable and the unseen. I watched the teenage girl at the next table, her tanned skin glowing, the light glancing off the curve of her bare arm as she dipped a spoon into her yogurt. It wasn’t just the yogurt, unfamiliar and faintly exotic, or her easy laughter as she spoke to the older man, presumably her father. It was the way she leaned back in her chair, utterly at home in a place where I shrank. I caught my reflection in the mirror—a pale, spectral figure, glasses catching the flicker of light like an accusation. My father sat stiffly, the lines on his face deepened by a furrow of discontent. The mashed potatoes, a mound of something that seemed to sneer back at us, bore the brunt of his irritation. "Pig slop," he muttered, too loud, earning a glance from the waiter that reeked of disdain. He repeated the phrase later, at home, his voice rising each time, but I knew it wasn’t the food. It was the yogurt, the girl, her easy privilege, the sharp reminder of where we belonged in the silent hierarchy of the dining room. He wanted to explain the indignity, to frame it in something tangible, and so he said, "pig slop." I, too, clung to the detail, though for me it was the yogurt, a symbol of a world I had not yet entered. In that moment, the line between us and them felt etched into the tablecloth, as indelible as the reflection in the mirror.
written_by_MFA033.Reason: The voice in excerpt 2 relies on overwrought imagery like "catching the flicker of light like an accusation" or "as inedible as the reflection in the mirror." Likewise, excerpt 2 struggles with showing what is happening and implying meaning from it. Instead, it states dynamics outright which excerpt 1 rightly implies. For instance, in excerpt 2 the second sentence refers to the narrator and her father's position as "place-second-class" in the restaurant, while excerpt 1 shows this through implication ("The waiter looked us up and down, seeing what we were immediately") and then emphasizes it at the end of the excerpt, while also explaining the tie to class ("We had been treated as second-class citizens because we ordered the prix fixe, instead of selecting expensive dishes à la carte like the more sophisticated clientele.").

written_by_MFA033.Excerpt1: My father wanted to take me to lunch. He found a restaurant unlike any I’d ever been to, unlike anything that existed in C. Any excitement I felt disappeared quickly. The waiter looked us up and down, seeing what we were immediately. I was pale from the winter, dressed in my worn, washed clothes. I wore spectacles, awkward and out of fashion, the kind you could buy at a steep discount. The waiter directed us to a shared table at the back of the restaurant, in front of the wash closet. At first my experience of discomfort was limited only to me. My father still had a big smile, ear to ear. But then I saw another father-daughter pair at a table in the restaurant’s big window. The girl was around my age, and pretty. She dealt with the restaurant staff confidently, with a confiding air, like they shared a special secret. I watched the girl longingly. Her tanned legs ended in delicate buckled shoes. I watched her eat food I could not identify. Back then, I’d never had yoghurt.As the waiter laughed and spoke to them in earshot of us, I saw my father growing red. “Those potatoes were pig slop,” he said after we left the restaurant, again and again. It embarrassed me. It was clear enough to both of us what had happened. At least, it was clear that we’d both had a bad time. I knew what he was saying. We had been treated as second-class citizens because we ordered the prix fixe, instead of selecting expensive dishes à la carte like the more sophisticated clientele. I wanted to forget about it. If we didn’t speak of the event, then perhaps it wasn’t real.
written_by_MFA033.Excerpt2: At the restaurant, a dim-lit corner housed a long table where we were seated, our pale faces barely catching the flicker of candlelight. The service was indifferent, the kind that signaled our place—second-class, among the unremarkable and the unseen. I watched the teenage girl at the next table, her tanned skin glowing, the light glancing off the curve of her bare arm as she dipped a spoon into her yogurt. It wasn’t just the yogurt, unfamiliar and faintly exotic, or her easy laughter as she spoke to the older man, presumably her father. It was the way she leaned back in her chair, utterly at home in a place where I shrank. I caught my reflection in the mirror—a pale, spectral figure, glasses catching the flicker of light like an accusation. My father sat stiffly, the lines on his face deepened by a furrow of discontent. The mashed potatoes, a mound of something that seemed to sneer back at us, bore the brunt of his irritation. "Pig slop," he muttered, too loud, earning a glance from the waiter that reeked of disdain. He repeated the phrase later, at home, his voice rising each time, but I knew it wasn’t the food. It was the yogurt, the girl, her easy privilege, the sharp reminder of where we belonged in the silent hierarchy of the dining room. He wanted to explain the indignity, to frame it in something tangible, and so he said, "pig slop." I, too, clung to the detail, though for me it was the yogurt, a symbol of a world I had not yet entered. In that moment, the line between us and them felt etched into the tablecloth, as indelible as the reflection in the mirror.
written_by_MFA033.Reason: The class differences are unnecessarily explained in the second excerpt, somewhat patronizingly: "The service was indifferent, the kind that signaled our place—second-class, among the unremarkable and the unseen." In the first excerpt, these class differences are made evident by concrete details in the characters' behavior and appearances: "I was pale from the winter, dressed in my worn, washed clothes. I wore spectacles, awkward and out of fashion ..." The slight comedy of the narrator being unfamiliar with yoghurt is played straight in the second excerpt, coming out in an awkwardly melodramatic way: "the yogurt, unfamiliar and faintly exotic." Nothing remains "unsaid" in the second excerpt; even the father's comment ("pig slop") is made too explicit: "He wanted to explain the indignity, to frame it in something tangible, and so he said, "pig slop," whereas the first excerpt simply states, more plainly: "It was clear enough to both of us what had happened. At least, it was clear that we’d both had a bad time. I knew what he was saying." The reader, too, can infer the father is saying, and leaving that inference to the reader is a sign of more sophisticated writing that trusts the reader's judgement.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: In the muted light of the restaurant, the stark class divide was as palpable as the stale odor clinging to the worn velvet seats.  My spectacles, magnifying the pallor of my reflection, seemed to amplify my sense of displacement.  At our table, a shared expanse with strangers, the service was a reluctant dance of neglect.  In contrast, a few tables away, a tanned teenage girl, radiating an aura of effortless confidence, shared an intimate meal with an older man.  Her laughter, light and carefree, bounced off the gilded mirrors, mocking my own constrained stillness.Her spoon, a silver arc, delivered a dollop of yogurt to her lips—a food so exotic, it was a whisper from another world.  My gaze drifted back to my plate, the food suddenly as bland as the pity I felt for myself.  Later, my father's voice, rough with suppressed resentment, dissected the meal, the "pig slop" mashed potatoes becoming a metaphor for our diminished status.  We were not "à la carte" patrons, and our presence was a mere tolerated intrusion.  The restaurant, a microcosm of society, had laid bare the invisible lines that defined our place.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: My father and I dined at an upscale restaurant in the 13th arrondissement. We each ordered chicken legs and mashed potatoes, and we sat stiffly while waiting for our food. It was clear that both of us felt uncomfortable with the opulence of the space, but neither of us knew how to say so. Nearby, a girl around the age of fifteen sat with an older man, presumably her father, eating a foreign-looking food that I didn't recognize—a bowl of yogurt, I later learned. She looked deeply at ease eating her meal, and I was disturbed to see myself in the mirror on the adjacent wall—spectacled, pale. Compared to the girl, I looked homely and unimportant, or at least I felt that I did at the time. For a moment I imagined myself as the girl, tan and comfortable among the trappings of wealth, though even then I knew that the hallmarks of the working class were written all over my face and my behavior. My father and I sat for a while in silence, and when the waitstaff brought out our plates, he remarked to me that his mashed potatoes looked like "pig slop." At the time, I thought he was just being fussy about his meal and I felt annoyed. Later I understood that he was deeply hurt at having been treated as second-class citizens who weren't ordering à la carte like the girl and her father, though he never said as much—he just continued talking about the potatoes, their unpleasant texture, their unsightly gray appearance.
written_by_MFA011.Reason: Excerpt 2 builds up to the idea of class division and inequity through the realistic lens of a teenager. The narrator of Excerpt 2 is imitating their experience in the restaurant that day, first captured by the sight of a peer, longing to be them, acknowledging the classic division in a distinctly teenage way (through desire for beauty and material items), and the discomfort and irritation with their father. The reflection at the end of the excerpt is from a later point of telling, explaining that they now understand why their father was so upset. Excerpt 1 opens with this off the bat, and dictates how the whole interaction is meant to read for the reader, instead of having them embody the narrator's experience.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: “I just cain't wrap my head 'round it, Ennis. Just give it to me straight up: you want me around or don't ya? Cause this here between us ain’t anything in full, and because it ain’t anything in full it ain’t hardly anything at all. All we see of each other is here, alone with ourselves. I only got you here. Out there, you ain’t anybody I ever known. All we got here are moments on Brokeback Mountain, and moments ain’t a life, ain’t close to living. How much more of ourselves are you willing to let die? Don’t you know how much less of me I feel of myself? You keep all that I am on the shortest leash, Ennis. You are the one keeping us from the fullness of what our lives could be. Maybe you can keep on like this, but I can’t. I’m at the end of that rope. God, Ennis. I want to quit you. I wish I knew how to quit you.” Nearing the tailend of these words Ennis’s knees buckled, his body softened, as if having taken birdshot to his backside, though to Jack any outer wound could not be found. Jack went silent then, and kept it, unsure what to do with Ennis screaming, “Jesus, Jesus…” And though Ennis calmed, and the air on the mountain steadied, nothing had changed. Still they would go on as they had before, no one in the world knowing what they had between them, except them. The pain on that mountain would go on with them, too, would follow them into the days and weeks ahead, so weighty, like clouds of steam rising between the two.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: Jack stood there, fists balled in his jacket pockets, words tearing out of him like barbed wire through flesh. "Twenty years we been at this, En. Twenty goddamn years of sneakin up here like outlaws, like we done somethin wrong. You got me on this short leash, always yankin me back when I get too close to somethin real. Christ, I'm sick of it. Sick of these few days we grab like scraps under the table. You think I wanted this half-life? Living off memories of Brokeback till they're wore thin as old leather?" His voice cracked, raw as windburn. "I wish I knew how to quit you." The words hung between them like smoke in still air. Ennis swayed, color draining from his face like water from a broken cup, then his knees buckled and he went down hard on the packed dirt. "Jesus," Jack shouted, lunging forward, thinking heart attack, stroke, something busted loose inside that couldn't be fixed. But Ennis's shoulders were heaving, great gasping sobs tearing out of him, the kind that leave a man hollow. Jack stood frozen, watching his friend shake apart, knowing any touch might shatter what was left. When the storm passed, Ennis climbed to his feet, brushed dirt from his jeans like nothing had happened. They stood in the heavy silence, steam rising between them from their breath in the mountain air, neither looking at the other. Nothing changed. Nothing could change. The moment passed like so many before it, settling into the collection of hurts they carried, weight added to weight until the burden seemed natural as breathing.
written_by_MFA015.Reason: Excerpt 1 is a little too voice-y, in my opinion, but it rings as something authentic, whereas Excerpt 2 feels a bit more writerly and inauthentic. That feeling comes partially, I think, from the sense that Excerpt 1 is "hitting the beats" -- we get Jack's statement, Ennis' collapse, and then Ennis righting himself all in a matter of a few sentences. Excerpt 1, meanwhile, lingers in the moment as necessary; it feels like Jack is given as long as he needs to amble through what he needs to say, and even Ennis is given space to collapse for however long he needs. (Though he calms, we end Excerpt 1 with Ennis still on his knees, whereas in Excerpt 2 he finds his feet again.) Overall, it feels like Excerpt 1 is concerned with allowing the characters the time and space to work through their emotions, verbally and physically, whereas Excerpt 2 feels more like it's working us through a scene.

written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: “You the storm that stranded me here,” said Jack. “Ain’t no other way to put it. I been thinkin on it, bustin my brain to try and fit the bits together, but it’s bullshit. You know it is, Ennis, don’t pretend like you don’t. I’ve called you, sent you letters first class, and you actin like the offseason applies to us. Brokeback’s just a little vacation, a couple ranch-hands in heat. Maybe you like it like that. You sure got me on a short leash. That’s all I am to you, Ennis: a bitch for the summer. I’d swallow glass if it meant I could spend the rest a my life on Brokeback, but you won’t even pick up the goddam phone.” Jack looked at the ridgeline. “I wish I knew how to quit you.” Ennis got down on one knee, and for a second Jack thought he was tying his shoe. Sobs wracked his ribs. “Jesus!” yelled Jack. Ennis kept crying. He looked down at the earth, the denim of his knee stirring up dust. To Jack he looked like a wounded horse, its hooves at rest. He feared for Ennis, this man for whom he had stored up so much love and hate. A cold distant man making a scene on the roadside—it didn’t make much in the way of sense. Jack had more to say but his jaw stayed shut. Ennis sobbed. After awhile he went still. Ennis pulled himself to his feet and pushed the dust off his jeans. Jack looked at him and Ennis looked back, but there was nothing there. Just the clouds of steam rising.
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: Jack leaned against the post, his chest heaving, words spilling out in a torrent, raw as the gouged earth beneath his boots. “I can’t do this anymore, Ennis. It ain’t just the damn mountain. You hold me like I’m some stray dog on a leash, pullin’ me close when you want and kickin’ me away when you don’t. Ain’t a life, this. Not for me.” His voice cracked, ricocheted into the dry air. “Wish I knew how to quit you, but it’s like tryin’ to wrench a fishhook outta your own throat.” He tipped his hat back, his eyes watery but fierce, daring the other man to respond. Ennis stood frozen, fists tight, the sinews of his neck stretched taut like old barbed wire. When the words hit their mark, it was like a shot fired too close—he crumpled, knees buckling, gasping for air as though Jack’s truths had knocked it clean out of him. “Jesus,” Jack muttered, rushing forward, unsure if he should steady Ennis or step away. The distance between them felt insurmountable, a chasm carved out of years of furtive touches and unspoken words. For a moment, there was only the rasp of their breath, mingling with the faint hum of crickets and the whisper of dry grass. Ennis lifted his head, the shadows on his face deep, his expression unreadable. He staggered to his feet, brushing off Jack’s hand, and the weight of their shared silence pressed in. Nothing was mended, no path forward uncovered. Just the same cycle of longing and restraint, heartbreak hanging in the air like steam from a kettle left too long on the flame, inevitable and unyielding, rising but never dispersing.
written_by_MFA012.Reason: Excerpt 1 conveys tricky, complex emotions in scene, the landscape and physical world complementing the depth of feeling expressed by dialogue. "A cold distant man making a scene on the roadside—it didn’t make much in the way of sense." The feeling between the two characters is tense and intense. Excerpt 2 relies on melodrama, over-explaining the sentiments expressed via dialogue.

written_by_MFA006.Excerpt1: “Thing is,” Jack said, “I’m fucking sick of it. Tired of goin nowhere but up the mountain with you. Givin me just Brokeback Mountain is bout as good as givin me nothin, and you know it. I want more–I want it all–and I don’t reckon you’ll ever give it to me. I’m like your dog, chokin on your short leash. All I want is to…it doesn’t matter, do it? Imma dog frothin at the end of your fuckin leash. Goddammit.” He paused for a moment, his breath coming out in short, steaming pants that warmed the tent. “Goddammit. I wish I knew how to quit you.”Jack’s words acted like a rusted arrow upon Ennis–tired, worn out, but not without their raw edge, dangerously sharp. They pierced through him, brought him down to his knees. He lay there on the ground, clutching himself, pale, his wide-eyed gaze fixed on the mountain. “Jesus–” Jack stooped down as if to help him. Was he sick? Jack wondered. Was he finally able to see? Jack’s hands hovered around the other man’s body, but Ennis looked so far away, as if dreaming, and impossible to touch. Ennis got up without his help, recomposing his face into that flat, familiar expression. He rose up from his knees, a man rewound–the dramatic act reversed, so that again he became just a man with a lockbox of feelings. Just Ennis, slumped against the valley. That same far off expression on his face, his hand, gently trembling, grasping at nothing. And that same pain was there too, a shared pain–hot, palpable, unresolved and unrelenting–like clouds of steam rising between them.
written_by_MFA006.Excerpt2: “Brokeback Mountain’s the only place I’ve ever felt happy. ” Jack’s voice, a raw rasp of longing and frustration, sliced through the quiet Wyoming air.“Four measly weeks a year, that’s all we get. Four weeks, Ennis, while the rest of the year you keep me on a goddamn short leash. Like I’m some kinda stray dog you picked up along the road. ” “I wish I knew how to quit you.”The words hung heavy, a confession and a curse.   Jack’s eyes, the blue of a high-desert sky, were clouded with torment.   “But I can’t.   I’m no good at quittin’. Never have been. Not you, not anything. ”Ennis, his face a mask of pain, crumpled to his knees.   Jack’s words, sharp as barbed wire, had pierced his defenses, drawing blood from his soul.The silence that followed was deafening, broken only by the wind whistling through the pines.“Ennis? ” Jack’s voice was thick with alarm. “What’s wrong? You sick? ”“Jesus,” Ennis choked out, his breath coming in ragged gasps.Jack watched, helpless, as Ennis wrestled with the emotional storm. He’d seen Ennis break horses, wrestle calves, but he’d never seen him like this.Raw, exposed, a man stripped bare by the force of his own feelings.Ennis slowly regained his composure, the storm within subsiding into a dull ache. He stood up, his legs shaky, his eyes fixed on the distant horizon, a vast expanse of sagebrush and sky. The confrontation had changed nothing. Their pain, unspoken yet palpable, hung between them like clouds of steam rising from damp earth on a cold morning.

written_by_MFA009.Excerpt1: It was Saint Patrick's Day when I watched my mother die, though there was nothing lucky about that bitter-bright morning. The sun bounced off snow banks outside her window, creating a cruel sparkle that seemed to mock the dimming light within. A cup of green Jell-O sat untouched on her bedside table – some nurse's attempt at festivity that now seemed obscene in its cheerfulness. My mother's eyes were the color of forgotten summers, a blue so startling against her pallid skin that it made my chest ache. They remained open, fixed on something I couldn't see, something beyond the sterile hospital walls and my desperate presence beside her. I watched death move through her like smoke through a burning house, slow and inevitable, claiming each room until nothing remained but ash. Those eyes – I saw everything in them. First came the bitterness, sharp as broken glass, then confusion that softened her face into something childlike, and finally, a quiet courage that broke my heart and rebuilt it in the same moment. The blue of her irises burned like pilot lights, struggling to stay lit even as the rest of her failed. Even now, I can close my eyes and see that color, that last fierce flag of life she waved, refusing to surrender until the very end. How wild it was, to watch someone both fight and accept their fate in the same endless moment.
written_by_MFA009.Excerpt2: It is one thing to know something and another other thing to live it. I knew that my mother would eventually leave. All of us eventually leave. I knew that it would be hard. It was Saint Patrick’s day. I’d brought her a green cup of Jell-O, which of course she didn’t eat. When she died, I had stepped into the bathroom. I was in the shower, running water through my hair. What a ridiculous place to be when someone dies. It wasn’t that I thought there would be some movie-scene ending. That she would wait to go until I was holding her hand, looking into her eyes. That death itself would wait until I could walk her to its door and burn with her until her fire turned to smoke and her sparkling blue eyes flipped through the stages of departure. From anger to confusion to something like heroism, the whispering heroism we all embody when we face our last moment. A heroism shining in the blue of her eyes, a deep, flickering blue which proclaimed how much she wanted to stay, here, with the rest of us, even as she left. I knew, after all, that death didn’t wait for anyone. And yet, no matter how much I thought I knew, when she went, what did I find myself shouting in my head? What other than “wait”?
written_by_MFA009.Reason: Excerpt 1 really expands the moment here in a way that Excerpt 2 does not. Excerpt 2 has a more simplistic perspective; this may be a choice. Excerpt 1, on the other hand, takes a more sentimental approach, which is more effective and evocative (ex. "I watched death move through her like smoke through a burning house, slow and inevitable"). It does not glide over moments that could benefit from expansion.

written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: The winter light was dimming, Saint Patrick’s Day fading into a muted gray.  I sat beside her bed, the green Jell-O untouched on the bedside table, a festive offering she couldn’t partake in.  Outside, the snow was falling, the last of winter’s icy grip, the sunlight reflecting off the white expanse in a dazzling display.  But in this room, there was a different kind of dimming, a slow, inevitable burning down to smoke.She wasn’t asleep, not quite, but somewhere between here and there, her breath shallow, her body still.  Yet, her eyes, those strikingly blue eyes, remained open, vivid against the pale skin, the stark white sheets.  It was in those eyes that I saw it all unfold – the bitterness that had clung to her like a shroud, the bewilderment at the body’s betrayal, and then, finally, a quiet heroism.  The blue, so vibrant, so alive, was a defiance, a refusal to let go, even as the current pulled her away.I watched her, my mother, her spirit flickering like a candle flame in the gathering darkness.  And in those blue depths, I saw the echo of the life she had lived, the love she had given, the strength she had shown.  It was a story written in the language of the heart, a story that would live on, even as the last embers of her life faded away.
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: On March 17th, the world was green, but my mother’s eyes were blue. Blue as the sky in early spring. Blue as the Joni Mitchell album. Blue as the bitterness within them, my mother’s undefeated eyes. I was losing her, on that snowy day in spring. Yet she didn’t try to sleep, she didn’t give in, she didn’t snuff out the inner fire of her. She gazed out the window, bewildered by the partiers, the people dressed for Saint Patrick’s Day. The city streets were alive with voices. Sunlight danced along the surface of the Jell-O. She didn’t eat, she just looked at it, that fucking glob of green. And when she looked away, I knew she would die. Her fire had burned away. All the years of shattered sparks and roaring flame and now she was only ashes. Twin flames burning low. I hadn’t always loved my mother in life. We had had our difficulties, that was for damn sure. But as she lay on that bed, showing the blue steel of her eyes, I knew what my mother was. She was a hero. She was a fighter. She was the strongest woman I’ve known. Her lips moved a little, and I leaned in close. Grasping for her life, she slipped away.
written_by_MFA012.Reason: I don't really love either of these but Excerpt 1 is my preference. Excerpt 2 both has a jarring shift in tones ("she just looked at it, that fucking glob of green") and ends with a series of cliches that can't really reach a reader emotionally ("She was a hero. She was a fighter. She was the strongest woman I’ve known," or "Grasping for her life, she slipped away"). The tone is more consistent in 1 and the images build gradually in a comparatively elegant way.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: My mother died on St. Patrick’s Day. There was snow outside, and sunlight glanced off the ice and back into her hospital room. A cup of green Jell-O lingered untouched on its tray. My mother was unresponsive, but not quite asleep. Her eyes were open and vivid. There was an alertness in them still, but what she was looking at, I could not say. The bright blue of her irises was like a frozen lake, contrasting the dull wash of beige and gray shrouding the room. The sky lived inside my mother. It lived inside her then, too, even as we bided time together at the very end, knowing there was only one thing left for her to do. Her fading life was a fire flickering down to smoke—it would only last as long as there was something to burn. There was bitterness too in her eyes, then bewilderment, then a stoic, quiet heroism. A commitment to her own dignity. A promise to endure this final test, no matter how unfairly it had been imposed on her. Her eyes were so blue, my mother’s eyes, a fierce blue, a frozen lake, a sheen of ice that refused to melt, even as the sun broke it apart.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: It was Saint Patrick’s Day, though there was no room for festivity in the hospital room where my mother lay suspended between this life and the next. Outside, the sunlight refracted sharply off the icy snow, casting a dazzling brilliance that mocked the stillness inside. Beside her, a bowl of green Jell-O sat untouched, its lurid color out of place in the solemnity of the moment. My mother’s eyes, blue and unyielding, remained open, vivid against the pallor of her skin and the muted sterility of the room. She was there but not there—unresponsive, yet undeniably present. I watched her, saw her dying like a fire slowly extinguishing into smoke, the embers of her vitality winking out one by one. Her eyes, once fierce with bitterness, shifted to bewilderment, and finally, to a quiet, unspoken heroism. They were the eyes of someone who clung to life even as it slipped from her grasp, a desperate yearning embedded in that piercing blue. The blue of her eyes became my lodestar, a symbol of her fight, her grace, her inevitability. And as I held her hand, I knew that when she closed those eyes for the last time, they would remain etched in me forever, as luminous as the snow outside.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: Excerpt 1 is more emotionally resonant. It gets right into the scene by beginning with "My mother died" as opposed to describing the setting, the emotions associated with the death, etc. Sentences like "The sky lived inside my mother." give me a sense of the narrator's connectedness to their mother, whereas "My mother’s eyes, blue and unyielding, remained open, vivid against the pallor of her skin and the muted sterility of the room" could've been written by anyone.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Aunt Nell used to tote Cousin Ernie Botts to the farm every summer like he was an old handbag or umbrella. He never seemed to mind, smiling banally to show off his fantastic straight, white teeth. He was a clean boy, a good boy, so much so that in the privacy of my own mind, I called him Earnest Bottom. When Aunt Nell passed, there was no one to drag sweet Ernie around, so we stopped seeing him for a while. Mother made sure to send him Christmas cards every year, and I’d doodle him little flowers and rainbows on the back. After I was accepted into college, I wrote him a little note instead, telling him I’d be moving to his city. He wrote back saying we really ought to get dinner once I was settled. We did, and it morphed into an every-other-Sunday affair. Ernie would pick me up at my dorm and drive me to a charming little restaurant called the Old Chelsea. Ernie insisted on us ordering two appetizers each, a main course, dessert, and of course, an after-dinner coffee. The checks, when I managed to glimpse them, always made my eyes bug. But Ernie was a good person, and the elaborate dinners never seemed to me a desire to show off, but rather a way to remain a part of the family. If he could spend so confidently every other week, I presumed he was working one of those legitimate office jobs. He never did talk all that much about himself.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Ernie Botts—Earnest Bottom, as I’d christened him in the foolish privacy of my head—was the clean and well-groomed sort of boy my mother admired.  He was always neat, pressed, and polite, the kind who’d never show up with grass stains or a ripped shirt.  Each summer, he’d arrive at our farm with his mother, Aunt Nell, a high-pitched echo of my mother’s pronouncements on how a young man ought to behave.  After Aunt Nell passed, the summer visits stopped, replaced by the steady arrival of Christmas cards—always signed “Ernie,” never the “Earnest Bottom” of my childhood.    Years later, when I found myself in his city for college, Ernie took it upon himself to take me out to dinner every other Sunday.  The Old Chelsea, the restaurant he chose, was the kind of place with heavy silverware and hushed conversations, the sort of place I figured Ernie frequented—though how a bachelor school teacher could afford it, I didn’t know.  Perhaps I’d underestimated a school teacher’s salary, or perhaps, like the old aunts I’d left back home, he’d scrimped and saved for the sake of appearances.  Ernie wasn’t much of a conversationalist, and I often found myself making idle chatter, filling the silences between his polite inquiries about my studies and his pronouncements on the weather.  I figured it was family duty that brought him, not any real desire for my company.  Still, there was something amusing about being seen in such a place with a man like Ernie—Earnest Bottom, the clean-cut boy turned proper bachelor.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: I preferred the language in Excerpt 1. Phrases like "tote Cousin Ernie Botts to the farm... like he was an old handbag" and "I called him Earnest Bottom" bring some freshness and originality to the passage, which is clear and effective and conversational. Excerpt 2 conveys a similar effect but its language is less finessed, less funny, and a bit more literal, leaving less room for the reader to fill in the gaps.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: During those summers on the farm, Ernie Botts, who we’d mischievously dubbed “Earnest Bottom,” became a predictable part of the season, like the first crop of sweet corn or the relentless hum of cicadas. He was always impeccably groomed—his blond hair neatly combed, his fingernails somehow untouched by dirt, even after a day spent traipsing through the fields. He was good-natured in a way that set him apart from the brashness of other cousins who fought over fishing rods or snickered at Aunt Nell’s awkward manners. Ernie simply smiled and carried on, often humming quietly as he helped with chores or indulged my younger siblings by playing checkers on the front porch. When Aunt Nell passed away, his visits ended, replaced only by his dutiful Christmas cards that seemed to grow shorter with each year. By the time I moved to his city for college, he was a figure shrouded in distant nostalgia, though he reappeared with an almost rehearsed sincerity, treating me to dinners at the Old Chelsea every other Sunday. The crisp white napkins, the polite waitstaff, the gleaming wine glasses—it all seemed to mirror Ernie himself, and I couldn’t shake the feeling that these outings were more about obligation than genuine kinship. But still, I didn’t protest. His generosity, even if tinged with a faint remoteness, filled the silences left by years and miles, a duty performed with meticulous care and quiet resolve.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: It is impossible to think of the Old Chelsea without thinking, too, of Earnest Bottom. His real name, of course, was Ernie Botts—my slightly younger and far more sophisticated cousin. We'd spent many summers together as children at my family's farm. Ernie was prim and manicured and always seemed to be dusting off his pants or scraping mud from the soles of his shoes. At Aunt Nell's funeral, he shook everyone's hands in his freshly pressed suit and thanked them for the flowers. He stopped coming to the farm after that, but we kept in touch through Christmas cards, which he always signed with a kind, personalized note. Our paths ran perpendicular again when I went to graduate school in his city. As soon as he heard I was in town, he locked me into his calendar for dinner every other Sunday. The Old Chelsea had an excellent fillet mignon, he told me, and it was true. The food offset the conversation, which was stale at best. Talk of work and school died out quickly, and I felt guilty talking about my social life—while I was making friends and had started going steady with a classmate, Ernie seemed to be suspended in self-imposed monkhood. Somehow, the bill always ended up in Ernie's hands. “It’s the least I can do,” he’d say, batting away the money I offered, and I couldn’t help but wonder what he thought he owed me.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: I prefer Excerpt2 because it paints a more vivid picture of Ernie Botts. Though both excerpts use specific, visual examples to show what Botts was like throughout time, these are a bit more fleshed-out in Excerpt2. For example, the description of Ernie at Aunt Nell’s funeral, where “he shook everyone's hands in his freshly pressed suit and thanked them for the flowers” is an active memory that shows Ernie doing something that would have been unusual for someone his age, whereas in Excerpt1, he’s described as playing checkers or helping with chores – something that anyone might do. The final lines in Excerpt2 are also more active, showing Ernie in “self-imposed monkhood”,  speaking and “batting” the narrator’s hand away, whereas in Excerpt1 Ernie is not shown speaking or moving and the  descriptions of Ernie’s “faint remoteness” and “meticulous care” are much less specific and could describe the behavior of distant relatives in general.

written_by_MFA033.Excerpt1: Ernie Botts. Ernie. My younger cousin, who was to remain a lifelong bachelor, had once spent each summer with us on the farm, showing up shyly in tow that first season in the shadow of my Aunt Nell. I hadn’t liked having to share a room with my sister, as I did when he came to visit. But he made up for it, with his good-natured affability, and his curious habit of punctilious grooming. I’d had the idea to call him Earnest Bottom-and my use of this nickname behind his back brought my sister and myself no end of amusement. The visits stopped when Aunt Nell passed, Ernie then thirteen. His presence in our house dwindled to a card each Christmas in his spidery handwriting. At eighteen I took the train out to the city, planning to start university at last and my new life. That my cousin lived there too was the last thing on my mind. It was my mother who reminded me. She told me I should look him up, conjuring at once his easy, slightly high-pitched laugh, his perfectly brushed wool sweaters. From then, Ernie and I had dinner every other Sunday, at a place called the Old Chelsea. I wasn’t sure why. I couldn’t tell if he had real fondness for me. His old habits of grooming were accompanied now by a certain formality of speech. It wasn’t a cheap restaurant either, but one of those old-style, stiff tablecloth establishments that used to be in vogue then. We always had three courses and wine. I assumed his loyalty to the Old Chelsea, and to me, meant he could easily afford such luxuries.
written_by_MFA033.Excerpt2: Ernie Botts—whom I privately called "Earnest Bottom" in those days of ruthless teenage cleverness—would arrive at our farm each summer with Aunt Nell, his clothes pressed and his hair neatly combed, as if the three-hour drive on dusty country roads had somehow failed to touch him. He had that particular quality of bachelor sons, a kind of pristine wholesomeness that spoke of carefully maintained routines and unspoken maternal guidance. After Aunt Nell died (a quick death, heart attack while hanging laundry), the summer visits stopped, though Christmas cards arrived without fail, bearing generic winter scenes and his meticulously penned signature. Years later, when I started college in his city, he began taking me to dinner at the Old Chelsea every other Sunday—a restaurant with heavy maroon drapes and waiters who wore black bow ties with an air of weary dignity. I suspected these dinners cost more than he should have spent, but there was something both touching and slightly oppressive about his insistence on maintaining this connection, as if he were fulfilling some deathbed promise to Aunt Nell that I'd never been told about. I assumed he could afford it; after all, he lived in an apartment building with a doorman and wore suits that looked expensive in their subtle way. But sometimes I'd catch him studying the menu with a carefully blank expression, and I'd remember how Aunt Nell used to darken last year's coat with shoe polish to make it look new. There are some kinds of family duty that run deeper than affection, I suppose, though I never quite knew which one brought Ernie to that restaurant every other Sunday, in his good suit, precisely on time.

It flows easily and simply, with simple and evocative sentences such as "At eighteen I took the train out to the city, planning to start university at last and my new life." Excerpt 2, on the other hand, while well written, sometimes falls into cliche territory, with phrases like "ruthless teenage cleverness" ad "weary dignity."

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: The plan was simple—if you could call it that—get the car, get the gear, and get out before anybody realized we were far too gone to be handling lethal machinery. My attorney had a phone jammed to his ear, barking demands at a salesman who clearly wanted nothing more than to shove a tire iron through his skull. “We need a convertible, the biggest one you’ve got. No, don’t give me that Chevy Impala bullshit, I want something with horsepower, something that howls like a dying wolf on the open road.” I could see the man on the other end hesitating, sensing that this was a deal he wanted no part of, but the law was clear—money talks, and we had just enough to sound legitimate. Meanwhile, across the room, a Stingray had just mowed down some poor bastard on Sunset Boulevard, the last frantic gasps of air leaking out of his ruined lungs as people stood around pretending not to see. My attorney watched, nodding approvingly, as if this was part of the deal. “That’s efficiency,” he muttered. I took a long drag from my cigarette and checked the time—not because it mattered, but because it felt important to note that this day had already spun out of control and it wasn’t even noon. The air smelled like hot asphalt and tequila. The salesmen were jittery now, fumbling with the equipment we needed—high-quality recording gear, something we could use to document the horrors we were bound to encounter in Vegas. The door cracked open just enough for us to reach through and grab our loot, an unspoken agreement that we would disappear into the desert and never return. “Load it up,” my attorney barked, shoving a crumpled wad of cash through the gap. “And throw in a few extra tapes. I have a feeling we’re going to need them.” He grinned like a man on the verge of a spectacular crime, then turned to me. “Time to move. The road waits for no one.” I nodded, already feeling the rush, the weight of reckless momentum pulling us forward. It was go-time, and there was no turning back.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: I was driving at an absurd speed and trying my best to keep to the road—though I could be excused for the rumbling moments when I veered into the orange moonscape, because it didn't matter at all as long as you didn't mind a few dings in your fender. I was hallucinating a chase and knew any dip in speed would end my life. My life was behind me, chemicals were in front of me and inside me, and this gave me some real pep as the tires screamed down the asphalt trail. The attorney sat in the passenger seat, even more delusional, leaning and bending with the rapidly changing momentum of the vehicle like an inflatable man. We went over a rock with a terrible chunking sound, and he didn't even wince as I turned us back toward the street and away from the cacti and boiled soil stretching endlessly around us. We were leaving Hollywood and aiming vaguely for Las Vegas. We rarely consulted maps or asked for directions. We would get there. The attorney slammed another acid tab into his mouth. The car, I realized, wouldn't do at all. It was too slow and too compact. It was terrible. What we needed was a big, rumbling convertible. We stopped for a few drinks at an ugly Polynesian bar, and the attorney made some frantic calls about a new rental, demanding the respect an esquire deserves. He did it. We turned off at a rental joint to turn in our desecrated piece of crap for a nice new Stingray. The salesman haggled with us, thinking we couldn't haggle back under the grip of heinous chemicals. We also required some high-quality recording equipment, which we would find when we finally tore into Vegas. There was something we needed it for, because this was a work trip, and all our expenses were dutifully covered as long as we did the interviews. We tried to enter an electronics store, and the clerk stopped us. "Go away," he said, holding the door shut. He waved a crowbar. The attorney negotiated quickly, sneaking company credit cards through the crack, and shortly after, recording equipment sat on the curb with us. We lay there, basking in the motion of our minds, when a Stingray convertible bashed into an elder across the road and left him to die.
written_by_MFA016.Reason: Excerpt 1 reads as frenetic, naturalistic, and seamless. "Meanwhile, across the room, a Stingray had just mowed down some poor bastard on Sunset Boulevard, the last frantic gasps of air leaking out of his ruined lungs as people stood around pretending not to see. My attorney watched, nodding approvingly, as if this was part of the deal." The quickness, ease, and lack of caring feels like a key facet of Gonzo journalism to me, unlike Excerpt 2, which feels more self-aware. "We rarely consulted maps or asked for directions. We would get there." At moments, Excerpt 2 read as more 'obvious.' For this reason, Excerpt 1 was more effective at expressing its ideas/movement in the characteristic Gonzo style.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: My life felt chaotic, and I decided the best way to deal with this would be to go on a reckless drive while indulging in loads and loads of heinous chemicals. We decided we would drive from Hollywood to Vegas, and I began to round up all my drugs—mescaline, amyl, and half a jar of cocaine that I had been keeping in my coat closet for a special occasion. At the same time, I sent my attorney out to look for a decent convertible with a high-quality stereo so that we could listen to music as loud as we wanted while driving through the desert. There were a lot of false starts; for several hours my attorney spoke aggressively on the phone with several car rental agencies while we sat at a Polynesian bar, with me sneaking off occasionally to do hits of acid in the bathroom. He kept needing to demand respect from these salesmen guys who were jerking him around, which I felt completely reflected the energy of Los Angeles at the time… everyone talking over one another and wanting desperately to wring the other’s neck, and yet nobody capable of listening to a single word the other is saying…eventually he got it straightened out, after hanging up angrily a few times and cursing while this ugly group of veins nearly popped out of his neck, and while we drive back to my place we saw a Stingray car hit a woman crossing Sunset Boulevard—she lay there, spread-eagled, and I remember thinking that this was what America had come to now, reduced to lying lifeless among the bird shit on the street. When we finally made it to the store with the audio equipment, things became even more unbearable, everything rushing down on me like a wave made from needles. written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: My life felt chaotic, and I decided the best way to deal with this would be to go on a reckless drive while indulging in loads and loads of heinous chemicals. We decided we would drive from Hollywood to Vegas, and I began to round up all my drugs—mescaline, amyl, and half a jar of cocaine that I had been keeping in my coat closet for a special occasion. At the same time, I sent my attorney out to look for a decent convertible with a high-quality stereo so that we could listen to music as loud as we wanted while driving through the desert. There were a lot of false starts; for several hours my attorney spoke aggressively on the phone with several car rental agencies while we sat at a Polynesian bar, with me sneaking off occasionally to do hits of acid in the bathroom. He kept needing to demand respect from these salesmen guys who were jerking him around, which I felt completely reflected the energy of Los Angeles at the time… everyone talking over one another and wanting desperately to wring the other’s neck, and yet nobody capable of listening to a single word the other is saying…eventually he got it straightened out, after hanging up angrily a few times and cursing while this ugly group of veins nearly popped out of his neck, and while we drive back to my place we saw a Stingray car hit a woman crossing Sunset Boulevard—she lay there, spread-eagled, and I remember thinking that this was what America had come to now, reduced to lying lifeless among the bird shit on the street. When we finally made it to the store with the audio equipment, things became even more unbearable, everything rushing down on me like a wave made from needles. Through a half-cracked open door, my attorney argued with the salespeople, who clearly wanted us out of there as quickly as possible. They held their tire irons like baseball bats, and I felt scared, but intrigued, although maybe it was the acid making me feel scared…I wanted to know what would happen, and I wanted, more than anything, for the rushing feeling to stop. Back and forth and back and forth and back and forth they went, until eventually, it was over and we started our drive through the desert.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: Christ almighty, here we are - trapped in this feverish documentation of a madman's journey, watching the words crawl across the page like speed-crazed insects searching for meaning in the neon wasteland between Hollywood and Vegas. The story reeks of desperate chemicals and the acrid stench of burning rubber on asphalt, all wrapped up in the frenzied quest for the Great American Convertible. My attorney, that chrome-domed harbinger of chaos, is barking into payphones at terrified salesmen while I hover near the bar of some godforsaken Polynesian tomb, mainlining Singapore Slings and wondering if we'll ever make it out of LA alive. The whole scene has the surgical precision of a hurricane - first the maniac phone calls, then the ugly business with the recording equipment, and somewhere in between, the grotesque spectacle of that poor bastard getting mowed down by a Stingray on Sunset. Jesus, what a place. What a time. The salesmen are wielding tire irons now, passing our gear through a crack in the door like they're feeding raw meat to a cage full of rabid wolverines. Can't blame them, really - not with what's happening out there in the streets. The whole country's gone belly-up with fear and loathing, and here we are, two professional journalists, supposedly documenting this circus of depravity. But the real story isn't in the facts - it's in the white-knuckled grip on the wheel at 110 mph, in the savage heart of the American Dream gone wrong. The evidence is everywhere: in the twisted metal on Sunset, in the paranoid eyes of the salesmen, in the heinous chemicals coursing through our bloodstreams like electric eels in a bathtub. And somehow we're supposed to make sense of it all, turn it into something resembling journalism. What a goddamn joke. But there's no going back now - we've bought the ticket, and by God, we're going to take the ride.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: With everything so fucked, there wasn't much to do but the usual heinous chemicals. Preparation for some kind of proper drive, driving on to forever and just past it. We were trying to find a suitable convertible and some recording equipment, but none of it was going well. The attorney met me at the Polynesian bar, and I was calling up the company, asking if I could get my good equipment and how soon. They weren't making sense—you could rarely make sense with these people—but the attorney grabbed the phone, and it seemed like soon enough we'd get it squared away. But the car situation was harder; the salesman took one look at us and shut down, as if we weren't respectable people with respectable money. The attorney stepped in again and got it sorted in his sweaty, loud, unpleasant sort of way. Some people just commanded respect. At the equipment store, we were hovering halfway in and halfway out while the salesman, tire irons in his hands like we were common thieves, was trying to get all our information from us pronto, and the motherfucker wouldn't even open the door. I kept saying I was just there for my equipment, and finally, exasperated, he came back with the stuff we'd asked for, sliding it through like a file in a prison cake. Just as we got in the car, we saw a Stingray hit a pedestrian on Sunset Boulevard. Real quick, it happening in a single breath—though I guessed the pedestrian wouldn't be breathing again after this accident. I looked at the attorney, and he laughed, shell-shocked, and I laughed too even though he was driving me crazy. After an hour on the road, he was still driving me crazy in the passenger seat. We did a little peyote and then a little ketamine, and I thought the two cancelled each other out, for the most part, and my foot was flat on the wheel. All around us we saw desert brush and mesas and nothing, the flat orange nothing that lived out there in the desert. Hollywood felt far away then, but Las Vegas felt further, and we hadn't done much by way of preparations for this Las Vegas trip. But the highway stretched out blissfully before us... and the drugs were good, real good. Sunset would come in a quick green flash.
written_by_MFA026.Reason: I prefer Excerpt2. Excerpt2 is more immersive, and the narrative progression is cohesive even if the events are frenetic. The narrator places the reader in a scene and his voice is vivid and personal ("At the equipment store, we were hovering halfway in and halfway out while the salesman, tire irons in his hands like we were common thieves, was trying to get all our information from us pronto...") By contrast, Excerpt1 reads more like a summary of the concept of a book, with broad, sweeping statements about the nature of narrative ("But the real story isn't in the facts - it's in the white-knuckled grip on the wheel at 110 mph, in the savage heart of the American Dream gone wrong..") rather than an immersive, chronological narration of actions as they are happening.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: I closed my eyes and thought about the nature of longing, how it shapes itself around absence like water flowing into an empty vessel, becoming more precise in its form the more complete the void becomes. Sylvie had left in that way of hers, without sound or ceremony, as if she had simply dissolved into the thick afternoon air, and I found myself studying the treeline where the shadows gathered, imagining her watching me pretend not to notice the solitude she had left behind. There is something about craving that makes the thing craved more vivid than itself could ever be—like the memory of a wild berry's tartness being sweeter than the actual taste, or how the thought of rain can feel more quenching than the drops themselves when they finally fall. I began to imagine crafting a statue, not of cold marble but of living stone that would draw up minerals from the earth like a tree draws sap, and I would place her among the pines where the light filters down in dusty columns. Unlike Lot's wife, who turned to salt in her backward glance of regret, this woman would be adorned with rare blooms that only grow in the deepest parts of the forest, and her face would hold all the forgiveness that Lot's wife could never find. The wild children—for there are always wild children in these woods, moving like shadows between the trees—would gather around her feet, marveling at the strange flowers that crown her head, at the way her stone hands, though forever still, seem to reach for them with infinite tenderness. They would sense in her something of mothers they barely remember, of homes they might have had in some other life, and they would leave small offerings at her feet: interesting pebbles, abandoned birds' nests, fragments of colored glass that catch the light like trapped pieces of sky. And I thought perhaps this is what Sylvie and I were both seeking: not the thing itself, but the holy shape of its absence, which holds more truth than presence ever could.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: I’ve realized that craving and fulfillment are not connected in the way I once thought. A craving is so intense and visceral that it cannot be truly satiated by consuming the thing you want. For example, berries are always sweeter before I eat them. I wonder if that’s how Eve felt in the garden after she tasted the forbidden fruit—disappointed, hungry, running her tongue over her teeth in search of satisfaction. I’ve been thinking about Sylvie, and how she disappeared silently into the forest and left me alone. I suspected she might be hiding somewhere, watching from a perch atop a spruce tree or huddled inside a hollow log. She liked to tease me. I didn’t want to give her the satisfaction of calling out for her, making her think I was afraid of being alone. I didn’t want her to feel like she’d rescued me by returning. I meandered around the little clearing and looked at the great towering tree trunks and their long shadows and the patches of grass poking up from the dark earth. In the center of it all, I imagined a statue. She was carved from some kind of pale, luminescent stone, something that seemed to give off its own light from within. Rare flowers were twined in her hair—orchid doves, lenten roses, midnight clematis. Blossoming vines wound up her body, not trapping her, but protecting her. My statue was a radiant mother, utterly unlike the barren, remorseful wife of Lot. She was vibrant and forgiving, always surrounded by children who marveled at her quiet beauty. The children, wild vagabonds of the forest, would be drawn to her through some mysterious summons, and they would huddle before her and bask in her gentle solace. Though her frozen hands would never touch them, she would look upon them with a kindness they had never known, and their happy tears would feed the vines and flowers that had made her their home. When the children were with her, they were not orphans, but children who had been made to be loved by a mother.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: I liked excerpt 2 better because it does a better job fitting complex ideas into more compact, rhythmic sentences. Compare the rambling idea, as expressed in excerpt 1, that longing "shapes itself around absence like water flowing into an empty vessel, becoming more precise in its form the more complete the void becomes," to the more elegant version from excerpt 2: "A craving is so intense and visceral that it cannot truly be satiated by consuming the thing you want." Sylvie had left in that way of hers, without sound or ceremony, as if she had simply dissolved into the thick afternoon air, and I found myself studying the treeline where the shadows gathered, imagining her watching me pretend not to notice the solitude she had left behind. There is something about craving that makes the thing craved more vivid than itself could ever be—like the memory of a wild berry's tartness being sweeter than the actual taste, or how the thought of rain can feel more quenching than the drops themselves when they finally fall. I began to imagine crafting a statue, not of cold marble but of living stone that would draw up minerals from the earth like a tree draws sap, and I would place her among the pines where the light filters down in dusty columns. Unlike Lot's wife, who turned to salt in her backward glance of regret, this woman would be adorned with rare blooms that only grow in the deepest parts of the forest, and her face would hold all the forgiveness that Lot's wife could never find. The wild children—for there are always wild children in these woods, moving like shadows between the trees—would gather around her feet, marveling at the strange flowers that crown her head, at the way her stone hands, though forever still, seem to reach for them with infinite tenderness. They would sense in her something of mothers they barely remember, of homes they might have had in some other life, and they would leave small offerings at her feet: interesting pebbles, abandoned birds' nests, fragments of colored glass that catch the light like trapped pieces of sky. And I thought perhaps this is what Sylvie and I were both seeking: not the thing itself, but the holy shape of its absence, which holds more truth than presence ever could.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: I’ve realized that craving and fulfillment are not connected in the way I once thought. A craving is so intense and visceral that it cannot be truly satiated by consuming the thing you want. For example, berries are always sweeter before I eat them. I wonder if that’s how Eve felt in the garden after she tasted the forbidden fruit—disappointed, hungry, running her tongue over her teeth in search of satisfaction. I’ve been thinking about Sylvie, and how she disappeared silently into the forest and left me alone. I suspected she might be hiding somewhere, watching from a perch atop a spruce tree or huddled inside a hollow log. She liked to tease me. I didn’t want to give her the satisfaction of calling out for her, making her think I was afraid of being alone. I didn’t want her to feel like she’d rescued me by returning. I meandered around the little clearing and looked at the great towering tree trunks and their long shadows and the patches of grass poking up from the dark earth. In the center of it all, I imagined a statue. She was carved from some kind of pale, luminescent stone, something that seemed to give off its own light from within. Rare flowers were twined in her hair—orchid doves, lenten roses, midnight clematis. Blossoming vines wound up her body, not trapping her, but protecting her. My statue was a radiant mother, utterly unlike the barren, remorseful wife of Lot. She was vibrant and forgiving, always surrounded by children who marveled at her quiet beauty. The children, wild vagabonds of the forest, would be drawn to her through some mysterious summons, and they would huddle before her and bask in her gentle solace. Though her frozen hands would never touch them, she would look upon them with a kindness they had never known, and their happy tears would feed the vines and flowers that had made her their home. When the children were with her, they were not orphans, but children who had been made to be loved by a mother.
