written_by_MFA009.Excerpt1: It was the longing itself that seemed to summon the essence of what I desired, as if yearning were a prayer that the world, in its quiet way, conspired to answer. The sweetness of berries unpicked lingered in the air, more vibrant for being out of reach. Sylvie had vanished again, her silence as deliberate as a shadow retreating with the sun, and I knew not to call for her. It was better to let the absence settle, to imagine her slender frame paused just out of sight, watching from the line of trees, her face half-lit by the dappled sun. The woods held their breath, alive with the hum of insects and the rustle of unseen creatures, and I found myself wondering if she had gone into them to become something wilder, freer, more elemental than her mortal self. It was then I imagined a statue, a woman wrought from the alabaster of my mind, her form unyielding yet softened by an artist’s hand. Her hair, an eternal cascade of rare blossoms, reached toward the ground like a benediction. She would not be like Lot’s wife, turned back toward despair, but a figure of grace, fixed in forgiveness, her face turned forward into the eternal now.Around her feet would gather children, wild-eyed and untamed, the sort that flit through the forest like whispers of untold stories. They would marvel at her beauty, her quiet presence, her promise of solace, though her hands, stiff and unyielding, could never stroke their hair or lift them from their loneliness. And yet, the children would linger, imagining themselves known, loved, by the depths of her unseeing gaze. Perhaps Sylvie, wherever she was, could understand such a figure—one who existed between the realms of presence and absence, neither gone nor wholly there. The trees would hold her as their own, casting shadows that shifted like whispers against her alabaster skin. And I, rooted in my own solitude, could only wonder if longing itself was a form of creation, if absence was a kind of grace, and if Sylvie’s silence spoke a language deeper than words.
written_by_MFA009.Excerpt2: Sometimes I wonder about the difference between craving something and fulfillment. Sometimes I want something so much I feel like I’m going to break open. Let’s say it’s a fresh berry, let’s say it’s like I’ve been really wanting a fresh berry, plucked from a bush in the orchard, even before that berry’s in my hands, it’s already got a taste in my mind, I’ve been building it up moment after moment until I have it in my brain like I’ve already got it on my tongue, so when Sylvie tells me she picked something for me and plops it in my mouth, it’s even sweeter because the sweetness confirms the foundation I’ve already built for it. I don’t know how to put it. Sylvie disappeared for a while, like a mouse, but then she came back. Sometimes she still goes out though, vanishes into the woods without saying anything. I think she’s out there right now, watching me ruminate. I don’t know what kind of solitude we can both get when we both are in each other’s minds. Could it be a way of being together? A very strange way? It’s beautiful out in the woods. The trees are older than I can fathom, really, old like stories can be old. I’d like to put a status out there, almost like somebody would always be watching, a statue of a woman, to stand in between all those old trees, a woman in a crown of new flowers, looking only ever ahead, forward, never letting any kind of barrenness touch her, like she was the opposite of Lot’s wife and all there was to her was the kind of forgiving vibrancy that children wonder at, the vibrancy that comes from a life well-lived. Even as a statue, I think they’d come to her, every child that’s ever felt lost-wild and orphan, and I think when they’d reach out to touch her stone hands, they’d find that that statue’s stone was warm for them. Sometimes I wish Sylvie were warmer. There’s warmth all around in all the beautiful trees and even the grasses. The problem is that trees don’t feel warm when you touch their bark unless it’s from the sun.
written_by_MFA009.Reason: Excerpt 2 seems to vibrate with a human subjectivity that makes its more simplistic observations seem more alive and coherent. Excerpt1 does have some beautiful language and lines, especially the final one, but it doesn't really demonstrate a progression of thought or fluency or chain of wrestling with uncertainty the way Excerpt2 does. Excerpt2 seems more accessible in its sensations, and doesn't need to insist on itself in order to be effective.

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: There are times when to long for something is almost as satisfying as to finally receive it, or when the essence of that which is desired is evoked so clearly that to receive it is no longer necessary. As when one yearns to pluck a berry from the vine and savor its ripeness, so that the sweetness seems to precede the taste of the juice itself. Sylvie had said earlier that in springtime we could pick berries here. I searched for Sylvie's hand beside mine, but I found that she had slipped away silently and left me alone in the clearing. Yet in some way, I felt I could sense her closeness and thought she might be watching me from the woods, so I showed no change in my expression and pretended to be ignorant of my solitude. Around me, the sun cast long shadows through the partings of the tree branches, from which the browned leaves had already begun to fall into the clearing. A thin layer of frost was formed on the mud around where I sat. I imagined forming out of this cold clay earth a statue of a woman whom I would adorn with rare flowers. She would be a calm presence standing among the trees, not the cold, hard pillar of salt into which Lot's wife was transformed as punishment for her desire, for turning back with regret to look at all she had lost. A figure free of yearning, around whom the wild children of the forest would gather to marvel at her beauty and warmth. They would take solace in the vivacious beauty of such a figure and cling to her almost as a mother, even as her frozen hands could not caress them as one would their own children. Again I looked for Sylvie and thought of how I was, in searching for someone who had left me, not unlike the poor woman who had been turned to salt. Unlike the taste of those imagined berries, I was not sure if my longing for connection could ever be quite enough to evoke the presence of the thing itself.

With all respect to heaven, scene of the miracle is here, among us.The eternal is idea much less preposterous than time, and this very fact should seize our attention.In certain contexts, improbable is called miraculous.What is eternal must always be complete, if my understanding is correct.So it is possible to imagine that time was created in order that there might be narrative – event, sequence and causation, ignorance and error, retribution, atonement.A word, a phrase, a story falls on rich or stony ground and flourishes as it can, possibility in a sleeve of limitation.Certainly, time is occasion for our strangely mixed nature, in every moment differently compounded, so that often we surprise ourselves, and always scarcely know ourselves, and exist in relation to experience, if we attend to it and if its plainness does not disguise it from us, as if we were visited by revelation.
written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2: There are times when to long for something is almost as satisfying as to finally receive it, or when the essence of that which is desired is evoked so clearly that to receive it is no longer necessary. As when one yearns to pluck a berry from the vine and savor its ripeness, so that the sweetness seems to precede the taste of the juice itself. Sylvie had said earlier that in springtime we could pick berries here. I searched for Sylvie's hand beside mine, but I found that she had slipped away silently and left me alone in the clearing. Yet in some way, I felt I could sense her closeness and thought she might be watching me from the woods, so I showed no change in my expression and pretended to be ignorant of my solitude. Around me, the sun cast long shadows through the partings of the tree branches, from which the browned leaves had already begun to fall into the clearing. A thin layer of frost was formed on the mud around where I sat. I imagined forming out of this cold clay earth a statue of a woman whom I would adorn with rare flowers. She would be a calm presence standing among the trees, not the cold, hard pillar of salt into which Lot's wife was transformed as punishment for her desire, for turning back with regret to look at all she had lost. A figure free of yearning, around whom the wild children of the forest would gather to marvel at her beauty and warmth. They would take solace in the vivacious beauty of such a figure and cling to her almost as a mother, even as her frozen hands could not caress them as one would their own children. written_by_MFA004.Excerpt1: The morning air reunited Clarissa Dalloway with Bourton, her younger face and younger days, her eighteen-year-old solemnity. She had a bright evening ahead, an ambition to entertain Rumplemayer's men. She was in wonder among the flowers, having traversed the market in lieu of her servant, Lucy. The young girl deserved a break, an evening to mind her own affairs. What else was a girl but this? But back to Bourton, where the air had kissed Clarissa's cheeks like the finest gentleman, where Peter Walsh had teased her over breakfast, asserting that cauliflowers were surely superior to men. He was on a sojourn in India, which he'd detailed in rambling letters. His letters were stiffened by truisms, cloyingly personal, a bore to spend one's evening with. What Clarissa recalled most were his teeth, their hue of yellow, not unhygienic but telling of inferior genetics. He had a laugh like a doctor's, inappropriate. He'd tell you about your muggy insides, then chuckle because there was nothing wrong with his. But alas, the flowers. Lavender or Rose? This called to mind Peter again and his oddly feminine smells. That he smelled unlike a man endeared Clarissa to him. Scent was a signature, a tell of how one moved through the world. To share a scent with a woman, one must also share her sensibilities, her gentleness, her sense of utter safety. If Peter were to return early, to meet Clarissa in the market right then, she'd recognize his teeth first, then his scent. She'd think how familiar the dull yellow of his mouth was. Admittedly, his remaining details might strike her as unfamiliar.
written_by_MFA004.Excerpt2: Clarissa Dalloway, a woman of exquisite sensibility, stepped out into the vibrant London morning. She had decided to buy the flowers herself, a small act of consideration for Lucy, her servant, who was already bustling about with the preparations for the evening's gathering. The crisp air carried a hint of the past, and Clarissa's thoughts drifted back to Bourton, her childhood home. She remembered the mornings there, the dew still clinging to the roses, the world awakening with a freshness that was both exhilarating and solemn.At eighteen, the world had seemed to stretch before her, a tapestry woven with infinite possibilities. Now, years later, the edges of that tapestry had frayed. But some threads remained bright, indelible marks on the fabric of her memory. Peter Walsh, with his sardonic wit and his penchant for the dramatic, was one such thread. "I prefer men to cauliflowers," he had declared one morning at breakfast, his eyes twinkling with amusement.Clarissa smiled at the memory. Peter was returning from India soon, his letters filled with tales of his adventures and misadventures. He was a man of contradictions, capable of great passion and profound melancholy. Clarissa had always found him both exasperating and endearing. His return would stir the waters of her well-ordered life, she knew, but it was a disruption she welcomed. For Peter, with all his flaws and foibles, reminded her of a time when life was less predictable, less constrained by the conventions of society. He was a relic of her youth, a symbol of a time when her heart was still open to the world, before the disappointments and disillusionments of adulthood had begun to close in.
written_by_MFA004.Reason: Excerpt 2 does a better job establishing conceits and building scenes. Compare the prosaic summary of Excerpt 1's "Peter Walsh had teased her over breakfast, asserting that cauliflowers were surely superior to men" to Excerpt 2's much more lively and scenic, "I prefer men to cauliflowers,' he had declared one morning at breakfast, his eyes twinkling with amusement." Look also to the conceit in excerpt too of the frayed tapestry, which brings so much life to Clarissa's sense of memory--missing completely from Excerpt 1.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: She had decided to buy the flowers herself, to spare Lucy the trouble — Lucy, who was rushing about with preparations for the party, and Rumpelmayer’s men were about also; Yes, thought Mrs Dalloway, I will buy them myself. It was all coming together as many parties had done before, with great bustle, and would come together in the end as all parties do, as did those parties from her youth when she was not the host. And the fresh morning air returns her to younger days at Bourton, stepping out into other early mornings — how exhilarating it was then, and how solemn also, to be eighteen and just beginning. The chill this air carries, and the slow warmth rising into one’s cheeks, and ears, and hands. What had Peter said to me: something about cauliflowers, about preferring men to cauliflowers. A conversation over breakfast with Peter Walsh, always teasing then; still teasing now, albeit separated by so many years and kilometres. Clarissa thinks of his letters, the glint in his eye she can still feel in those pages — his promise, too, steady as his voice, to return from India, to return and to see her. Cauliflowers! Such a thing to remember as clearly as if their breakfast was shared only yesterday, when in fact yesterday Clarissa had been deciding about the flowers, deciding to buy them from the yellow and blue shop she now rapidly approaches, with the vibrant window displays; the freshest flowers, she knew, those with the richest and most enduring smell, must come from this shop, and now she would buy them herself.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: Mrs. Dalloway, stepping out into the June morning, thought how she would fetch the flowers herself, for Lucy had quite enough to manage with those men from Rumpelmayer's coming. The fresh air caught her face (how young she felt, how perpetually astonished!) and sent her mind spinning back to Bourton, to those mornings when she was eighteen, when she would burst out onto the terrace and feel the world pause, crystalize, become both solemn and effervescent in that early hour. Peter Walsh (he was coming back from India, his letters said) had laughed at her that morning at breakfast, saying she preferred men to cauliflowers — how like him to say such a thing, to pierce through to some truth while making it all seem ridiculous! His letters, scattered now across her desk at home like fallen leaves, still carried that sharp wit, that capacity to wound and heal in the same breath. And how strange it was, she thought, pausing at the corner of Bond Street, that while whole years dissolved into nothing, that single moment remained: Peter's fork suspended, his eyes twinkling with mischief, the morning light streaming across the breakfast table at Bourton. The way he would tilt his head when amused (she could see it now, with perfect clarity) while all else blurred and shifted like patterns in water. For that was what memory did, was it not? It preserved these fragments, these bright shards of experience, while whole seasons fell away into darkness, into that great pool of forgotten things that lay beneath the surface of one's daily life.
written_by_MFA026.Reason: Excerpt 2 has a more fully formed voice to me. The use of parentheses results in sophisticated, winding sentences (for instance: "Peter Walsh (he was coming back from India, his letters said) had laughed at her that morning at breakfast, saying she preferred men to cauliflowers — how like him to say such a thing, to pierce through to some truth while making it all seem ridiculous!"). The language also feels slightly more precise. The same anecdote feels forced in excerpt 1 ("What had Peter said to me: something about cauliflowers, about preferring men to cauliflowers.") the "something" like it is pushing too hard to feign the probing quality of memory.

written_by_MFA032.Excerpt1: Clarissa stepped into the brisk morning air, her gaze lifting to the soft haze of London streets, a breath catching in her chest, carrying with it the scent of fresh blooms and the faint rumble of Rumpelmayer’s men unloading their crates. She would buy the flowers herself, sparing Lucy the trouble, and in the act, indulging that faint, persistent thrill of slipping out unencumbered, her steps crisp, her thoughts unfurling. Bourton, as if summoned by the cool touch of the breeze, rose vivid before her. The mornings there had carried a peculiar gravity, the air saturated with the promise of youth, of life, at eighteen—the world trembling on the cusp of discovery. She could feel it still, the dewy grass against her shoes, the sharp burst of laughter carried on the wind, and Peter Walsh, always Peter, his voice teasing yet tethered to something deeper. “I prefer men to cauliflowers,” he had said once, over breakfast, as if the absurdity of the phrase could mask the intensity beneath it. And now, after all these years, Peter was returning. From India, of all places, with letters she could scarcely recall opening properly, their pages crammed with the tangents of a restless mind. She had always thought of him as a man on the edge of some revelation, never quite within reach. His words lingered, some sharp, some softened with time, like the murmur of a distant wave retreating. Yet it was the texture of him she remembered most—the way his presence filled the room, the peculiar weight of his silences. The day unfolded before her, rich and strange, and as the sunlight broke through the fog, she felt herself poised, a solitary figure on the cusp of past and present, out in the world, yet curiously, utterly alone.
written_by_MFA032.Excerpt2: She was in danger of a mood; if I am to remain still, Clarissa thought, it will overtake me, it will make the world unwelcome with me, turn it dim and desiccated, and poor Lucy will bear the brunt, or Rumpelmayer’s men, who were laying the table. “I’ll do it,” Clarissa said, and she said it again, as if worried that the words had not escaped the confines of her thought, “I’ll get the flowers, Lucy.” She left the house. Outside, it was almost Bourton—the air was sharp, like a country wind, she thought; at eighteen, in Bourton, it had felt more like a gale; yes, at eighteen years old, simply placing one foot in front of the other had lent Clarissa purpose—a stroll around the garden was as grand as an expedition to India. Yes, at Bourton, the thought of sending Lucy would not have arisen; Clarissa would purchase the flowers and admire them freely. But in London, a strong wind carried the brine of the Thames; it stank; it irritated her lungs, her heart; the odor of the flowers would, too. And there came Peter Walsh, sailing in on an airy, unnamed ship, saying, “What match is a cauliflower for a man?” (Around his voice, Clarissa recognized the faint crunch and tinkling of a decade-old breakfast.) Peter will return from India like that—on which date and at which time his ship would dock in England should have been unimportant to Clarissa, and yet she wondered; she called up his last letters, filed away in a familiar groove, and read them again, and with each word, London decayed, fell away like petals, and in its place, she erected another cathedral. Inside it, relics, some potent to the touch, some no more than shriveled digits, long-empty boxes.
written_by_MFA032.Reason: Excerpt 2 has more beautiful sentences; "She was in danger of a mood" is much more memorable than "Clarissa stepped into the brisk morning air." In addition, Excerpt 2 feels like it is much closer to Clarissa's point of view than Excerpt 1.

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: Orin woke up next to the subject, mentally flaying himself for referring to this person as such, but using the same voice to berate himself that he used to describe this person as a subject, so the whole process became moot. The subject roused and pantomimed closeness, holding Orin’s clammy ribs, giggling at nothing, suggesting they fry or filet or bake the byproducts of various animals for breakfast. Orin’s beady little button eyes shimmered the reflections of the Subject's own eyes, through which they saw, perhaps, a glimpse of their own happiness, their own attempts at it, their own failures towards it. Orin longed to be alone, to return to his routines. Four coffees, each more burned than the last, a shower where he contemplated cleaning the mold spots that grew imperceptibly over the evening, perceptibly over the month, and perhaps a run after to justify the next day’s shower. But he knew that all of it, the loneliness, the mundane, was just a steep climb towards something crested and flat, a plain he wished to never see.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: That it's somehow both pathetic and profound how Orin's post-dream consciousness becomes this sort of infinite regression of anxieties, each one feeding into and sort of birthing the next, like those Russian nesting dolls except imagine each smaller doll is progressively more damaged than its container. The whole morning routine thing becoming this desperate assemblage of shields — the multiple coffees and showers and runs — against whatever nameless thing the dreams have excavated in him, and the presence of these "Subjects" (which is exactly the kind of clinically distant terminology someone would use when they're terrified of actual connection) only amplifies the awareness of his own emotional vacancy, which then of course makes him feel even more alienated, which then makes him need more coffee, etc., ad infinitum. That there's something almost liturgical about how he processes these mornings, these rituals of purification that never quite purify. The dreams themselves being less about actual spiders or heights than about the sensation of being watched while being alone, which is possibly the most contemporary form of existential terror there is. And it's worth noting that even in his solitude he's performing for some imagined audience, his anxiety itself becoming a kind of entertainment, the way everything does in our self-conscious age, even our own private sufferings being transformed into these sort of avant-garde performances for audiences that don't exist.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Orin awoke in the cold post-dream anxiety and discomfort of a spider’s web, a fall from a height, a suffocating loss of control.  The tendrils of the dream clung to him, their grotesque forms and unspeakable anxieties lingering.  Even multiple coffees, showers, or a morning run could barely rinse him of the feeling of being spectacularly tiny and yet at the mercy of something vast and unknowable.  Waking up alone was bad enough, but waking up with a Subject—an overnight guest whose name and details were best left unscrutinized—was a special kind of hell.The Subject, oblivious to the roiling psychic storm within him, would engage in the usual banalities of morning—the vapid small talk, the cuddling, the attempts at cooking breakfast.  Orin would lie there, trapped beneath the weight of their normalcy, feeling like a creature from another dimension.  Their cheerful voices sounded like the chirping of alien insects; their well-meaning touches were suffocating him.  Even when alone, these mornings were a bleak and desolate landscape.  The day stretched before him like a vertical climb or a fall, depending on the dream’s residue.  Either way, it was an ordeal to be endured, a performance to be staged.  The world was a stage, and he was a fraud—a fraud who longed for authenticity but found himself perpetually trapped in the performance of it.  The irony was not lost on him, but neither was it a source of amusement. It was simply a fact, as bleak and inescapable as the morning itself.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Orin wakes up feeling miserable. It’s always the same thing for him, that feeling of being wrenched out of a bottomless pit, the spiders, the heights, the tsunamis, the teeth falling out and clattering to the floor, the cliché and the boilerplate, dreams and fears so ordinary and yet completely destabilizing. He wants to go through his ritual, the multiple black coffees and the boiling hot shower and the run around the block in his sweatpants, just to get to a state resembling normalcy. But on this particular day, he has woken up next to a Subject, and he feels that rage, at the person he was last night, and also at the person lying in bed beside him. He has been doing this more and more lately, finding somebody to go to bed with, and he always hates himself for it. He wants to go back to the heights and the spiders to avoid the cuddling, the mindless small talk, the fried eggs, the depressing attempts at morning sex, the way the Subjects are chronically unable to recognize his torment. When he is alone, he feels suffocated, but with the Subjects, it’s worse. He wants to go back to the tall building he was teetering on the edge of the moment before he woke up, though now he feels, strangely, like he is already there. The subject rolls over and Orin imagines himself losing balance on that building, and tumbling through the agonizing, nauseating remainder of a lonely and empty day.

Sentences like "It’s always the same thing for him" feel more colloquial than "The tendrils of the dream clung to him, their grotesque forms and unspeakable anxieties lingering." The ideas in Excerpt 2 flow more naturally whereas the ideas in Excerpt 1 feel more choppy. Excerpt 2 uses more memorable details like "fried eggs, the depressing attempts at morning sex," etc.

The walls of his apartment took on the sheen of inevitability, the day ahead a Sisyphean incline of meetings and errands and human interactions that he already knew would leave him feeling as drained as the coffee grounds spiraling down his sink. This, he thought, was life’s greatest irony: that waking up alive could feel so much like falling.

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: Orin’s mornings often began as a kind of existential residue, the aftermath of dreams that seemed to gnaw their way out from the deep recesses of the psyche’s cellar, dreams that were equal parts spiders and sheer verticality, both suffocating and vertiginous. Yet the presence of a Subject—the capital "S" both deliberate and derisive, a holdover from what Orin thought of as his internal marketing manual for coping with emotional distance—would complicate the sequence. Subjects had a tendency toward earnest, unbidden gestures: talking as though morning were a shared phenomenon, attempting to wrap him in the tangled warmth of their limbs, even cooking eggs with a kind of oblivious cheer that Orin could only describe as offensive. The worst was the silence, the gap in conversation where their gaze hung too long on him, expectant. Alone, though, wasn’t better. The walls of his apartment took on the sheen of inevitability, the day ahead a Sisyphean incline of meetings and errands and human interactions that he already knew would leave him feeling as drained as the coffee grounds spiraling down his sink. This, he thought, was life’s greatest irony: that waking up alive could feel so much like falling.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: I stumbled into the job because I heard about it from the local drunk. The local drunk had uneven stubble and a feminine watery quality around his eyes. It was seasonal, but I was fine with that. I never liked to stay in the same job too long. It was free and it was simple, and I don’t know of a man who doesn’t value those things above all else. It was a small amount of work compared to most jobs, monotonous, sure, but I could think about other things, like girls or what I wanted to eat. Some people didn’t, but I always liked to work around Christmastime. It was only my second day when I met the big woman. She had a mole over the left side of her lip shaped like a heart. She had short hair, and her breasts were small for how big she was. Her eyes were thin and suspicious. She opened the door when I came to put her mail in the box. She wore a white, lace robe that was meant for a smaller woman, and it made her hips look nice and round. She was smoking a cigarette delicately like a movie star, and she asked me to give her the mail. I did, three letters, and somehow we ended up talking, and I found out her husband was stationed somewhere in California. “It’s sorta dark, the loneliness,” she said, and I agreed with her. “You’re alone?” she asked. “No,” I said. “But you’re still lonely.” I shrugged and looked right at the sun. We organized it so we’d meet that night, at her house. It was her idea, but I didn’t exactly turn it down. I went over there after dinner and it was nice enough. We fooled around on her couch and I was pleasantly surprised by how good her figure was. She wasn’t all lumpy and stretched like big women can be. It went on like that for a couple nights, but by the third I was tired of it and that was the end of that. It was a good experience, all in all, and reminded me why I liked that job so much.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: I drove down the street with a bag of letters slung over my shoulder like some half-assed Santa Claus in a postal uniform. Got the job from some drunk at the bar who said they were desperate for Christmas help, didn't even check my record. Perfect setup - walk around all day, drop paper in boxes, nobody breathing down your neck about quotas or time cards. Second day in, I'm working this neighborhood of tired houses with paint peeling off like dead skin when I see her. Big woman, not the Hollywood type, more like a female wrestler gone soft. She was watering dead flowers, her dress pulled tight across her ass, and when she bent over I nearly dropped the whole damn bag. "You the new mailman?" she asked, straightening up. I nodded, handed her some circulars and bills. She told me her husband was stationed in Germany, hadn't touched her in 8 months. Christ, the way she said it made my balls ache. I had a woman at home but she was always bitching about the rent, about my drinking, about everything. This one just wanted company. "Come by tonight," she said, giving me her address. I showed up at 9, half-drunk on cheap wine. The house smelled like potpourri and desperation. We didn't waste time talking - she led me straight to the bedroom, peeling off that housedress like a snake shedding its skin. For three days I'd deliver her mail, then deliver something else at night. But like everything else, it got old fast. The smell of her perfume started making me sick, her neediness felt like a noose. By the fourth day I was taking different routes, ducking behind hedges when I saw her watering those dead flowers. Looking back, being a mailman wasn't half bad - good hours, easy work, and lonely housewives with too much time on their hands. Hell, you didn't even have to try - they were so desperate they'd fuck anything in a uniform. Sometimes the best jobs are the ones that give you just enough money to drink and just enough time to fuck.
written_by_MFA008.Reason: Excerpt 1 has a more coherent, effective style than Excerpt 2. Where Excerpt 2 reaches for similies like "peeling off that housedress like a snake shedding its skin," or, "her neediness felt like a noose," Excerpt 1 delivers its action in a punchier, more matter-of-fact way: "It went on like that for a couple nights, but by the third I was tired of it and that was the end of that."

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Cheerfulness was not in the job description for "Christmas mail carrier," so every day I showed up and delivered the damned mail. It was fitting that I found out about the job from our local drunk. Five bottles in at nine in the a.m. and the guy was babbling about being an elf for the US postal system. I'd rather have been six sheets to the wind than selling my soul for employment. And yet, I found the work to be rather freeing. I got to swan around town all day, moseying up to people's houses and eyeing their letters before dropping them off, washing my hands of them until tomorrow. It was simple, easy.I met the big woman my second day on the job. When I say big, she was actually quite short, but her tits were so massive they came up to her chin. My kind of woman. Until she opened her mouth and gave me her sad sap story. Her husband was enlisted some place far away. I couldn't tell what possibility bothered her most—that he was blowing guys' heads off or that he was getting blown. She went on and on about how it wasn't right for a married woman to be all alone. The big diamond ring was apparently a cure-all. This was news to me. I had a lady, myself, but I was lonely with her.After our shift, when the big woman invited me to come over later that night, I thought, to hell with being lonely ever again! The sex was great, the kind you think about the next time your old lady "has a headache" and you're on your own for the night, but not great enough. Five days later I found her to be so one-note that I split. Besides, even when we were together, we were both still alone. I think recent events showed I was perfectly suited to being a temporary mailman, what with the great benefits like steady pay, leisurely work, and ill-conceived romantic escapades.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: I took the job because I needed something easy, something that didn’t ask too many questions, didn’t make me think too hard. A local drunk had mentioned they needed Christmas help at the post office, and that was enough for me. Walk around, dump letters in boxes, pretend to care. Not bad. My second day, I met her—big woman, bigger than me, with those arms that looked like they’d been lifting more than just grocery bags. She stood at the door like she’d been waiting for me all day. “Cold out,” she said, her breath heavy, warm, sweet and rotten at the same time. “Yeah,” I said, “but I don’t mind.” I minded, but I wasn’t about to tell her that. She took the envelope from my hand, but didn’t let go. “Lonely here,” she said. Her husband was stationed somewhere far off, wearing a uniform, probably shining his boots and thinking about her. Poor bastard. “I make good coffee,” she said. That wasn’t coffee she was offering. And I was lonely too, despite having a girl waiting for me somewhere, someone who wasn’t enough, someone who made too much sense. That night, I went back. The place was warm, smelled like burned toast and old carpet. She poured me whiskey instead of coffee, and that was better. We moved from the kitchen to the couch to the bedroom like it was something we’d done before. A few days passed like that. But the thing about loneliness is, it doesn’t go away just because you put your hands on someone. Eventually, the whiskey bottle emptied, the room started feeling smaller, and her laugh turned into something I didn’t want to hear. The job was still there, but the excitement was gone. So I delivered the mail, took my paycheck, and let her find another man to fill the spaces her husband left behind. Being a mailman wasn’t bad. Good work if you like walking. Better work if you don’t mind a little company along the way.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: Excerpt 1 has clearer sentences and more precision in its descriptions. It also has a comedy in its voice that is charming. I'm thinking of lines like: "the guy was babbling about being an elf for the US postal system" and " When I say big, she was actually quite short, but her tits were so massive they came up to her chin. My kind of woman." The narrator is allowed to be unpleasant and distasteful. While the final sentence, stumbles, it feels more coherent as the work of a single voice. Excerpt 2 does a better job situating the narrative in a single scene, but the scene is confusing as one excerpt and the narrator's voice occasionally moves into strange imagery ("smelled like burnt toast and old carpet"). The snake-bitten feeling of the narrator doesn't match the pace with which the narrative proceeds and instead of feeling tragic, it feels off-kilter.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: I’d spoken with Reva last week, but it was a short conversation filled mostly with platitudes. She’d seemed distracted and said she was at the gym. When the news broke about the towers, I called her a few times, but she didn’t pick up. Without thinking, I went immediately to the store to purchase a TV/VCR machine. Suddenly the most important thing was to record all the news footage that was blaring at me from out of my TV. I thought briefly about calling Trevor, then remembered that he was in Barbados on his honeymoon, probably sipping a drink with some spiky, inedible part of a fruit in it, completely unaware of what had happened. Once the sun went down and I still hadn’t heard from her, I realized that Reva was lost, likely for good. For days I sat watching and rewatching the footage I’d taped of the attacks, unable to move from in front of the TV save to piss or search the bathroom cabinet for more pills. There was a video of a woman leaping from the North Tower, and though it was too grainy for me to ever be able to tell if it was Reva, I liked imagining that it was.She wore a grey pencil skirt with black tights and stilettos – one still gripping her foot while the other had torn free, suspended in the air. She looked so beautiful, jumping like that into the unknown, that I took a kind of strange and holy comfort in her courage.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: I stared at the television screen, the pixelated image of the Twin Towers collapsing, a grotesque loop of destruction playing over and over.  Reva, my dear Reva, was lost in the chaos, her voice a distant echo on the other end of a dropped phone call."Are you there?" I had asked, the dial tone buzzing in my ear.Hours earlier, the news had crackled to life, the blue glow of the television illuminating the room.  Trevor was away in Barbados, his honeymoon a cruel irony in the face of the unfolding tragedy.  I watched the towers crumble, the smoke billowing, a woman leaping from the inferno, her body a fragile arc against the backdrop of the burning sky. "She looks like Reva," I whispered, a strange sense of admiration washing over me.The woman's beauty, even in the face of death, was mesmerizing. Her courage, her desperation, her final act of defiance against the inevitable.I watched her fall, the image burned into my mind, a haunting reminder of the fragility of life.Reva, my wild, untamed friend, was gone, swallowed by the chaos, her laughter and vibrancy extinguished.  I mourned her loss, the emptiness a gaping hole in my soul.Days turned into weeks, the world a blur of muted colors and hollow sounds.  I watched the footage repeatedly, the woman's fall a morbid fascination, a symbol of our collective mortality.  In her final act, I saw a reflection of my own struggles, my own search for meaning in a world that often felt meaningless.
written_by_MFA011.Reason: Excerpt 1 is the stronger piece of writing. Where Excerpt 2 goes out of its way to over-determine easy ideas, Excerpt 1 maintains a similar level of coherence while leaving its most devastating insights to the imagination. Notice, for instance, the bathetic overstatement in Excerpt 2 of "Reva, my dear Reva," compared to Excerpt 1's simple use of Reva's name, or how Excerpt 2 refers to Trevor's honeymoon as a "cruel irony in the face of the unfolding tragedy," while Excerpt 1 simply tells you he's "unaware of what happened" and allows you to experience the irony yourself.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: I stood in the dim light of my living room, the boxed TV/VCR perched on the coffee table, its plastic wrapping still intact, a strange relic of the morning. I’d bought it not because I needed it, but because the weight of a new object felt like an anchor. Something solid. I didn’t know what else to do with myself after the towers fell, after I’d called Reva at the gym and heard her voice on the line—distant, tinny, preoccupied. That voice haunted me, replaying in my head, a loop of “Can we talk later?” as if she had known this was coming and had somewhere better to be. I could have told her to stay on the line, begged her to come over, but I didn’t. Later, I’d sit on the floor, knees pulled to my chest, watching footage of a woman leaping from the North Tower. Her dress caught the wind like a parachute, her body poised, graceful, falling as though she’d chosen to fly instead of burn. The likeness to Reva—her height, her hair—was undeniable, but I didn’t cry. I pressed pause, rewound, played it again, squinting at the screen, wondering if courage could be beautiful or if beauty was just what we saw in things we didn’t understand. Reva was gone. Lost. And yet, in that leap, she was eternal.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: The last time I spoke to Reva, she was distant. Eager to get back to sweating on the elliptical, or stair-master, or whatever absurd machine she was convinced would keep away the horrors of arm flab. She’s distant now, too, but in a new way. That day, Trevor was on his honeymoon in Barbados, but Reva felt farther. She was gone, lost. I still feel a faint throb of theft when I think of them. On the morning of September 11th , I bought a TV/VCR and recorded the towers going down. When I find myself drifting, floating back to the state I had been in that previous year, I turn on the recording and watch. The footage isn’t soothing, it’s scalding—it wakes me up and keeps me conscious. In one clip, my favorite clip, a woman leaps from a window ledge in the North Tower. She looks enough like Reva that if I were feeling sentimental, I could pretend it’s her. The edge of her pencil skirt whipping up could be Reva’s knock-off designer, her shoes flying from her feet and floating up past her head could be Reva’s second hand Manolos, the glints of sunlight that could be Reva’s grandmother’s ring. But it doesn’t have to be. I don’t need her to be Reva. In dreams, when you feel like you’re falling, you jolt awake. I need her to wake me up.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: I prefer Excerpt2. The imagery and language used is more specific and less cliched than in Excerpt1. For example, in Excerpt2 the description of the woman falling using specific details about Reva’s appearance – her “second-hand Manolos” and her “grandmother’s ring” – that help to characterize her in relation to the narrator. I also prefer the ending in Excerpt2 – the way the action of falling is used to segue from the mystery woman in the 9/11 footage to the narrator, who needs to wake up from her “dream”. The ending of Excerpt1 is hackneyed and cliched, and it’s hard to believe the detached narrator would actually be wondering “if courage could be beautiful”.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: The last time I spoke to Reva, she was distant. Eager to get back to sweating on the elliptical, or stair-master, or whatever absurd machine she was convinced would keep away the horrors of arm flab. She’s distant now, too, but in a new way. That day, Trevor was on his honeymoon in Barbados, but Reva felt farther. She was gone, lost. I still feel a faint throb of theft when I think of them. On the morning of September 11th , I bought a TV/VCR and recorded the towers going down. When I find myself drifting, floating back to the state I had been in that previous year, I turn on the recording and watch. The footage isn’t soothing, it’s scalding—it wakes me up and keeps me conscious. In one clip, my favorite clip, a woman leaps from a window ledge in the North Tower. She looks enough like Reva that if I were feeling sentimental, I could pretend it’s her. The edge of her pencil skirt whipping up could be Reva’s knock-off designer, her shoes flying from her feet and floating up past her head could be Reva’s second hand Manolos, the glints of sunlight that could be Reva’s grandmother’s ring. written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: I stood in the dim light of my living room, the boxed TV/VCR perched on the coffee table, its plastic wrapping still intact, a strange relic of the morning. I’d bought it not because I needed it, but because the weight of a new object felt like an anchor. Something solid. I didn’t know what else to do with myself after the towers fell, after I’d called Reva at the gym and heard her voice on the line—distant, tinny, preoccupied. That voice haunted me, replaying in my head, a loop of “Can we talk later?” as if she had known this was coming and had somewhere better to be. I could have told her to stay on the line, begged her to come over, but I didn’t. Later, I’d sit on the floor, knees pulled to my chest, watching footage of a woman leaping from the North Tower. Her dress caught the wind like a parachute, her body poised, graceful, falling as though she’d chosen to fly instead of burn. The likeness to Reva—her height, her hair—was undeniable, but I didn’t cry. I pressed pause, rewound, played it again, squinting at the screen, wondering if courage could be beautiful or if beauty was just what we saw in things we didn’t understand. Reva was gone. Lost. And yet, in that leap, she was eternal.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: The second excerpt is more cliched and sentimental; the relationship to the lost Reva is "haunting" and the woman's jump from the towers makes her "eternal." It also doesn't quite make sense - the TV/VCR is described as "a strange relic of the morning" and "an anchor" that the narrator doesn't "need," though it's clear that the tape is played beyond that morning and is ever-important to the narrator. In the first paragraph, the narrator speaks with a much more original voice, rendered with cruelty and humor: "whatever absurd machine she was convinced would keep away the horrors of arm flab." The image at the end of the excerpt is much more effective, a clash between the horror of the burning towers with luxury (or knock-off luxury) commodities, a contrast that feels both authentic and surprising: "The edge of her pencil skirt whipping up could be Reva’s knock-off designer, her shoes flying from her feet and floating up past her head could be Reva’s second hand Manolos."

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: I'd stared at my cheap TV/VCR combo for hours that day, recording endless footage while sprawled on my beige couch, still warm from my body's perpetual indent. The towers fell again and again on my screen – I'd rewind, watch, rewind, watch, like some demented projectionist in a theater of one. Reva had called from her gym that morning, rambling about calories and men and whatever else filled her anxious mind. I'd barely listened, picking at a hangnail until it bled. Now she was gone, vanished into that cloud of debris and paperwork and human ash that coated lower Manhattan like toxic snow. Trevor was in Barbados with his new wife, probably slathering on coconut-scented sunscreen while I watched people jump from burning buildings. But there was one woman who caught my eye, her body arcing through the air with such grace, such impossible beauty, that I felt a sick surge of envy. She looked like Reva – same dark hair, same slight build – but she moved like a dancer, like she'd chosen this terrible performance. I watched her fall hundreds of times, memorizing the way her skirt billowed, how her arms stretched wide as if embracing the sky. She became my obsession, this falling angel in sensible office wear. I understood her choice in a way that frightened me. There was something pure in it, something almost holy – to leap into nothingness rather than wait for it to claim you. I never told anyone how much I admired her courage.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Reva seemed distant the last time we talked, though maybe I’m just imagining that now. She was breathing heavily into the phone when she picked up. It sounded like she was having sex, and I made a mean joke about it, and she laughed in a forced way and told me she was at the gym, on the elliptical, which I could imagine easily, her in that ugly little workout set, climbing toward nothing. She told me she’d call me back later, but she never did. Then she went missing after 9/11, and I knew she was dead. Not in any kind of mystical or spiritual way, but because I knew there was no other option. That same day, I bought a TV/VCR from Best Buy with cash because I wanted to record the news coverage. Now, I watch it, not in a morbid way, but hoping I’ll find a clue, about something, maybe about Reva, maybe about something else. It’s not about Trevor anymore. He’s in Barbados on his honeymoon, probably slathering sunscreen on his anorexic wife and pretending to be happy. Or maybe he is happy. I was watching one of the recordings today when I spotted something. From the smoking North Tower, a woman poked her torso out of a window. She was wearing a blue sweater and jeans. She had brown hair, short like Reva’s. She hovered on the edge for a moment, then let go and plunged into the unknown. She sailed weightlessly through the air, and then she disappeared out of frame.
written_by_MFA008.Reason: I prefer Excerpt2. The language is more evocative and specific, with adjective and phrasing choices (“ugly little workout set” “slathering sunscreen on his anorexic wife” “I knew there was no other option”) that reveal the narrator’s cynical and depressive personality. The language in Excerpt1 is not as colorful, so less is revealed about the narrator’s personality, and some of the metaphoric language - “like some demented projectionist” “like toxic snow” - is generic, unnecessary and adds little to the narrative.

written_by_MFA013.Excerpt1: Wendy could barely breathe as she ran up the old, creaking staircase, Jack close behind. “I’m gonna cave your head in, Wendy!” he screamed gleefully up at her, swinging his roque mallet back and forth in the air. Blood oozed out of his grinning mouth and down his chin. He looked like a real maniac, some deranged and bloodthirsty maniac. That gave Wendy the push she needed to block out her pain and pick up her pace. As she reached the next floor and darted through a connected corridor, a door suddenly swung open. A man emerged. He wore a rubbery and ghoulish green mask that seemed to be part of a Halloween costume. “Sing, dance, come celebrate! The party’s just starting!” he shouted, voice booming like a thunderstorm, and pulled the string on a party popper. A crack like lightning. The startling party favor spit confetti into the hallway, and Wendy gasped. The man slammed the door, vanishing back into the room. For a moment Wendy felt ridiculous, as if this whole thing were staged and harmless, like a haunted house attraction at an amusement park. But her body’s brief relaxation brought back her pain, which burst through her side. She crumpled in agony to the floor, vision blurring, battling to keep herself conscious; the carpet moved under her fingers. She heard the elevator rumble again, and knew that Jack had caught up. “There she is! Smile for me!” He lunged at her, narrowly missing her head with his mallet. Too much momentum. He lost his balance and crashed to the floor beside her with a thud. Blood spraying out of his mouth and onto the carpet as his cheek hit the ground. His eyes stayed closed. Wendy’s heart skipped a beat and for a moment she thought it was over. Then Jack opened one eye, almost playfully, and reached for her. She crawled forward, pushing herself back up and into a gradual sprint but Jack’s heavy footfalls trailed not far behind.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: Wendy’s breath came in ragged gasps, the sharp pain in her side like a splintered knife twisting deeper with each step. Jack’s laughter echoed up the staircase, a sound that was both guttural and gleeful, like a hyena that had found its prey. His mallet thudded against the bannister, a syncopated rhythm to the rising panic in her chest. She clawed at the handrail, her legs burning, her mind screaming for her body to keep moving.The corridor at the top of the stairs stretched out like a warped funhouse hallway. Shadows wavered on the walls, flickering with the uneven glow of the overhead bulbs. Wendy’s vision blurred, the carpet beneath her feet seeming to ripple like water. She stumbled but didn’t fall, her hand brushing the wall for balance as she pushed forward. A door burst open on her left, and a man in a green ghoul mask leapt out, his arms wide in mock celebration. “Party time!” he bellowed, the sound shrill and manic, accompanied by the wheezy squeal of a party favor. Wendy recoiled, her scream caught in her throat, as the ghoul slammed the door shut behind him, the sound echoing like a judge’s gavel.Jack’s voice boomed behind her, slurring threats that mixed rage with twisted humor. “Here’s Johnny!” The mallet whooshed through the air, missing her by inches as she collapsed against the wall. Her fingers dug into the carpet, her nails scraping the fibers, as the texture seemed to undulate beneath her touch. The elevator chimed in the distance, and her stomach turned as she realized he’d found another way up. Jack lunged forward, his momentum carrying him past her, and he hit the floor with a wet thud. Blood pooled beneath his face, staining the carpet in a grotesque bloom of crimson. Wendy blinked, the world tilting, as she willed herself to rise. The monster was down, but not out. Her escape depended on seconds, and the clock was still ticking.
written_by_MFA013.Reason: Excerpt 1 describes the scene clearly, and uses speech ("I'm gonna cabe your head in," and imagery (blood oozed out of his grinning mouth) to effectively deliver the danger and suspense. Excerpt 2 replies on cliched similes ("like a hyena that had found its prey," "ripple like water") that contrast with the overall more direct language in Excerpt 1, which more effectively captures the spirit of the scene. The varying sentence lengths in Excerpt 1 create momentum and immediacy ("A crack like lightning"). Overall, Excerpt 1 is more effective.

written_by_MFA018.Excerpt1: Wendy’s breath hitched in her throat, a sob trapped in the cage of her ribs. Pain splintered through her side, a white-hot fire that threatened to consume her. But Jack was coming. She could hear his ragged breathing, the scrape of his workboots on the stairs, each footfall a hammer blow against her terror.He was grinning, she knew, a rictus of madness splitting his face, blood trickling from the corner of his mouth like a macabre smear of lipstick. The roque mallet, clutched in his fist, was an obscene promise of violence. “Wendy, my dear,” he’d croaked, the words thick with menace, “time for your medicine.”She scrambled to her feet, the pain a living thing in her side, a clawing beast that wanted to drag her down. But she couldn’t stop, not now. The corridor stretched before her, an endless tunnel of shadows and dread. A door flew open, and a man in a green ghoul mask lurched out, bellowing, “Party time!” He thrust a plastic horn at her, confetti raining down like grotesque snowflakes. Then he was gone, the door slamming shut behind him, leaving her in the echoing silence.The elevator whirred, the cables groaning like a tortured beast. Jack was still coming. She stumbled, her legs leaden, the carpet a treacherous bog beneath her feet. He was close now, she could feel the heat of his rage, smell the stale beer on his breath. The mallet whistled through the air, a whisper of death that grazed her shoulder. He lurched forward, off balance, and crashed to the floor with a sickening thud. Blood bloomed on the carpet, a crimson flower against the sickly green.He lay there, a broken doll, the mallet clattering away like a discarded toy. A moment of respite, a stolen breath in the suffocating darkness. But the elevator was moving again, its gears grinding like the teeth of a hungry monster. He would be back. He would always be back.
written_by_MFA018.Excerpt2: Wendy gasped as she stumbled up the stairs, holding onto the railing with one hand. Each step sent a sharp pain through her side. She would’ve liked nothing better than to take a short rest but Jack’s voice behind her kept her going. “Wendy,” he slurred, grinning through bloody teeth, “come back here, sweetheart, so I can crush your bones like garlic cloves, what do you say?” She imagined feeling a gust of wind from the swing of Jack’s mallet behind her. At least the thundering of her pulse dulled the pain in her side. She turned corner after corner. Her feet barely touched the steps. The stairs seemed to stretch on endlessly. Finally, she reached the landing. She thought she had a second to breathe, when suddenly, a man—or something similar to a man— burst from a door. He wore a green ghoul mask and his suit reeked of mildew. Blowing a party favor that flapped in the air like a severed tongue, he shrieked, “Party time!” Wendy screamed and not knowing where else to go, stumbled backwards. The man vanished as abruptly as he’d appeared, slamming the door behind him. Wendy’s chest heaved. She collapsed to the floor. Her eyes felt heavy, but she told herself to stay awake, to just stay awake. Beneath her trembling fingers, the carpet seemed to writhe, its pattern shifting back and forth. She heard a ‘ding’ from the elevator. Jack’s footsteps followed. The mallet whistled past her shoulder, but Jack’s momentum betrayed him as he crashed to the floor. Blood splattered in jagged streaks across the still shifting carpet. This was her moment. If not now, then when? Wendy got up, staggered, pain exploding in her side, and started running. Every step felt slow and heavy, as though she moved through quicksand. She imagined Jack rising behind her, unstoppable, coming closer by the second. She glanced back once, only once, before running headlong into the dark corridor.
written_by_MFA018.Reason: I don't love either of these - both are packed with imagery and high-stakes action, but feel hard to follow because the prose is dense and the scene lacks clear spatial grounding. The mix of intense physical movement, internal sensation, and surreal elements overwhelms the pacing, making it difficult to track what's happening moment to moment. But on the whole 1 is more scary and immersive, whereas 2 has some weird lines ("like garlic cloves") that take you out of the moment.

written_by_MFA018.Excerpt1: Wendy’s breath hitched in her throat, a sob trapped in the cage of her ribs. Pain splintered through her side, a white-hot fire that threatened to consume her. But Jack was coming. She could hear his ragged breathing, the scrape of his workboots on the stairs, each footfall a hammer blow against her terror.He was grinning, she knew, a rictus of madness splitting his face, blood trickling from the corner of his mouth like a macabre smear of lipstick. The roque mallet, clutched in his fist, was an obscene promise of violence. “Wendy, my dear,” he’d croaked, the words thick with menace, “time for your medicine.”She scrambled to her feet, the pain a living thing in her side, a clawing beast that wanted to drag her down. But she couldn’t stop, not now. The corridor stretched before her, an endless tunnel of shadows and dread. A door flew open, and a man in a green ghoul mask lurched out, bellowing, “Party time!” He thrust a plastic horn at her, confetti raining down like grotesque snowflakes. Then he was gone, the door slamming shut behind him, leaving her in the echoing silence.The elevator whirred, the cables groaning like a tortured beast. Jack was still coming. She stumbled, her legs leaden, the carpet a treacherous bog beneath her feet. He was close now, she could feel the heat of his rage, smell the stale beer on his breath. The mallet whistled through the air, a whisper of death that grazed her shoulder. He lurched forward, off balance, and crashed to the floor with a sickening thud. Blood bloomed on the carpet, a crimson flower against the sickly green.He lay there, a broken doll, the mallet clattering away like a discarded toy. A moment of respite, a stolen breath in the suffocating darkness. But the elevator was moving again, its gears grinding like the teeth of a hungry monster. He would be back. He would always be back.
written_by_MFA018.Excerpt2: Wendy gasped as she stumbled up the stairs, holding onto the railing with one hand. Each step sent a sharp pain through her side. She would’ve liked nothing better than to take a short rest but Jack’s voice behind her kept her going. “Wendy,” he slurred, grinning through bloody teeth, “come back here, sweetheart, so I can crush your bones like garlic cloves, what do you say?” She imagined feeling a gust of wind from the swing of Jack’s mallet behind her. At least the thundering of her pulse dulled the pain in her side. She turned corner after corner. Her feet barely touched the steps. The stairs seemed to stretch on endlessly. Finally, she reached the landing. She thought she had a second to breathe, when suddenly, a man—or something similar to a man— burst from a door. He wore a green ghoul mask and his suit reeked of mildew. Blowing a party favor that flapped in the air like a severed tongue, he shrieked, “Party time!” Wendy screamed and not knowing where else to go, stumbled backwards. The man vanished as abruptly as he’d appeared, slamming the door behind him. Wendy’s chest heaved. She collapsed to the floor. Her eyes felt heavy, but she told herself to stay awake, to just stay awake. Beneath her trembling fingers, the carpet seemed to writhe, its pattern shifting back and forth. She heard a ‘ding’ from the elevator. Jack’s footsteps followed. The mallet whistled past her shoulder, but Jack’s momentum betrayed him as he crashed to the floor. Blood splattered in jagged streaks across the still shifting carpet. This was her moment. If not now, then when? Wendy got up, staggered, pain exploding in her side, and started running. Every step felt slow and heavy, as though she moved through quicksand. She imagined Jack rising behind her, unstoppable, coming closer by the second. She glanced back once, only once, before running headlong into the dark corridor.
written_by_MFA018.Reason: Though Excerpt 1 is a bit too image-heavy for my own preferences, Excerpt 2 relies upon numerous cliches: "thundering of her pulse" "her eyes felt heavy" and "as though she moved through quicksand." For this reason, I prefer Excerpt 1, which also captures Wendy's fear and panic in a visceral way. Excerpt 1 includes some great phrases like "a rictus of madness" and "the carpet a treacherous bog beneath her feet." The movement of the chase is rendered coherently and fluently.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Wendy looked back and wished she hadn’t. Jack had a malevolent smile on his face, and blood dripped from his open mouth down his chin like fruit juice. He swung a roque mallet steadily from side to side as he advanced up the staircase toward her. “C’mere, Wendy,” he said, “or I’ll paint this wall with your pretty, pink little brains.” Wendy turned back around and willed herself to keep going up the staircase. Her side was electric with pain, but she grit her teeth and kept going until she was in the corridor, where she broke into a run. She was almost at the end when a large figure jumped out in front of her. “You’ve gotta come to the party!” he shouted. He wore a green mask with hideously contorted plastic features. “Party favor?” he said, and jammed a little box toward her. She darted around him and continued down the hall, running faster this time. A door slammed violently behind her, and she turned to see that the man had disappeared.The pain in her side was becoming so severe that, when she took her next step forward, she collapsed under the agony of it. She tried to contain her scream, but it came roaring out of her anyway. She balled her hands into fists and pounded them into the carpet, which appeared to move beneath her, the patterns snakelike and fluid.The elevator made an ominous noise as it crept up the shaft, and she got on her knees, gripping the wall to try and stand. The elevator doors peeled open, revealing Jack with his heavy mallet. He spotted her and smiled. “Those pretty brains,” he said, and staggered in her direction. She began to run again, and he was behind her quickly. She felt the whoosh of the mallet, the air from its force grazing the back of her neck. She ducked away, and watched as Jack’s momentum sent him tumbling face-down onto the carpet, blood scattering like gory diamonds. She continued down the hall without looking back, her gasps so loud they blocked out all other sound.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: The pain exploded in Wendy's side like a grenade of glass shards as she clawed her way up the stairs, each step a new universe of agony. Behind her—too close, Christ, too close—came the whisper-thump of Jack's feet, a sound she'd once found comforting during their late-night kitchen raids but now sent ice-water terror coursing through her veins. His laughter floated up, thick and wet with blood, a madman's carousel music. "Honey, come back! I just want to bash your brains in!" The roque mallet whooshed through the air, stirring her hair like a lover's caress. She reached the top landing, lungs burning, heart thundering against her ribs like it wanted to escape her chest—and why shouldn't it? Getting away seemed like the only sane response to this nightmare. That's when the door to her left burst open and a figure lurched out, wearing a moldering green ghoul mask that might've been funny at some teenage Halloween party twenty years ago. "GREAT PARTY, ISN'T IT?" it screamed, blowing a party favor that unrolled with a wet, obscene sound. Then it was gone, door slamming with such force it shook dust from the ceiling. Wendy's legs betrayed her and she went down hard, the carpet beneath her fingers writhing like living things—thousands of insects fleeing from the violence above. The elevator hummed to life somewhere in the bowels of the hotel, its ancient gears grinding like arthritic teeth. She tried to push herself up, but her side shrieked in protest. Jack's shadow loomed over her, distorted and massive on the wall. The mallet swung down in a silver arc of death, missing her by inches as Jack stumbled, his momentum carrying him forward. He crashed face-first into the carpet, blood spraying from his mouth in a fine crimson mist. But Wendy knew he wouldn't stay down long. In the Overlook Hotel, nothing stayed dead for long.
written_by_MFA008.Reason: The second excerpt is overly filled with similes and metaphors, which slows down and lessens the impact of this action-heavy and violent scene: "the pain exploded in Wendy's side like a grenade of glass shards," "each step a new universe of agony," "ice-water terror," "stirring her hair like a lover's caress" (this last simile is also inappropriate, considering the domestic violence of this scene). The use of figurative language is much more restrained in the first excerpt, which allows the reader to focus on the disturbing set of actions being described; when figurative language does come into the excerpt, its use is much more effective, as in "blood dripped from his open mouth down his chin like fruit juice." The childish image of fruit juice running down someone's chin is nicely discordant with the actuality of the blood, an effective bit of grotesquerie.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: You fucked up, straight up. No way to pretty it up with words your fancy-ass MFA taught you—fifty mujeres over six years, all those emails stacked up like bodies, like evidence in one of them CSI episodes your girl used to love watching with you on the couch, back when she thought you were something else, something better, something more than just another Dominican tigre con su vaina. Your bad-ass salcedense who survived the Bar exam like a warrior, who held your hand through all your broke-ass teaching days eating mangú for dinner three times a week, who cried against your shoulder when her pops passed—she warned your ass about cheating, told you straight up how her old man did her mom dirty, how that shit was unforgivable, how it lived in her bones like a curse. But you did it anyway, thinking you were too smooth to get caught, thinking them delete buttons would save your ass forever, thinking you had some special blessing from Ochún herself. Then comes the fucking emails, each one like a bullet, like them killing blows they teach you about in them martial arts movies. Your girl, she give you them three extra months though—three months of plane rides and hotel rooms, three months of you watching her turn into somebody else, somebody with eyes that looked right through you like you was a ghost. In New Zealand, watching her walking that beach she dreamed about since forever, since that movie with the piano, you knew it was done. She wouldn't let you touch her, wouldn't let you near. Y'all drove past some happy-ass couple all wrapped up in each other and the silence in that rental car could've drowned a thousand islands. Later in the hotel room, when she finally broke down, tears coming like they'd never stop, you knew: some things you break, they don't never get fixed. Some betrayals cut too deep for even the ocean to wash away.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: How this went was, you go about your post-cheating days with your bad-ass  from Salcedo, unworried about what you’d done, how you’d done it, who you’d done it with, and for a good long while the two of you are what you might call happy. You were happy. Then out of nowhere you one day walk in on her reading your emails. The emails. Upwards of fifty women over six years she discovered, and for some reason you thought you had messaged more. No significó nada, you said, it was foolish, you said, and what she’d said and told you over and over again over the years, she said again: that cheating was unforgivable. Prohibida. Grounds to shout, Pack your shit and go. Just go. But she stayed. Maybe it was her father’s death or your failures, all those failures, that she stayed with you through, maybe it was her success in passing the bar, but in the end what bound the two of you, why she stayed as long as she did––who the hell knows. After the emails you made an attempt to make good. Travelled with her everywhere from the Dominican Republic, Mexico, to New Zealand. New Zealand. There on the beach she had long dreamed of visiting, that one from The Piano, and that you thought bringing her to would fix everything, she walked on ahead, and you walked in her smaller footsteps in the sand. Mi amor, you said. Walk by my side. You are so far away. Please, she said. Just leave me alone. On the ride home, the two of you shared a cab with a laughing couple tumbling over one another, besar, holding each other’s faces in their hands, and you wanted to die. Back in the hotel room she broke down for good. You never saw such tears, never felt that shame you felt then for having caused them. No more, she said to you. No mas.
written_by_MFA015.Reason: Excerpt 1 effectively delivers the challenging task of creating compelling, coherent long sentences despite their straying off course (e.g. "CSI episodes" reference in sentence 1). The writing is percussive and fluid, and the tone is consistently self-deprecating and manic. Excerpt 1 also uses hyperbole ("tears coming like they'd never stop" and profanity effectively. The storytelling in Excerpt 2 is somewhat forced instead of natural and fluid ("How this went was," "After the emails you made an attempt to make good"). Overall, Excerpt 1 is more effective.

Excerpt 1 has very successful images with the walking in the smaller footprints of his partner, the image of the happier couples holding one another's faces, etc. But there seems to be a deeper network of lived experience with the way Excerpt2 flows, where in Excerpt1 the death of the father is vaguely linked but in Excerpt2 we see how the woman's father's death motivates the way she sees the relationship and cheating now. So because of the greater transition and fluency between the cheating and the trip and how the father's death acts as a bridge between, Excerpt2 seems more fluent and coherent.

written_by_MFA006.Excerpt2: She was the one who said it, mi amor. "If you cheat on me, it's over." Maybe it was the years woven together, the memories of her father's funeral, the echo of your own failures, the triumph of her passing the bar.  You clung to those shared moments like a life raft in a sea of your own making.You tried to mend the shattered pieces with trips – the Dominican Republic, Mexico, even the beach in New Zealand she'd dreamed of since "The Piano."  But on that windswept shore, her sadness was a tangible thing, a wall you couldn't breach.  She walked alone, the sand stretching out like a metaphor for the distance between you.In the rental car, a giddy couple, their love a bright, painful contrast, drove past, and you saw the reflection of your guilt in her eyes.  Later, in the hotel room, the tears came, a torrent that mirrored the storm inside you.  You knew then that some things, once broken, can never be truly fixed.The weight of your betrayal pressed down on you, a suffocating blanket of remorse. You remembered her fierce independence, her unwavering loyalty, the way she could light up a room with her smile.  And you had dimmed that light, extinguished it with your own selfishness.You had broken the trust that had been the foundation of your relationship, and the cracks were irreparable.  The guilt gnawed at you, a constant reminder of the pain you had caused.  You had betrayed the woman you loved, and the consequences were devastating.
written_by_MFA006.Reason: Excerpt one opens with a clear statement of the premise, whereas Excerpt two implies the premise through an indirect reference. Instead Excerpt 2 rushes into the emotional stakes, informing the reader of their history. Excerpt one delays a moment of emotional release ("It is only later ... that she cries") until the very end, when it is most potent. written_by_MFA028.Excerpt1: You come home. It’s hot--dead hot, like a puta in church. She’s home, and rat-fucking pissed, but that’s what you liked about her, isn’t it? Bad-ass salcedense, short hair, ass is the stuff of rumors. Throw a brick at a homeboy for looking at her funny. And this salcedense had to throw a couple bricks in her day. But she found out, and it’s bad. Fifty women bad, and for six years. Plus you knew. Of course you fucking knew. She told you, you chancla-headed fuck, you slip once and she’s out. written_by_MFA028.Excerpt2: You should have known better. You should have remembered her face that night in Salcedo, when she told you—plain as day, no flourish, no smile—that if you ever cheated, she’d be gone. Pero no, you had to be that dude. Fifty women, six years. A whole-ass archive of receipts, every click, every email, every I-miss-you-ma written out like a confession just waiting for her to find. And she did. You came home that night and there she was, sitting on the couch, laptop on her knees, the kind of quiet that makes your bones go soft. You tried to talk, to explain—mi amor, please—but she cut you off with a look. Not screaming, not throwing things, not even crying, just staring at you, eyes dark as road tar, full of something you couldn't name yet but would come to know real well: the slow, suffocating unravel. And for some stupid reason, she stayed. Maybe because you had history, because you were there when her father died, because you let her practice cross-examining you for the bar. Because habit is its own kind of handcuff. So y’all tried. A few months, a few trips, trying to patch up something that was already dust. The D.R., Mexico, New Zealand—her dream trip, the one she’d been talking about since The Piano. You watched her walk down that beach alone, black sand, gray sky, the Pacific pulling at her feet like it wanted her too. When you reached for her hand, she flinched, like touching you might burn. The drive back was long. Silent. Until you passed some couple, arms locked, glowing like they’d never known heartbreak. You knew she saw them too. That night in the hotel, when she curled away from you, when she finally let the tears come, you lay beside her, knowing you’d already lost, knowing it was over, knowing it had been over since the moment she clicked that first email.
written_by_MFA028.Reason:
Both excerpts here are effective in their aims, though their methods and aims themselves are quite different. Excerpt 2 has a more novelized prose that flows well with evocative sequences of images like "eyes dark as road tar, full of something you couldn't name yet...because you were there when her father died, because you let her practice cross-examining you for the bar." There's a sense that the narrator knows the woman deeply, and vice-versa, which helps the ending feel more tragic, the relationship something with real gravity.

On the other hand, Excerpt 1's strength is that the prose is a truly unique fit for the content, and renders the narrator's internal monologue as though they are both an archetype and wholly distinctive. We get insights into the linguistic texture of their world, but also subtle revelations of the deeper issues they face, like colorism's connection to their masculinity: "She wants nothing to do with your black ass." Despite the more singular focus on the narrator, for its higher ambitions and incredible execution, Excerpt 1 feels like the stronger here.
