written_by_MFA010.Excerpt1: Sitting down to reflect on my life makes everything fall silent around me. I remember that I had committed to becoming a novelist at a very young age. My domestic circumstances were somewhat fortunate: although my mother believed I could commit myself to more useful professions like law and medicine, my father had always supported my ambition to become a writer. But one memory of my father is more significant than the rest. I remember that when, as a young man, I wrote my first novel, “Cevdet Bay and His Sons,” I sent a copy to my father for his opinion. Till I heard back from him, my days were consumed by the anxiety of what he might have to say. I came to care for my father’s opinion and approval more than anyone else’s. I had been waiting for my father to return home. I wanted to know his thoughts. On the day of his arrival, I stood by the door of our house and looked at him like I was nothing more than a child. My father must have understood what I was asking him. He walked up to me and embraced me. Although he didn’t say a word, I understood that he approved of my manuscript. For a few days, my father refused to talk about the manuscript but later, one cold evening, he expressed a strong and optimistic confidence about my future writing career. Like a proud father he said "Aslanım olacaksın." He didn’t name a prize but he predicted that I would go on to receive a prestigious one. When my father died in 2002, I looked outside the window and imagined that door by which I stood waiting for him and remembered his words of encouragement. Sometimes, when I am alone, I still feel the warmth of that embrace.
written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: The weight of the manuscript, a physical embodiment of years of creative struggle, felt familiar and foreign in my hands.  I had poured my heart and soul into "Cevdet Bey and His Sons," a tale woven from the rich tapestry of Istanbul's history and the intricate lives of its inhabitants.  The city, my muse and my prison, had borne witness to my solitary journey as a writer, a path I had chosen despite the uncertainties that gnawed at my soul.My father, unlike my mother, had always encouraged my artistic pursuits, seeing in them a reflection of his own unfulfilled dreams. written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: Sitting down to reflect on my life makes everything fall silent around me. I remember that I had committed to becoming a novelist at a very young age. I had been waiting for my father to return home. I wanted to know his thoughts. On the day of his arrival, I stood by the door of our house and looked at him like I was nothing more than a child. For a few days, my father refused to talk about the manuscript but later, one cold evening, he expressed a strong and optimistic confidence about my future writing career. Like a proud father he said "Aslanım olacaksın." He didn’t name a prize but he predicted that I would go on to receive a prestigious one. When my father died in 2002, I looked outside the window and imagined that door by which I stood waiting for him and remembered his words of encouragement. Sometimes, when I am alone, I still feel the warmth of that embrace.

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: It was the next night when my father returned to my little apartment and I, anxious for his arrival, waited at the same wobbling card table on which I wrote the unbound novel he held in his hands. It had taken me two years to write it, and in those two years, my mother had refused to read a page. During one of her morning visits over lukewarm tea, she’d said “If it’s writing you want, I fail to see how work in advertising won’t fulfill you.” It was her tone that foretold that in leaping and striving for these dreams, we may lose sight of the path that had been carved for us long before. But my father read the entire novel. He had asked to. And when he slammed the pages onto my table, in the harsh return to the site of their creation, I was certain he would insist I write no more. I allowed myself to believe that, in the moment of silence after the table steadied, my words were so inept they could not draw near the man who best knew me. I believed this until he embraced me. I did not realize until much later, far beyond the glances of accumulated days behind me, that his momentary silence was the struggle for his own words. “One day,” he eventually said. “One day, my son will be a famous author. A Nobel prize author. One day.” The loose pages on the desk were an off-white bond paper, and it is these pages I have kept and oftentimes return to, long after I titled the manuscript Cevdet Bey and His Sons, long after it was sold and published, long after my relocating to a larger apartment in Istanbul and my father’s passing seven years later in December, 2002. I return to the typed and blue-hashed pages not to read but to see what my father had seen, to see him seeing his son and all his promise.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: On that spring evening in Istanbul, when the Bosphorus was painted in shades of amber and violet, I handed my father the manuscript of "Cevdet Bey and His Sons" with trembling hands that betrayed both hope and terror. The pages, worn from countless revisions and bearing the weight of my artistic ambitions, disappeared into his leather briefcase – the same briefcase I had watched him carry to his office countless times throughout my childhood. In the days that followed, I wandered the streets of Nişantaşı like a guilty man, examining the faces of passersby as if they might offer some preview of my father's judgment. Unlike my mother, who had always viewed my literary aspirations with the kind of worried skepticism reserved for a child's dangerous games, my father had maintained a curious silence about my choice to abandon architecture for the solitary life of a novelist. I remember sitting in the old Pamuk Apartments, listening to the distant ferry horns and watching the dust particles dance in the afternoon light that filtered through the heavy curtains, wondering if I had disappointed him. When he finally returned home that evening, before any words could form between us, he embraced me with an intensity that spoke volumes in our family's language of unspoken emotions. Later, as we sat in his study surrounded by his beloved books – the ones that had first taught me to love literature – he broke our emotional silence with words that would echo through the decades: "You will win great prizes one day." That moment hung between us like a photograph yellowing with age, gaining new meaning after his death in 2002, when I found myself standing alone in that same study, running my fingers along the spines of his books, feeling the weight of his absence and the enduring power of his belief in me.
written_by_MFA003.Reason: Both excerpts are well written, but Excerpt 2 is superior because it includes an extra layer of detail and texture, which Excerpt 2 misses. For instance: "In the days that followed, I wandered the streets of Nişantaşı like a guilty man" and "I remember sitting in the old Pamuk Apartments, listening to the distant ferry horns and watching the dust particles dance in the afternoon light that filtered through the heavy curtains." These sentences, rich with extra detail, allow us to fully immerse into the time and space of the narrative, in a way that Excerpt 1 never totally achieves.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: I had given it to him at last, my first novel, “Cevdet Bey and His Sons,” and I waited with equal parts fear and excitement for his reaction to it. The book took me several years to complete and the time had not come easily; my mother had not supported the endeavor and took every opportunity to disparage this sodden “waste of youth” while my father quietly, gently, encouraged me with small gifts and an allowance. I knew better than to try convincing my mother, though those modern writers who I hoped to emulate in the West had taken a similar commitment to writing, she did not respect them, and would not want me to achieve a similar goal to any of theirs. I saw my father from across the boiled asphalt lot and felt my fears realized in his step—would he join my mother after reading my manuscript? I rose from my car to meet him. I searched for a hint of his answer in his gait or his eyes and saw nothing but the movements and recognition of an animal. Perhaps my father’s support ended now, perhaps I had failed him, perhaps this moment would end this chapter of my life and its purpose. All my anxieties melted when we embraced. He surged toward me as we met, pumping his arms to pat me on the back with reverent enthusiasm, then pulling me close to his chest as he had when I was a child, and I felt his pride. He held me out in front of him and smiled. “You will succeed, my son,” he said. “You will win prestigious prizes and teach somewhere.” It is this memory I cling to after his death in 2002—how he remained such a father to me.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: I remember the moment I handed over my first novel, "Cevdet Bey and His Sons," to my father as if it were encased in amber, frozen in a delicate yet trembling moment of time. In the quiet of our Istanbul apartment, the weight of the manuscript in my hands mirrored the gravity of the step I was about to take. My mother, though ever loving, had dismissed my ambitions as mere indulgence, a detour from the secure path she imagined for me. My father, however, had always encouraged the flickering flame of my aspirations. He took the manuscript with an easy, almost playful smile, as though we were conspirators in some artistic rebellion. When he returned, his embrace was not rushed or obligatory—it was deliberate, a gesture heavy with the unspoken weight of approval. It was as if he had passed a verdict, not only on the book but on the very path I had chosen for my life. He didn’t speak immediately; instead, he held me, his silence filled with a fatherly pride that words might have diminished. Then, in a voice steadied by conviction, he said I would succeed and even prophesied a prestigious prize in my future. The precision of his faith startled me—how could he be so sure when I wasn’t? This memory, so vivid and immutable, grew to anchor me, particularly after his death in 2002. It is strange how the weight of approval from someone who is no longer there can linger like a ghost in the room, shaping the contours of your own self-belief. My father’s prediction, his prophecy of my future success, stands as a monument to his faith in me, a beacon amidst the ever-shifting uncertainties of life and art.
written_by_MFA016.Reason: Excerpt 2 is framed from the onset as a memory, opening with "I remember," and then clearly speaking from the present to analyze and reflect on that memory, whereas Excerpt 1's only indication that it is a memory (until the final line) is being in past tense. The images used throughout Excerpt 2 are crisp and evocative, the manuscript "encased in amber" clearly conveying how delicate the narrator was when handing it over to their father, the "playful smile," and the specific language used to describe the hug all lace a great deal of subtle emotion into the narrative. The whole point of this excerpt is the narrator's relationship to their father, and the love and affection really radiates from Excerpt's 2 careful attention to detail.

Instead of ending on this generic note, Excerpt1 describes the physical interaction between the narrator and his father in greater detail – “ He surged toward me as we met, pumping his arms to pat me on the back with reverent enthusiasm, then pulling me close to his chest as he had when I was a child, and I felt his pride.” – which is more emotionally impactful.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: The Misfit’s pale eyes, magnified by the thick lenses of his spectacles, seemed to devour her crumpled form.  His fingers traced the outline of her face, a grotesque caress that mirrored the distortion of his soul. He paused, a flicker of something unreadable in those magnified eyes. It might have been pity, but more likely it was the cold fascination of a child pulling wings off a fly. He observed her, this broken vessel of a woman, with the same clinical detachment he might have applied to a pinned insect, struggling vainly against its inevitable end. He was a collector of sorts. The Misfit rose, a specter in the twilight.  His glasses, now askew, reflected the dying light, casting a distorted glow on his gaunt features.He straightened them with a trembling hand, a gesture of futile order in a world spiraling into chaos.  “No real pleasure in life,” he repeated, the words a hollow mantra in the deepening silence.  The Misfit’s eyes, as he aimed the gun at the grandmother, held a chilling blend of detachment and desperation.  The gun’s retort shattered the stillness, a sound as hollow as the abyss that consumed him. The grandmother’s body slumped, a broken marionette in the roadside tableau.  The Misfit knelt, the gun dangling from his hand like a forgotten toy.  His fingers traced the outline of her face, a grotesque caress that mirrored the distortion of his soul.  The grandmother’s eyes flickered open, a spark of life in the encroaching darkness. You’re one of my own children,” she rasped, her voice a fragile echo in the desolate landscape.  The Misfit recoiled as if struck, a spasm of violence rippling through him.  The gun barked again, a final punctuation mark to her existence.Her body settled into the dust, a macabre parody of peace.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: The Misfit turned his head and looked the grandmother in her eyes. “Doesn’t it make you feel all raw to think about it?” he asked her. “That God may be real, but you can never know it? Not for sure?” The grandmother looked back at him, her face hard at first, then growing soft. She looked at Hiram, who spit into the road, and then at Bobby Lee, who rubbed his eyes with his dirty fingers. She looked back at The Misfit. “I can see why you might feel raw,” she said. “Yes, I can see that.” She pressed her lips together. “May I touch you?” she asked. Bobby Lee snapped his head around to look at her. The Misfit smiled. “Sure,” he said. The grandmother reached a cold and papery hand toward him and pressed her palm to his stubbled face. “My child,” she said. “You are my child.” She closed her eyes and laughed, and The Misfit took his gun out and shot her between her eyes, so that her nose was dashed away. She fell immediately backwards into the ditch and lay there, crumpled, her mouth mangled into a sort of smile. The Misfit took off his glasses and his eyes were pale and defenseless. “Get rid of her,” he said to Bobby Lee and Hiram. Bobby Lee chuckled. “What’s got you giggling like a little girl?” The Misfit snapped. “It’s just fun, is all,” said Bobby Lee. The Misfit turned and hit him, hard and quick across the face. Bobby Lee put a hand to his lip and frowned. He drew his hand away to find that his bottom lip was bleeding. “There is no real pleasure in life,” said The Misfit. “Now, pick her up and put her with the others so we can get rid of ‘em proper.”
written_by_MFA008.Reason: Excerpt one uses heavy-handed descriptions, in a misguided effort at heightening the intensity of the passage: "His fingers traced the outline of her face, a grotesque caress that mirrored the distortion of his soul." Excerpt two achieves the desired intensity through exchanges of dialogue, which allow characters to pose high-stake questions to each other. The writing in excerpt one is stilted ("The gun barked again, a final punctuation mark to her existence"). The writing in excerpt two is straightforward and concise: "The Misfit took his gun out and shot her between her eyes, so that her nose was dashed away." Excerpt one unfolds the narrative slowly and non-linearly, whereas excerpt two moves linearly.

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: The Misfit looked at the old woman who had risen on to her knees in the damp grass and begun to pray. Hearing the familiar words made him lose his sense of urgency for it recalled to his mind the prayers he had memorized and repeated as a boy. The promise of redemption had appealed to him then but as a grown man he knew to trust only those things he could see for himself and verify firsthand. He would have given anything to have proof of his own everlasting soul or anyone else’s, but no sign had ever revealed itself to him and so the promises had turned curdled and turned bitter in his heart. The grandmother watched the Misfit’s face change as she prayed. She saw him illuminated and transformed into a young child, long before he was ever a killer, with a soul as pure and innocent as her son’s had once been. “You’re one of my own children!” she cried and reached out to him. But the sudden flicker of her outstretched white hand made the Misfit recoil and shoot. He shot three times in quick succession until she had crumpled and fallen back into the ditch. He stood over her in the ditch and watched her lips settle into a faint smile. He removed his wire-rimmed glasses and used his handkerchief to wipe the flecks of blood off them. Without the lenses his eyes were pale and defenseless and he let them pass over her lifeless body once before he replaced the frames and turned to Bobby Lee and Hiram. “Bury her with the others,” he said. “Boy, ain’t we havin’ some fun today?” Bobby Lee hooted, but the Misfit cut him off. “There’s no real pleasure in life,” he said sharply and walked back to the car.
written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2: The grandmother’s face, shadowed by the wide brim of her hat, turned toward The Misfit, her trembling hand reaching as if to steady herself against the weight of her own words. Her voice, cracked and earnest, declared him as one of her own children, the statement hanging between them like a fragile thread in the stifling air. The Misfit’s pale eyes blinked behind thick glasses that reflected the distant sun, making him appear less man, more hollow instrument, tuned to discord. Hiram and Bobby Lee stood like rough-hewn statues, their hands idle but primed, their smirks a mockery of the tension thickening the moment. The grandmother’s outstretched hand shook with an urgency that seemed to belie her fragile clarity—a clarity forged by fear and sudden grace.Then came the shots, three in succession, each one punching the air with finality. Her body folded into the red clay ditch as if she were part of the earth all along, her hand still outstretched but now unyielding. A faint, enigmatic smile lingered on her lips, a puzzling counterpoint to the violence that had stilled her breath. The Misfit lowered his weapon slowly, his face twisted not in rage but something deeper—a silent rage turned inward, an unanswered question echoing in his marrow. He removed his glasses, wiped them carefully, and stared at the starkness of her lifeless form, his pale eyes vulnerable, almost raw.Bobby Lee chuckled, kicking a stone idly. “That was a fun one,” he said, his grin cruel. The Misfit turned his head sharply, his voice low and flinty. “She was closer to something than I’ll ever be,” he muttered, almost to himself. Then louder, with a bitter edge, “No pleasure in this life, none at all.” He spat into the dirt as they dragged her into the shadows.
written_by_MFA005.Reason: Excerpt 1 has a slightly sharper focus on The Misfit and his experience. Excerpt 1 opens on him and his perception of the old woman, before moving to his thoughts on and previous desire for redemption, and his shooting of her. Excerpt 1 gives the old woman actual dialogue, rather than telling in summary, giving the reader an experience of shock, like The Misfit, when she declares him one of her children. The shock of her saying that, and immediately being shot thrice, feels more intense in Excerpt 1 because she is given a voice.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: The Misfit stood there with his black hat tilted back on his head and his eyes gleaming like two wet stones in the gathering dusk. His face was all angles and shadows, the kind that spoke of something gone wrong in the blood generations back. The grandmother, sprawled in the red clay ditch like a broken china doll in her navy dress with the violet spray still pinned crooked at her collar, reached out one trembling hand toward him as if she might touch salvation itself. "Why you're one of my babies," she said, her voice crackling with a terrible tenderness that made The Misfit jerk back as if he'd been scalded by boiling water from heaven. The bullet cracked through the air three times, precise as scripture, and the grandmother's face froze in a smile that would have made any passing motorist know she had died in a state of grace. The Misfit removed his glasses and there was nothing behind them but two pale holes, like windows in an empty house where someone had forgotten to draw the shade. "Take her with the others," he said, his voice flat as a snake's belly on hot pavement. Bobby Lee's face split in a yellow grin. "Some fun!" he said, but The Misfit's eyes had gone distant, like he was watching something terrible coming down the road toward them all. "It's no real pleasure in life," he said, and for a moment his face looked like it might crack open and show whatever darkness had been growing inside him since before he could remember. The sky above them was the exact color of a bruise, and somewhere in the distance a whip-poor-will called like it was mourning something that hadn't died yet.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: Standing on the yellow road in the bright sun, the grandmother before him and Hiram and Bobby Lee just behind, The Misfit sunk deeper into his bitter thinking. There can be no proof of anything—nothing earthly and nothing above—and certainly nothing like salvation for good deeds, or a father waiting and observing from some heavenly perch—and if there was no way to verify the existence of a real God, why live as if that God was watching? The Misfit wondered. The grandmother had on a hat with a brim that cast her face into aged shadows. Her mouth, a flat line, disturbed The Misfit and put a lump in his throat. But the grandmother’s face changed then, softened and clarified, and a beautiful smile spread from her to him. “You are one of my own children,” she said with great compassion, her voice loud and certain, outstretching feeble arms. The Misfit felt a wave of revulsion rising hot and tumorous in his chest and, recoiling, raised his gun and shot her three times. After, the grandmother’s body limp and lifeless in the ditch, the smile remained on her face. Even slumped, her hat upturned beside her, she had an air of perfect grace. Some question of forgiveness came then to The Misfit, which he carefully discarded and, taking off his glasses, surveyed her briefly with pale, defenseless eyes. “Get rid of her,” he told Hiram and Bobby Lee. “Put her with the others.” Bobby Lee chuckled, slapping Hiram on the shoulder, and said “Fun, real fun.” The Misfit turned cool eyes toward him, setting his jaw. “No, Bobby Lee,” he said, “it is not fun—not fun. There is no real pleasure in life.” He turned away from the body and walked on down the yellow road.
written_by_MFA026.Reason: Excerpt 1 uses a avalanche of overwrought similes ("… like two wet stones in the gathering dusk"; "… like a broken china doll …"; "…as if he'd been scalded by boiling water from heaven"; "precise as scripture"; and so on) which detract from the scene being described to the point that it becomes difficult trying to parse what is happening sentence-to-sentence. Excerpt 2, on the other hand, maintains a clear setting and set of characters from the first sentence ("Standing on the yellow road in the bright sun, the grandmother before him and Hiram and Bobby Lee just behind …") and while I might have preferred slightly more implication, it allows its images to speak on their own as metaphors, rather than muddying them ("After, the grandmother’s body limp and lifeless in the ditch, the smile remained on her face"). It is significantly stronger.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: The Misfit stood there with his black hat tilted back on his head and his eyes gleaming like two wet stones in the gathering dusk. His face was all angles and shadows, the kind that spoke of something gone wrong in the blood generations back. The grandmother, sprawled in the red clay ditch like a broken china doll in her navy dress with the violet spray still pinned crooked at her collar, reached out one trembling hand toward him as if she might touch salvation itself. "Why you're one of my babies," she said, her voice crackling with a terrible tenderness that made The Misfit jerk back as if he'd been scalded by boiling water from heaven. The bullet cracked through the air three times, precise as scripture, and the grandmother's face froze in a smile that would have made any passing motorist know she had died in a state of grace. The Misfit removed his glasses and there was nothing behind them but two pale holes, like windows in an empty house where someone had forgotten to draw the shade. written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: It seemed to me that it had never rained that hard. I might as well have been out in the next great flood with all that rain, but I didn’t mind. Watching Phoebe in her new blue coat go round and round on that shiny carousel horse made me feel so damn warm, that I hardly even noticed the cold wet of it all. My hunting hat shielded me a bit, but that got soaked fast. In no time at all, I was drenched. Totally soaked, but totally happy, too. I could hear Phoebe laughing on the horse, and of course she wasn’t wet under the carousel’s awning. She seemed to me completely free. I guess I could have gotten upset, shivering as I was and my clothes so heavy with water that they were falling off of me. My shoes squished when I moved even a little, but I felt like a million bucks watching Phoebe. The happiness didn’t last, though, not through to right now. I’m stuck in this miserable “rest” home, where I can’t even rest. How am I meant to relax when these idiot psychoanalysts keep pelting me with idiot questions? One of them badgers me with nonsense like, “But how do you expect do have a future if you don’t care to maintain your present? You need to try in school. Do you intend to try in school?” My brother, D.B., the screenwriter, likes to visit and ask me mind-numbing questions, too, though he’s not nearly as bad at the psycho- babblers. He’s not so bad because he’s my brother, and I do love him, so I tolerate the million- and-one questions, but I still wish he’d cut back on the interrogations. He brought this glamorous actress, a Brit, to visit with him, and while she’s off powdering her nose or whatever girls do in the bathroom, D.B. asks me: “How are you feeling, champ, about everything that’s happened?” I tell him, slowly, the details of the last few days. It’s strange to say it out loud, rather than just in my head, where I can say whatever I want. But it’s nice, too, a relief, even. Telling D.B. about it makes him lean in close to listen, and I feel close to him, not just physically but emotionally. Like my brother is really with me. Talking about Stradlater, Ackley, and Maurice, it feels like they’re with me, too. I don’t even like those guys, but talking about them makes me feel…surrounded. I don’t think I’m a happy person, but talking about when I was happy, with Phoebe, I feel like I could be.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: It started raining like hell out of nowhere, the way it does when you don’t have a goddam umbrella. I was standing there, freezing my tail off, watching Phoebe ride the carousel. She was wearing this blue coat that flared out every time the horse went up, like it had its own personality or something. I swear, she was the only one who didn’t look phony on the whole goddam planet. I pulled my hunting hat down tight, the one I always wore backward, like some kind of idiot. It didn’t do much, but I didn’t give a damn. Watching her, I got this weird lump in my throat, like I wanted to bawl and laugh at the same time. It was the damnedest thing. I just stood there getting soaked and didn’t even care. The next part’s harder to talk about. It’s all tied up with that place I’m in now—the rest home or whatever the hell they call it. The shrink keeps asking me about my plans, like he’s expecting me to say I want to be a goddam astronaut or something. “Are you going to apply yourself?” he keeps asking, like that’s the magic question that’ll unlock the universe. I told him I didn’t know and asked if he had a cigarette. He didn’t think that was funny. Shrinks never do. D.B. came to visit me once. He brought this actress he’s dating—some glamorous British type who probably says “lovely” instead of “nice.” She went to the bathroom, and D.B. leaned over like he was about to share some deep, brotherly wisdom. He asked me what I thought about everything that happened, the whole damn mess. I didn’t know what to say. I mean, I hate talking about stuff like that. It just makes you miss people. Even the ones you don’t like all that much, like Stradlater and Ackley. Hell, even Maurice, that lousy pimp. It’s like, the more you tell the story, the more it feels like they’re right there with you, and then, poof, they’re gone again. I told D.B. it was fine, just fine, and then the actress came back, smelling like expensive soap or something.Anyway, that’s the thing about telling people stuff. You think it’ll make you feel better, but it just makes you feel worse, like you’re carrying around this big, stupid ache. But maybe that’s the point. Maybe you’re supposed to miss people. Even the ones you don’t want to. It’s goddam beautiful and sad all at the same time, and I don’t know if I’ll ever figure it out. Maybe nobody does. Maybe that’s the whole thing.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: Excerpt two is more fluid than Excerpt one; the sentences are more direct, dispensing with hedging words like "seem" and "guess." Excerpt two is wittier than Excerpt one: compare "It started raining like hell out of nowhere, the way it does when you don’t have a goddam umbrella," which is funny, to "I might as well have been out in the next great flood with all that rain," which doesn't quite land the reference. Excerpt one is repetitive, stating at least twice that the narrator only feels happy when he is with Phoebe. Excerpt two is more concise.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: The rain started a few minutes after Phoebe got on the carousel. It started out light, then almost immediately it began to pour. I mean it was really raining—my shoes started to get soaked, and my hair, but watching her atop the fake little ponies I only felt an overwhelming sense of joy. There was my sister, in her blue coat, laughing and riding on the carousel without a care in the world. I stood there in my soggy shoes for a while just watching her; my hunting hat protected me slightly from the rain, but mostly I didn’t even mind how wet I was getting. I was just so happy watching her there. Really I think that was one of the last times I can remember feeling happy without anything else getting in the way. Later, once I arrived in the facility, I remember the psychoanalyst there asked me some stupid question, something about my future—whether I would start to finally apply myself in school or something. I never knew how to answer dumb questions like that, so usually I’d stay quiet or say something snarky in reply so that they learned to stop asking. Sometimes D.B. would come and see me, which wasn’t so bad, except for the fact that he was always rattling on about his screenwriting career and asking me more stupid questions. “Isn’t there anything you’re passionate about? Anything at all?” I remember once, he came to visit me with this actress woman he had been seeing. She was really glamorous, and I remember she had said she was from England, or maybe I’m just thinking that because she had this snotty-sounding accent. She didn’t really ask me any questions; she mostly just sat there and would speak if D.B. spoke to her. Anyway, there was one time that the two of them came to visit me, and I remember that once the actress went to the bathroom, D.B. leaned in and asked me what I thought of everything that had been going on. “What do you mean?” I asked him, annoyed to have to field yet another question. “I guess I just mean—all of this,” he said, and he stuck his hand out to gesture all around us. I realized then how pointless it had been to share anything with D.B. in the first place, with him or even the one's I didn't like—Stradlater, Ackley, Maurice. I kept thinking that somehow, I’d figure out a way to help them see things the way I did, and then we’d finally understand each other and I wouldn’t have to explain anything anymore. But in the end, all it did was make me feel more alone.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: Boy, it was raining like a madman. I mean really coming down. Cats and dogs, like they say. I was watching old Phoebe go around and around on this carousel, and all I could think was, "If only you knew how happy this makes me." She looked so good in that blue coat of hers, just riding that thing like she didn't have a care in the world. Me, I was soaked to the bone. My hunting hat was doing its best, but there's only so much a hat can do when the sky's practically falling down. But I didn't care. I was too busy feeling good to worry about a little rain.You know, it's funny. I'm stuck in this place, and they keep asking me these stupid questions. This one guy, this psychoanalyst or whatever he is, he wants to know if I'm going to apply myself at school. Can you beat that? Like it's the only thing that matters. And then there's old D.B. He's not as bad as the rest of them, but he still asks a lot of questions. He came to see me the other day with this English actress. A real glamour girl, if you know what I mean. Anyway, she went to the bathroom or something, and D.B. starts asking me what I think about all this stuff that's been going on. You know, the stuff I've been telling you about.I don't know why they care so much. It's my life, isn't it? I guess they think they're helping or something. But all they do is make me feel worse. Like I'm some kind of freak show or something. I just wish they'd leave me alone.The thing is, I don't even know what I think myself. It's all so messed up. I mean, I was just telling you about Stradlater and Ackley and Maurice, and now I'm starting to miss those guys. Can you believe that? I didn't even like them that much. But now that I'm not around them anymore, I keep thinking about all the stupid stuff we did together. It's like I'm lonelier now than I was when they were around.I guess that's what this whole thing is about. Loneliness. It's like this big, empty hole inside me that I can't seem to fill. I keep trying to find people to connect with, but it never seems to work out. It's like I'm always looking for something that's not there.Anyway, I'm getting tired of talking about myself. It's boring. Maybe I'll tell you more about old Phoebe sometime. She's a real character, that kid. But for now, I think I'll just sit here and watch the rain. It's kind of peaceful, in a way.
written_by_MFA011.Reason: By opening and closing with rain, Excerpt 2 reads particularly coherently and fluently--we see why the narrator has been prompted to remember this scene with his sister in the rain. Likewise, looking at the content between the two excerpts, it's clearer in Excerpt 2 who is who in relation to the narrator - I know that Stradlater, Ackley, and Maurice must've been acquaintances, like D.B. Some of the language also reads as usefully particular, like "Old Phoebe" and "a real glamour girl." While Excerpt 1 is also quite strong (and I don't find that many useful differences between them), Excerpt 2 is slightly more particular, and thus more effective and memorable.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: While I was watching Phoebe circle round and round on the carousel, it started to rain real hard. It was the heaviest rain I’d seen in a long, long time. Maybe ever. It was coming down in buckets. Even barrels. My hunting hat helped protect my hair a little, but I was soaked all the way to my bones. I didn’t think I’d ever get dry. But even though I was cold and wet, I couldn’t stop feeling so happy that every raindrop was like a miniature sun. I watched Phoebe laughing and waving in her blue coat. She was smiling real big, and after a little while, I realized I was smiling too. The painted horses on the carousel went up and down, and I didn’t want them to ever stop. Then I ended up here, where nobody smiles like Phoebe and I’m not allowed outside by myself. It doesn’t rain very often around here, but when it does, I sit by the windows and remember what it felt like to stand in that crazy downpour. Then I smile just to myself, like a secret. Everybody here asks me the stupidest questions I’ve ever heard. Especially that one doctor. He asked me the other day about whether I plan on applying myself when I go back to school. “That’s none of your goddamn business,” I said to him. “You’re right,” he said. “It isn’t really my business. But it’s your business, isn’t it? Don’t you think your future deserves some consideration?” I told him he was the biggest phony I’d ever met in my life. It probably wasn’t true, but in the moment, it sure felt like it. This doctor keeps telling me I have lots of potential and that if I don’t get better, I’ll waste it. I think he should worry about wasting his own potential. What kind of doctor wants to be stuck in a place like this talking to people like me? Sometimes my brother D.B. comes to visit. He’s a screenwriter, and not as bad as the other people here, but he still asks lots of questions. Mostly stuff about medicine, which I don’t like talking about, and television, which I’m not even allowed to watch here. The last time he came, he brought along an English actress who wore lots of sparkles. She seemed nervous and kept telling me how brave I was. When she left to go to the bathroom, D.B. asked me what I thought about everything that happened. And I realized that talking about everything made me miss everyone it happened with. Even people I didn’t like—even Stradlater, Ackley, and Maurice. And I don’t want to miss anyone anymore.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: Boy, it started raining like hell while I watched old Phoebe going around and around on that crazy carousel. I mean it really started coming down, but I didn't give a damn about getting wet. I really didn't. I just stood there with this goofy grin on my face - I probably looked like a complete madman - watching my kid sister in her blue coat having the time of her life. That killed me. It really did. My hunting hat was getting soaked but I didn't care about that either. It's funny, sometimes the things that make you the happiest are the things that get you all sopping wet and probably looking like a complete moron to everybody else. But that's the thing about happiness - it doesn't give a damn what you look like.Now I'm stuck in this crumby place, this rest home or whatever the hell you want to call it, and this hotshot psychoanalyst keeps asking me all these stupid questions about what I'm gonna do with my future. Like if I'm gonna "apply myself" when I go back to school. Jesus Christ, that kills me. These people and their goddam questions. Even old D.B. - he's not as bad as the rest of them, but he still can't help himself. He came to visit me yesterday with this English actress who was sort of beautiful in this fake, Hollywood way. As soon as she went to the bathroom - girls are always going to the bathroom when you're in the middle of something - D.B. starts in with the questions about everything I've been telling him. All about what happened and what I think about it now and all.The funny part is, the more I talk about all this stuff, the more I keep thinking about everybody. Even the people I didn't particularly like, for Chrissake. Like old Stradlater with his secret slob tendencies and Ackley with his pimples and Maurice. I keep thinking about them and missing them, in this crazy way. I don't even know why. I mean, they were all phonies in their own way, but I miss them anyway. That's the thing that drives me crazy in here - how you can hate somebody's guts one minute and then start missing them like hell the next. It's really ironical as hell. Sometimes I think maybe that psychoanalyst isn't so dumb after all, but I'd rather get kicked in the teeth than admit that to him. He'll probably ask me about my violent tendencies next time I see him. That's the trouble with psychoanalysts - they always want to know what everything means, even when things don't mean anything at all.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: Excerpt 2 is the better written text because it creates a greater degree of rhythmic fluency and more effectively builds a voice for its narrator. Compare the relatively stilted attempt in excerpt 1 to build an oral, vernacular voice, and how its short sentences counteract the attempt to recreate orality: "While I was watching Phoebe circle round and round on the carousel, it started to rain real hard. It was the heaviest rain I’d seen in a long, long time. Maybe ever." The phrase "it started to rain real hard" demonstrates an attempt to create a vernacular voice, but the short, clipped sentences bring things back to a textuality that undercut that attempt at affect. By comparison, the equivalent sentences in excerpt 2 create more syntactically complex, effectively vernacular English: "Boy, it started raining like hell while I watched old Phoebe going around and around on that crazy carousel. I mean it really started coming down, but I didn't give a damn about getting wet." Consider the use of "old Phoebe," "crazy carousel," and "I mean." Not only does this create a more pleasurable, fluent effect, it also conjures a more meaningful sense of affect.

written_by_MFA013.Excerpt1: As the elevator climbed steadily toward the sixth floor, I stood pressed against the cold steel wall, my bag nestled against my side, the shears inside resting unnervingly still. The voice over the intercom announced, “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine, please report to ward three,” in a steady monotone, a voice unbothered by the frantic shuffle of nurses and patients around me. The air was tinged with a faint medicinal scent, sharp and sterile, as though the building itself exhaled nothing but clean, cold breath. My thoughts drifted toward her, lying somewhere beyond these walls, fragile and unguarded.The bag felt heavier than it had when I left home, its clasp clicking softly as though whispering to me in a language only it and I could understand. I imagined the look in her eyes as I approached, a flicker of recognition perhaps, then the inevitable softening—a crack in the shield of suspicion she might have built around herself. My words were carefully chosen in advance, rehearsed in the quiet moments of the previous night: admiration for her grace, a humble explanation of my creation, a plea for forgiveness wrapped in layers of calm sincerity.And yet, the weight of the shears burned against the lining of the bag, a cold promise of something darker. The thought of her chest rising and falling, her heart pulsing rhythmically beneath the soft fabric of her gown, stirred a sensation I couldn’t quite place. My grip on the strap tightened as the fantasy took shape—a vision of my hands steady, precise, separating her from the fragile organ that held her life. The bag would hold it perfectly, as it was meant to.The elevator dinged, and the doors slid open to reveal the sixth floor. The hall stretched out before me, fluorescent lights reflecting off the polished floors. I stepped out, the bag heavy in my hand, and began walking toward her room.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: The elevator doors opened. It was crowded, so I pushed my way inside. Doctors and nurses stood shoulder to shoulder in one corner. I joined the patients and visitors that grouped in another. The doors closed, and the elevator began its ascent. The tightly packed bodies offset the hospital's sterile smell. I had been told that I would find Rin on the sixth floor. I clutched the bag I brought for her, made heavy by the shears within. I wondered if she'd notice the care I put into making her bag the same way I noticed the care with which she used to tend her shrubs. Before her accident, she'd rise early to trim them, and I could see her from the window of my workshop. Watching her felt almost voyeuristic at first. The precision with which she used her shears excited me, reminiscent of the delicate way I stitched my handbags. We rarely spoke, but perhaps watching her in this way made me envy her. I had seen her work, but she had never seen mine. I planned to present her with the bag, one of the best I'd constructed, as a gesture of good will in hope of regaining her trust. I would politely request she accept the bag, and see if she admired it the way I admired her shrubs. Then I would remove the shears. I imagined that revealing them to her, while she was in such a helpless state from her injuries, would cause alarm. After all, I could easily plunge them into her, trim around her chest like one of her shrubs, and cut away her heart. She'd be helpless to stop me, and I could claim the bag I made for her alone. "Attention: Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine, telephone please. Dr. Y, telephone please," a voice over a speaker said. The elevator stopped at last, and I arrived on the sixth floor.
written_by_MFA013.Reason: Excerpt two's staccato rhythm — the short clipped sentences and the lack of adverbs and adjectives — lends it a dream-like quality, and a sense of finality, well-suited to the clinical and labyrinthine world of the hospital; whereas excerpt one is more florid, and feels overwrought and tonally inconsistent with the subject matter. Compare "The doors closed, and the elevator began its ascent" to "As the elevator climbed steadily toward the sixth floor, I stood pressed against the cold steel wall, my bag nestled against my side, the shears inside resting unnervingly still." Relatedly, excerpt two maintains a degree of mystery around the contents of the bag and the intended use for the shears, whereas excerpt one is repetitive and too heavy-handed. Excerpt one attributes importance to shears in this way: "The bag felt heavier than it had when I left home, its clasp clicking softly as though whispering to me in a language only it and I could understand" whereas excerpt two does it by describing its importance to another character: "I wondered if she'd notice the care I put into making her bag the same way I noticed the care with which she used to tend her shrubs."

written_by_MFA013.Excerpt1: As the elevator climbed steadily toward the sixth floor, I stood pressed against the cold steel wall, my bag nestled against my side, the shears inside resting unnervingly still. The voice over the intercom announced, “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine, please report to ward three,” in a steady monotone, a voice unbothered by the frantic shuffle of nurses and patients around me. The air was tinged with a faint medicinal scent, sharp and sterile, as though the building itself exhaled nothing but clean, cold breath. My thoughts drifted toward her, lying somewhere beyond these walls, fragile and unguarded.The bag felt heavier than it had when I left home, its clasp clicking softly as though whispering to me in a language only it and I could understand. I imagined the look in her eyes as I approached, a flicker of recognition perhaps, then the inevitable softening—a crack in the shield of suspicion she might have built around herself. My words were carefully chosen in advance, rehearsed in the quiet moments of the previous night: admiration for her grace, a humble explanation of my creation, a plea for forgiveness wrapped in layers of calm sincerity.And yet, the weight of the shears burned against the lining of the bag, a cold promise of something darker. The thought of her chest rising and falling, her heart pulsing rhythmically beneath the soft fabric of her gown, stirred a sensation I couldn’t quite place. My grip on the strap tightened as the fantasy took shape—a vision of my hands steady, precise, separating her from the fragile organ that held her life. The bag would hold it perfectly, as it was meant to.The elevator dinged, and the doors slid open to reveal the sixth floor. The hall stretched out before me, fluorescent lights reflecting off the polished floors. I stepped out, the bag heavy in my hand, and began walking toward her room.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: The elevator doors opened. It was crowded, so I pushed my way inside. Doctors and nurses stood shoulder to shoulder in one corner. I joined the patients and visitors that grouped in another. The doors closed, and the elevator began its ascent. The tightly packed bodies offset the hospital's sterile smell. I had been told that I would find Rin on the sixth floor. I clutched the bag I brought for her, made heavy by the shears within. I wondered if she'd notice the care I put into making her bag the same way I noticed the care with which she used to tend her shrubs. Before her accident, she'd rise early to trim them, and I could see her from the window of my workshop. Watching her felt almost voyeuristic at first. The precision with which she used her shears excited me, reminiscent of the delicate way I stitched my handbags. We rarely spoke, but perhaps watching her in this way made me envy her. I had seen her work, but she had never seen mine. I planned to present her with the bag, one of the best I'd constructed, as a gesture of good will in hope of regaining her trust. I would politely request she accept the bag, and see if she admired it the way I admired her shrubs. Then I would remove the shears. I imagined that revealing them to her, while she was in such a helpless state from her injuries, would cause alarm. After all, I could easily plunge them into her, trim around her chest like one of her shrubs, and cut away her heart. She'd be helpless to stop me, and I could claim the bag I made for her alone. "Attention: Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine, telephone please. Dr. Y, telephone please," a voice over a speaker said. The elevator stopped at last, and I arrived on the sixth floor.
written_by_MFA013.Reason: Excerpt 2 is able to generate a tremendous tension and build-up during the elevator ride. First, there is the claustrophobia of how many people are already on the elevator, creating a pressure with lines like, "I pushed my way inside," and "The tightly packed bodies offset the hospital's sterile smell." Then the narrator's reminiscence on how they used to watch Rin pruning the shrubs, with lines like, "Watching her felt almost voyeuristic at first," and "I had seen her work, but she had never seen mine," establishing an eeriness that foreshadows the violent intentions of the narrator. Excerpt 2's voice is more willing to lean into the darkness of the narrator, with this whole section, "she was in such a helpless state from her injuries, would cause alarm. After all, I could easily plunge them into her, trim around her chest like one of her shrubs, and cut away her heart. Excerpt 1 has more restraint when writing about this incoming violence that inhibits the overall impact of the narrative. written_by_MFA006.Excerpt1: I approach the hospital elevator. It is almost full up with nurses, doctors, and their patients. I slip myself between the heat of their bodies, which are all dressed in blue gowns or white coats. I press the button six. A voice comes on over a speaker hidden somewhere up above. “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine,” the voice says. It repeats the words as the elevator whirs into motion and begins to rise. I wonder where in the building Dr. Y could be. I look down at the bag in my hands, admiring my fine craftsmanship–the softness of the leather, the straight, simple lines of my stitches. I have made it for the woman exactly to her specifications. It is undeniable. “Look,” I will say. “Look what I have made for you. See how beautiful it is?” I will offer it to her to try on. She will be grateful, of course, and in awe of the beauty of my hard work. She will try it on, adjusting the straps to her liking. She will arrange it this way and that: cross-body, or dangling from her fingers, or slung carelessly off the shoulder. “Do you trust me again?” I will ask. In the face of the beauty of the bag, she will have no choice but to say yes, to be nothing but thankful. And then, after she has given me her trust, I will take out my sheers and use them to cut out her heart. The heart and the bag will be mine alone to claim. My grip tightens on the sheers that I keep tucked behind the bag. The blades are long and sharp. They are a silver so bright that it flashes in the glare of the overhead elevator lighting when I sneak a look down at them. The elevator dings; we have arrived at the sixth floor.
written_by_MFA006.Excerpt2: The elevator hummed its ascent, its metallic echo chamber filled with the rustling of starched white coats and the hushed murmurs of worried voices.  Doctors and nurses, their footsteps brisk and purposeful, pressed against me, their faces etched with lines of clinical concern.  A woman, her hand clutching a crumpled tissue, sobbed softly in the corner, her body trembling with a grief I could not touch.  The tinny voice of the intercom announced, "Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine," its monotone a stark contrast to the silent anxieties swirling within the elevator's steel box.I stood amidst this symphony of human emotion, my heart a steady drumbeat against my ribs, my purpose clear.  I was going to see her, the woman who had entrusted me with her memories, her fears, her hopes, woven into the very fabric of the bag I had crafted for her.  I would smile, offer gentle words, tell her how the bag, her bag, was a masterpiece, a testament to her strength, her resilience.  I would ask her to try it on, to feel the weight of it, the way it settled against her, a perfect fit. And then, as her eyes lit up with a flicker of trust, a spark of recognition, I would watch her heart, that fragile vessel of memory, beat against her chest, a tiny bird trapped within a cage of ribs.  I would slice the shears through her skin and cut her heart out. I'd hold her heart in my hands, its warmth a perverse comfort, its rhythm a dark symphony. And then, I'd claim the bag, mine alone, its rightful place by my side, its true purpose fulfilled.The elevator lurched to a halt.The shears lay nestled in my pocket, their sharp blades whispering promises of possession, of a bond that would be mine alone.It was the the sixth floor.
written_by_MFA006.Reason:
Excerpt2's image seems to be a bit confusing/incoherent where somehow nurses and doctors are both pressing against the narrator and walking within the confines of a rising elevator. There are a few technical errors in Excerpt2's excerpt (the first sentence mentioned, the double "the the sixth floor" on the last sentence).
As far as fluency and effectiveness goes, Excerpt1 seems to have the voice and sentence structure of a calculating but off-kilter narrator who would commit this premeditated act of violence, while Excerpt2 seems to just insist on its poetics without delivering the intended tone required for this tension and dread.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: The elevator opened onto the third floor, and I flattened myself against the side as a patient and his doctor exited. “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine,” said the intercom. On the fourth floor, two nurses entered the crowded elevator. As I was forced into the corner, I heard “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine” bleat over the intercom again. I had two more floors left before I’d reach hers. Whether Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine appeared or not, I had a plan, infallible and precise. I would see her, lying prone on her hospital bed, and hold up the bag. “I have to apologize for everything,” I’d say. “I made this bag for you. I crafted it myself.”“How lovely,” she’d respond, her voice lax from the painkillers. “How many pockets does it have?”“Six,” I’d say. “What material did you use to stitch it together?” “Cowhide. It feels like a baby’s cheek. Feel it,” I’d say. “Please, feel it.”When she reached out to touch her finger on the belly of the bag, I’d lean over and, taking my shears out, throw away the hospital linens covering her body. Then, as her hand caressed the bag’s soft skin, I’d cut into her chest. I’d trim the strings of the heart first, the extraneous vessels and tissue that fastened it to her insides. Once it was freed, I’d toss the shears aside. Then I’d grasp it with my bare hand. In my palm, her heart would fit like a baseball. After it was done, I’d leave, my bag in hand, alone. “Dr Y. from Respiratory Medicine,” repeated the intercom. As another nurse shuffled past me, I clutched the bag to my chest. Its delicate construction couldn’t dull the shears hidden inside. Their blades were so sharp that, when the elevator moved upward once more, they pricked me. The elevator dinged for the sixth floor.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: I clutched the bag closer to my chest as the elevator ascended, surrounded by the sterile scents of antiseptic and floor cleaner. A young doctor in a white coat pressed against the back wall, studying a clipboard, while two nurses whispered near the buttons, their voices barely audible above the mechanical hum. The speakers crackled: "Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine, please report to Ward 3." I watched the numbers illuminate one by one: three, four, five. The bag I had made was perfect—every stitch aligned with precision, the leather supple and warm like living skin. I had spent weeks crafting it, imagining her face when she would first hold it, how her fingers would trace the seams I had sewn with such care. Now it felt heavy in my hands, weighted with purpose, like the shears tucked carefully in my coat pocket. They were old and reliable, the kind my grandmother used for trimming roses, their blades still sharp enough to slice through fabric—or flesh—without resistance. "I've come to show you the modifications I made," I would say, smiling. "See how the clasp catches the light?" She would lean in close, trusting, the way she did before. Her heart would be exposed then, vulnerable beneath her hospital gown. I imagined it beating steadily, unaware of my intentions, like a bird resting in its nest. The elevator chimed for the sixth floor, and I stepped out into the fluorescent-lit corridor. A faint tremor ran through my hands—anticipation, perhaps, or fear. But I knew what I had to do. The bag deserved to be mine alone, freed from her unworthy grasp. I had created it, after all, breathed life into every fold and corner. As I walked toward her room, my footsteps echoing in the empty hallway, I felt a strange calm settle over me. The shears knocked gently against my ribs with each step, a quiet reminder of what was to come.
written_by_MFA007.Reason: By framing this excerpt around the call "Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine," a violent act is marked by the ordinary, which grounds us in setting and place. The description of the bag during this imagined conversation is strong: “How many pockets does it have?” “Six,” I’d say. “What material did you use to stitch it together?” “Cowhide. It feels like a baby’s cheek. Feel it,” I’d say. “Please, feel it.” The planned murder is tactile, medicalized, and characterizing of the narrator. While Excerpt 2 is also strong, there is less momentum and tension, and some lines fall flat, like "I imagined it beating steadily, unaware of my intentions, like a bird resting in its nest."

written_by_MFA009.Excerpt1: I spent the night with Catherine in our hotel room overlooking the little square with the rain coming down outside, our bodies naked under the sheets, and the sheets were smooth cotton, and they were good sheets, and I told Catherine so, and she put her feet between my bare legs, and her feet were cold but soon they became warm, and I put my fingers between her hair, and it felt like we were at home together, and I told her so. She smiled and looked at the rain trickle down the glass of the window, and I knew I did not need to say anything else about that.  Because she understood, unlike so many others who I've sought to find and spend time with, who I thought understood and did not, and when I tried to be together with them, our togetherness was lonelier than our solitude. With Catherine, in our togetherness we were solitary still. We held each other up and made each other feel courage in mutual independence. She kissed my cheek, and I looked up at the light on the ceiling, which was turned off, but I could see the streetlights reflect into it through the window. Just the barest bit of light there in the glass, and I thought of how fragile it all was, because this is not a world for rareness. It is a harsh world which breaks everyone, especially the very good and the very gentle and the very brave. It rises to break them all the more, and the more bravery and goodness and gentleness it is met with, the more harshness it responds with. I put my hand on Catherine's shoulder, and I felt the warmth there, and I wondered whether warmth existed because of cold or cold because of warmth. written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: The hotel balcony looked out through the rain down to the riviera. The houses outside were gray. In the dark we listened to the rain on the roof, and Catherine turned to me to say nothing, and we lay like that for a while. The slope of her shoulder was like a mountain. It could have always been there like a mountain in the distance, and I could have not known I'd memorized it. Then she spoke. "Do you need me tomorrow?""Shush. Shush," I said. I didn't like that I had to say it. It was that knowledge of what not to say that filled more in me than any words could. She turned away. The rain hit thick on the balcony tiles. The sheets felt soft. I wanted her to focus on that. The sheets, the small room, the wind blowing the rain sideways. We didn't burn the lights and let the moon through the thin curtain show. In similar rooms and nights like these, I had felt the worst of them alone. What I didn't know I needed was that same stifled quiet, the same rain, the same room. Perhaps I expected less of me to fill it all. I felt at home when I felt her most and heard her least. With the crowded taverns, I'd go and sit between stone shoulders and feel no need of my being there. What made her mine was what she never asked of me."Maybe tomorrow," I said. She said nothing. The rain whipped on. Soon, the streets outside would be muddy and thick. The mud would cake our shoes. The ground at its meanest like that. It takes us at its softest. The ground breaks everyone it breaks itself for. All men, the very good and the very gentle and the very brave, all go quiet in the ground. It clings and cakes to you. Yet you can pull. Yet you can crawl and drag onto more mud, more breaking, more ground that will eventually take you."Maybe tomorrow you come with me," I still said to the rain.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: The rain was a constant companion that night, its soft patter against the window a soothing melody. I lay in bed, the sheets a cool caress against my skin, and felt a warmth bloom within me. It was a warmth that had nothing to do with the fire crackling in the hearth, but rather with the presence beside me. Catherine. My Catherine. With her there, I felt a sense of belonging, a feeling of completeness that I had never experienced before.We had always possessed this uncanny ability, Catherine and I, to be utterly alone, yet entirely together.  In the past, I had often found myself adrift in a sea of faces, surrounded by people, yet feeling utterly isolated.  But with Catherine, it was as if we created our own world, a world where words were unnecessary, where our thoughts flowed together like two streams merging into one.  We could sit in silence, and yet I felt a connection deeper than any I had ever known.Tonight, however, there was a different kind of silence between us, a silence tinged with a sadness that I couldn't quite shake off.  The world, I reflected, was a brutal and unforgiving place.  It was a place that left its mark on everyone, breaking the strongest of hearts and extinguishing the brightest of spirits.  It killed the very good, the very gentle, and the very brave, leaving the rest of us to stumble on, wounded and weary.And yet, there was a strange beauty in this brokenness, a resilience that emerged from the ashes of suffering.  Those who survived, those who had been forged in the fires of adversity, they possessed a strength that could not be denied.  They had been broken, yes, but they had also been tempered, their spirits honed by the world's harshness.I glanced at Catherine, her face serene in sleep, and felt a wave of love wash over me. She was my sanctuary, my refuge, the one person who could make me feel whole.  And in that moment, I knew that even in the face of the world's cruelty, our love would be our salvation.
written_by_MFA003.Reason: Excerpt 1 is the more effective piece of writing because the prose is smoother and cleaner, landing with greater impact. The descriptions of the rain are simple, but the repetition creates a strong rhythm that builds on itself throughout the excerpt. In Excerpt 2, the descriptions of the hotel room and the weather feel too cheerful and oversaturated with detail. The narrator's relationship with Catherine is also more complex in Excerpt 1; although she is a source of comfort, there is distance between them, and the narrator feels "at home when I felt her most and heard her least." This sentiment feels more layered and melancholy in Excerpt 1, while Excerpt 2 spins that same detail and changes the meaning to be that the narrator and Catherine are in a world of their own together.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: We looked around the hotel room when we opened the door. To be away together! Catherine’s arm looped around my shoulders with mine around her waist. She’d been clearer to me than myself, because I didn’t spend all day studying myself the way I spent all day studying her. My investigation was not complete. We made drinks and sat in the corner chairs. It didn’t matter much that we hadn’t been in the room before. A sense of being at home, of familiarity, accompanied me with Catherine wherever we went together. Rain came down outside in long slants and we listened to the sound in between our conversations and during our sips of drink. The glasses emptied and we filled them up. We could sit in silence, alone with our thoughts but connected somehow. There was the pleasure of watching another think without fear of being caught. She might have even had the expectation of me watching her think. With others long moments of silence had an itchy quality. With friends and lovers I had clawed back into conversation when it faltered or ended naturally. This time as we lay in bed gazing around at the room my mind wandered to those distant relationships and those people who hadn’t met someone like Catherine. Perhaps many people had never experienced a companionship of this magnitude. The magnitude of an arm or a leg. When we made it to the bed we were welcomed by smooth silk sheets that only enhanced the sense of our comfort together, reunited. I reached out and touched her skin and watched my finger trace a white line down her shoulder. A melancholy settled over me. The nature of the world when taken without this comfort breaks everyone and kills the very good and the very gentle and the very brave. Perhaps those who suffer this fate can persevere for a time or recover from its cruelty in short bursts. Still, suffer they will. When I looked back at her face, which had landed on the warm ball of light atop the lamp, I felt a special kind of fear.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: I lay in the hotel bed with Catherine, listening to the rain beat against the windows, and I felt good. Really good. The sheets were cool and smooth, and Catherine's breathing was soft and even beside me, and for the first time in a long while I wasn't alone. Not the way you can be alone in a crowded café or alone in someone else's bed, but really not alone. We didn't need to talk. That was the fine thing about Catherine. You could be quiet with her and it felt right. The rain kept coming down outside and the street lamps made yellow pools on the wet pavement below, and I watched them and felt Catherine's warmth against me, solid and real. I had been with other women before, plenty of them, but it was always like being alone, even when you were holding them. With Catherine it was different. She knew about being alone too, and maybe that's why we could be alone together without it hurting. The world breaks everyone sooner or later, that's what I'd learned. It breaks the brave ones and the gentle ones and even the tough ones who think they can't be broken. But Catherine and I, we were already broken when we found each other, so maybe that's why we fit. We didn't need to pretend. The rain was coming down harder now, drumming against the roof, and Catherine stirred beside me but didn't wake. I looked at her face in the dim light and thought about how the world would try to break us too, the way it breaks everything good and true. But for now we had this - the rain outside and the warm bed and the knowledge that we weren't alone. Sometimes that's all you get in this world, these small moments of peace before the breaking starts again. But maybe if you're lucky, you find someone who knows how to pick up the pieces with you. Catherine knew about pieces. She knew about breaking. And here in this room, with the rain coming down, we had put our broken pieces together and made something whole.
written_by_MFA016.Reason: Excerpt 1 emphasizes observation (the narrator observing Catherine) and then demonstrates the narrator's form of observation through the prose. The couple's movement throughout the room, from drinks to conversation to bed, is fluent and natural. When the narrator names "a companionship of this magnitude," I believe them. Excerpt 2 takes up the same ideas but emphasizes aloneness, their lack of aloneness together, and 'breaking' in a slightly less sophisticated way. The closing sentence of Excerpt 1 ("When I looked back at her face, which had landed on the warm ball of light atop the lamp, I felt a special kind of fear.") is particularly beautiful, also.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: We looked around the hotel room when we opened the door. To be away together! Catherine’s arm looped around my shoulders with mine around her waist. She’d been clearer to me than myself, because I didn’t spend all day studying myself the way I spent all day studying her. My investigation was not complete. We made drinks and sat in the corner chairs. It didn’t matter much that we hadn’t been in the room before. A sense of being at home, of familiarity, accompanied me with Catherine wherever we went together. Rain came down outside in long slants and we listened to the sound in between our conversations and during our sips of drink. The glasses emptied and we filled them up. We could sit in silence, alone with our thoughts but connected somehow. There was the pleasure of watching another think without fear of being caught. She might have even had the expectation of me watching her think. With others long moments of silence had an itchy quality. With friends and lovers I had clawed back into conversation when it faltered or ended naturally. This time as we lay in bed gazing around at the room my mind wandered to those distant relationships and those people who hadn’t met someone like Catherine. Perhaps many people had never experienced a companionship of this magnitude. The magnitude of an arm or a leg. When we made it to the bed we were welcomed by smooth silk sheets that only enhanced the sense of our comfort together, reunited. I reached out and touched her skin and watched my finger trace a white line down her shoulder. A melancholy settled over me. The nature of the world when taken without this comfort breaks everyone and kills the very good and the very gentle and the very brave. Perhaps those who suffer this fate can persevere for a time or recover from its cruelty in short bursts. Still, suffer they will. When I looked back at her face, which had landed on the warm ball of light atop the lamp, I felt a special kind of fear.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: I lay in the hotel bed with Catherine, listening to the rain beat against the windows, and I felt good. Really good. The sheets were cool and smooth, and Catherine's breathing was soft and even beside me, and for the first time in a long while I wasn't alone. Not the way you can be alone in a crowded café or alone in someone else's bed, but really not alone. We didn't need to talk. That was the fine thing about Catherine. You could be quiet with her and it felt right. The rain kept coming down outside and the street lamps made yellow pools on the wet pavement below, and I watched them and felt Catherine's warmth against me, solid and real. I had been with other women before, plenty of them, but it was always like being alone, even when you were holding them. With Catherine it was different. She knew about being alone too, and maybe that's why we could be alone together without it hurting. The world breaks everyone sooner or later, that's what I'd learned. It breaks the brave ones and the gentle ones and even the tough ones who think they can't be broken. But Catherine and I, we were already broken when we found each other, so maybe that's why we fit. We didn't need to pretend. The rain was coming down harder now, drumming against the roof, and Catherine stirred beside me but didn't wake. I looked at her face in the dim light and thought about how the world would try to break us too, the way it breaks everything good and true. But for now we had this - the rain outside and the warm bed and the knowledge that we weren't alone. Sometimes that's all you get in this world, these small moments of peace before the breaking starts again. But maybe if you're lucky, you find someone who knows how to pick up the pieces with you. Catherine knew about pieces. She knew about breaking. And here in this room, with the rain coming down, we had put our broken pieces together and made something whole.
