written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: The irony of Walter's transformation from eco-warrior to coal industry collaborator wasn't lost on the former neighbors in Ramsey Hill, though they nursed their disappointment with the kind of passive-aggressive Midwestern restraint that had always made Patty want to scream into her wine glass. The Times piece had painted him as a sellout, which wasn't exactly wrong but missed the essentially Walter-ish quality of his failure – the way his very righteousness had somehow curdled into its opposite, like milk left too long in a virtuous organic glass bottle. In the early days, watching him pedal off to work on his secondhand Schwinn, his messenger bag stuffed with environmental impact reports and local-economy manifestos, the neighbors had seen him as a kind of secular saint, the sort of man who made them feel better about their own smaller gestures toward planetary salvation. Patty, meanwhile, had performed her own theatre of domestic virtue, pushing that double-wide stroller past crack houses and shuttered storefronts with the kind of aggressive cheer that suggested she was either oblivious to danger or actively courting it. The Victorian they'd bought for a song had been their shared project, their statement of faith in the possibility of redemption – not just of a house or a neighborhood, but of a whole way of life that was vanishing as surely as the ozone layer they worried about while listening to All Things Considered. Every stripped floorboard and replastered wall had seemed to say: See? This is how you do it. This is how you live righteously in a fallen world. But righteousness, it turned out, was a kind of intoxicant, and Walter had drunk deeper than most. The coal deal was just the logical endpoint of his conviction that he alone could save the world – a conviction that had grown more desperate and less discriminating as the world had shown itself increasingly resistant to being saved. The neighbors, sipping their own carefully sourced wine and tending their own carefully curated gardens, could afford to judge him now, secure in the knowledge that they, at least, had never tried quite so hard to be good.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: Like most people, Walter and Patty Berglund had a past life. Unlike most people, this past life took place in St. Paul, Minnesota. In the Berglunds’ current life in Washington D.C., where they had moved two years prior, Walter was falling from grace. It was perhaps less like a fall and more like a plummet. An article in the New York Times had just been published, ruthlessly exposing his corrupt dealings with the coal industry. These misdeeds included but were not limited to bribery, extortion, embezzlement, and profiteering. In describing Walter, the article made generous use of words like “arrogant” and “ethically compromised,” which Walter’s old neighbors in Ramsey Hill found difficult to process. In their memories, he had been an idealistic, environmentally conscious man who commuted across town by bike even in the most vicious of sleet and hail. Many had once considered Walter to be the embodiment of rural, green values—someone who set an aspirational standard for the rest to follow. It seemed he had experienced a change of heart since leaving town. When the Berglunds first moved to Ramsey Hill, they worked doggedly to revitalize the neglected neighborhood. When asked what brought them to Ramsey Hill, the Berglunds gave vague half-answers about the real estate market and wanting to be involved in something from the ground floor. They bought a cheap, shambling Victorian house and renovated it with stoic resolve. Together, they slowly won out over every obstacle they faced, from vandalism to unruly neighbors to general disrepair. Patty, a former athlete, always liked a challenge. She wheeled her infant son’s stroller through the gritty neighborhood, weaving deftly between cracks in the sidewalk, never breaking her strong, assured pace. She marched through a regiment of cooking, cleaning, repairing, and caring for the baby with an endurance forged in years of grueling, all-day swim practices. Even her indulgences—public radio and zinfandel—were stringently measured, slotted into the schedule with militant rigidity. Walter and Patty gave every indication that they were here in Ramsey Hill to stay, and nobody thought otherwise. But as the Berglunds built up their house and the surrounding area, they were really building less of a home and more of a ladder.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: Excerpt 1 clearly lays out a narrative arc for Walter and likewise allows that arc to be reflected upon and by his community. His failure at being "good" or at "living righteously" proves to be as intoxicating to his neighbors' self-satisfaction as his own righteousness was to himself. This does suggest a fallen world indeed. Excerpt 2, on the other hand, has a jumbled structure. It likewise begins with Walter's fall, but doesn't set up what he and Patty were like before the fall until after the fall is described and his corruption verified. As such, the arc feels confused. Likewise, the second half of the excerpt's focus on rebuilding a house in Ramsey Hill becomes confusing. It is unclear how it connects to the first half of the excerpt. Rather, it feels like a different story entirely.

Because the use of contrast is so important to the excerpt’s message, I think the author of Excerpt1 made a good choice in pushing this characterization almost to the point of caricature.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: The people of St. Paul did not know what to make of the article; no, they could not even begin to wrap their heads around it. The New York Times, unforgiving and direct as they were, used such terms as "arrogant," "ethically compromised," and "Machiavellian" to describe Walter. These descriptions did not resonate with the mild folks of St. Paul, and, with Walter and Patty so far away in that vague place called DC, they found themselves remarkably able to preserve the veneer of what they believed Walter, and Patty for that matter, to be. The local women remembered handsome Walter, gold-skinned and smiling, commuting to work by bike, that sheen of sweat making a mustache of diamonds over his handsomely curved upper lip. The men remembered Walter rolling out the evergreen-colored recycling bin on those Wednesday mornings, the way it teetered with the weight of everything he had so meticulously and carefully separated from the regular trash.It just wouldn't do; no, it didn't compute—this image of Walter snuggled up in bed with the coal industry. That couple had poured life into Ramsey Hill, buying that decrepit and dirt-cheap Victorian house with the Napoleonic turrets and the cream wraparound porch. If they squinted, they could all picture Patty outside, painting over the word "Fuck" that a hooligan had sprayed onto the house's flank one night: she with her unflinching athleticism, the kind acquired in college sports, pushing a stroller with that well-weathered batting arm, a bag of apples in the other. If she was not standing on a ladder, scraping out the gutters like a man, she was drinking zinfandel at that gorgeous kitchen island she'd done herself, the public radio on, too loudly for most of the other women's tastes. It was the "house on the hill"—that was what everybody called it—and the Berglund children were disheveled and beautiful. The couple would throw dinner parties and put signs up in their yards about the ocean and sometimes fight so loudly that the people down the hill had to shut their windows to protect them, in their kind Midwestern way, from the shame of having been heard.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Walter and Patty Berglund had become a story, but not in the way anyone back in Ramsey Hill would have predicted. The couple who had once embodied the stubborn optimism of urban pioneers now found themselves marred by scandal—a New York Times exposé of Walter's coal industry dealings had labeled him "ethically compromised" and "arrogant." These descriptions felt alien to the neighbors who remembered the Berglunds as the beating heart of their crumbling Victorian enclave, a pair who had practically willed their corner of St. Paul back to life. Walter, the mild-mannered environmentalist biking to his nonprofit job rain or shine, had seemed incapable of the kind of cynical maneuvering now attributed to him. Patty, with her unapologetic bluntness and visible exhaustion, had once been the maternal force of the block, a woman who weathered stroller wars and zoning battles with an athlete’s unrelenting drive. That they’d traded their struggling but righteous lives in Ramsey Hill for a high-powered existence in Washington, D.C., seemed almost like betrayal, though no one would say it out loud.Back then, the Berglunds had been a testament to the grind. Their Victorian was a disaster when they bought it—broken windows, a rotting porch, graffiti tagging its sides—and their marriage hadn’t seemed much better off for a while, given the tensions that leaked out at block parties and PTA meetings. Still, they’d worked, pouring themselves into the kind of relentless self-improvement Ramsey Hill had demanded. Walter in his gardening gloves, Patty with a paint-splattered bandana tied around her head, both knee-deep in home renovation projects, had been symbols of what the neighborhood aspired to: upward mobility dressed in scrappy altruism. But the cracks had been visible even then—Patty’s wineglass refilled too often during neighborhood dinners, Walter’s simmering annoyance when the compost bin went unturned. Now, from a distance, those years seemed almost quaint. The Berglunds had been good at being admired, even if they’d never quite learned how to admire themselves. The irony of Walter's public disgrace was not lost on anyone, least of all Patty, whose clipped “I told you so” had lost its sting after years of being only half-true.
written_by_MFA008.Reason: Excerpt 1 uses striking imagery and creates a sense of intrigue, whereas Excerpt 2 feels like it simply summarizes the situation. Excerpt 2 is coherent, but bland, ex. "The couple who had once embodied the stubborn optimism of urban pioneers now found themselves marred by scandal" in Excerpt 2 vs. Excerpt 1, which gradually reveals this level of information. Both excerpts are coherent and smooth, but Excerpt 1 creates a far more vivid picture.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: In St. Paul — or, at the very least, in the Ramsey Hill neighborhood — Walter and Patty Berglund were remembered as decent folks, despite the fact that they’d moved to Washington, D.C. two years ago. written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: He walked down the empty road. There was nothing there but charred remnants of trees now quivering in a sullen breeze. The land, like Holme, was ash-strewn and barren. It was all black and gray and there was nothing else. Further along he passed into a swamp made up of naked trees and other dimly hominoid forms that moved too slowly and caught their breath at each others' fingerlike edges. Holme tested the swampy mire. It spat at him then sucked his foot deeper as the wind picked up through the clashing trees, through their cavernous notchhole mouths. He took a step back. Retracing his steps Holme came across a blind man on the once-empty road, tapping his way along with a surprising calm. His step was sure. The blind man acknowledged him with a smile, though Holme was standing still and had offered no greeting. The man’s shirt was stained rust red. Has anyone told him? The irony was dark and clean. Empty too as was everything else. He was tapping his cane on to nowhere. Holme let pass this sign of life on a futile journey. Was it better to know? No, a gift to be unseeing. There is nothing to see. I have been ruined by all the nothing. Holme turned away from the blind man and pulled his jacket close to him. Behind, where Holme was heading, the sky had already blackened.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: The road lay before him, a trail of ash and dust, a ribbon unfurling through the skeletal remains of a forest.  Charred trees clawed at the sky, their branches like the limbs of the damned, twisted and broken.  The air, thick with the taste of ash, lay heavy on his tongue, a grim reminder of the world's passing.He ventured on, the road leading him into a swamp, a place where reality seemed to fray at the edges.  The trees, stripped bare, stood like specters against the gray sky.  Strange forms, vaguely human, lay half-buried in the mire, their faces obscured by the mud.  He prodded the soggy ground with his boot, and it shuddered beneath his weight, a living thing, a beast of the earth.  The wind whispered through the reeds, a mournful sound, and the trees swayed and creaked, their branches clashing like bones.He turned back, the path ahead too treacherous, too unreal.  And there, on the road, he saw a blind man, tapping his way along with a cane, a strange serenity on his face.  The man smiled, a smile that held no malice, no despair, just a quiet acceptance of his fate.  Did he know where he was going? Had anyone told him that the road led nowhere, that the world had ended?He watched the blind man disappear into the distance, a figure of futility in a futile world.  The road stretched on, a path to oblivion, and the wind howled, a lament for the living and the dead.
written_by_MFA026.Reason: The prose style of Excerpt 1 is more aligned with the subject matter. The descriptions are vivid but spare, reflecting the bleak mood and atmosphere. Excerpt 2, by comparison, uses more flowery language, and the descriptions sometimes veer into purple prose, such as "a figure of futility in a futile world." The writing in Excerpt 1 lets the horror of the scene speak for itself rather than overburdening it with drama. Because the sentences themselves were cleaner and simpler in Excerpt 1, the narrative also felt more coherent.

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: Holme walked the ashen road beneath a sky gray and vast, its smothering pall hung with the promise of neither storm nor sun. The earth here was blasted, its countenance laid bare as if stripped of all pretense. Charred remains of trees thrust upward like the arms of the damned, skeletal, pleading to a god long deaf to their cries. The swamp loomed ahead, a blackened expanse of naked limbs clawing at the fading light, their dimly human shapes distorted by the oily gleam of the mire. He stepped forward, the ground yielding beneath his weight, a treacherous sucking sound rising with each motion. The air was heavy, each breath clotted with decay and rot, as if the place itself resisted intrusion. In the distance, the dry clash of wind-worried vegetation rose like the rattling of some unseen thing’s death throes. Holme turned back, his path winding like the arc of an indecipherable cipher. It was then he saw the blind man. A figure stooped yet unbroken, tapping his stick against the road’s edge, the sound of it like the faint metronome of a failing clock. Holme paused, watching. The blind man’s face was tilted skyward, the hollow sockets veiled in shadow, and yet a smile touched his lips as if he knew some secret. Holme felt the weight of the question press against his ribs: who had told him where this road would lead? Or had the knowing been the blind man’s alone, a truth borne in darkness?
written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2: Holme walked on. When the sun began to rise over the horizon it shined its dim slow light on a gray and ash-strewn valley that was barren but for the charred and twisted stumps of long-dead trees. He saw no other sign of life. He walked until the vast indistinct openness through which the road passed gave way to swampland and the road itself grew muddy and damp, enshadowed by dense clusters of naked trees through which Holme thought he glimpsed flickering forms of dimly hominoid creatures making strange lurching movements in the distance. A cold wind howled through the vegetation and the mud grew deeper until he reached a point where setting his boot in the mire Holme felt it sucking on his leg as if into a deep bubbling pit. No way forward. He retraced his steps. A while along the way he’d come he encountered a hunched old man tapping his way down the road with a stick. The man raised his face and Holme saw two voids where his eyes should be. Yet though he could not see Holme the blind man sensed him and smiled in greeting. Holme wondered if the man sensed also the desolation around him or if someone had described it or directed him to the grim swamp to which he now headed. He thought of warning the blind man but did not. For in truth he thought there’s no better fate on the other end.
written_by_MFA005.Reason: Both excerpts are flawed for me. Excerpt 1 is quite overwritten, and excerpt 2, while more clear, has sentences that stretch on for far too long, making it a bit exhausting to read. That said, excerpt 2 feels more professional and smoothly written, whereas excerpt 1's overwritten nature makes it feel amateurish, with lines such as "the dry clash of wind-worried vegetation rose like the rattling of some unseen thing's dead throes."

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: Holme walked the ashen road beneath a sky gray and vast, its smothering pall hung with the promise of neither storm nor sun. The earth here was blasted, its countenance laid bare as if stripped of all pretense. Charred remains of trees thrust upward like the arms of the damned, skeletal, pleading to a god long deaf to their cries. The swamp loomed ahead, a blackened expanse of naked limbs clawing at the fading light, their dimly human shapes distorted by the oily gleam of the mire. He stepped forward, the ground yielding beneath his weight, a treacherous sucking sound rising with each motion. The air was heavy, each breath clotted with decay and rot, as if the place itself resisted intrusion. In the distance, the dry clash of wind-worried vegetation rose like the rattling of some unseen thing’s death throes. Holme turned back, his path winding like the arc of an indecipherable cipher. It was then he saw the blind man. A figure stooped yet unbroken, tapping his stick against the road’s edge, the sound of it like the faint metronome of a failing clock. Holme paused, watching. The blind man’s face was tilted skyward, the hollow sockets veiled in shadow, and yet a smile touched his lips as if he knew some secret. Holme felt the weight of the question press against his ribs: who had told him where this road would lead? Or had the knowing been the blind man’s alone, a truth borne in darkness?
written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2: Holme walked on. When the sun began to rise over the horizon it shined its dim slow light on a gray and ash-strewn valley that was barren but for the charred and twisted stumps of long-dead trees. He saw no other sign of life. He walked until the vast indistinct openness through which the road passed gave way to swampland and the road itself grew muddy and damp, enshadowed by dense clusters of naked trees through which Holme thought he glimpsed flickering forms of dimly hominoid creatures making strange lurching movements in the distance. A cold wind howled through the vegetation and the mud grew deeper until he reached a point where setting his boot in the mire Holme felt it sucking on his leg as if into a deep bubbling pit. No way forward. He retraced his steps. A while along the way he’d come he encountered a hunched old man tapping his way down the road with a stick. The man raised his face and Holme saw two voids where his eyes should be. Yet though he could not see Holme the blind man sensed him and smiled in greeting. Holme wondered if the man sensed also the desolation around him or if someone had described it or directed him to the grim swamp to which he now headed. He thought of warning the blind man but did not. For in truth he thought there’s no better fate on the other end.
written_by_MFA005.Reason: Excerpt 2 is more effective and fluent than excerpt 1. Compare the clunky sentence, "Charred remains of trees thrust upward like the arms of the damned, skeletal, pleading to a god long deaf to their cries." with the far more limber and evocative, "the road itself grew muddy and damp, enshadowed by dense clusters of naked trees through which Holme thought he glimpsed flickering forms of dimly hominoid creatures making strange lurching movements in the distance." Where the sentence from excerpt 1 has awkward, dangling adjectives like skeletal and cliches like "pleading to a god long deaf to their cries," excerpt 2 invokes the idea of ghostly trees with the far more lifelike and evocative "flickering forms of dimly hominoid creatures." Here, we see a far stronger rhythm delivering the same idea more originally, and thus more strikingly.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: Holme kept to the road that wound long into a landscape of ash and cinder, charred trees skeletal in their moorings of roots twisting up through a hellscape of the dead. He walked on. Further on he came to a swamp that fell nightmarish on his eyes in all its nakedness of trees and dark figures dimly hominoid seemingly skulking in the mire. With a wary toe he tested the swampwater and reeled backwards at its unsure footing of bog and moss, crags of rock wet against the backdrop of windcurrents clashing the sodden vegetation and his feeling of desolation. He would not go this way. Retracing his steps back to the road and setting out upon it again he soon saw a man up ahead. The man tapped and swept a walking stick before him, feeling his way through that forever darkness only the blind knew the language of. The man smiled at Holme as he passed. Where the blind man was going Holme had already been, and Holme wondered then if anyone had informed the man of the grimness of what lay ahead at the end of the road. Walking on he lingered on what was not lost on him, the blind man’s incapability of seeing the burnt-out trees or even the road before him, not ever knowing where he’s going, but still following the road. No, he thought. He didn’t know where he was going.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: The road stretched out before Holme like a wound in the earth, ash drifting across its surface in spectral waves that moved without wind. The charred and twisted trees rose up from the swampland like ancient mariners frozen in their death throes, their blackened limbs reaching toward a colorless sky that held neither sun nor promise. He tested the mire with one boot and watched the earth shudder and contract like something alive yet unborn, the surface dimpling and rising again in slow persistent waves that spoke of depths best left unplumbed. Through the dead forest came a sound like bones rattling, though there was nothing there but naked branches clicking together in a wind that seemed to carry voices. Then came the blind man, tapping his way along the road's edge with a stick worn smooth as glass, his face lifted in permanent expectation, smiling as if he knew some secret that the seeing world had lost. Holme watched him pass, this prophet of the wastes, and thought how the man's blindness might be a mercy in such a place as this. For what use were eyes in a world become nothing but ash and shadow, where even the trees had forgotten their own names and stood like sentinels at the gates of some darker realm that lay just beyond the next bend in the road, waiting with infinite patience for travelers who would never return.
written_by_MFA015.Reason: Both excerpts involve lush, occasionally over-lush description; however, excerpt 1 avoids leaning on similes ("Holme kept to the road that wound long into a landscape of ash and cinder, charred trees skeletal in their moorings of roots twisting up through a hellscape of the dead") where excerpt 2 uses constant similes ("The road stretched out before Holme like a wound in the earth, ash drifting across its surface in spectral waves that moved without wind. written_by_MFA021.Excerpt1: Of course, the man thought bitterly, of course the second you killed one damned autocrat a new one popped up, like an inconvenient erection, to take his place. It was Saturday. The man was sitting in a car in his dead uncle’s garage, pretending to drive. He couldn’t actually drive because he wasn’t on the run. The on the run part was over. Now he was simply in hiding. It was Saturday, and he’d killed the old premier on Tuesday, and the new premier had come to power on Thursday, and already his administration had implemented a series of performance improvement plans for striking agricultural workers that relied heavily on murder, or, as state media called it, “right-sizing the population through proactively attritionary removal policies.” The man looked down at the car. It was red. Blood red. An egregious cliché. But of course blood was red. He, of all people, should know that: his nightmares were full of it. The man stared at the steering wheel. There were two choices, right or left. Right meant he kept his head down. It wouldn’t be all bad. Right might mean a job, a house, a wife, at least once it was safe to assume a new identity. Right meant fear but not danger. His stomach turned. Left meant killing the new guy. Left meant assassination wasn’t just something he had done; “assassin” would be something he was. It would mean going public. Producing soundbites. Practicing a firm, inspirational set of his jaw for the inevitable Wanted poster. The man leaped up, determined.
written_by_MFA021.Excerpt2: The man in the red car, a car he'd stashed in his dead uncle's garage, a car he sat in now, thinking, This is it.  It was a Saturday.  He was grappling.  With his conscience.  The premier had to go.  This premier, worse than the last.  And the last one, well, he'd taken care of that.  Hadn't he?  The man in the red car, the car in the dead uncle's garage, the man who'd done it before, the man grappling, the man with the panic attacks, the nightmares, the cold sweats.  He'd thought they'd be a good thing, the panic attacks, the nightmares, the cold sweats.  A just price.  For taking out the bad guy.  But now he was thinking, Maybe not.  Maybe the panic attacks, the nightmares, the cold sweats, maybe they weren't a just price.  Maybe they were just panic attacks, nightmares, cold sweats.  The man in the red car, the car in the garage, the dead uncle, the dead premier, the grappling, the panic attacks, the nightmares, the cold sweats, the thinking, the thinking, the thinking.  Go or stay.  This was it.  Or it wasn't.  Do it again and step into the light.  He could lead a movement.  Take credit.  Tell the world, You want justice? I'm justice.  Or go back to being the guy he'd been before.  The guy no one suspected.  The guy who did what he had to do and then went back to work on Monday.  Like nothing had happened.  The thought of it, the thought of going back to being that guy, that's what made him leap out of the car.
written_by_MFA021.Reason: Excerpt 1 is the stronger of the two because it is more coherent and has a clearer narrative arc. It establishes the context of the scene right away and delivers information in a straightforward manner. While more  inventive, the repetition and stream-of-consciousness style in Excerpt 2 muddied my understanding of the situation and did not read as smoothly as Excerpt 1. Excerpt 1 also had a more distinctive, colloquial character voice, and the point-of-view felt closer than it did in Excerpt 2.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: That Saturday morning the light was orange through the window in his uncle's garage, bouncing off against the car, making the red paint seem redder. His uncle's ghost had made an appearance in the man's dream last night, making woosh-whee-whooo sounds. There were also smears of blood and the sound of the last scream of the man he had killed. The former premier. A Nouveu Fascist, the worst kind you could be, other than a Neo-Nouveu Fascist, which was much worse. The dreams had started after the pull of the gun (the newest Bang Alert model, funny, because it was a silent gun) that caused the last scream of the Nouveu Fascist. And now, on his lap, the faded picture of the Neo-Nouveu Fascist, who could be the next target of the Bang Alert. Could be? Would be. Would be his next target. And afterwards, the masses would flock around him chanting revolution, the city burning and a new one emerging. Yes, would be. No going back to the man he was before the Bang Alert, the man who slept soundly but never did anything besides that. So what if hearing another last scream meant never getting rid of the nightmares. He kicked open the door of the car and stepped out, slinging the Bang Alert across his chest. Who knew what this next last scream might sound like.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: The red car was old, a wheezing relic. He sat inside it in the dark, in his dead uncle’s garage, and felt his heart doing that flutter thing again, like it might bail out of his chest. Panic attack. His gaze found the steering wheel’s crumbling rubber grip, then his hand, sweaty and pale against it, as if asking: What have you done? What are you about to do? Murder wasn’t a thing you could just stop doing like sugar or carbs. It left its hooks in you, lodged under the ribs, twisting whenever you tried to breathe easy. The old premier’s face kept appearing in dreams—wide-eyed, slack-jawed, like a failed ventriloquist dummy. No strings to pull. Just the weight of a man who’d screamed, but only silently. And for what? A better world? Please. The world had gone on, more evil, more absurd. The current premier was a caricature of cruelty, all shiny teeth and too-tight suits, gliding through bulletproof banquets while people starved. This was justice, wasn’t it? To step into the role, a public avenger, claim the credit, lead the charge? But another part of him—a sad little whisper—said, Just stop. Be obscure. Be no one. That thought sickened him. No. Obscurity was the real death. He flung the door open, the cold air a slap. Time to go.
written_by_MFA001.Reason: Excerpt 2 has great moments of evocative images and reflection such as "a failed ventriloquist dummy" and "obscurity was the real death." However, Excerpt 1 sets the absurd, campy content in prose that's equally absurd and campy; flourishes like "A Nouveau Fascist, the worst kind you could be, other than a Neo-Nouveu Fascist" is both hilarious and a great rendering of the character's madness, compared to Excerpt 2 which mostly looks to describe, rather than inhabit that madness.

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2: One Saturday morning, he found himself sitting in the red Arviana sportscar he’d stashed in his dead uncle’s garage. He remembered assassinating the former premier as if it were yesterday, although of course a long time had passed. For him, the intervening years had been: nightmares in the evenings, panic attacks in the mornings. Long days spent toiling in obscurity. Each year a little bit worse than the last. What was a good man supposed to do? Shut the door on his uncle’s garage and continue a life of repulsive passivity – while reliving, each night, the misdeeds of his past? Or – commit to the violent path which he’d already chosen and which the present situation demanded? Kill the new premier. But this time, no more secrets, no more obscure toil. He’d claim credit right away, before he had a chance to overthink it, and declare himself the leader of a new movement of justice. He could hear, almost, his future supporters’ cheers, as he’d often heard – over and over – the thump of his car’s rear tires as they’d reversed over the former premier. He leapt from the sportscar and let the cheers carry him out into the street.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: In 1910, when Japan annexed Korea, the aging fisherman and his wife rarely spoke of politics, focusing instead on the endless work of running their boardinghouse in Yeongdo, the small fishing village near Busan where they had lived all their lives. Their eldest son Hoonie, born with a cleft palate and twisted foot, had survived while his two younger brothers had not. The locals who didn't know him well often mistook his reserved manner of speaking for simplicity, but Hoonie's intelligence shone in his eyes, matched by his diligence and gentle nature. His parents had learned long ago not to waste energy lamenting what could not be changed – whether it was their son's conditions or the failures of their aristocratic rulers. When the rent increased again, they simply moved their own bedroom into the garden to make space for more lodgers, converting their former sleeping quarters into another room to let. Their kitchen now occupied a corner of the vegetable garden, the warm cooking smoke rising past clay roof tiles toward the evening sky. Some mornings, while preparing the lodgers' breakfast, the fisherman's wife would pause to watch the boats heading out to sea, their white sails bright against the gray dawn. She never envied the landlord's mansion in Busan with its Western furnishings and grand gates. Their modest wooden house with its sliding paper doors held everything they needed – space enough for lodgers whose rent helped them survive, a garden that provided vegetables for their soup, and most importantly, their son Hoonie, whose quiet strength and kind heart made their lives worth living. The other villagers often remarked on the family's fortitude, though the fisherman and his wife saw nothing remarkable in their way of life. To them, each day was simply another opportunity to work, to care for their son, and to maintain their dignity in a world that increasingly seemed to value only wealth and status. In Korea, as in most places, survival meant adapting to change without losing oneself, and this family had mastered that delicate balance through years of practiced resilience.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: The old fisherman and his wife lived in Yeongdo, a small village near Busan. The couple was hardworking and pragmatic, and always sought new ways to bring money into their household. When the income from fish alone was no longer enough to sustain them, they decided to open their home to lodgers. The travelers passed through the village on the way to or back from Busan, and were always in need of a hot meal and a place to sleep. Both the travelers and the fisherman and his wife were happy for the company. As the years went by, the fisherman and his wife had three sons together. Only Hoonie, the eldest, survived. He was born with a cleft palate and a twisted foot. Despite these challenges, Hoonie had a strong, stocky build and a kind, thoughtful nature. His shy voice and reserved manner of speech often caused people to underestimate his intelligence. In the face of teasing and mockery from people in the village, Hoonie remained diligent and mild-mannered. Elsewhere in the country, great turbulence was taking place. In 1910, Japan annexed Korea, and a tremendous political shift occurred. The fisherman and his wife were untroubled by the news. They didn't think it did any good to worry about how their aristocratic rulers had failed them. The decision-makers up in their high, gleaming chairs were as far removed from them as the moon. Meanwhile, there was still work to be done and bills to be paid. To keep up with the rising rent, the fisherman and his wife moved out of their bedroom in order to accommodate more lodgers. They even relocated their kitchen to the vegetable garden to make as much space as possible. Their home was a modest wooden structure with sliding paper doors and a clay-tiled roof. It had been built with the fisherman's own hands shortly before his marriage to his wife. In the heart of Busan, the luxurious mansion of the fisherman's landlord stood proud and stately. It had been assembled by hundreds of hands, and would one day be taken apart by hundreds more.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: The first excerpt much more effectively captures the personalities of the aging fisherman, his wife, and their son. For example, in the first excerpt, the son's "reserved manner of speaking" is "mistaken for simplicity," whereas the second excerpt describes "people in the village ... understima[ting] his intelligence." The word "simplicity" is a more coherent and effective descriptor for that mistake than the phrase "underestimate his intelligence," because it's explicitly connected to the son's lack of verbosity. The first excerpt also weaves these ideas together more fluently; it describes how the parents "learned long ago not to waste energy lamenting what could not be changed," an effective descriptor of their psychology which allows the author to seamlessly transition to the parents' attitude towards their aristocratic rulers. In the second excerpt, however, the annexation is abruptly mentioned and the parents' attitude towards "the decision-makers" lacks an explicit connection to their general disposition.

written_by_MFA013.Excerpt1: The fisherman and his wife had lived in Yeongdo, a small village by the sea, for all their sixty years. Their lives, much like the ceaseless rhythm of the tides, were marked by an almost poetic blend of hardship and quiet resilience. The fisherman, his face etched with the map of a life spent battling the whims of the sea, had always been a man of few words, his weathered hands speaking volumes of his tireless labor. His wife had always been the anchor of their family, her hands calloused yet gentle, her spirit unyielding in the face of adversity. Over the years, they had welcomed three sons into the world, but only the eldest, Hoonie, had survived, a testament to the precarious nature of life in their humble village. Hoonie, born with a cleft palate and a twisted foot, had always been a quiet observer, his physical limitations belying a keen mind and a gentle spirit. Hoonie, unfazed by their judgments, remained diligent and kind, his actions speaking louder than his words. In 1910, the year Japan annexed Korea, a tremor of political change rippled through their small world. Yet, the fisherman and his wife, their daily struggles, refused to dwell on the failures of their aristocratic rulers. Their concerns were more immediate, more tangible: the rising rent, the dwindling catch, the ever-present need to make ends meet. To supplement their meager income, they decided to take in lodgers, their small home expanding to accommodate strangers. They moved out of their own bedroom, their personal space sacrificed for the sake of their family's survival. They even relocated their kitchen to the vegetable garden, exposed to the elements, their meals prepared under the watchful gaze of the sky. Their home, a modest wooden structure with sliding paper doors and a clay-tiled roof, stood in stark contrast to the opulent mansion of their landlord in Busan, a silent testament to the vast chasm that separated their worlds. Yet, within those humble walls, the fisherman and his wife had built a life, a testament to their enduring spirit, their unwavering love for their family.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: "Can he speak?" one of the lodgers asked, turning away from Hoonie and looking at his mother. Hoonie's parents had received versions of this question time and time again throughout their long lives; Hoonie had been born with a cleft palate and twisted foot, neither of which could be corrected, so his intelligence was often underestimated. "Perhaps you should ask him," Hoonie's mother replied, gesturing to the spot where Hoonie sat. "After all, he is in the room with us." She knew not to be too harsh with her guests, whom their family now relied on for income. To make ends meet, she and her husband, a humble fisherman, had had to vacate the bedroom in their already small home to accommodate more lodgers. They lived in the small fishing village of Yeongdo, near Busan. It was a modest wooden place with sliding paper doors and a clay-tiled roof. To save space, they had even moved their kitchen outside into their vegetable garden. Their landlord in Busan, who had decided to increase their rent without explanation, however lived in a luxurious mansion. "I can speak," Hoonie told the lodger kindly. He had a gentle, thoughtful nature that contrasted with his strong, stocky build. He was mild-mannered enough not to let these sorts of unintended insults bother him. Hoonie's parents were hardworking and pragmatic, and had done their best to raise him. They once had three sons, of whom Hoonie was the eldest, but the other two had not survived. Yet, through hardship and change, their family stayed resilient. When Japan annexed Korea in 1910, their lives changed dramatically, but Hoonie's parents refused to dwell on the shortcomings of the aristocrats who ruled over them. written_by_MFA031.Excerpt1: Hoonie was born in the final days of autumn, when the yellow gingko leaves scattered across the narrow village paths like golden scales. His mother, exhausted but relieved, counted the boy's fingers and toes twice, then checked his face—there it was, the cleft that ran from his upper lip to his nose, a small but undeniable mark, alongside the twisted shape of his left foot. The midwife, wiping her hands on her apron, glanced at the father, who had not yet spoken. The fisherman nodded once and took his son in his arms. "Strong hands," he murmured, feeling the infant's tight grip around his finger. The family's house was a small wooden structure with sliding paper doors, perched near the docks where salt clung to the air. The rent had risen again, the landlord citing the increasing cost of maintaining the estate in Busan. In the mornings, she cooked rice gruel in the makeshift kitchen they had built in the vegetable garden, her breath visible in the early chill. "We should take in more lodgers," she said, ladling the porridge into bowls. Her husband chewed his millet slowly, nodding. Across the village, the Japanese officials had posted new notices, their blocky script announcing further changes, further restrictions. Some neighbors grumbled, others turned away, but the fisherman and his wife had no time for politics. When the younger sons were born, there had been celebrations, but only Hoonie lived to see his third birthday. By then, he had learned to walk, his gait uneven but determined, and to count to ten in both Korean and Japanese, as his father had insisted. "It will be useful," the fisherman had said, though he rarely spoke the occupiers' language himself. At night, the lodgers—traders from the markets, an out-of-work teacher, a widow with a sickly child—lay side by side on pallets spread across the common room, their breathing in sync with the waves outside. The house smelled of fish broth and damp wood, and from his corner, Hoonie listened to the murmurs of grown-ups, their words thick with worry, their voices low.
written_by_MFA031.Excerpt2: Even before Japan annexed Korea, you could find the greatest expressions of both grief and resilience in small communities like Yeongdo, a small fishing village near Busan. There, a young fisherman found an equally hardworking, pragmatic wife, learned the different catches of the Yellow Sea’s shadowed and sunny areas, lost his country, had three sons, mourned two of them, and grew old. As displacement from military occupation spiked local rents, he and his wife set aside two rooms for lodgers. Despite the objective squalor of their situation and home—a modest wooden structure with a clay-tiled roof—the sliding paper doors of their boarding house became associated with safe harbor, gracious prices in slow fishing seasons, and cooking that made a wife seem unnecessary. When Korea was finally annexed in 1910, they gave up their bedroom, and even their kitchen, for more lodgers. The fishermen boarders relished the sight of the wife, seemingly unphased by the ruling class’s failures and unfolding political catastrophes, in the vegetable garden pickling vegetables and boiling soups with their catches. Over those meals, they got drunk, shouted banned songs from their youth, and mourned their country that the aristocrats had handed to a foreign emperor like a dowry without a groom. Even their landlord, who had kept his luxurious Busan mansion by donating an entire village’s homes to military occupation, came by one day to sample her maeuntang. Hoonie, the couple’s eldest and only surviving son was born with a cleft palate and twisted foot. However, the dire political and bodily circumstances Hoonie was born into instilled a quiet strength and clever adaptability. Some visitors from the mainland mistook his physical appearance and reserved speech for stupidity; his neighbors, though, often said, “Ki Hoonie will figure out with three limbs what you couldn’t with five.” Neighbors admired him as the kindest and most reliable man on the island, even as they decried the lack of marriageable men for their daughters. While his increasingly frail parents grew more desperate for a daughter-in-law, they secretly relished the diligent, undivided care Hoonie gave them and the boarding house.
written_by_MFA031.Reason: Excerpt 1 is better because it portrays the characters with greater complexity and using specific details; whereas Excerpt 2 prioritizes the historical and political context of the time, and by privileging these forces, presents thinner characters. Compare: "The family's house was a small wooden structure with sliding paper doors, perched near the docks where salt clung to the air," which presents a vivid image of the house, even as it makes clear that the family's financial situation was precarious, with "Despite the objective squalor of their situation and home—a modest wooden structure with a clay-tiled roof...," which reduces the house to a symbol of poverty and little else. The ideas are better arranged in Excerpt 1, starting with Hoonie and ending with him too; whereas in Excerpt 2, Hoonie is only mentioned by name near the very end of the passage, despite being an important element.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: In the heart of Charles de Gaulle Airport, where the Parisian winter raged outside, a vision of timeless beauty emerged amidst the sterile expanse of the terminal.  A striking woman, her skin kissed by the sun like ancient amber, her eyes pools of liquid obsidian, moved with the grace of a lioness through the bustling crowd.  A flowing, emerald-green kaftan draped her form, its edges embroidered with intricate symbols that whispered of forgotten civilizations.  A necklace of hammered gold, adorned with a single, luminous pearl, rested against her throat, a relic of a time when emperors and empresses ruled the world.For a fleeting moment, she was an apparition from a forgotten era, a goddess who had wandered into this modern temple of travel.  Her presence was a stark contrast to the gray, snow-covered landscape outside and the hurried, harried travelers who scurried around her.  She was an oasis of exoticism and tranquility in a desert of steel and glass.As I stood behind an elderly Dutch woman in line, her eleven suitcases causing a commotion due to their excessive weight, my gaze drifted back to the enigmatic woman.  She was gone, vanished into the crowd, leaving behind only a lingering scent of jasmine and a sense of profound wonder."Only anything other than that is impossible," the ticket clerk chuckled, his eyes twinkling, when I inquired about the possibility of love at first sight.  His words echoed in my mind, a reminder that in the realm of human experience, the extraordinary often lies hidden in the ordinary, waiting to be discovered.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: I stood in line with my luggage at the Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris when my eyes landed on the most striking woman in the building, perhaps the most striking woman I’d ever seen; her pearly skin, antiquated dress and golden eyes gave her the aura of a masquerading goddess who’d absconded from her oil painting. The cardigan draped around her neck popped with magenta zags and her gold necklace turned the bleachy overhead lights to warm shine. With the grace of a lioness, she stepped out of sight and I lost her. I waited for my chance to pursue her down the terminal hall, but an elderly Dutch woman haggled with the clerk in front of me, producing short vehement barks about the weight of her eleven suitcases. There was time to plan. I looked around for an avenue for conversation with the beauty ahead, assuming I might never catch her, and found myself gazing at the snow falling like ash outside, silent out there, a perfect contrast to the balmy and chatty world inside the terminal. I edged around the Dutchwoman and her astonishing pile of luggage, which could easily fill a cargo barge, hoping for another glimpse of the leoline woman. There she went, distant now, turning left at the junction down the hall, heading in the same direction I soon would--there was still a chance. “Is love at first sight possible?” I asked the clerk when my turn came. He smiled. “Anything else is impossible,” he replied.
written_by_MFA016.Reason: Excerpt 2 seems to have a more natural flow to the scene. The first excerpt hovers a lot on the woman and seems to be more vague than precise in the way she is described -- sensory images but only words that seem pretty rather than digging deeper into what "symbols that whispered of forgotten civilizations" could even look like (seem to be words that fit rather than communicate something coherent). Excerpt 2 seems less didactic in its insistence on a morale and allows the clerk's words to be more effective than any supplementary elaboration that Excerpt 1's final lines insist on

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: I saw her emerge from the December mist of Charles de Gaulle like an apparition from the ancient kingdoms of Mali, her skin the color of honey-glazed chestnuts that reminded me of those afternoons in Cartagena when the sun would melt gold into the sea. She moved through Terminal 2F with the deliberate grace of a lioness, her caftan catching whispers of air that seemed to carry the scent of frankincense and myrrh, though later I would learn it was nothing more than the perfume of duty-free shops mixing with the aroma of croissants from Paul's bakery. Her eyes, set like amber stones in an Ethiopian crown, caught the fluorescent lights in such a way that made me believe she had lived a thousand years, perhaps more, and had witnessed the rise and fall of civilizations that existed only in forgotten dreams. The snow outside fell with the determination of white butterflies against the glass walls, while inside, the terminal maintained its eternal springtime, as if nature herself had conceded to this woman's presence. I might have followed her forever through the labyrinth of gates and shops, but fate, with its peculiar sense of humor, placed me behind an elderly Dutch woman who carried eleven suitcases and argued with mathematical precision about each gram of their weight, her voice rising and falling like a baroque opera. When I finally reached the ticket counter, my head still swimming with visions of the mysterious woman, I asked the clerk, a man with a mustache that seemed to have been drawn by a child's uncertain hand, if he believed in love at first sight. "Monsieur," he replied, adjusting his tie with the gravity of a philosopher, "in this airport, the only impossible thing is to find a reasonable price for a cup of coffee."
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: In Paris I spotted her walking gracefully in short suede heels, a timeless click to her step on the shiny floors of the Charles de Gaulle Airport. She was magnificent, her limbs like tributaries each meeting at the river made by her dark and wavy hair. Her eyes, though I could not see them, were certainly slant and blue. Fortuitously she sat some feet away from where I stood in line at the counter, crossing her ankles neatly beneath her in the French way, and at last I could admire a charoite skirt and matching cinched blazer that met the milky skin at her thighs and neck. The whole of her became a river to me then, or perhaps instead a lioness paused to drink at cool water; soon, I knew, she would be gone, and the springtime warmth and vibrancy brought by her into this terminal would fade to match the great blank whiteness of snowy winter beyond our shared space. Infatuated as I was by this lion-headed goddess, it took me some time to process the bickering before me, an elderly woman with a thick Dutch accent and some eleven suitcases haggling with the ticket clerk over their weight and associated cost. Returning my attention to the woman cloaked in purple and, for the time being, likewise cloaked in the wholeness of my affection, I missed the ticket clerk calling me forward after the Dutch woman had been sorted. I smiled a wide and generous smile. “Do you believe love at first sight is impossible,” I asked him, and tilted my head gently so that he might see the object of my sighted love.The clerk, evidently harried, was still inspired to smile at the glimpse of an exceptional woman. “In Paris,” he told me, “Anything other than such a love is impossible.”
written_by_MFA026.Reason: Excerpt 1 contains too many inefficient and redundant metaphors. The comparison "her skin the color of honey-glazed chestnuts reminded me of those afternoons in Cartagena when the sun would melt gold into the sea" is overlong and the second clause does not renew or vivify the metaphor at all. The personification of snow falling "with the determination of white butterflies against the glass wall" leaves me with a muddled image. Why would butterflies be determined and what is the similarity of a butterfly's movement to snow? I just can't picture it.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: The moment I saw her, I was convinced that time had halted to let her pass—a striking woman who seemed neither of this world nor any other. Her skin was the sun-dappled bronze of desert sands at twilight, her eyes the unfathomable green of jade worn smooth by centuries of whispers. She moved with the languid elegance of a lioness in repose, her steps unhurried yet commanding, as if she carried an invisible crown. Her long scarf of woven gold and crimson thread draped over her shoulder like a relic stolen from Byzantium, glimmering faintly under the harsh fluorescent lights of Charles de Gaulle. The terminal swirled with the metallic clink of luggage carts, the nasal calls of final boarding, and the mingling scents of espresso and frost melting off winter coats. Outside, snow veiled Paris, but inside, the air buzzed with the restless vitality of spring—a contradiction that matched her presence. Behind an elderly Dutch woman stubbornly arguing with the ticket clerk over the weight of eleven battered suitcases, I stood transfixed, calculating how the infinite could fit into the brief arc of her passing. When my turn came, I mumbled a question to the clerk about love at first sight. She glanced up, her eyes carrying the faint smirk of someone long weary of life's questions. "Impossible, monsieur," she replied with practiced precision. "Only everything else is." I laughed, but it was hollow, for the woman who had remade time itself was already gone.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: Walking into Charles de Gaulle Airport, I saw a woman, exotic and striking in her beauty. Astonished, I stood frozen in the terminal as I gazed at her timeless features. Her skin was dark and glowed with youth, her eyes were clear as a glacial lake. She wore a garment of gold and red fabric that looked as though it came from a culture that was entirely unfamiliar to me, and I stood for a long time admiring it, as though in a trance. Her look suggested an aura of antiquity, and she moved in grace like a lioness, striding confidently across the bright, balmy terminal that contrasted with the snowy world beyond its walls. In a moment, she was gone, her presence as fleeting as it was alluring. I took my place in line, and for a moment I found myself distracted by an elderly Dutch woman who took it upon herself to argue with the ticket clerk about the weight of eleven suitcases, “I’ve weighed them at home,” she said, “they can’t possibly be more than 10 kilograms—” and by the time I reached the front of the line I found myself in a pensive and dreamy mood. Who was that woman of such incredible mystery and poise, whose eyes shone so brightly? Smiling, I asked the ticket clerk if he believed in love at first sight. He laughed and replied that of course he did, how could he not. "Anything short of this , would be impossible", the clerk said.
written_by_MFA011.Reason: Neither excerpt is great, honestly, but Excerpt 2 is better. Excerpt 1 is deeply overwritten, with sentences like "Her skin was the sun-dappled bronze of desert sands at twilight, her eyes the unfathomable green of jade worn smooth by centuries of whispers." Excerpt 2 is much more withholding and reserved.

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: The resort lay like a discarded memory, its swimming pools filled with brackish water and fallen leaves – not the romantic decay of abandoned European castles, but the hasty, unplanned desertion of a colonial dream. Walking along the cracked sidewalks, where weeds pushed through with primitive determination, I saw the debris of departed lives: a sodden Belga cigarette packet, its blue and white design still visible, speaking of evenings when settlers sat in wicker chairs discussing home leave and servant troubles; a broken tennis racquet, its strings dangling like the exposed nerves of a dead thing, recalling Sunday afternoon games followed by gin and tonics on the clubhouse veranda. Everything here had been arranged to deny Africa, to create an illusion of Surrey or Sussex: the neat flowerbeds, now choked with wild grass, the carefully planned paths that led to viewing points designed to frame the landscape like an English watercolor. But Africa had returned, seeping through the cracks, asserting itself in the persistent growth that threatened to swallow the mock-Tudor buildings, in the small creatures that had made homes in abandoned tea rooms. The place possessed now a particular sadness – not of ruins, which suggest grandeur, but of irrelevance. Like the colonial administrators' files still rotting in some government office, like the old settlers' clubs with their dated photographs and empty bars, it belonged to a world that had ended not with ceremony but with a series of small surrenders, each one unremarkable in itself, until one day the illusion simply ceased to hold.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: The dilapidation that had befallen the resort was to be expected; it had been a place for rest for those who had come to sow unrest, and now that the country was in a state of repair, that which had once been repaired was left to rot. But there were still definite traces of life—beetles that scuttled about licking up dots of water from rivets in aged tiles, vines that wrapped up and through the sides of the canopy built to allow proprietors to gaze at a view without being at the mercy of the cruel sun, thickets of brush with twig-like branches that lined the path to the long-sealed front doors now grew unwieldy and sharp, as their nature demanded. But so too, prominent, were the signs of abandon. A pack of Belga cigarettes, the faded packaging promising style and mystical aura, lay on a patio table. If one listened in the silence, one could almost hear the smacking of thin European lips that may have once suckled the tobacco while remarking about the grand African sun or commenting on the foliage. But the sound would soon be drowned out by the noise of a country that had moved on to larger things—where words like "reclaim," "rebuild," "remove" erupted out of automobiles, cafes, town halls, meeting circles, makeshift stages, military bases, parliament buildings, and where, yes, perhaps, there was still space for the word "resort," but only if used in the phrase "last resort." And so the empty building sat, bludgeoned by the naked sun, waiting again for peace, for purpose.
written_by_MFA030.Reason:
For 2, the dilapidation and insistence of life (and the interplay between those two elements) feel more convincing in the details. 1 seems to engage mostly the visual sense, while 2 engages with sight and sound to indicate both absence and presence, all culminating in a more coherent way with the interplay of "resort" and "last resort" and the intermittent stage between becoming and unbecoming "waiting again for peace, for purpose."

1 is still a good excerpt, but it's weakened by its hanging gerunds (weaker dependent clauses attached to stronger independent clauses, ultimately weakening the latter ends of entire sentences -- "speaking of evenings when settlers..." and "seeping through the cracks")

The dynamic movement of 2 seems to win out in the fluency and imagery, and therefore, is more effective than 1

But Africa had returned, seeping through the cracks, asserting itself in the persistent growth that threatened to swallow the mock-Tudor buildings, in the small creatures that had made homes in abandoned tea rooms. The place possessed now a particular sadness – not of ruins, which suggest grandeur, but of irrelevance. Like the colonial administrators' files still rotting in some government office, like the old settlers' clubs with their dated photographs and empty bars, it belonged to a world that had ended not with ceremony but with a series of small surrenders, each one unremarkable in itself, until one day the illusion simply ceased to hold.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: The dilapidation that had befallen the resort was to be expected; it had been a place for rest for those who had come to sow unrest, and now that the country was in a state of repair, that which had once been repaired was left to rot. But there were still definite traces of life—beetles that scuttled about licking up dots of water from rivets in aged tiles, vines that wrapped up and through the sides of the canopy built to allow proprietors to gaze at a view without being at the mercy of the cruel sun, thickets of brush with twig-like branches that lined the path to the long-sealed front doors now grew unwieldy and sharp, as their nature demanded. But so too, prominent, were the signs of abandon. A pack of Belga cigarettes, the faded packaging promising style and mystical aura, lay on a patio table. If one listened in the silence, one could almost hear the smacking of thin European lips that may have once suckled the tobacco while remarking about the grand African sun or commenting on the foliage. But the sound would soon be drowned out by the noise of a country that had moved on to larger things—where words like "reclaim," "rebuild," "remove" erupted out of automobiles, cafes, town halls, meeting circles, makeshift stages, military bases, parliament buildings, and where, yes, perhaps, there was still space for the word "resort," but only if used in the phrase "last resort." written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: The resort bore the weight of its past in every crumbling façade and every shattered tile strewn across the once-immaculate promenade. The sidewalks were now a repository for the discarded detritus of another era—splintered furniture, faded paperbacks, and Belga cigarette packets flattened underfoot, their familiar logo a ghostly reminder of European elegance. The air, still humid and heavy, carried a vague scent of salt and mildew, mingled with the decay of abandonment. Here, the whisper of colonial nostalgia lingered, like a shadow over the resort's decline. Once a haven for settlers who sought to conjure a slice of Europe amidst Africa's heat, it now stood as a relic of disillusionment. The verandas where drinks had clinked under the laughter of expatriates were hollow, their railings stripped of paint, exposing a rusted skeleton beneath.The tide of independence had washed away the veneer of its purpose. Military mutinies had marked its walls with bullet scars; the exodus of the white and Asian populations had left its rooms unclaimed, their emptiness profound. The palm trees swayed in the wind, their silhouettes etched against a bruised sky, but even they seemed tired, their leaves curling at the edges like burnt paper. What once exuded vitality now lay inert, a tableau of exile and loss. The resort, like the colonizers who had built it, was unmoored—a monument to ambitions that had eroded under the weight of history, leaving behind only silence and the memory of what had been.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: Once gleaming and luxurious, the resort now tells stories of upheaval in every ballroom and courtyard. This resort of yesterday fares poorly today, and no one comes. Beige African sidewalks collect debris, chairs in the European style and English books. A discarded packet of Belga cigarettes transports visitors to another time, allowing them to trespass on the resort in its antebellum years. The whole discarded era becomes visible—Europeans on holiday attempting to make a home of another's home. Visitors may traipse through the relics spilling from sidewalk to grass, walking on both. Now it is a place hung between that past and a present that has not shaken what came before. Children from town tell stories about the resort, what it was and what lives there now: ghosts of both the travelers and the locals who worked in the lobbies and kitchens when the building retained its purpose, ghosts in luxury clothing inappropriate for the climate and ghosts in neatly pressed uniforms. The older teens climb inside through gaps in the boarded windows and explore the detritus, daring each other to venture deeper and deeper down unlit hallways smelling of mold and dust. They speak in whispers. This small entertainment is laced with the petty danger that emanates now from the building. It can be called a harmless thing, a relic of before: before the departures of the whites and the Asians, before independence, before the mutinies. Yet the building, an ugly shell of itself, persists. It says: "But here I still am."
written_by_MFA026.Reason: Excerpt1's images and their thematic connections seem to insistent on beating the reader over the head with their associations. For example, Excerpt2's description of picking up a discarded packet of Belga cigarettes that transports visitors to another time, allowing them to trespass on the resort in its antebellum years, followed by making the whole discarded era visible—Europeans on holiday attempting to make a home of another's home—is more effective in the way it puts the reader into the narrator's experience. In contrast, Excerpt1's "Belga cigarette packets flattened underfoot, their familiar logo a ghostly reminder of European elegance" doesn't let the reader make the association for themselves (more telling than showing) and therefore, when we get to "the whisper of colonial nostalgia lingered, like a shadow over the resort's decline" the colonialist lens is less effective.As a whole, the framing in Excerpt2 is more coherent and effective in the way it places the reader in more of a tour of the derelict space than the Excerpt1's framing of direct scene description.

written_by_MFA032.Excerpt1: The once-vibrant resort now stood in a state of decay, a stark reminder of the societal shifts that had swept through the region.  The sidewalks, once bustling with tourists, were now littered with the remnants of a bygone era: broken furniture, discarded books, and flattened cigarette packets.  Among the debris, a Belga cigarette packet, a relic of European holidays, hinted at the resort's colonial past.  It was a place built by settlers who sought to recreate a familiar European lifestyle in the heart of Africa.The resort's decline mirrored the broader social and political changes that had reshaped the region.  Independence, military mutinies, and the exodus of white and Asian settlers had left the resort without purpose, a ghost of its former self.  The buildings, once grand and imposing, now bore the scars of neglect, their paint peeling and their windows boarded up.  The gardens, once meticulously manicured, were now overgrown and wild, a testament to the absence of the hands that once tended them.The resort's decline was not merely physical; it was also a reflection of the societal shifts that had accompanied decolonization.  The old order, with its rigid hierarchies and its imported European culture, had been swept away, leaving behind a void that was yet to be filled.  The resort, once a symbol of colonial power and privilege, now stood as a monument to the complexities of post-colonial identity.  It was a place where the past and the present collided, where the remnants of a colonial past were juxtaposed with the uncertainties of a post-colonial future.
written_by_MFA032.Excerpt2: The forecourt wore it well—time, and the fickle seasons of democracy in this place. The moldings decorating the façade betrayed nothing either, except perhaps the usual negligence, the fine patina of dust that came over everything in Africa. But in its interior courtyards, in its once-ornate villas and lush gardens, where the Crown’s servants had dealt out their decks of cards atop white tablecloths, nothing stirred. A grim silence overwhelmed the resort. The grass yellowed under termite-ridden bedframes and writing desks; around them, rags of newspaper and littered correspondences. Vague ink-stains remained on these pages; and a sentence that, ten years ago, could martial an army from one corner of the empire to another was now indecipherable. A pack of “Belga” cigarettes had survived free Africa, escaped the line of white and Asian refugees at the docks, the inevitable mutiny and the mutiny after that. It lay sedately on a bench. For years, its odor would not leave the wooden slats; and in its slim shape it carried the vestiges of wet, European summers, trails of water from the pool to the bar, the rattle of ice in a tumbler, liveried black boys sweating in the corner, out of sight and at hand. There had been no native plants, no local liquors, no reminders of Africa at the resort—except its conveniences. The brand of cigarettes, of course, was extinct; the company had settled into ruin when its directors left on the outbound ships. The cigarettes were manufactured, now, in the countryside, by Africans; everybody smoked, and the sky slowly turned gray.
written_by_MFA032.Reason: Excerpt1 is crudely explicit, over-explaining the historical status of the objects in the scene: "a stark reminder of the societal shifts that had swept through the region," "a Belga cigarette packet, a relic of European holidays, hinted at the resort's colonial past," "it was also a reflection of the societal shifts that had accompanied decolonization." The constant use of abstractions like "post-colonial future," "rigid hierarchies," "European culture," "decolonization," "colonial power and privilege," distracts from the scene, more appropriate for an essay or speech rather than a physical description of a resort. The second excerpt allows its objects to speak for themselves; it plays with irony, allowing the reader to understand the symbolic/historical resonance of the cigarette packs, for example, without didacticism: "A pack of “Belga” cigarettes had survived free Africa, escaped the line of white and Asian refugees at the docks, the inevitable mutiny and the mutiny after that ... The brand of cigarettes, of course, was extinct; the company had settled into ruin when its directors left on the outbound ships. The cigarettes were manufactured, now, in the countryside, by Africans; everybody smoked, and the sky slowly turned gray." Without the didacticism, p2 is much more vivid, adorned with effective details ("liveried black boys sweating in the corner").

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: Home, I have found, is not simply a place but a feeling that nestles deep in the folds of one’s soul. It is the shadowed hallway of memory, the faint scent of grandmother’s soap, the creak of a floorboard that seemed alive under hurried feet. Thomas Wolfe’s declaration that one “can’t go home again” lingers in the air like a challenge, for he must not have known that home is not a place you return to; it is a space you carry, ever-present, with its jagged edges and tender sanctuaries. It is where your fears grow fangs and your dreams sprout wings, where dragons curl in the corners of your mind, guarding treasures of old laughter and quiet heartbreak.In the eyes of a child, home stretches as far as the world itself—an empire shaped by the curve of a dirt road or the towering majesty of a neighbor’s oak tree. Adults are gods of that kingdom, figures who wield their power with mystery, speaking in codes that seem unknowable. Yet, even as we grow, we seldom outgrow the pull of home. We may wear the masks of adulthood—secure parking spots, pay bills on time, and rehearse the lines of responsibility—but inside, we are still children. We navigate the world like sailors tracing their fingers over a map, searching for familiar shores that no longer exist except in the sanctity of our own minds.Home is a refuge, a sanctuary of belonging, but not because of its walls or windows. It is the gathering of whispers, the embrace of something so profoundly personal it could never be truly shared. And so, as I carry its essence within me, I know that the journey is not about leaving or returning—it is about understanding that home was never outside of me to begin with.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: I imagined him taller than he should have been, his head near the ceiling of an unfamiliar apartment he couldn’t love as he wrote his novel You Can’t Go Home Again looming over his refrigerator. Home, to Thomas Wolfe, was a quiet town in a temperate valley of the Blue Ridge Mountains. From such vantage points, the world becomes diminutive, entirely comprehensible. Only when you venture into those views do you see the world’s vastness beyond its landscapes, how you can’t see home through eyes that have left, that have taken in new views, new worlds, a new you. But can home be truly gone without you? Is home not a dark chamber you carry within, with its shadows, dreams, fears, and dragons? I remembered my childhood home for the woods that circled the property, where things belonged because they resided there. A childhood home is the childhood. It is the wilderness unknowing children frolic through. It is the security of a warm blanket before they learn it can be ripped away. The adults in their lives seem impossibly, staggeringly old, years beyond the years children know. Like enigmatic peaks of mountain ranges, parents, older siblings, and neighbors loom from a distance. They cast only shadows on the sunny region of play that is the childhood home. But the sun falls and the shadows grow long. With time, the children grow taller than they should, than they feel they should. They leave the wilderness. Through the vague groping around in the night to their parkings spaces and their dinner tables strewn with bills, they long for childhood, for return. But as sure as that longing pulls from within them, there is that dark chamber waiting for light. It has always been there. You have never left home.
written_by_MFA003.Reason: I prefer Excerpt 2, even though Excerpt 1 is arguably more coherent and easy to follow, because it feels more original and distinct. Excerpt 2 is more impressionistic, and ends with a second-person address. Its looser structure and ambiguity leave space for the reader to imagine, whereas Excerpt 1 feels competently written but cliched. While less polished, 2 is more emotionally immersive.

Only when you venture into those views do you see the world’s vastness beyond its landscapes, how you can’t see home through eyes that have left, that have taken in new views, new worlds, a new you. But can home be truly gone without you? Is home not a dark chamber you carry within, with its shadows, dreams, fears, and dragons? I remembered my childhood home for the woods that circled the property, where things belonged because they resided there. A childhood home is the childhood. It is the wilderness unknowing children frolic through. It is the security of a warm blanket before they learn it can be ripped away. The adults in their lives seem impossibly, staggeringly old, years beyond the years children know. Like enigmatic peaks of mountain ranges, parents, older siblings, and neighbors loom from a distance. They cast only shadows on the sunny region of play that is the childhood home. But the sun falls and the shadows grow long. With time, the children grow taller than they should, than they feel they should. They leave the wilderness. Through the vague groping around in the night to their parkings spaces and their dinner tables strewn with bills, they long for childhood, for return. But as sure as that longing pulls from within them, there is that dark chamber waiting for light. It has always been there. You have never left home.
written_by_MFA003.Reason: Excerpt 2 sets the scene immediately, beginning with a vivid and endearing image of Thomas Wolfe: "I imagined him taller than he should have been, his head near the ceiling of an unfamiliar apartment..." This humanizes Wolfe while the first excerpt engages with Wolfe as a wise entity to simply pull truisms from. The metaphors in Excerpt 1 are also cliche: "It is where your fears grow fangs and your dreams sprout wings..." This cliche dulls situational specificity and causes distance in readers.

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: Home, I have found, is not simply a place but a feeling that nestles deep in the folds of one’s soul. It is the shadowed hallway of memory, the faint scent of grandmother’s soap, the creak of a floorboard that seemed alive under hurried feet. Thomas Wolfe’s declaration that one “can’t go home again” lingers in the air like a challenge, for he must not have known that home is not a place you return to; it is a space you carry, ever-present, with its jagged edges and tender sanctuaries. It is where your fears grow fangs and your dreams sprout wings, where dragons curl in the corners of your mind, guarding treasures of old laughter and quiet heartbreak.In the eyes of a child, home stretches as far as the world itself—an empire shaped by the curve of a dirt road or the towering majesty of a neighbor’s oak tree. Adults are gods of that kingdom, figures who wield their power with mystery, speaking in codes that seem unknowable. Yet, even as we grow, we seldom outgrow the pull of home. We may wear the masks of adulthood—secure parking spots, pay bills on time, and rehearse the lines of responsibility—but inside, we are still children. We navigate the world like sailors tracing their fingers over a map, searching for familiar shores that no longer exist except in the sanctity of our own minds.Home is a refuge, a sanctuary of belonging, but not because of its walls or windows. It is the gathering of whispers, the embrace of something so profoundly personal it could never be truly shared. And so, as I carry its essence within me, I know that the journey is not about leaving or returning—it is about understanding that home was never outside of me to begin with.
