written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: Home, that perennial thing. The place we’ve heard a million aphorisms about—telling us how much it matters, that it’s always there for us, and trying to answer the biggest question: where to find it. Thomas Wolfe’s novel, You Can’t Go Home Again, seems to offer a concerning counter to this, but this is actually a trick of the light, for one can never truly leave home to begin with. Home is in the sinew, in the flesh, home, in all of its shadows, dreams, fears, and dragons, is a place deep in the bosom, straight in the center, right up the spine and down through the feet. And what is truly at the core of home is not the wood beams, the forest hills, the patio furniture, metal gates and paved roads—it’s the youthful perception, those rose-tinted glasses, a time of understanding before the world laid its full hands on us. It is childhood, not just the memory or the idea of it, but the physical self that was once to a child, learning the way of the world, ignorant to the ways of man, the race, the place, the pace. It is a version of the self that navigates only through imagination, through interaction with those mysterious figures of the land, the adults, the mailman, the clerk, the aunt, the neighbor, the siblings. And it is this version of the self, the child, that we try to run to when we get older when the bills pile, when you can’t find a place to park, when the kids won’t listen, when we crave that time again, that little pocket in our chest we can tuck into to know that there was life before these little bothers. When we nestle in there, we find the key to ultimate return, to a place of comfort, to belonging to your own world— to coming home.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: When Thomas Wolfe declared you can't go home again, he hadn't reckoned with the stubborn geography of the heart, that relentless compass that forever points to our beginning place. Home isn't merely the creaking floorboards beneath our feet or the worn doorknobs our palms remember—it's the shadow-dance of memory that lives in our bones, as natural as breathing and just as necessary. I've watched children, those clear-eyed prophets of truth, who know nothing of north or south, east or west, but understand perfectly the latitude of belonging. In their world, grown folks move like planets in a universe they haven't yet learned to question, their orbits unbroken by doubt. Mama's laugh rings true as church bells, and daddy's footsteps mark time like drums in the evening, while neighbors drift through the streets like familiar ghosts, their stories settling into the soil of young minds like seeds waiting to bloom. Lord, how we fool ourselves thinking we've grown up just because we've learned to navigate parking meters and mortgage payments! The truth is, most of us are still those wide-eyed children wearing adult clothes, playing at being grown, while deep inside we're running home through twilight streets that exist now only in memory. We carry our dragons and dreams tucked away in secret pockets, and when the world proves too sharp, too cold, we retreat to that internal sanctuary where everything makes sense according to the logic of childhood. Home isn't a place you leave behind—it's the story that writes itself in your blood, the mirror that shows you your truest face, the song that keeps singing long after the music has stopped. It's the place where our first tears fell and our earliest laughter echoed, where we learned the shape of love and fear, and where we return, again and again, in the quiet moments when our hearts need healing.
written_by_MFA030.Reason: Excerpt 2 relies on overwrought imagery. While it avoid too much simile, its metaphors serve the same function ("… children, those clear-eyed prophets of truth…"; "We carry our dragons and dreams tucked away in secret pockets …") and they repeat structure in a way that is slightly uncanny ("… still those wide-eyed children …"). Excerpt 1 still relies on cliches ("… rose-tinted glasses …"), but it tones back its rhetoric enough that when it does embark on lengthy run-on sentences they feel impactful rather than hackneyed ("… it is this version of the self, the child, that we try to run to when we get older when the bills pile, when you can’t find a place to park, when the kids won’t listen, when we crave that time again, that little pocket in our chest we can tuck into to know that there was life before these little bothers.") and the rhythm of sentences is varied to sell moments of excess.

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: I disagree with Thomas Wolfe. Home, it seems, is something you can never leave. It is a shadow, a dream, a fear, a dragon that follows you, forever tucked away in the deepest corner of your heart. It is the space you were first allowed to be yourself, the place where you learned to see the world through your own eyes, a child's eyes, where everything seemed as it should be.The adults in this region of your world, your parents, neighbors, siblings, were mysterious figures, moving in and out of your awareness like fleeting shadows. Their voices echoed in the hallways of your mind, their laughter and tears shaping the contours of your memories. You never questioned their presence, their belonging. They were as much a part of your world as the sun and the moon, the trees and the stars.And then, one day, you grew up. Or so they said. But did you really? Did you ever truly shed the skin of your childhood, the innocence of your youth? Or did you simply grow old, fulfilling the roles and responsibilities that society thrust upon you, finding parking spaces, paying bills, all the while carrying that child within, seeking the safety and comfort of home?Home is not a place, not really. It is a feeling, a sense of belonging, of being truly known and accepted. It is the refuge you seek when the world becomes too much, the place where you can always return, no matter how far you may have strayed. It is the echo of your childhood, the whisper of your dreams, the shadow of your fears, the dragon of your heart. It is the place where you are always welcome, the place where you are always loved.
written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2: Though I understand the meaning behind ‘You Can’t Go Home’, the title of that great novel by Thomas Wolfe, I myself cannot agree with his sentiment. I have found myself returning home many times over the years. There may no longer be a geographical place that bears more than a passing resemblance to the home of my girlhood, yet “home” itself is something inescapable and internal, a place of shadows, dreams, fears and dragons that is formed in childhood and carried deep inside for the rest of one’s life. I have returned again and again to that place, an imaginative landscape mapped and defined not by geography nor by cultural differences but by our youthful perceptions, during a time when the adults in our lives—parents, neighbors, siblings—are but shadowy figures whose actions are an enigma to us even as they shape our very selves. Many of us will grow old without truly growing up. We may fulfill the roles demanded of us as we age, whether by paying a bill, finding a parking space, or any of those actions that comprise an adult life. We may wander to other continents and may never return to the physical houses of our pasts, if these houses even remain standing for us to visit. But we are always one moment away from retreating to this inner world. It is here where we immerse ourselves in the comforts that defined our sense of home as children, whether those comforts were real or half imagined and exaggerated by our childlike innocence. I have returned home in spirit countless times, to this inner world that is a refuge and sanctuary, a place of ultimate belonging. It is this home which keeps me whole, a place I will never fully leave.
written_by_MFA005.Reason: The language in the first excerpt is more repetitive, abstracted, and incoherent than the language in the second excerpt, so it doesn't quite fully communicate this idea of "the imaginary landscape" that is home. For example, the first excerpt references "a dragon that follows you" and "the dragon of your heart," but it's not clear why the excerpt is referencing a dragon or what those phrases mean (dragons are not known for following people nor are they often in people's hearts). In the second excerpt, the dragon is explicitly tied to childhood's dreams/fears, so it's incorporated more appropriately: "'home' itself is something inescapable and internal, a place of shadows, dreams, fears and dragons that is formed in childhood and carried deep inside for the rest of one’s life." Because the second excerpt references concrete experiences like "girlhood," "wander[ing] continents," and the reality of homes from our past being demolished, the narrator feels more grounded and real. The idea of home is also more nuanced in the second excerpt; whereas the first excerpt repetitively describes it as "a sense of belonging, of being truly known and accepted ... the refuge you seek when the world becomes too much," the second excerpt acknowledges that this comfort may come from an imaginary place that existed only in one's youthful perspective: "It is here where we immerse ourselves in the comforts that defined our sense of home as children, whether those comforts were real or half imagined and exaggerated by our childlike innocence."

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: Kant, a connoisseur of solitude, had always envisioned his coming-out as a cataclysmic event, a meteor strike that would leave a crater in his life.  He'd spent weeks crafting the perfect email, a digital dove carrying the olive branch of his truth.  His imagination, a master of disaster, painted vivid scenes of his mother's tearful rejection, his friends recoiling in horror, and his colleagues whispering behind his back.But reality, it turned out, was a terrible painter.  The email launched, and instead of a meteor shower, there was a gentle rain of heart emojis from friends, muted acknowledgments from coworkers, and a carefully worded acceptance from his parents.  No drama, no disinheritance, not even a decent argument. Kant was baffled.  Where was the transformative growth?  The epic struggle he had envisioned himself overcoming?  Instead of relief, he felt a perverse disappointment, a sense of anticlimax that left him feeling strangely unfulfilled.His post-coming-out life was marked by inertia, an endless parade of solitary evenings and damp socks.  He'd walk home alone, his footsteps echoing in the cavernous silence of his apartment, the air thick with the scent of unwashed laundry and existential loneliness.He'd spend hours on the internet, scrolling through endless feeds of other people's curated lives, each post a tiny dagger to his heart.  He'd watch reality TV, the inane chatter of the contestants a poor substitute for human connection. He'd even tried dating, but his heart wasn't in it.  Each date felt like a performance, a carefully choreographed dance of small talk and forced smiles.  He'd find himself longing for the solitude of his apartment, the comforting embrace of his damp socks. Kant's year of damp feet was a testament to the enduring power of fear, a fear that had not only kept him closeted for years but had also robbed him of the joy of his own liberation.  He was free, but he was alone, a prisoner of his own making.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: For seven months, thirty-one-year old Kant tried to come out. He had decided that the most optimized method would take the form of mass email, as text could be perfected, and, in these many months, perfected the text: it was nearly a work of art, forthcoming without oversharing (he’d received feedback from internet forums), and grammar checked. It was four sentences. He’d created a listserv for the recipients: family, friends, and coworkers. After he closed his eyes, downed two shots of vodka, and hit “send,” he knew what was going to come to him. His colleagues would whisper about his deviant sexual activity; inevitably, he’d get kicked out on the street with his box of desk supplies (a dried-up fern and a hand gripper). Not to mention his poor mother—her wracking sobs, her inevitable refusal to speak to him, the prodigal son, ever again. After sending, he paced around the room, drank four additional shots, and cried in the bathroom. written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: Kant writes the email and spends a long time editing it, making minor changes to the wording only to change them back to exactly what he’d written before. He thinks about his upbringing and all the years that this information has weighed on him: the kids in middle school who tackled him in the locker room and forced him to eat dog shit, the fact that he couldn’t even admit to himself that he wanted to watch gay porn until he was twenty-five. Paralyzed, still editing, he imagines his mother’s disgust upon reading the email, imagining her 31-year-old son doing exactly what he’d done for the better part of the last two decades: that is, fanatasizing about some buff, hairy dude he saw online. He imagines himself dying alone, ostracized from anyone who might love him, the nerves in his dick beginning to desensitize from too much dry-hand masturbation. When he sends the email, though, the responses are surprisingly anticlimactic. He gets a few heart emojis from friends; some coworkers reply with “nice,” and “good for you!” Even his parents are mostly supportive, though his mom expresses some mild annoyance that he hadn’t called first to warn them. Kant feels a mixture of intense relief, combined with an unpleasant sense of disappointment that he finds difficult to face. Where was the fallout, the dramatic messages and cut-off relationships from family members? Why didn’t anyone care? He had once imagined his post-coming out life as a time of transformation, a new life like a beautiful patterned carpet rolling out before him, but instead he finds himself stuck in the exact same state of stasis that emboldened him to write the email in the first place. He begins to call this period his “Year of Damp Feet,” as his feet are constantly sweaty despite the fact that he rarely moves them from beneath his computer desk.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: Kant spent hours drafting the email, toggling between subject lines (“A Word to Everyone,” “FYI,” and, finally, “Coming Out”) like they were tarot cards predicting his fate. In his head, each recipient’s reaction unspooled in unrelenting technicolor: his mother, weeping silently in the kitchen as she diced onions for the biryani she thought would fix his mood; his old college roommate forwarding the email to their group chat with the caption, “Knew it”; his boss, furrowing his brow at the computer, typing, “Not sure why this concerns me professionally.” These imagined catastrophes paraded through his thoughts as he clicked send, his trembling hand a cheap metaphor for the fear wedged in his sternum. Then: nothing. The world didn’t combust. Instead, his notifications flooded with low-stakes affirmations—heart emojis from friends, a “proud of you, dude” text from a cousin, even a begrudging “love you” from his father, which Kant suspected had been typed under duress from his mother. He should’ve felt relief, triumph even, but instead, there was this sneaking, hollow ache. He’d braced himself for rejection, a narrative arc with stakes, but life handed him a shrug and a pat on the back. What was the point of all that dread if no one made it cinematic? The next few weeks stretched out like an overcooked spaghetti noodle—soft, limp, no bite. Without the anticipated martyrdom, Kant drifted into what he called his “Year of Damp Feet,” shuffling around his apartment in unwashed socks, ignoring texts inviting him to “finally celebrate.” He scrolled through his inbox, rereading replies, hoping to stumble on something more… dramatic. Wasn’t this supposed to be the pivot point of his life? Instead, he remained unchanged, realizing that even monumental self-revelations couldn’t save him from the everyday inertia of being Kant. A hero’s journey, sure—but with no villain, no fight, just the lukewarm end credits rolling over silence.

written_by_MFA024.Excerpt1: Kant's coming out email sat in his drafts folder like a grenade with the pin half-pulled, while he spent weeks A/B testing subject lines, as if the right combination of words could defuse three decades of queerness into something digestible for his mother's WeChat circles. He'd crafted seventeen versions, each more baroque than the last, padding them with disclaimers and preemptive responses to imagined objections, until the final draft read like a corporate merger announcement crossed with a hostage negotiation. The responses, when they finally came, were an anticlimactic parade of heart emojis and "love you no matter what"s—the kind of tepid acceptance that made him wonder if perhaps he wasn't gay enough to warrant proper drama. His coworkers replied with the practiced neutrality of people who'd attended exactly one diversity training, while his mother's response ("Ok. Did you eat dinner?") felt like being handed a participation trophy for surviving thirty-one years of internal torment. He'd prepared for scorched earth but got lukewarm validation, and now here he was, somehow lonelier in his freedom, spending his newly authentic life watching YouTube compilations of gay wedding flash mobs and ordering rainbow-colored socks he'd never wear. The Year of Damp Feet, he called it in his journal, though he knew the phrase would sound better in someone else's memoir. His therapist called this "adjustment period" progress, but it felt more like trading one closet for another—this one just happened to have better lighting and an Amazon Prime subscription. The truth was, he'd gotten good at being afraid, had built his personality around it like a pearl around grit, and now that the fear was gone, he couldn't shake the suspicion that he'd peaked at being closeted, that he'd somehow gentrified his own identity into something too palatable to matter, too sanitized for the revolution he'd imagined himself starring in.
written_by_MFA024.Excerpt2: Kant wrote thirty versions of his coming-out email over the course of ten months. Though he knew better, he couldn’t keep from anticipating and meticulously addressing, in the email itself, the various surprised, dismissive, or condemnatory responses of his friends and family, to the point where the email was less an act of claiming his own reality than a bullish bracing of himself against an incoming bilgewater tide of others’ realities. He clicked send. Feeling noble, self-satisfied, and above all ready, he camped at his laptop with an energy drink and spammed refresh. A couple hours later, an email from his father sent a spike of fear into his chest: he was about to be disowned. But while not exactly celebratory, the message indicated uncomplicated respect and acceptance. An email from an old college friend came in next, composed only of emojis. Where was their disgust? Their bitterness and disdain? The underwhelm was itself an overwhelm: he felt ridiculous, mocked by precisely an absence of mockery. Coming out should feel like something, shouldn’t it? He considered, by way of analogy, his own naïve expectation every birthday that he might experience an inner shift adequate to the day’s significance, a radiance, a spiritual lift, some kind of internal popping sound at least—I’m twenty-nine!—and instead met again and again just another day. Wasn’t this exactly how all life’s big events felt? A non-feeling? Supportive replies rolled in, and each refused to move the plot of his life forward. He’d imagined that this one symbolic action would release something huge and wild in him, that he’d start going on dates, he’d kiss the real flesh of a real guy; but months later he was still eating the same Cheez-Its and masturbating to the same porn, only now he didn’t even bother to clean up after himself. What he’d imagined calling The Year of Freedom had become The Year of Damp Feet.
written_by_MFA024.Reason: While I appreciate excerpt 1's maximalism in some respects, I find the torrent of similes and imagery to distract from the feeling it intends to provoke ("… like a grenade with the pin half-pulled …"; "… like a corporate merger announcement crossed with a hostage negotiation …"; "… like a pearl around grit …"). Excerpt 2 maintains the feeling of maximalism through its run-on and near-run-on sentences, but avoids these bursts of garish imagery in favor of what feels like a more specific internal thought process, which is more affecting to me and more painful ("He’d imagined that this one symbolic action would release something huge and wild in him, that he’d start going on dates, he’d kiss the real flesh of a real guy; but months later he was still eating the same Cheez-Its and masturbating to the same porn, only now he didn’t even bother to clean up after himself")
